parties:
Jahangir Alam (Md) and others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Shabdir Ahmed and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-2-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2919 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 3-2-2009 passed by a single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2919 of 2007 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 11-4-2007 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2006 allowing the appeal in part and reversing the judgment and decree dated 25-7-2006 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 23 of 2003 dismissing the suit.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are that Samadullah was the owner of 2.74 acres of land appertaining to plot No. 2906 of SA khatian No.553 as described in schedule-1 to the plaint. Samadullah gifted the said land to his 4 sons, namely, Mattober Ali, Mokaddas Ali, Abdul Nojibor and Idris, who used to possess the same by cultivating paddy. Similarly, Samadullah used to possess another 0.10 acre of land appertaining to plot No. 2905 of khatian No. 301 after getting the said land from his father Ayet Ali by way of amicable partition with other brothers. Samadullah's son Mukaddas Ali got the said 0.10 acre of land of plot No. 2905 by way of amicable partition after the death of Samadullah. Thus Mukaddas Ali got 1/4 share of plot No. 2906 measuring 0.6850 acre of land and 0.10 acre of land of plot No. 2905. He sold 0.22 acre of land and 0.08 acre of land from plot Nos.2906 and 2905 respectively to the predecessors of the plaintiffs, Muddasir Ali and Muzammel Ali by 2 registered deeds of sale dated 3-11-1968 and 1-4-1969 and delivered possession thereof to the purchasers. At the time of execution and registration of the deeds, the plot number was wrongly mentioned as 2693 instead of plot Nos.2905 and 2906 which was detected in 1975. As soon as, the matter was informed to Mukaddas Ali, he executed and registered another deed dated 14-1-1975 mentioning the correct plot Nos. 2905 and 2906 and the area of land was correctly mentioned in rectified deed as 0.30 acre. Subsequently, Mudassir Ali and Muzammel Ali died leaving behind 4 sons, plaintiff Nos.1-4, 2 daughters, defendant Nos.5-7 and wife plaintiff No.6 who used to possess the suit land.

3. It was also contended by the plaintiffs that defendant Nos. 1-2 claimed title to the suit land in August 2002 as they got a decree from the court in a partition suit and on query, the plaintiffs found that in Title Suit No. 30 of 1998 for partition they were not made parties and defendants obtained an ex parte decree. On 4-1-2004, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land. Hence the suit has been filed.

4. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint. Their case, in short, is that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. The suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiffs have no possession in the suit land. The land of plot No. 2906 of the 1st schedule to the plaint belonged to Samadullah. During continuance of his title and possession in that land, Samadullah sold 0.45 acre of land to Most. Ekramunnesa, the mother of these defendants, by a registered deed dated 25-9-1964 and handed over possession to her. Subsequently, Samadullah died on 25-6-1972 leaving behind 4 sons, Mohabbat Ali, Mokaddas Ali, Mosabbir Ali and Idris Ali along with 2 daughters Shamsunnessa and Suratunnessa. Idris Ali died leaving behind his wife, 4 sons and 5 daughters, defendant Nos.5-11 and Raina Begum and Badana Begum.

On 10-2-1983, Mohabbat Ali died leaving behind 2 sons, defendant Nos.3-4. On 12-12-1991 Mokaddas Ali died leaving behind wife and 1 daughter and 1 son. After death of his wife, on 14-5-1997, his son and daughter, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 became the leaving heirs of Mokaddas Ali. Abdul Mosabbir died leaving behind his son, defendant No.16 and 4 daughters. Defendant Nos.1-2 have got 0.45 acre of land from their mother Ekramunessa and 0.46 acre of land from their father and mother as heirs and in total they got 0.91 acre of land. On 18-2-1998, defendant No. 1 came to know that at the time of SA operation, the land of plot No. 2906 had been recorded in the names of 4 sons of Samadullah in respect of 0.74 acre of land instead of 2.74 acres of land. These defendants asked the co-sharers to make partition of their shares but they refused to do so. Finding no other alternative, these defendants filed Title Suit No. 30 of 1998 for partition impleading all the co-sharers. After getting notices, some of the co-sharers appeared before the Court but they did not file written statement and as a result, the suit was decreed ex parte in preliminary form on 13-9-2000. Then an Advocate Commissioner was appointed who filed a report on the basis of which final decree was passed on 9-5-2002. After that, Execution Case No. 04 of 2003 has been filed which is still pending. The plaintiffs had no right, title and interest in the suit land and as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court, upon hearing the parties, by the judgment and decree dated 25-7-2006, dismissed the suit.

6. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 114 of 2006 before the learned District Judge, Sylhet. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet, who by the judgment and decree dated 11-4-2007 allowed the appeal-in-part reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, the plaintiffs moved the High Court Division by filing a revisional application and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2919 of 2007. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 3-2-2009 discharged the Rule.

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiffs as the leave-petitioners have filed this Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1176 of 2009, in which, leave was granted on 12-1-2011, resulting in the instant Civil Appeal No. 61 of 2011.

9. Mr Shaheed Alam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellants, submits that the Court of appeal below reversed the finding of the trial Court and held that the appellants have title and possession and that they are not bound by the judgment of Partition Suit No. 30 of 1998 but did not allow the appeal in full on the ground that the appellants did not implead the daughters of Samadullah in the suit and that the High Court Division wrongly discharged the Rule without considering that the daughters of Samadullah were not necessary parties since the appellants suit was not a suit for partition and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside.

10. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate and Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, appearing on behalf of respondents, on the other hand, submit that the appellate Court rightly found that a suit for declaration simpliciter is not maintainable as admittedly the original owner Samadullah had two daughters and that admittedly the jote left behind by Samadullah was not partitioned by metes and bounds. In support of their submissions, the learned Advocates relied on three cases which we shall discuss in the body of the judgment.

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants and the learned Advocates for respondents, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

12. Leave was granted to consider whether a suit for declaration of title was maintainable without prayer for partition and whether the High Court Division was justified in affirming the judgment of the appellate Court when the appellate Court came to the finding that the appellants could prove their title to and possession in the suit land.

13. Admittedly, Samadullah was the owner of 2.74 acres of land of plot No. 2906 of SA Khatian No. 553. The plaintiffs alleged that Samadullah gifted the aforesaid land to his four sons. The plaintiff, however, could not produce the deed of gift alleged to have been executed by Samadullah. It is also stated Samadullah got 0.10 acre of land from his father Ayet Ali in plot No. 2905 of Khatian No. 301. Mukaddas Ali one of the sons of Samadullah sold 0.22 acre of land from plot No. 2906 and 0.08 acre of land from Plot No. 2905 to the plaintiffs' predecessors by two registered deeds of sale dated 3-11-1968 and 1-4-1969. Later it was detected that in both the deeds Plot No.2693 (1693) was wrongly written in place of plot Nos. 2905 and 2906 which was detected in 1974. Subsequently, the vendor Mukaddas Ali executed and registered a rectification deed on 14-1-1975.

14. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2, the contesting defendants stated that admittedly, Samadullah was the owner of the land shown in the first schedule to the plaint. Samadullah sold 0.45 acre of land to Ekramunnessa, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by a registered deed of sale dated 25-9-1964. These two defendants also became owners of 0.46 acre of land as the heirs of their father and mother and in total they became owners in 0.91 acre of land.

15. Admittedly, Samadullah died leaving behind four sons and two daughters. The claim of the plaintiffs that Samadullah gifted 2.74 acres of land of plot No. 2906 of SA Khatian No. 553 to his four sons could not be substantiated by producing any documentary evidence. It is also admitted that the jote left behind by Samadullah was not partitioned by metes and bounds.

16. The trial Court came to the finding that the plaintiffs could not prove their title to and possession in the suit land. The trial Court also found that the plaintiffs had claimed declaration of title to the suit land measuring 0.30 (0.22 + 0.08) acre out of 2.74 acres in which admittedly several co-sharers had been possessing and that they could not prove the specification of the suit land properly. The trial Court, therefore, concluded that the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for partition as consequential relief apart from declaration of title.

17. The Court of appeal, however, found that the plaintiffs could prove their deeds of sale by adducing evidence. The appellate Court also found that they had been able to prove their possession as well in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah. The appellate Court, however, found that as per evidence, Samadullah apart from four sons had two daughters and that the daughters are also co-sharers in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah. The appellate Court held that the disputed jote was not partitioned by metes and bounds and that the daughters of Samadullah were also necessary parties. The appellate Court noted that the plaintiffs without impleading the daughters claimed title to the suit land. Therefore, the plaintiffs should have filed a suit for declaration of title as well for partition.

18. The appellate Court, however, came to a finding that the plaintiffs became owners in the disputed jote by purchase and that they were not impleaded as defendants in Partition Suit No. 30 of 1998 filed by the defendants and that the aforesaid partition suit was not disposed of legally. The appellate Court held that since the plaintiff-appellants are co-sharers in the disputed jote they are entitled to get relief against the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 30 of 1998. Accordingly, the appellate Court declared that the plaintiff-appellants are not bound by the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 30 of 1998 for partition.

19. The High Court Division merely concurred with the findings and decision arrived at by the appellate Court.

20. Admittedly, Samadullah died leaving behind four sons and 2 daughters. The plaintiff-appellants became co-sharers in the disputed jote left behind by Samadullah by purchase. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed that they also became owners in the disputed jote left behind by Samadullah by purchase and inheritance. The plaintiff-appellants claimed title to the disputed jote left behind by Samadullah without impleading the admitted co-sharers to the suit. While seeking declaration of title in an undivided jote, the plaintiffs should have prayed not only for declaration of title but also for partition as a consequential relief as envisaged in the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. If declaration of title is allowed to the plaintiffs in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah, the other co-sharers, who are not impleaded in the suit are likely to be affected. Admittedly, many co-sharers and successive co-sharers of Samadullah were not imleaded in the suit for declaration of title filed by the plaintiff-appellants. In a suit for partition, the share of each of co-sharer is determined and such determination is necessary so that at the time of calculation of shares, the share of none of co-sharers is affected or reduced. If declaration of title is allowed to the plaintiff-appellants in the absence of other co-sharers, the left out co-sharers are likely to be affected.

21. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Enjaheruddin Mia alias Md Enjaheruddin Mia, (1998) 18 BLD (AD) 77 = 50 DLR (AD) 84 where it has been held as under: "The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act 1 of 1877) provides that no court shall make any declaration as to the plaintiff's legal character or his right to any property where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. So far as the instant case is concerned the plaintiffs could have asked for either joint possession or partition as a co-sharer of the defendants in the disputed land, but they did not take any such stand in the lower appellate Court or even before the High Court Division. In such view of the mater it will not, at all be fair to put blame either upon the lower appellate court or the High Court Division that they did not declare plaintiffs title to the part of the suit land."

22. Reliance may also be placed on the case of Mrs Shabiha Khanam vs Jaitun Bibi @ Mrs Syed Moazzem Hossain being dead her heirs: Syed Nurul Hasan, (1998) 3 MLR (AD) 15 = 3 BLC (AD) 175 where it has been held as under:

"It must however be said that in the absence of any evidence of partition of CS plot No. 42 the plaintiff-petitioner is not without right and title to his portion of purchased land. Admittedly his purchase is through a co-sharer. But he cannot claim declaration of title simpliciter unless he claims a partition for determining the respective shares of the four brothers in CS plot No. 42 and thereafter his own share of 0.13 acres therein. Hence although the suit has ultimately been dismissed the issue is still open and the plaintiff is free to agitate the question of his title and entitlement to specific portion of 0.13 acres from CS plot No. 42 in a properly framed partition suit."

23. Reliance may also be placed on the case of Tayeb Ali vs Abdul Khaleque, 43 DLR (AD) 87 where it has been held that the suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified share of an undivided plot of land is not maintainable without prayer for partition.

24. The principle expounded in the cases is that in the absence of partition of the undivided jote the plaintiff cannot pray for simple declaration of title without praying for partition by impleading all the co-sharers. The plaintiff-appellants in the case in hand could have asked for joint possession in the disputed undivided jote left behind by Samadullah but they omitted to do so at any stage of the suit. Thus they are not entitled to declaration of title within specific boundary in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah in the absence of left out co-sharers.

<u>25. The plaintiffs without impleading all the heirs of Samadullah prayed for declaration of title in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah. The plaintiffs should have prayed for not only declaration of title but also for partition impleading all the co-sharers of Samadullah. The appellate Court was, however, justified in decreeing the suit in part holding that since the plaintiffs were not impleaded in previously filed Title Suit No. 30 of 1998 for partition, they were not bound by that decree. The appellate Court was perfectly justified in giving the above declaration. The plaintiff-appellants are, however, entitled to file a properly framed suit if so advised and the question of limitation will not stand on the way.</u>

In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any substance in this appeal Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, Advocate ------ For the Petitioners.

parties:
Parsuram Malo and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Niyat Ali Dewan ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
In this civil revision leave was granted under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 22-7-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka allowing the Civil Revision No. 313 of 2008 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 9th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 rejecting the application under Order XXII, rule 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. It appears that the present opposite party filed an application on 15-1-2006 under Order XXII, rule 10(1) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for adding him as assignee in place of his vendors, defendant Nos. 1(1), 4 and 5 and the heirs of defendant No. 3 in Title Suit No. 215 of 1976, subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 and transfer to the court of Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka stating that during the pendency of the suit, he purchased 0.81 decimals of the suit land by four registered kabalas being Nos. 10490, 10491, 10492 and 10489 all dated 3-6-2004 and has been possessing the same by the aforesaid purchase. It was also stated in the application that the present suit was decreed in preliminary form by judgment and order dated 5-5-1987 and challenging the said decree the present applicant instituted Title Suit No. 367 of 2005 in the Court of Second Joint District Judge, Dhaka and the same is now pending.

3. The present petitioner contested the said application by filing written objection and upon hearing the parties, the learned Senior Assistant by order No. 46 dated 22-7-2008 rejected the application with a finding that the opposite party instituted Title Suit No. 367 of 2005 in the Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka challenging the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 and declaring the same is illegal void ab-intio and not binding upon him and further found that in the application under Order XXII, rule 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure applicant failed to mention specifically how much land he purchased from whom, in which plot of land.

4. Against the order dated 22-7-2008, the present opposite party filed Civil Revision No. 313 of 2008 under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka and the same was eventually transferred to the Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka for disposal. After hearing the parties, the learned Additional District Judge by judgment and order dated 22-7-2009 made the Rule absolute and set aside the order dated 22-7-2008 passed by the learned Assistant Judge on the finding that the original Title Suit being Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 relates to partition and after passing of the preliminary decree on 28-4-1987 no final decree has yet been passed in this suit and further found that the suit for partition kept pending till passing of the final decree. Thus there is no legal impediment to implead/add the petitioner as defendant in this suit and allowed to prosecute the suit as defendant. Moreover, High Court Division by judgment and order dated 15-4-2009 gave similar observation and directed to disposed of the Civil Revision No. 313 of 2008 filed by the present petitioner within two months from the receipt of the order and same was disposed of by judgment dated 22-7-2009.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 22-7-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 313 of 2008 the plaintiff-decree holder-opposite party as petitioner filed the instant Civil Revision and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, the learned Advocate argued this case on behalf of the petitioner. He firstly submits that this is not proper stage of the proceeding to implead the opposite party as defendant in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 after passing of the preliminary decree in the said suit. Where the vendors of the opposite party were made party as defendants and the present petitioner got saham of '72 decimals of land and the defendant is the vendors of the opposite party got only '9 decimals of suit land and the said decree was upheld by the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 627 of 1998 by judgment and order dated 7-3-2000. He further submits that when the vendors of the opposite party had no saleable right, then purchase of the suit land from them, he is not entitled to add him as assignee in place of his vendors in the final decree of Title Sit No. 1 of 1985. He next submits that the vendors of the present opposite party surrendered possession of the suit land in favour of the petitioners and in pursuant to the decree passed in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 the RS record was corrected and after mutated their names they have been paying rents to the government. He also submits that the learned Additional District Judge without considering of the above vital aspect of the case allowed the revision to add the opposite party as assignee of his vendors in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 and thus committed an error of law. He submits that the deed of declaration dated 3-6-2004 does not create any title over the suit land. He finally submits that the learned Additional District Judge failed to consider the findings of the learned trial court that the present opposite party filed Title Suit No. 367 of 2005 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka praying for a declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 is illegal, void and not binding upon him and that in the application under Order XXII, rule 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no mention how much land purchase from whom in which plot of land and thereby committed gross error of law and accordingly prayed that Rule should be made absolute. In support of his contentions the learned Advocate refers decisions reported in AIR 1975 (SC) 733 and 7 BLT (HCD) (1999) 43.

7. Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, appearing with Mr Md Motahar Hossain, the learned Advocates for the opposite party. Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder submits that the learned trial court failed to consider that the present opposite party in his application under Order XXII, rule 10(1) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure sufficiently described the facts how much land he purchase from whom in which plot of land and accordingly, the learned Additional District Judge rightly set aside the order of the learned trial court. He further submits that the Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 being a suit for partition and has pending in which till now no final decree of partition has been passed yet, there is no legal bar to re-open the case of the entitlement opposite party share in the suit land. A suit for partition remains pending till the passing of the final decree. He next submits that the preliminary decree was passed in Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 without considering the title deed dated 29-7-1935 and if the said deed was produced by the defendants in the suit and considered, the preliminary decree would have been otherwise.

He lastly submits that the learned Additional District Judge after considering the materials on record and the principle of law and assigning cogent reasons allowed the revision by setting aside the order dated 22-7-2008 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, which is liable to be affirmed and prayed for discharged the Rule.

8. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate has made reliance to the decision in the case of Rezaul Karim vs Md Amanullah reported in 1 BCR (1981) (HCD) 51.

9. In the present revision the principal question to be decided is that after decreed the Title Suit No. 1 of 1985 in preliminary form whether the order of assignment passed by the Additional District Judge of the present opposite party as defendant in the said suit is maintainable or not.

10. The learned Advocate for both the parties made extensive argument in this revision touching with the merit of the suit. But I will concentrate myself only with the impugned order passed by the learned Additional District Judge in respect of assignment of the defendant.

11. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties, perused the application, counter affidavit, supplementary counter affidavit filed by the opposite-party on 14-1-2013, 27-1-2013, 26-2-2013 and supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioner on 24-2-2013 and the annexures annexed thereto.

12. Before I deal with the revisional application I like to dispose of the application for substitution filed by the petitioners on 7-10-2012 after condoning the delay of 773 days. This court on 5-11-2012 passed order that the application for substitution should be heard first and the same was kept with the record. Subsequently the petitioner on 12-2-2013 filed supplementary affidavit stating the facts of delay in not substituting the heirs of the deceased petitioner No.1, Parsuram Malo. Against the application for substitution the opposite party filed counter affidavit stating that the petitioners were very much negligent in substituting the heirs of the deceased petitioner No.1 and prayed for rejection of the application for substitution.

13. The petitioners in their application for substitution stated that the petitioner No.1 Parsuram Malo died on 25-8-2010 and since the petitioner No. 2 was seriously ill he could not file this application within time. Subsequently, the petitioner in paragraph No.3 of the supplementary affidavit stated the reasons for delay of filing this application for substitution. Learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that although the delay is inordinate in this case, it should be condoned considering the helpless position of petitioner No. 2. That the aforesaid delay is bonafide and unintentional and beyond the control of the petitioners. That unless the delay of 773 days in filing the civil revision is condoned, the petitioners shall suffer irreparable loss and injury and prayed for condonation of delay.

14. I have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the application. It appears from the statements made in paragraph No.3 of the substitution application and paragraph No.3 of the supplementary affidavit that the reasons for delay in filing the application has been satisfactorily explained and which seems bonafide and reasonable. Accordingly, the application for substitution is allowed and for ends of Justice, the delay of 773 days in filing the revisional application is hereby condoned. The heirs of deceased petitioner No. 1 be substituted as petitioner Nos. 1(ka) and 1(kha) in place of deceased petitioner No.1 Parsuram Malo Accordingly, office is directed to note the same in the cause title of the revisional application.

15. It appears that the opposite party is the assignee being a subsequent purchaser during the pendency of the suit and he has acquired substantial interest in the suit property. The provision as laid down under Order XXII, rule 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not contemplate the addition of a new party, but the person having interest obtained through purchase from person who was a party in the suit may be impleaded enabling him to continue the suit.

16. In the present case it appears that the opposite party after purchase of the suit land by 4 (four) registered kabalas all dated 3-6-2004 and possessing the same by the aforesaid purchase and there is no other person on behalf of the defendant to prosecute the suit. In the circumstances stated above the opposite party being an assignee resorted to an alternative procedure which guarded against the danger that the defendant being no longer interested in the suit may not prosecute the suit or collide with the plaintiff.

17. It appears that the opposite party wanted to be impleaded as defendant on the ground that he purchases the suit land. Order XXII, rule 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure lays down that in case of an assignment, creation or devolution on any interest during the pendency of a suit, the suit may, by leave of the court, be continued by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved.

<u>18. The provisions are of an enabling character and entitle an assignee to do so, if so desired. It does not make incumbent upon an assignee to make the application if he thinks that his interests are being well looked after by his assignor. It is merely an alternative procedure which guards against the danger that the original defendants are no longer interested in the suit may not prosecute it or may even side with the adversary. Furthermore, under the said provision of the Code the right to apply is a continuing right accruing from day to day and is not subject to the law of limitation.</u>

<u>19. It appears that the order of assignment was passed in a suit for partition. A suit for partition remains pending till the passing of the final decree. The court maintains its seizin over the entire dispute, there would obviously be no bar to the court taking any steps which it could have been before the preliminary decree.</u>

20. The learned Additional District Judge considering the facts and circumstances of the case rightly found that opposite party has subsisting interest and locus-standi to be impleaded as defendant in the suit by way of assignment. In such view of the matter the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error causing failure of justice in allowing the application under Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the petitioner. I do not find any ground to interfere with the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge.

21. I have already observed that the extensive argument was made by the learned Advocates for both the parties in respect of the merit of the suit, but sitting in the revisional court there is no scope to consider the merit of the suit which should be decided by the trial court in the suit.

22. Learned Advocate for the petitioners has referred the case of Harihar Prasad Singh vs Balmiki Prasad Singh reported in AIR 1975 (SC) 733 and Md Azimuddin Talukder vs Md Abdul Mannan Talukder reported in 7 BLT (HCD) (1999) 43 but the aforesaid decisions have got any bearing on the question involved in the present case. So the reported cases will not be any help of the petitioners.

22. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

23. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Communicate the order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Musherrof Hossain Majumder Advocate ----- for petitioner.

parties:
Moulana Mohammad Baquer Siddiqui 
Vs.
Tamizuddin Khan Trust Estate and others
full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali, J: In the instant Rule, the petitioner challenged the judgment and order dated 17.2.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 rejecting the prayer under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for stay of the subsequent Judge (Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Dhaka.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, title and interest of 2/3 share in the eastern portion of the 3 schedule property and for cancellation of the Tamizuddin Khan Trust Deed No. 5915 dated 6.3.1985 and for permanent injunction restraining the Defendant No. 1 from claiming the title over the schedule property.

3. The schedule as has been stated in the said Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 runs thus" one storied" pucca building measuring approximately 8,400 sqf. on plot no. 22/1. Block-B.Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Mouja Barba, P.S. Mohammadpur, Measuring about 1000 sqf. yards now known as No. 1, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. In the said suit Mrs. U.K. Siddiqua Huda was shown as principal Defendant and Mrs. Razia Khan Amin and Mrs. Nina Jamaly as proforma Defendants.

4. After appearance in the said suit the Tamizuddin Khan Trust represented by its chairman filed title Suit No. 237 of 2002 against the Devendant Zaber Siddique, Adnan Siddique, Moulana Mohammad Baker Siddique Jounpuri, Babor Sidique before the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration that the 'A' Schedule property as stressed property, a decree for khas possession of the B & C schedule property after evicting the Defendants, a decree for permanent injunction 'restraining the Defendants from evicting the tenant of the plaintiff from the 'D' schedule property and changing the natured and character of the vacant land and giving lease or transfer or construct any stracture in the 'C' schedule property to any other party and for a declaration for profit of Taka 20,000/- per month.

5. Defendant No. 3 after appearance of Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 filed an application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 14.11. 2002 stating that regarding the same schedule property Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 is pending before the same Court to determine the same issues between the same parties and as such the subsequent suit being Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 should be stayed till disposal of Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 now pending before the same court.

6. The plaintiff filed written objection against the said application dated 14.11.2002 denying the assertion made by the Defendant No. 3 of Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 stating that the Tamizuddin Khan Trust deed was created with the consent of the Defendant No. 3 who was a signatory in the deed. It was further stated that the parties of both the suit are not same. In the earlier suit Tamizuddin Khan Trust Estate was not made party in the suit and Mrs. U.K. Siddiqua Huda, Mrs. Razia Khan Amin and Mrs. Nina Jamely are not party in the subsequent suit. Zabbar Siddique, Adnan Siddiqui and Babor Siddique are not the party in the earlier Title Suit No. 371d of 1998. The schedules are not the same, which are apparent in the plaint of both the suits. The reliefs claimed are not the same, which are apparent from the paper of both the suits. The relief claimed in the subsequent suit cannot be granted in the previous instituted suit. The title as claimed in both the suits is different. The issues, which will be settled in both the suits, are also different. It was further stated that if the earlier suit fails, the Plaintiff of the subsequent suit will not get any relief and that the application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is premature.

7. The trial Court after hearing the parties and on consideration of the materials on record rejected the said application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure by his judgment and order dated 17.2.2003 in Title Suit No. 237 of 2002.

8. Against the said order dated 17.2.2003 passed by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title suit No. 237 of 2002 the Defendant No. 3 preferred application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained instant Rule.

9. Mr. Md. Musherrof Hossain Majumdar, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that Defendant No. 3 Moulana Mohammad Baquer Siddiqui Jonpuri filed Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 before the learned Subordinate Judge (joint District Judge), 2nd Court Dhaka for declaration of right, title and interest over the suit property and permanent injunction and for cancellation of the truest deed No. 5915 dated 6.3.1985. In the said suit who are beneficiary of the Trust deed were made party as Defendant Nos. 1-3. He further submits that point of both the suits to be decided as to whether the trust deed is a genuine document or not and as such the issues in both the suits are same and the parties of both the suits are same and the schedule property in both the suits are same and as such the subsequent suit being, Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 to be stayed to avoid the multiplicity of the proceeding.

10. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, Learned Advocate appearing with Mr. T.M. Sakil Hossain submits that the trial Court on consideration all the aspect of the case has rightly rejected the application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial Court considered that the parties involve in both the suits are different. The issues are also different. He further submits that the plaint of Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 shows that the schedules are also different. The relief claimed in both the suits are different. He further submits that the relief claimed in the subsequent suit cannot be granted in the previously instituted suit. The title of the suit are also different; cause of action arrived in both the suits are different. The title of the suit are also different; cause of action arrived in both the suits are different. The issues are to be framed in two suits are different. He further submits that if the earlier suit being Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 is failed. The plaintiff of the subsequent suit in Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 will not get any, relief and the relief claimed in the subsequent suit will be barred by limitation. He further submits that Defendant No. 3d without submitting the written statement in the subsequent suit has filed the application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such at this stage it cannot be said that the issues of the subsequent suit are same. He further submits that the issue will be framed according to the relief claimed by the parties and on consideration of written statement. Lastly, he Submits that the application under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a pre-matured one. Until and unless the issues are framed by the Courts below in both the suits it cannot be said that the issues are same. In support of his contention he cited the case of Askar Ali and another Vs. Shamsul Islam alias Md. Shamsuddin and others reported in 4 MLR(AD)-193.

11. We have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused the revisional application and the grounds there under and papers and documents and annexures of the application and the counter affidavit filed by opposite party No. 1.

12. It appears that Begum Atika Khanam, the wife of late Tamizuddin Khan created Tamizuddin Khan Trust Estate vide trust deed No. 5915 dated 3.6.1985. The defendant No. 3 challenged the said trust deed in Title Suit No: 371 of 1998 by making defendant No. 1 Mrs. U.K. Siddiqui Huda. Mrs. Razia Khan Amin, Mrs. Nina Jamaly. Thus Defendants appeared in the suit and filed written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint. While the said suit was pending for disposal Tamizuddin Khan Trust itself filed Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 praying for declaration that the 'A' schedule property is a trusted property after evicting the Defendants, a decree for permanent injunction restraining the Defendants from evicting the tenants from the schedule property by the defendants forcefully and from changing the nature and character of the suit property in order to giving lease to any other persons or for transferring newly constructed 10 shops to the 3rd party as described in the schedule 'G' and a decree for monthly profit of Taka 20,000/- per months against the Defendants.

13. The plaintiff of Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 being Defendant No. 3 of Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 filed an application under Section 10 of the Civil Procedure (Annexure—'C') praying for stay Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 till ,disposal of Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 stating that the schedule property is the same and parties of both the suits are same and issues are the same but we find that the earlier suit was field against the Defendant No. 1 Mrs. U.K. Siddique Huda Defendant No. 2 Mrs. Razia Khan Amin, Defendant No. 3 Mrs. Nina Jamaly who are not made party in the subsequently instituted suit. It further appears that Kabir Siddique, Adnan Siddiqui and Babor Siddiqui are also not made party in the earlier instituted suit and as such it cannot be said that both the suits are related between the same parties.

14. It appears from the schedule of the plaint of Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 which are as follows:

Schedule of the property.

One three storied, pucca building measuring approximately 8400 sft. on plot No. 22/1, Block-B, Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Mouza Baraba, P.S. Tejgaon, District-Dhaka measuring about 1000 sq. yeards now address as No. 1, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka.

The schedule of subsequent Title suit No. 237 of 2002 are as follows:

SCHEDULE—' A'

All that piece and parcel of 4800 sft, or 0.20625 acre (1000 sq. yrds) non agricultural land appear training to Housing and settlement plot No. 22/1 of Block-B, Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Mouza- Tejgaon at present Mohammadpur, District-Dhaka commonly known as No. Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka with three storied building and all its appurtenances which has been shown by red border line in the attached sketch map.

SCHEDULE—`B’

Out of the said 'A' schedule entire property two bed rooms , one drawing room, one kitchem room, one dining room, one store room, two bath rooms and one dreassing room of the ground floor which has been shown by bellow border line in the attached sketch map.

SCHEDULE—`C’

Out of the 'A' schedule entire property 7 (seven) semi pucca under construction shop rooms facing to the Mirpur road and another 3(three) under construction shop room facing to the Babor road as shown by colour sky blue in attached sketch map.

SCHEDULE-‘D’

The 1st and 2nd floor and the 3(three) garages of the ground floor and 3 store rooms upon the said garages and vacant place out the 'A' schedule property which is under the possession of monthly tenant, Directorate of Archaeology.

15. The schedule as has been described in Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 has been described by hand made sketch as such we find that the schedule of both the suits are not same. It further appears that the cause of action of both the suits are different. The relief claimed in the earlier Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 the plaintiff prayed for declaration of right, title and interest over the suit property to the extended of share and for cancellation of Tamizuddin Khan Trust deed No. 5915 dated 6.3.1985 and for permanent injunction against the Defendant claiming the right, title and interest over the schedule property. It appears from the prayer of the Title Suit No. 371 of 1998 that the Defendants No. 3 claimed 2/3 share of the schedule property and as such we find that share of the schedule property admittedly remains with the Defendants Nos. 1-3.

16. The prayer as stated in the plaint of the subsequently instituted Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 that the Trust claims a decree over the 'A' schedule property. Recovery of khas possession 'B' and 'C' schedule property permanent injunction against 'D' and 'E' schedule property and as such we find that the reliefs claimed are not the same.

<u>17. We find that the issues has not yet been framed in both the suits even Defendant No. 3 of Title Suit No. 237 of 2002 has not yet submitted any written statement and as such it cannot be said at this stage that the issues are same. It has been held in the case of Askar Ali and another Vs. Shamsul Islam alias Md. Shamsuddin and others reported in 4 MLR(AD)-193 that the subsequent suit may be stayed only when the matter in issue of the previously instituted suit is directly and substantially the same, the parties are the same title and the court is competent to grant the relief so claimed. Unless the Court is satisfied with the above tests of law, no stay can be granted. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1 submits that if the earlier suit fails or in the alternative the plaintiff of the earlier suits unable to get a decree the plaintiff of the subsequent suit will not set relief due to the law of limitation. Such submission merits consideration. We find that both the suits are not between the same parties; not in the same schedule; not with the same cause of action not with the same prayer; though no issues are framed, the issues may not be same. The relief claimed in subsequent suit cannot be determined and granted in previously instantiated suit. From the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above we do not find any reason to interfere in the impugned judgment and order passed by the trial Court.</u>

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The order of stay granted by this Court stands vacated. The trial Court is directed to expedite the trial of both the suits.

19. Communicate the order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Afzal Hossain Ahmed, J: This Rule is directed, at the instance of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners, against the judgment and decree dated 20.1.2000 and 27.1.2000 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur in Title Appeal No. 5 of 1998 reversing those dated 30.11.97 and 4.1.98 respectively passed by the Assistant Judge, Damudya, Shariatpur in Title Suit No. 18 of 1996 allowing the appeal.

2. The case of the plaintiff-petitioners, in brief, is that the plaintiff-petitioners filed Title Suit No. 18 of 1996 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Damudya, Shariatpur for declaration of title to the suit land and for declaration that the recent survey record in the name of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instead of the names of the plaintiffs alone in respect of the suit land is illegal and without any basis and for permanent injunction restraining the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 from entering into the suit land and from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land alleging, inter alia, that 5.72 acres of land in different plots under C.S. Khatian No. 99 of Purba Kandi mouza within P.S. Goshairhat was owned and possessed by Miah Chand Chowkidar. He died leaving behind his only son Bahar Ali @ Bahar Ali Chowkidar, only daughter, Joygun Bibi and wife Miajan Bibi. Bahar Ali Chowkidar, as per his share, while possessing in the suit land sold out .44 decimals of land of plot No. 666 under schedule I by kabala, dated 11.10.23 to Shafizuddin Sarder, Abe predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs. The said land was duly recorded in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs in R. S.Khatian No. 187 as plot No. 469. In the title column of B.S. Khatian, the name of the heirs of Mia Chand Chowkidar and Shafizuddin Sarder and others are seen. Though their names were recorded but in the remark column of the said record, possession in respect of the suit plot was shown in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs. In the last S.A. operation the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs was recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 210 in- ejmali with Babu Kha and defendant No. 1 in respect of 3.83 acres of land where the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor was also shown alone in the possession column against the suit plot and that does mean that plaintiffs predecessor -in-interest used to possess the suit plot exclusively. While the predecessor of the plaintiffs had been in exclusive possession in the suit plot he sold out .11 decimals of land out of the suit plot to Abdur Rahim Sarder, son of Abdul Hashem Sarder, by kabala dated 1.4.1976 and handed over possession to him who then sold out the same to one Delwara Begum. Thereafter Delwara Begum sold out her said purchased land to plaintiff No. 4 by kabala dated 19.4.1987 and he has been possessing the same since then. Shafizuddin Sarder died leaving behind sons , plaintiff Nos. 1-3 as his heirs , thus the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land within the knowledge of the defendants and general people for more than 12 years. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land, in collusion with the employees engaged for survey records, illegally got the suit land recorded in their names with the plaintiffs in the recent Khatian. On the basis of the said illegal and wrong record, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the last part of Ashar , 1404 B.S. threatened the plaintiffs with forcible dispossession from the suit land and hence the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations contending, inter alia, that the land under suit Khatian was owned and possessed by Joygun Bibi and Mohammad Bepari who sold 1.28 acres of land out of the suit, khatian including the land of C.S. Plot No. 666 in favour of Shafizuddin, the predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and Babu Kha and Chamol Bibi, the father and mother of the defendant No. 1 and handed over possession to them. Thereafter Bahar Ali Chowkidar sold out 1.62 1/2 acres of land out of the suit land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 99 by registered deed dated 1.1.1944 to Shafizuddin, predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and defendant No. 1 and his father Babu Kha. The S.A. Khatian No. 210 was rightly recorded in respect of the suit land in 1/3 share in the names of Shafizuddin Sarder, Babu Kha and Jobbor Kha each. Thereafter defendant No. 1 sold out some land out of the suit land to the defendant No. 2. The present hal record in respect of the suit land has been prepared correctly. The suit land being an ejmali property, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief as prayed for without asking for partition and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

4. During trial of the case both the plaintiffs and defendants adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases.

5. The trial court on hearing both the parties and on consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendants preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 5 of 1998 before the District Judge, Shariatpur. The appeal was heard and disposed of by the Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties without considering the points involved in the case reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court holding that the trial court had erred in law in decreeing the suit declaring the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land which appertains to an ejmali Khatian and as such without seeking for partition simple suit for declaration is not maintainable.

8. Being aggrieved by that judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Shariatpur the plaintiffs have preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

9. Heard Mr. A.B. Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners and Mr. Muhammad Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 2 and perused the revisional application, impugned judgment and decree as well as the judgment and decree passed by the trial court, oral and documentary evidence and the L.C. Record.

10. Mr. A.B. Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the land of the previous suit jote measuring 5.72 acres appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 99 (Ext. 1) previously belonged to one Miajan @ Mia Chan Chowkidar who died leaving wife Manijan Bibi, son Bahar Ali Chowkidar and daughter Joygun Bibi and then Manijan Bibi died leaving Bahar Ali Chowkidar and Joygun Bibi as son and daughter respectively . He further submits that Bahar Ali Chowkidar, while he had been exclusively possessing .44 acres of land appertaining to R.S. Plot No. 469 out of the suit land sold out that 44 decimals of land by kabala in the year 1923 ( Ext.7) to Shafizuddin Sarder, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and in R.S. Khatian No. 187(Ext.2) which was admittedly prepared and published during 1942 to 1948 under the provision of Bengal Tenancy Act and that in Ext. 2 Shfizuddin Sarder's possession by purchase was recorded in .44 decimals of land appertaining to R.S. Suit Plot No. 469. He further submits that the plaintiffs' predecessor Shafizuddin had been possessing the suit land since 1923 and after him the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land and thereby acquired valid title thereto but the Court of Appeal below failed to appreciate that aspect of the matter as well as the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the plaintiffs and thereby arrived at an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice which caused serious prejudice to the plaintiff-petitioners.

11. Admittedly, the original suit jote measuring 5.72 acres of land including the suit land measuring .44 acres of land of B.R.S Plot No. 1088 corresponding to C.S. Plot No. 666 and R. S and S.A. Plot No. 469 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 99 (Ext. 1 ) previously belonged to one Miajan @ Miachand Chowkidar and he died leaving wife Manijan, son Bahar Ali and daughter, Joygun Bibi and Manijan died leaving Bahar Ali Chowkidar and Joygun Bibi as son and daughter respectively. It is also an admitted fact that Bahar Ali thereafter sold out .44 decimals of land of C.S. Plot No. 666 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 99 to one Shafizuddin Sarder, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs by a registered deed in the year, 1923 A.D. (Ext. 7). The R.S. Khatian No. 187, marked Ext. 2, corresponding to C.S. Khatian No. 99 shows that the lands of the original suit jote with an area of 5.75 acres were recorded in the names of the riyots with their specific share in the jote and in the "remark column" it is mentioned that the plot No. 469 with an area of .44 decimals was being possessed by one Shafizuddin Sarder son of Tither Ali Sarder on the basis of purchase. In Ext. 2, against all other plots, names of the respective possessors were also mentioned showing their respective share in each of the pion. Ext. 3 is the S. A. Khatian No, 210 which relates to 3.83 acres of land including the suit land measuring .44 decimals of plot No. 469 wherein against suit plot No. 469 exclusive possession of Shafiz Ali @ Shafizuddin, the predecessor of the plaintiffs has been mentioned in its entire .44 decimals of land. Rent receipt Ext. 5 shows that An Sarder (plaintiff No. 1) son of Shafizuddin paid rent for the suit land in respect of Plot No. 469 appertaining to Khatian No. 210 upto 1397 B.S. The BRS Khatian No. 282 marked Ext. 6 shows that this khatian stands prepared exclusively in respect of only suit Plot No. 1088 with an area of 44 decimals which is admitted to have been finally published in the meantime. Ext. 6 appears to have been recorded in the names of both the plaintiffs and the defendants. Plaintiffs asserted through a registered deed executed in the year 1923 marked Ext. 7 that by this deed Bahar Ali Chowkidar, who had admittedly 2/3rd share in the original suit' jote, sold out 44 decimals of land in R.S. Plot No. 469 corresponding to C.S. Plot No. 666 which has subsequently been transformed into BRS plot No. 1088 to Shafizuddin Sirder, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs . From R.S. Khatian, marked as Ext. 2, it appears that the share of all the co-sharer-tenants has been specifically mentioned therein against their names along with their individual and specific possession in each plot of the jote wherein in 'remark column' exclusive possession of Shafizuddin Sarder predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs in .44 decimals of land of R.S. Plot No. 469, on the basis of purchase, stands mentioned: The facts dis-closed in the Ext. 2 give rise to presumption that there was at amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of the C.S. jote before the preparation of the R.S. record which reflects in the R.S. Khatian No. 187 (Ext. 2). Had there been no such amicable partition the specific share of each of the co-sharer tenants with their specific possession along with specific possession of the transferees from them in each individual plot of the suit jote would not reflect in R.S. Khatian (Ext. 2). In S.A. Khatian No. 210, marked. Ext. 3, too the exclusive possession of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs has been mentioned in .44 decimals of land of Plot No. 469.

12. In view of the above evidence (Ext. 2 ,3 and 7) it is apparent that Shafizuddin Sarder, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs had exclusive possession in .44 decimals of land of R.S. and S.A. Plot No. 469 which has been subsequently transformed into BRS Plot No. 1088.

13. The R.S. Khatian No. 187, marked Ext. 2 and S.A. Khatian No. 210 marked Ext. 3 show that exclusive possession of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs was mentioned therein over .44 decimals of land of suit plot No. 469 amongst other plots of the khatian belonging to other co-sharers. In view of the facts, circumstances and evidence as referred to above it appears that the plaintiff-petitioners have been able to make out a good case than the case of the defendant-opposite parties.

14. In S.A Khatian No. 210 (Ext. 3) the exclusive possession of -the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs in the suit land measuring 44 decimals of land in plot No. 469 has been mentioned . Thereafter the BRS khatian No. 282 marked Ext. 6 has been prepared exclusively in respect of only one plot, i.e., the suit plot No. 1088 which corresponds to A.S. and S.A. Plot No. 469 and C.S. Plot No. 666 measuring .44 decimals of land. Ext. 6 has been prepared in the names of both the plain-tiffs and the defendants. In view of Ext. 6 it is apparent that co-sharership in the tenancy no. longer remains and it seized to exist.

15. Admittedly, Plaintiff-petitioners 1-3 are the sons of Shafizuddin Sarder and plaintiff-petitioner No. 4 is the purchaser from the transferee of Shafizuddin. Plaintiffs claimed that the predecessor-in-interest Shafizuddin Sarder had been exclusively possessing the suit land by purchase since 1923 (vide Ext.7) and after him they have been possessing the suit land. Ext. 5 is the rent receipt which shows that the plaintiff No. 1 paid rent for the suit land measuring .44 decimals of land appertaining to plot No. 469 upto 1397 B.S. Plaintiffs examined 3 P.Ws who affirmed plaintiffs' exclusive possession in the said land and there is nothing to disbelieve their evidence. Moreso, P.W.I has deposed stating that the defendants threatened them with dispossession of the suit land in the last part of Asarh 1404 B.S. The possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land has also not been denied by the defendants. On the other hand, although the defendants claimed their possession in the suit land they could not substantiate that by adducing any independent and reliable evidence which was also disbelieved by the lower appellate court.

<u>16. Considering the facts, circumstances and evidence as discussed above I find that Shafizuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs had been in exclusive possession of the suit land measuring .44 decimals of land of R.S . and S.A. Plot No. 469 corresponding to C.S. Plot No. 666 and BRS Plot No. 1088 by purchase since 1923 and after him the plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession thereof and thereby the plaintiffs acquired their valid title to the suit land. Since co-sharership in the tenancy seized to exist and in spite of having their exclusive title and possession in the suit land since the names of the defendants have been recorded in the hal BRS khatian No. 282 (Ext. 6) along with the names of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land the title of the plaintiffs thereto is found to have been clouded and when the defendants on the basis of that wrong BRS Khatian No. 282 (Ext. 6) threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession of the suit land , the plaintiffs are en-titled to seek relief in a suit for declaratory relief with a view to removing the cloud on their title created due to wrong recording of ROR, because in such a suit declaration of title is all that the plaintiffs require, the plaintiffs may also seek for injunction along with the declaration of title if there is threat of dispossession. So the plaintiffs are not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition.</u>

17. Of course the provision of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act forbids a suit for pure declaration without further relief but it does not compel the plaintiff to sue for all the relief which could possibly be granted or debar him from obtaining a relief which he wants unless at the same time he seeks for a relief which he does not want. It may be that the plaintiff requires nothing more than a mere declaration and in those circumstances to refuse to make the decree asked for, will be a denial of justice. Accordingly, since cloud has arisen on the title of the plaintiffs because of wrong recording of ROR, a simple decla7 ration of title is enough.

18. In 46 DLR 419 cited by Mr. Siddique our High Court Division also held that in a case of original ownership the plaintiffs and defendants being in joint possession of the suit property, suit for declaratory relief in respect of the share of the plaintiff in a specified land without seeking partition is maintainable.

19. Even, if the plaintiffs were in joint possession of the immovable property before seizing of the co-sharership in the tenancy, they were entitled to file a suit praying for declaratory relief only in respect of their share in a specified land without praying for any consequential relief with a view to removing the cloud on their title created due to wrong recording of ROR, because in such a suit simple declaration of title is enough. So, the plaintiffs were not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition. This view also finds support from the decision in the case of Md. Giasuddin and others Vs. Md. Noab Ali and others reported in 22 BLD (HCD), 586.

20. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the decisions referred to

above the instant suit is found to have been framed properly.

21. Mr. Muhammad Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite-party No.2 has submitted that the plaintiff-petitioners can not seek for any relief in a declaratory suit without asking for consequential relief by way of partition since the suit land is an ejmali property. As it is already found from the oral and documentary evidence that the co-sharership in the tenancy seized to exist and when the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and after him the plaintiffs are found to have acquired valid title to the suit land by their exclusive possession since 1923 without any interruption from any quarters the above submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite-party cannot be sustainable in the eye of law.

22. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the discussions above, I hold that the impugned judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and causing prejudice to the plaintiffs and as such the same can not be sustained in the eye of law.

23. In the result, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court in Title Appeal No. 5 of 1998 are hereby set aside and those of the trial court are hereby restored.

Send down the L.C. Records at once.

End.
