19. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order passed in the said civil revision the plaintiffs preferred Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 297 of 1992 before the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division while dismissing the leave petition observed as under:

“……….. The learned Subordinate Judge observed that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree roe permanent injunction for their unspecified and unidentifiable 7 annas share (if at all) in view of these and other findings, we are of the view that it has been rightly decided that a simple suit for permanent injunction notwithstanding plaintiff s possession is not maintainable in the circumstances of the case."

20. A reading of the judgments passed in Title Appeal No. 196 of 1984, Civil Revision 76 of 1987 and Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 297 of 1992 it is primafacie clear that the plaintiffs suit was dismissed as complicated questions of title were involved, but all the courts found their possession in the suit property. It is also a well settled legal proposition that in a suit for permanent injunction regarding an immovable property the court shall see whether the plaintiffs are in exclusive possession of the suit property and it can see title of the plaintiffs incidentally, so all the courts rightly refrained from giving any finding as to the title of the parties to the suit property as well as the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. When all the 3 (three) courts dismissed Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 on the categorical finding that complicated questions of title being involved the suit was not maintainable then how the stray observations even if any made regarding the auction purchase by plaintiffs vendor's predecessor Ali Ahmed can be said to be a constructive res-judicata to nonsuit the plaintiffs, the instant suit being one for title along with the consequential reliefs. We are of the view that in order to non suit the plaintiffs from maintaining a suit of the instant nature on the plea of constructive res-judicata as conceived of in explanation IV to section 11 of the Code the defendants were obliged to prove that in the earlier suit the plaintiffs did not at all plead their title on the basis of the auction purchase by their vendor's processor Ali Ahmed or that there was a conclusive decision in the previous suit on the title of the plaintiffs or the auction purchase but the plaintiffs could prove none. At the risk of repetition we hold that since no issue as to the title of the parties to the suit property and the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed was raised and decided in neither of the suits fought by the parties and the plaintiffs vendors vendor having pleaded in the very first suit his own right title to the suit property it cannot be said that the plaintiffs claim was barred by the principle of constructive res-judicata. So, we find no substance in the submission Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, on the first point and hold that the instant was quite maintainable in law.

21. Now let us see whether the plaintiffs proved their title to the suit property. The whole basis of the plaintiffs title to the suit property was the auction purchase by Ali Ahmed on 20.06.1953. Further case of the plaintiffs was that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953, the sale certificate was issued on 19.11.1953 and Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court 20.01.1954 and since then he had been in possession thereof. After the death of Ali Ahmed his wife Khatibunnesa inherited his entire property and on her death Abdul Mannan, her full brother inherited the same. In support of the said case of the plaintiffs they filed the sale certificate (exhibit 2) and the writ of delivery of possession (exhibit 2 (ka). In the written statement exhibit 2 and 2 (ka) were not challenged as spurious or forged. In the deposition of D.W. 1 only a general denial was given to the effect:

“………. ইহা সত্য নয় যে, আলী আহম্মদ নিলাম খরিদ করিয়া ভোগ দখলে ছিলেন। তিনি, ভাড়াটিয়া হিসাবে ভোগ দখলে ছিলেন।”

22. From exhibit 2 it is clear that the sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953. From exhibit 2 it is further clear that the entire suit land measuring .568 ajutangsha was sold in auction and not 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit plot. From exhibit 2 it further appears that the said 568 ajutangsha was the 7th annas share of the "হিস্যে" of the touzi being No. 61/1 of Dhaka Collectorate. `Touzi' refers to a page of the register of the tenant. When a property is sold in auction giving specific description thereof and mentioning the area how can it be said that 7 (seven) annas share out of the plot mentioned in the schedule of the sale certificate was sold. Mr. A. J. Mohammad vehemently argued that since in the compromise applications dated 16.11.59 filed in Title Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 and in the two registered agreements of the same date Ali Ahmed claimed to have purchased 7 (seven) annas share out of the suit land, in no case the plaintiffs could claim more than said 7 (seven) annas share of the suit property. But we do not find any substance in the said submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, our reason being that when the alleged agreements and the compromise applications were cancelled at the instance of the defendant's predecessor Rasheda Begum in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 how reliance could be put on the said agreements and the compromise applications. Further as those were not filed in the instant suit neither the trial court had any chance to see the recitals therein nor this court has any chance to go through the same to verify the submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali. In the plaint the plaintiffs claimed the entire suit property which is clearly mentioned in the sale certificate as well as in the writ of delivery of possession, but the defendants never challenged the identify of the suit property or the area of the suit property.

23. The submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali that auction purchase by Ali Ahmed being after the transfer of the suit property to Salimunnesa by the admitted rightful owners, namely, Khiroda Sundari Shaha and Lalit Mohan Das Shaha no title accrued to him appeared to us absolutely fallacious. Because, though the auction sale took place on 20.06.53, yet the number of the certificate case shows that it was started in 1952 being No. 60 of 1952-53. It is also very pertinent to keep in mind that before auction sale notice under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 (the Act) must have been served after observing the other requirements as mandated in sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act. The said provisions of the Act deal with filing of certificate for public demand payable to the Collector, requisition for certificate in other cases and the filing of certificate on requisition. Rules framed under section 38 of the Act have provided the details as to how the notice under section 7 of the Act shall be served. Section 8 of the Act has clearly stipulated that from and after the service of notice of any certificate under section 7 of the Act upon a certificate debtor any private transfer or delivery of any of his immovable property situated in the district in which the certificate is filed, or of any interest in any such property, shall be void against any claim enforceable in execution of the certificate and the amount due from time to time in respect of the certificate shall be a charge upon the immovable property of the certificate-debtor, wherever situated, to which every other charge created subsequently to the service of the said notice shall be postponed. Section 9 of the Act has clearly provided for filing petition denying the liability and section 10 thereof has spelt out about the hearing and determination of such petition. The defendants in their written statement did not specifically challenge the auction sale, what they pleaded was that Ali Ahmed having earlier claimed that he purchased 7 (seven) annas share of the suit plot the plaintiffs could not claim the entire suit property. Whether the certificate of demand and certificate of requisition were filed before the certificate officer prior to the alleged sale by Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha to Salimunnessa are questions of fact and as the defendants did not challenge the certificate proceedings in which Ali Ahmed auction purchased the suit property the plaintiffs were not required to prove all those facts. In support of the plaintiffs claim of title through auction purchase by Ali Ahmed they having filed the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession their onus was discharged. Further, as per the own admission of the defendants that Ali Ahmed disclosed the fact of auction purchase as far back as in 1959 when he allegedly created two deeds of agreements and two applications for compromise filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and in House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 which were ultimately cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, but Rasheda Begum never took any attempt to set aside the said auction purchase by Ali Ahmed. In this regard we like to observe that in a revenue matter proceeding follows the land not the person, so even if Khiroda Sundari Daishaya and Lalit Mohan Shaha sold the suit property prior to the auction sale but that shall not automatically make the auction sale a nullity. It was obligatory upon Rasheda Begum to take step to set aside the sale. In this regard we like point out that rule 39 of the Rules as detailed in schedule 11 to the Act which have binding effect in view of the provision of section 38 of the Act (hereinafter refereed to as the Rules) has clearly provided that if any claim is preferred to or any objection is made to the attachment or sale of, any property in execution of a certificate, on the ground that such property is not liable to such attachment or sale, the certificate officer shall proceed to investigate the claim or objection. Rule 40 has provided that the claimant or the objector must adduce evidence to show that (in case of immovable property) at the date of service of the notice under section 7 of the Act he had some interest in, or was possessed of, the property attached. Rule 41 has given power to the certificate officer to release the property from attachment or sale. Rule 43 has provided that the party against whom an order is made may instant a suit in a civil court to establish the right which he claims to the property in dispute, but subject to the result of such suit (if any) the order shall be conclusive. But Salimunnessa or Rasheda Begum did not take shelter under the said provisions of law to set aside the sale. In the Act or in the rules nothing has been provided for as to when an auction sale shall take its effect, but we can easily take the aid of section 65 of the Code which reads as under:

"65. where immovable property is sold in execution of a decree and such sale has become absolute, the property shall be deemed to have vested in the purchaser from the time when the property is sold and not from the time when the sale becomes absolute."

24. It is true that the auction sale in question was not held in execution of a decree of a civil court, but we do not see any wrong in borrowing the concept from the Code it being a civil proceeding and appeared to us quite akin to an auction sale held under the Code in execution of a decree. Mr. Mohammad Ali like a drowning man who catches a straw tried to challenge the auction sale by submitting that the sale certificate does not tally with Form 28 and Rule 74 of the Rules, so on such defective sale certificate the plaintiffs could not claim their title to the suit property. On such submission of Mr. Mohammad Ali we have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or noncompliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate void or voidable. We are of the view that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property.

25. Admittedly the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property which was clearly found by all the courts in connection with the proceedings which arose out of Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 of the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka. The plaintiffs by amending the plaint prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit property and also for mesne profit stating categorically that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants therefrom forcibly on 16.09.1997. All along plaintiff's case was that their predecessor's predecessor Ali Ahmed got possession of the suit property through court on the basis of his auction purchase and in support of their said case they filed the writ of delivery of possession, exhibit 2 (ka). From exhibit 1 (ka) and 1 (kha) it appears that the S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed. Exhibit 5 shows that plaintiffs names were mutated and a new khatian being No. 197 was opened in their names. Exhibit 6-6 (Na) series show that Ali Ahmed paid rents to the government and then the plaintiffs paid rents to the government after mutation of their names. Exhibit 7-7 (Nia) series show that the holding in respect of the suit property was recorded with the Dhaka City Corporation in the name of the plaintiffs and they paid City Corporation tax. Exhibits 8. 9 and 10 series show that it is the plaintiffs who paid the utility bills such as Dhaka Was a, gas and electricity in respect of the suit property. Exhibits 11 and 12 series show that the plaintiffs inducted tenants in the suit property who paid rents to them. And those documents primafacie proved that it was Ali Ahmed and the plaintiffs who exercised their right of ownership in the suit property and had been in possession thereof uninterruptedly since the delivery of possession on 20.01.54 by virtue of the auction purchase. On the other hand, the contesting defendants failed to file a single scrape of paper to show that their so-called vendor Rasheda Begum and before that Salimunnesa ever exercised their right of ownership and possession in the suit property or that Ali Ahmed or his wife had ever attorned Salimunnessa as land lord after purchase from Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Shaha or they ever paid any rent to Rasheda Begum attorning as their land lord. Not only that the defendants also failed to file/produce any original deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum. It is a well settled legal proposition that though the khatians and rent receipts are not the documents of title, yet they can very much be used for collateral purpose to prove title. The very fact that S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared in the name of Ali Ahmed and he paid rents to the government and after his death the plaintiffs paid rents and they also paid other utility bills proved their title to the suit property. It is also a salutory legal proposition that possession follows title, so even if it is presumed for argument's sake that the plaintiff's vendor's vendor Ali Ahmed purchased the 7th share of the suit plot as argued by Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, yet due to the long and continuous uninterrupted possession in the suit property since 20.01.1954, the plaintiffs acquired absolute title to the suit property.

26. From the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 it is apparent that Rasheda Begum filed Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 in the Court of the then Munsif 3rd Court, Dhaka for realization of arrear rent and also House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 in the same court for eviction of her tenant and although Ali Ahmed allegedly took attempt to nullify the result of the said suit and the house rent case by filing two compromise petitions and eventually the said two compromise petitions were declared cancelled in Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, yet thereafter no step was taken by her either to realize arrear rents from Ali Ahmed and his wife Khatibunnesa or to evict them from the suit property. From exhibit 13 it appeared that Rasheda Begum filed Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 on 13.04.70 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against Khatibunnesa and others for declaration of title and injunction. Exhibit 13 further shows that the said suit was dismissed for default on 28.06.72. The said fact was asserted in the plaint as well as in the deposition of p. w. 1. Rasheda Begum did not take any step to set aside the said order of dismissal by filing an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code. Exhibit 14, the application filed by the plaintiffs for the certified copy of the plaint of said Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 also shows that the said order of dismissal was passed on 28.06.72; the certified copy of the plaint could not be supplied as the record was destroyed. Rule 9 of Order 9 of the Code has clearly spelt out that where a suit is dismissed wholly or partly under rule 8 of Order 9 of the Code the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit on the same cause of action. Section 12 of the Code has clearly debarred a plaintiff from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action where he is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit. In this regard we may also refer to the provision of sub rule (3) of Rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code which is as under:

"Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim."

27. Thus, it appeared to us that in fact, Rasheda Begum defendant's so-called vendor abandoned her claim to the suit property by not taking any step to set aside the order of dismissal of Title Suit No. 106 of 1970. It is true that it is not the defendants who have come for title, but when they set up a specific case of their title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum by obtaining an ex-parte decree for specific performance of contract and tried to justify their possession in the suit property we can very much see whether their vendor had any right and title to the suit property. From the above, it is clear that Rasheda Begum failed to establish her title to the suit property, so how the defendants could claim title to the suit property through Rasheda Begum in their defence to deny the plaintiffs title when they proved their story of acquisition of title and possession in the suit property by filing documents without any gape right from the auction purchase of the suit property by, Ali Ahmed. In this regard it is also very pertinent to state that the plaintiffs in theft plaint categorically stated that after a few days of the liberation of Bangladesh Resheda Begum left Bangladesh for Pakistan Via Nepal and did not enter into any contract with the defendants to sell the suit property, but they created a forged bainapatra. P.W.1 also deposed in court to the said effect. But the defendants failed to produce any evidence whatsoever to show that at the time of bainapatra which was allegedly executed on 12.08.72 or thereafter Rasheda Begum was in Bangladesh. Rather, the evidence of D.W.1 in his cross-examination to the effect:

“……. প্রদঃ ‘ছ’ এর ১ম পাতার পিছনে পৃষ্ঠার রাশেদা বেগম ২৫/০৩/৭৫ ইং তারিখে স্বাক্ষর করিয়াছে মর্মে লিপি আছে। তখন রাশেদা ঢাকার কোথায় ছিল মনে নাই। প্রদ ‘ছ’ এর ২য় পাতায় উল্টে পৃষ্ঠার রাশেদা বেগমের নাম লিপি আছে। উক্ত ৩/১১/৭৬ ইং তারিখে রাশেদা বেগম কোথায় ছিল আমার মনে নাই্ ইহা সত্য নয় যে, পূর্বোক্ত ২টি মানি রিসিট একই কালিতে একই বৈঠকে ও একই  হাতে লিখা হইয়াছে। রাশেদা বেগম বায়না পত্র সম্পাদনের পর ১২/৮/৭২ ইং তারিখে খুব সম্ভবতঃ ডি ও এইচ এস তে ছিল। ………….উক্ত মোকদ্দমাটি দায়েরের পর রাশেদা বেগম কোথায় থাকিত সুনির্দিষ্ট ভাবে বলিতে পারিব না। পরবর্তীতে যে ডিক্রীজারী মামলা মূলে দলিলটি পাইয়াছি উক্ত ডিক্রীজারী মামলাটি দায়েরের সময় রাশেদা বেগম কোথায় থাকিত বলিতে পারিব না। উক্ত জারী মামলার দলিলে খসড়া কপি জারী হইয়াছিল। কোন ঠিকানায় জারী জারী হইয়াছিল বলিতে পারিব না। আমাদের দায়েরকৃত দেঃ ৬২/৭৯ নং মোকদ্দমার রাশেদা বেগমের ঠিকানা এই মহুর্তে বলিতে পারিব না। ইহা সত্য নয় যে, দেঃ ৬২/৭৯ নং মোকদ্দমা ও ডিক্রীজারী ৩/৮০ নং মামলা রাশেদা বেগমের উপর যোগাযোগী ভাবে নোটিশ জারী দেখাই���াছি। ইহা সত্য নয় যে, তখন রাশেদা বেগম বাংলাদেশে ছিল না বা আমাদের বায়া দলিল ও কাগজপত্র সমূহ তঞ্চকী ও অকার্য্যকর বা আমি মিথ্যা সাক্ষ্য দিয়াছি।”

corroborates the plaintiff's case that at the relevant time of execution of the alleged bainapatra by Rasheda Begum and during the period of filing of Title Suit No. 62 of 1979, at the time of passing of the decree as well as up to the execution and registration of the kabala in favour of the defendants she was not in Bangladesh. Our view is further strengthen from the further fact that Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 brought by Rasheda Begum was dismissed for default on 28.06.72, had she remained present in Bangladesh after liberation then she would not have allowed the suit to be dismissed for default. Further though the defendants filed the bainapatra, yet none proved the same and none deposed as to the fact of passing of consideration to Rasheda Begum as part performance of the contract. Since the plaintiffs were not party in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 filed by the defendants and they were claiming title to the suit property on the basis of a decree passed therein the plaintiffs had every right to challenge the propriety of the decree passed in the suit, particularly when they prayed for a declaration to the effect that they were not bound by the judgment and decree passed therein. As the plaintiffs challenged the bainapatra allegedly entered into by Rasheda Begum and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 as fraudulent the onus was upon the defendants to prove that the bainapatra was genuine and the decree in the said suit was obtained in a regular course on due service of summons of the suit upon Rasheda Begum in Bangladesh but they failed to discharge the said onus. It is also very significant to state that the defendants could not file any original title deed of their alleged vendor Rasheda Begum which also creates primafacie doubt about their case of bainapatra entered into by Rasheda Begum.

28. We conclude by holding that the plaintiffs proved their 16 (sixteen) annas title to the suit property.

29. Now let us see whether the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs and their tenants from the suit property forcibly on 16.09.97 or the plaintiffs themselves vacated the same on 05.10.97 on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 from the defendants on 30.09.97. Admittedly the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property. In Civil Revision No. 76 of 1987 a single Bench of this Division gave a clear observation to the effect:

"…………..It is true that plaintiffs are in possession and filed suit for permanent injunction. Mr. Gafur submits that since the plaintiffs are in possession, they cannot be evicted by the defendants. It is now well settled that a person in possession of a property should be evicted in due process of law. So, the plaintiffs are liable to be evicted in accordance with law. "

30. So, the plaintiffs could not be evicted from the suit property other that due process of law. The defendants levied Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for execution of the decree. The defendants admitted in the written statement that though the bailiff went to the suit property yet he could not deliver possession thereof to them because of the resistance put by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs specific case was that the defendants dispossessed them and their tenants forcibly on 16.09.97 and looted away the goods for which they amended the plaint and prayed for recovery of khas possession along with other reliefs including mesne profit. Whereas the defendant's case was that the plaintiffs of their own delivered vacant possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.97 on receipt of, a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 on 30.09.97 on the basis of a salish/mediation done by Hajee Md. Selim, the local member of the parliament and the other respectable people of the locality. Defendant's further case was that Abdul Majid, father of the plaintiffs acknowledged the receipt of the said amount of money in writing in a paper by putting his signature which was subsequently signed by plaintiff No. 2 on 05.10.97. P.W.1 categorically denied the said assertion of the defendants. In support of the forcible dispossession by the defendants from the suit property the plaintiffs besides examining plaintiff No. 2 as p.w.1 also examined 3 (three) other witnesses and filed documentary evidence. P.W.1 in his examination-in-chief categorically stated that while the suit was pending the defendants entered into the suit property along with 20/30 terrorists and dispossessed them and looted away the goods which included gold ornaments. The defendants also looted away the goods of their tenants. P.W.1 further stated that over the said incident their father lodged a complaint with Lalbag Police Station which gave rise to Case No. 32 (9) 97. On behalf of the 'bharatias' Wazir Ahmed also lodged a general dairy with Lalbag Police Station being No. 940 dated 16.09.97. The certified copy of the First Information Report (FIR) was filed and marked as exhibit 16 and the copy of the general diary was filed and marked as exhibit 17. The p. w. further stated that the news of their illegal eviction from the suit property and the looting away of goods therefrom were published in the daily Inquilab and the Bhorer Kagaj on 18.09.97 and 20.09.97 respectively. The copies of the said news papers were filed and marked as exhibits 18 series. P.W.1 further deposed that on 30.09.97 the defendants by force obtained a writing from his father in a white paper to the effect that he received taka 16,60,000/00 and then on 05.10.75 also obtained a similar writing from him in the same paper though they did not receive any money. In cross-examination p.w.1 further asserted that no salish took place on 30.09.97 at the house of the ex-member of the parliament. Hajee Selim at the presence of the plaintiffs and the Ward Commissioner and they did not put their signature on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand). P.W.1 further asserted that his signature was obtained in the receipt on 05.10.97 by force. P.W.2, Abdul Majid, the father of the plaintiffs categorically stated in his examination-in-chief that Rasheda Begum was never the owner of the suit property and she never possessed the same and Title Suit No. 106 of 1970 filed by her for declaration of title was dismissed for default. This P.W. further stated that on 16.09.97 the defendants being accompanied by 20/25 goondas dispossessed the plaintiffs and their bharatias by force and looted away the goods. After eviction the defendants took him to court forcibly and got the suit withdrawn on the threat that if he did not withdraw the suit they would kill his sons (the plaintiffs). On 30.09.97 the defendants took him to their office and then got a paper written by him to the effect that he received taka sixteen lacs and sixty thousand. At first it was written as 16,000/00. He further stated that he did not receive any money from the defendants. P.W.2 denied the defendant's case that he, on 30.09.97 in presence of the former member of the parliament Hajee Selim and others demanded taka 20,00,000/00 (twenty lacs) from the defendants as compensation and on receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 delivered possession of the suit property and withdrew the civil and criminal cases. This p. w. corroborated P.W.1 on all other points. By cross-examining these two P.W. s the defendants could not at all shake the credibility of their testimony in examination-in-chief.

31. P.W.3, Wazir Ahmed was a tenant in respect of a shop in the suit property. He stated in his examination-in-chief that his father was a tenant of a shop at 1/B Atash Khaha Lane in 1955 under Doctor Manjurul Haque. In the last part of 1955 his father also took a family quarter on rent at the suit property and he was born there in 1958. He further stated that they remained in the said family quarter till 1980 and then they shifted to their own house. In the suit land there were 13 (thirteen) shop rooms and 10 (ten) family quarters and he was a tenant in one of the shop rooms in the suit property till he was evicted by the defendants and the "গুন্ডা পান্ডা" on 16.09.97 at 10 a.m. He further stated that 20/25 “গুন্ডা পান্ডা” under the leadership of the defendants attacked the tenants, looted away the goods and committed ''ভাংচুর" and pushed them away (সরাইয়া দেয়) and over the said incident he lodged a general diary on 16.09.97 being No. 940. No Salish took place on 30.09.1997 and he was also not present in the salish. The G.D. entry lodged by him was exhibited as exhibit 17. By cross-examining this p.w. the defendants could not at all dislodge the assertion that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit property forcibly on 16.09.97 with the help of `goondas' by committing looting and "ভাংচুর" and the further fact that no shalish was held on 30.09.97 as asserted by the defendants and that he lodged the G.D. entry over the said incident. This p. w. appeared to us independent and disinterested and we do not see any reason to disbelieve him.

32. P.W.4, Shafique Ahmed unequivocally corroborated P.W.s 1-3 as to the fact of dispossession of the plaintiffs from the suit property by the defendants with the help of 20/25 gondas. Ext. 16 is the certified copy of the F.I.R of Lalbag P.S. Case No. 32(9)97 corresponding to G.R. No. 3094 of 1997. A reading of the said F.I.R shows that the same was lodged by Abdul Majid, the father of the plaintiffs against the defendants and others on 17.09.97. In the F.I.R. it was clearly stated that on 16.09.97 under the leadership of Akram Hossain (defendant No. 2) the terrorists being armed with fire arms such as pistol, revolver, kata rifle, pipe gun and lathi attacked them and they out of fear of life left the area; taking the advantage of their absence the defendants looted away the furniture's, ornaments, money and the other articles from the dwelling house and the shop rooms and also demolished structures on the suit land and thus caused damage to the tune of taka 50,00,000/00 (fifty lacs). From the G.D. entry dated 16.09.97 lodged by P.W.3 Wazir Ahmed being No. 940 dated 16.09.97 (exhibit 17) it appeared that there is clear mention of “দোকান ভাংচুর” and “মালামাল তছনছ” in the suit land over the dispute of ownership and the taking of possession of the shop by driving out the owners. Exhibit 18 series show that news were published in the daily Inquilab and the daily Bhorer Kagaj on 18.09.1997 and 20.09.97 respectively as to the fact of dispossession of the actual owners and their bharatias from the suit property on gun point by defendant No. 2 and the looting away of the goods therefrom. D.W.1, (defendant No. 2) in his cross-examination clearly stated to the effect:

“প্রদঃ ১৮ ও প্রদঃ ১৮(ক) আমার বিরুদ্ধে ধেনিক পত্রিকায় প্রকাশিত ২টি সংবাদের বিরুদ্ধে প্রতিবাদ করি নাই। এম, পি, সাহেবের পরামর্শে প্রতিবাদ করি নাই”

33. The defendants examined 9 (nine) witnesses, of them D.W.1 is defendant No. 2. D.W.1 admitted that the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit property but asserted that the plaintiffs were not the owners of the suit property. D.W.1 asserted in his examination-in-chief that on 30.09.1997 at the mediation (মধ্যস্থতায়) of the former local member of the parliament Hajee Md. Selim, Ward Commissioner of Ward No. 61, Hajee Md. Masum, ex-ward Commissioner of Ward No. 60 Mosharaf Hossain and the others, namely, Janab Lal, Janab Md. Uzir (p.w.3), Md. Yousup, Md. Aziz, Md. Shawkat, Md. Mesbahuddin including the plaintiffs, their mother, their maternal uncle Abdul Gani, the plaintiffs father admitted that it was the defendants who were entitled to get the suit property and on demand of compensation to leave the suit property as well as to settle somewhere else Hajee Selim settled the amount of compensation at taka 16,60,000/00 on the further condition that the plaintiff's father would withdraw the cases both civil and criminal and that in the very salish they paid the said amount which was received by the plaintiffs, their father and maternal uncle. D.W.1 further asserted that Abdul Majid in his own hand wrote in a paper to the effect that he received the said amount and put his own signature which was also signed by the plaintiffs maternal uncle Abdul Gani on 30.09.97 and thereafter plaintiff No. 2 wrote similar thing on 05.10.73 in the said paper and then he put his signature. D.W.1 further asserted that after receiving the money on 30.09.97 the plaintiffs shifted their goods from the suit property to the house of their maternal uncle from 01.10.97 to 04.10.97 and then on 05.10.1997 delivered possession of the suit property to them. D.W.2 is one Md. Islam. He did not say a ward about the salish/settlement and payment of money on 30.09.97 at the mediation of Hajee Selim and others. He stated that the plaintiffs and their father delivered possession of the suit property to the defendants on 05.10.1997 and he was present at the said time. After 7/8 months therefrom the process server from the court went to the suit property and having found the defendants in possession gave the report which he signed. In cross-examination he stated that Din Mohammad father of defendant No. 2 was his tenant. In the suit land there were shops and the plaintiffs also used to live there. He further stated to the effect:

“না সম্পত্তি হইতে উচ্ছেদ হওয়ার পূর্ব পর্যন্ত বাদীরা সববাস করিত।”

34. D.W.3, Lal Mia is a rickshaw puller. He said nothing about the salish and the payment. He stated that on 3rd, 4th and 51 of October, 1997 in his “ভেনগাড়ী” he took the goods from the house of the plaintiffs at No. 1 Atash Khana Lane to Paltan. In cross-examination he stated:

“আমি বিবাদীদের বাসায় সব সময় থাকিতাম।”

35. D.W.4, Md. Rafique is a meat seller. He deposed that he used to sell mutton at No. 1 Atash Khana Lane. He was a bharatia of the defendants and previously he was the tenant of the plaintiffs. He further stated that while he was the bharatia of the plaintiffs the defendants did no commit any "ভাংচুর" and create any obstacle and also did not threaten them to leave the suit premises. In cross-examination he stated to the effect:

“……..না। সম্পত্তিতে বাদীদের এক তলা একটি বিল্ডিং কিছু ফেমিলি কোয়ার্টার এবং দোকানগুলি ছিল।”

36. D.W.5, Md. Mesbahuddin stated in his examination-in-chief that the knew the plaintiffs, the defendants and the suit property. He further stated that he knew that the there was a case over the suit property between the plaintiffs and the defendants. The defendants got judgment in their favour. Subsequently the plaintiffs on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 from the defendants through salish delivered possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.1997 and since then they have been possessing the same. The salish took place in the drawing room of the former member of the parliament Hajee Selim and a deed was executed on 30.09.97. On receipt of the money plaintiffs father and maternal uncle acknowledged the same in writing and he was present at that time. Before getting possession the defendants did not commit any “সন্ত্রাসী কার্য��লাপ কিংবা ভাংচুর অথবা জবর দখল করে নাই।” In cross-examination this P.W. stated that he was the manager of Dodge Industrial Company of which the defendants were the directors. He further stated that the defendants used to supervise the affairs of the said company directly. He gave affidavit as tadbirvar of the defendants in Transfer Case No. 38 of 2002. He further stated:

“…… আমার বর্ণিত ষোল লক্ষ ষাট হাজার টাকা নগদে দেওয়া হইয়াছে। উক্ত টাকা কোথায় হইতে দেওয়া হইয়াছে আমি জানি না।

……. না। সম্পত্তির পূর্বের Structure গুলি ভাঙ্গিয়ে ফেলা হইয়াছে। বাদীদের বাসায় আমার যাতায়াত ছিলনা এবং বাদীদের আত্মীয় স্বজনকে চিনি না।”

37. D.W.6, Md. Mosharraf Hossain deposed that he knew the plaintiffs, the defendants as well as the suit property. On 30.09.1997 he along with others namely, the ex-commissioner, the sitting commissioner Kazi Masud sat in a salish at the office of the then local member of the parliament Hajee Md. Selim in his residence and on the basis of the consent of both the parties the plaintiff s father and matemal uncle received taka 16,60,000/00 from the defendants and then vacated the suit property. He further stated that he was present when money was paid and it was reduced into writing on the pad of the M.P Shaheb. He further stated:

“আমার মনে হয় বাদীর অথবা মামা নিজেরা লিখা টাকা বুঝিয়া নিয়াছে। আমার মনে (sic) টাকা বুঝিয়া নেওয়ার কাগজে কে কে স্বাক্ষী আছে। আমার যতটুকু মনে (sic) বাদীর মামা আঃ গনি স্বাক্ষী ছিল। যে কাগজ লেখা হইয়াছিল তাহা জাতীয় সংসদের পেড ছিল এবং সেই কাগজে হাজী সেলিম আমাদের সম্মুখে দিয়াছিল।”

38. In cross-examination this p.w. stated:

“লিখিত ভাবে কোন সালিশ হয় নাই। হাজী সেলিমের জাতীয় সংসদের নিজস্ব প্যাড থাকেনা। তবে, বানাইয়া নিতে হয়। আমি একটিু আগে জাতীয় সংসদ লিখা পেডের কাগজটি দেখিয়াছি। ইহা সত্য নয় যে, আমি দেখার পর বলিয়াছি যে, সেখানে বাদীর মামা সাক্ষী আছে। আমি ভোরের কাগজ এবং ইনকিলাব পত্রিকা রাখি না। আমার জানা নাই বিবাদীরা ১৬/০৯/৯৭ ইং তারিখে গুন্ড পান্ডা নিয়া না। সম্পত্তি হইতে বাদীদেরকে বেদখল করে ও ভাংচুর করে। ইহাও আমার জানা নাই যে, এই নিয়া দৈনিক ইনকিলাব ও ভোরের কাগজে বিস্তারিত প্রকাশিত হইয়াছে কিনা।”

39. P.W.7 is Gopal Chandra Das. He was a Moharar of the record room of the Sadar Registration Complex. This p. w. was examined to prove the sale deed of Rasheda Begum. P.W.8 is Hajee Abdul Aziz. This P.W. stated that he knew the plaintiffs, the defendants as well as the suit property. He further stated that there was a salish on 30.09.1997 in respect of the suit property. In the salish it was decided that Babul Mia would be given a sum of taka 15,00,000/00 but he having raised objection finally it was decided that he would be given taka 1,50,000/00 (one lac fifty thousand) more and the said money was given in the Majlish. Akram Shaheb (defendant No. 2) gave the money to Babul Mia when his sons and younger brother-in-law (শ্যালক) were present. There was a writing on the pad of the M.P, Hajee Selim. On receipt of the money Babul Mia told that he would withdraw all the cases and subsequently he heard that Babul Mia had withdrawn all the cases. The actual name of Babul Mia was Abdul Majid. In cross-examination he stated to the effect:

“…….. সালিশটি লিখিতভাবে হয়।

………… আমার বর্ণিত প্যাডে লিখা ছাড়া উক্ত সালিশে আর কোন লেখা হয় নাই। উক্ত প্যাডে লিখাতে আমি সাক্ষী হয় নাই।

উহাতে কেহ সাক্ষী হয় নাই।

40. P.W.9, Abdul Rouf stated in his examination-in-chief that he knew the plaintiffs, the defendants and the suit holding which was No. 1 Atash Khana Lane. But he stated that he knew nothing about the suit property. He further stated that he went to the suit property on 05.10.97. He saw the occupant of the suit property to take away their goods by a van by handing over the key to Mr. Akram. In cross-examination he stated to the effect:

“……….. বিবাদীর সাতে আমার ব্যবসা আছে ঘটনার ৩/৪ বছর পূর্ব হইতে। আমি হার্ডওয়ারের ব্যবসা করি। আমি বিবাদীদের কবজা, ছিটকানী, হেঙার পাইব ছকেট, যোঘা কাটা ইত্যাদি আইটেম নিয়া থাকি। আমি ০৫/১০/৯৭ ইং তারিখের পূর্বে ১৫ দিনের মধ্যে না। সম্পত্তির পাশ দিয়া যায় নাই। উক্ত ১৫ দিনের মধ্যে না সম্পত্তি কি ঘটিয়াছে আমি জানি না।”

41. Of the 9 (nine) D.ws. D.W.1 is defendant No. 1 and of the remaining witnesses D. w. s D.W.S 5, 6 and 8 deposed as to the holding of the alleged salish and payment of taka 16,60,000/00 to the plaintiffs. But these D.w.s cannot be believed, our reasons being:

(a) D.W.5 stated in his examination-in-chief that salish tok place in the drawing room of the former member of the parliament Hajee Selim and a deed was executed on 30.09.97; P.W.6 stated that salish was held at the office of Hajee Selim situated at his (Hajee Selim) residence. He further stated that no salish was held in writing. P.W.8 did not say anything about the place of salish but said that salish was held in writing. Thus it is clear that the P.W.s contradicted each other as to the place of salish and as to the mode as well.

(b) D.W.5 appeared to us to be a very partisan and interested witness, he being the manager of Dodge Industrial Company of which the defendants were the directors who used to supervise the affairs of the company directly. This P.W. also had sworn affidavit on behalf of the defendants as their tadbirkar in Transfer Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 2002 of the Court of District Judge, Dhaka.

(c) D.W.6 deposed in supposition without asserting the fact of payment and the writing by Abdul Majid and the maternal uncle of the plaintiffs in a positive manner. (d) Although all the 3 (three) D.Ws. were allegedly present at the salish, yet none figured as a witness in the document allegedly written and signed by Abdul Majid and plaintiff No. 2. Had they remained present definitely they would have figured as witnesses.

(d) Neither Hajee Selim nor the Ward Commissioners who were allegedly present in the salish figured as a witness in the said alleged writing.

42. The evidence of the D.W.S does not inspire confidence in our mind to believe defendant's case that the plaintiffs voluntarily handed over possession of the suit property to them on 05.10.1997 on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 (sixteen lacs sixty thousand), on 30.09.97, as it sounded absurd to us that when the plaintiffs fought upto the Appellate Division to maintain their possession in the suit property by filing Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the defendants and then filed application in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 so that they could not be evicted through the execution of the said case and fought upto this Division they would leave the same on receipt of a sum of taka 16,60,000/00 the suit being ready for peremptory hearing. Defendant's story of delivery of possession by the plaintiffs also appear to us against the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in relation to the facts of the case as articulated in section 114 of the Evidence Act. If the plaintiffs handed over the vacant possession of the suit property to the defendants voluntarily then why there should be “ভাংচুর” as deposed by P.W.3 and evident from exhibits 16, 17 and 18 series. Had such a huge amount been paid as a. prize for the compromise then it would have been written in a form of document signed by both the parties and duly witnessed by the witnesses stating in detail the terms of compromise and the fact of voluntary delivery of possession. And what prevented the defendants to take step to file a compromise application in the suit to dispose of the same as per terms of the compromise. We have seen the alleged writing of Mr. Abdul Majid as to the receipt of taka 16,60,000/00 allegedly paid to him by the defendants as a settlement to leave the suit property as incorporated in the additional paper book. It is to be noted that original money receipt was not filed but from the evidence of D.W.1 it appeared that the same was written on the pad of Hajee Selim local member of the parliament. Though a photostat copy of the same was allegedly filed when D.W.1 was examined, we could not find out the same from the record. However, the said writing is as under:

বাংলাদেশ জাতীয় সংসদ সচিবালয়

"I Mr. Abdul Majid (Babul) S/0 Late Abdul Mannan, 1/B Atash Khana Lane, Lalbagh, Received Tk. 16,60,000/- sixteen Lakh & sixty thousand only from, Akram Hossain S/o Deen Mohammad.

Sd/= Eligible

30.09.97

Sd/= Eligible

30.09.97

ষোল লক্ষ ষাট হাজার টাকা বুঝিয়া পাইলাম

Sd/= Eligible

05.10.97"

<u>43. The very writing as relied upon by the defendants as a proof of their payment of taka 16,60,000/00 to the plaintiffs appeared to us shocking and repulsive. It is unbelievable that when the bailiff from the Court failed to deliver possession of the suit property due to the resistance put by the plaintiffs they would hand over vacant possession of the same to the defendants on the basis of a mere money receipt written on a pad of a local member of the parliament; and that to in four lines having no reference to the suit property and the names of the parties. None of the persons who were allegedly present in the salish including the local member of the parliament Hajee Selim and the local Ward Commissioner was examined in court. What business the local member of the parliament had to meddle in the matter when both the suit and the execution case were pending in Court. Further, from the evidence of the D.W.S it is apparent that the alleged salish was held only on one date, that is, on 30.09.97, if that be so, how is that on the same sitting such a huge amount could be arranged and given by the defendants. How did they know that there would be a settlement on that very date and they would be required to pay the said amount. How is that in the alleged money receipt Abdul Majid put his signature on 30.09.97, whereas defendant No. 2 put his signature on 05.10.97. Moreno, if possession of the suit property was delivered voluntarily as claimed by the defendants then there must be a paper showing delivery of possession by the plaintiffs or their father executed in favour of the defendants. In this regard it is very pertinent to state that after the plaintiffs failed to resist the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 by filing an application under Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code they filed an application in the suit on 28.11.94 for temporary injunction praying for restraining the defendants from evicting them from the suit property till disposal of the suit. On the said application a notice was issued upon the defendants asking them to show cause within 10 (ten) days as to why an order of temporary injunction as prayed for shall not be granted. As the said application for temporary injunction could not be heard and the defendants were taking desperate attempt to dispossess them the plain-tiffs on 14.09.97 filed an application under section 151 of the Code praying for an order of temporary injunction with a prayer for ad-interim injunction so that they could not be evicted through the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980. Copy of the said application was duly served upon the learned Advocate of the defendants. The court below fixed the said application for hearing on the next date, that is, on 07.10.97. In the meantime the plaintiffs were evicted on 16.09.97 and the reason for such action by the defendants is obvious. P.W.1, categorically asserted the said facts in his deposition but he was not cross-examined on the said facts. The fact of forcible dispossession is also borne out from the photographs taken from the suit property after the eviction and exhibit 18 series which show that the structures on the suit property were damaged by resorting to vandalism. D.W.1 also admitted that he did not protest the news item published in the two dailies, namely, the Bhorer Kagaz and the Inquilab in that respect. From the evidence as discussed hereinbefore, it appeared to us that the defendants by taking law in their own hands dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit property forcibly just to frustrate the result of the suit which is very much deplorable and shocking and if such action of the defendants is countenanced to that would bring the whole legal system of dispensation of justice through court into jeopardy.</u>

44. The fact that there was a one storied building, 10 (ten) family rooms and 13 (thirteen) shops in the suit property and after taking possession of the suit land those were demolished are also admitted by the D.W.S apart from the evidence of the p. w. s particularly,P.W.3, an independent and disinterested witness as already discussed hereinbefore. Therefore, we find no reason to disbelieve plaintiffs case that because of their forcible dispossession from the suit property by the defendants on 16.09.97 and then demolition of the 10 (ten) family quarters and 13 (thirteen) shop rooms they were deprived of monthly rent from the tenants and so they were entitled to get the mesne profit as decreed by the court below.

45. In view of the discussions made above, we hold that the court below rightly decreed the suit in the terms as noted at the very beginning of this judgment and, therefore, we do not see any reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree.

46. In the result this appeal is dismissed. The impugned judgment and decree is confirmed.

47. There will be no order as to costs.

48. Send down the lower court's record immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: All these rules are taken up for hearing simultaneously inasmuch as the petitioner is one and the same company and common question of law and facts are involved in these rules.

2. In Writ Petition No. 2431 of 2000 the petitioner company opened a letter of credit on 7.4.99 for importation of 100 metric tons of Zinc Ingot covered by H.S. Code No. 7901. After the arrival of the goods the petitioner submitted in bond bill of entry on 19.05.1999 and warehoused the goods in Bond. Thereafter the petitioner submitted bill of entry from bond dated 09.03.2000 to release the goods on payment of customs duty, VAT and other charges. The customs authority in assessing the goods levied customs duties and other charges and also charged supplementary duty @ 5% pursuant to the SRO No. 45-Law/2000/258-VAT dated 14.2.2000. The petitioner raised objection on the imposition of supplementary duty @ 5% on the goods in view of the facts that when the letter of credit was opened there was no supplementary duty and also when the goods were in bond at that time also there was no supplementary duty for the goods in question and it is only after the in bonding of the goods the supplementary duty @ 5% was imposed pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000.

3. In Writ Petition No. 2389 of 2000 the petitioner opened letter of credit on 4.2.1999 for importation of another consignment of 100 metric tons Zinc covered by H.S. Code No. 7901. In this case the petitioner after the arrival of the cargo at Chittagong Port submitted in bond bill of entry registration No. C-38881 on 24.5.1999 and warehoused the goods in bond on 25.5.1999. Thereafter the petitioner submitted bill of entry for releasing the goods from bond on 2.4.2000. In this case also the customs authority in assessing the customs duties and other charges of the goods levied supplementary duty @ 5% pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000 and in this case also on the self same ground the petitioner disputed the imposition of supplementary duty on the goods in question.

4. In writ petition No. 2392 of 2000 theme petitioner opened letter of credit on 15.03.1999 for importation of 100 metric tons B.P. sheet (Cold Rolled Sheets) Coil covered by H.S. Code No. 7208 and 7209. In the usual course of business in this case also after the arrival of the consignment at Chittagong Port the petitioner submitted in bond bill of entry registration Nos. C-38242 and C-38245 both dated 20.5.99 and accordingly warehoused the goods. Subsequently they submitted bill of entry on 9.3.2000 to release the goods from bond on payment of customs duties and other charges. This time also in making the assessment of the goods the customs officials imposed supplementary duty @ 5% on the consignment in question pursuant to SRO No. 45-Law/2000/258-VAT dated 14.2.2000 as by the said SRO supplementary duty on this goods have been re-imposed on and from 15.2.2000. In this case also the supplementary duty @ 5% on the B.P. Sheet coil was disputed by the petitioner on the ground that neither at the time of opening of the letter of credit nor at the time of registering the in bond bill of entry there was any such supplementary duty on the goods in question. Therefore, the petitioner in respect of all these consignments acquired a vested right to get the goods assessed at the rate which was prevalent on the date of in bonding the goods in question.

5. Mr. Borhanuddin, the learned Advocate appeared for the common petitioner in all these rules and advanced common argument in support of the rules. He at the very outset drawn our attention that there are two cases decided by the Appellate Division which apparently appears to be against the petitioner, namely — the case of Shah Dairy, reported in 5 BLC(AD) 160 and 8 MLR (AD) 128, that is, the case of Haji Md. Selim.

6. After referring to these two decisions he tried to distinguish the present rules from the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid cases. The first contention raised by him is / that section 7(1) of the VAT Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant rules inasmuch as a plain reading of the provisions as contained in sub-section (1) of section 7 of the Act shows that only in case of those commodities which are socially undesirable and/or luxury items, a supplementary duty can be imposed provided those goods find place in the third schedule to the Act. In the first two rules the goods imported are zinc in bulk which is used as raw materials for producing G.I. and C.I. Pipes and in the other rule it is the B.P. Sheet coil which is used for manufacturing of B.P. Sheet. Mr. Borhanuddin in elaborating his submission submits that by no stretch of imagination these two goods can be categorized either as luxurious items or as socially undesirable one. More so, when the products are used by common people who are the vast majority of the population and these items are required to sustain the reasonable standard of living for the common people, namely- the poor middle class and middle class. There-fore, inclusion of these items in the third schedule of the Act, is in fact, outside the provision of section 7(1) of the Act, that is, the inclusion of these items in the third schedule is in fact ultra vires of that section. Then Mr. Borhanuddin advanced a new and noble argument that section 30 of the Customs Act cannot be applied in collecting and realising supplementary duty pursuant to the provisions of section 7(1) of the Act because section 7 of the VAT Act has nothing to do with section 30 of the Customs Act inasmuch as section 30 refers to the value as determined under the provision of section 25 of the Customs Act and the rate of customs duties on any goods As imposed pursuant to the provisions of sections 18, 18A, 18B of the Act. Therefore, the customs authority most illegally and without jurisdiction, in fact, took shelter under the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act in the matter of imposing supplementary duty on the goods in question. Mr. Borhanuddin then submits relying on the later portion of para-graph No. 15 of the case of Mizanur Rahman, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 = 5 BLC(AD) 134 wherein it was observed by the author judge of the Appellate Division that had it been a case of general exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act then probably the arguments of vested right or promissory estoppel were available. Relying on this observation of the Appellate Division Mr. Borhanuddin tried to bring home his contention that the instant rules are covered by the principles of law laid down by the Appellate Division in Ahmed Hossain's case which is reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and in that case our Appellate Division once for all settled the principle of law that if there is exemption from any amount of customs duty at the time of opening of letter of credit the importers acquired a 'vested right and that vested right cannot be taken away subsequently by the Government by issuing SRO to the detriment of the interest of the importer, that is, either by withdrawing the exemption or enhancing the rate of duty.

7. In writ petition No. 2389 of 2000 the respondents did neither enter appearance nor make any submission at the time of hearing. In writ petition Nos. 2431 of 2000 and 2389 of 2000 the respondents filed power but they did not appear at the time of hearing of these rules.

<u>8. We have perused the applications along with annexures and noted the relevant facts. The admitted position is that at the time of opening of the letter of credit and at the time of in bonding the goods there was no supplementary duty for the goods in question and in all these three rules when the petitioner submitted bill of entry for ex-bonding the goods there was supplementary duty on those goods pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000.</u>

<u>9. Now let us examine the contention raised by Mr. Borhanuddin in support of these rules. His first plank of attack against the impugned assessments is that the provision of section 7(1) of the Act is not attracted in these cases inasmuch as it has been clearly spelt out in section 7(1) of the Act that in case of luxurious goods, non-essential and socially undesirable goods, supplementary duty can be imposed by the Parliament by adding the goods in the third schedule of the Act. Therefore a cursory reading of the provisions of sub-section (1) shows that the Parliament is obliged to add any goods in the third schedule pursuant to the provisions of sub-section (1) of Section 7 of the Act provided the Parliament is of opinion that the goods is luxurious, non-essential and socially undesirable and also in the public interest Government can include an item in the third schedule for the purpose of imposition of supplementary duty. The expression used in sub-section (1) is very much clear. It categorizes three kinds of goods, namely — those which are luxurious, unessential and socially undesirable. Besides, on top of this the Parliament could add any' goods in the third schedule in the public interest. These are the four elements and if any one of these four elements are found to be present the Parliament is empowered to add that commodity in the third schedule of the Act for the purpose of levy and collection of supplementary duty. Mr. Borhanuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submitted that the nature of the goods imported by the petitioner clearly indicates that these do not fall in any one of the three categories which have been spelt out in sub-section (1) of the Act. Therefore, since these goods cannot be said to be luxury, unessential or socially undesirable, no question of levy of supplementary duty on these goods do arise at all. To repel this contention suffice it to say that this question previously, on two occasions, came up before this Division and also before the Appellate Division of this Court and the self same argument was advanced in those cases and both the Divisions repelled the submissions on the ground that it is the domain of the Parliament to decide which commodity is luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable. Even if a goods which according to the common sense of a citizen answers the description of an essential goods that too can be treated by the Parliament as luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable. It is the Parliament which is empowered to enact laws and therefore when they categories a commodity as luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable for the purpose of levy of supplementary duty this Court sitting in its writ jurisdiction cannot substitute its opinion for the opinion of the Parliament. It is the absolute prerogative of the Parliament and in the aforesaid two cases the Appellate Division observed that if the goods are found to be in the third schedule of the Act at once the Court shall jump to the conclusion that the goods have been so categorized by the 'Parliament and this Court should apply `hands off doctrine and will not make any attempt to undo the legislation. Therefore, first contention which is raised by Mr. Borhanuddin that this Court can enter into the factual aspect to determine as to whether the goods in question, in fact, is luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable cannot be sustained as this issue is well settled by the aforesaid two decisions of the Appellate Division. In this connection it may also be added that by the Finance Act No. 16 of 1999 a further element has been added in sub-section (1) and that is `public interest'. The legislation has provided that in the public interest at any time the parliament can place a goods in the third schedule of the Act for the purpose of imposition and collection of supplementary duty and in the instant case all the three letters of credit were opened in 1999 as such this amendment which has been brought about after the opening of the letters of credit in question we need not advert to that part of section 7(1) of the Act as these rules can be disposed of without adverting to that aspect of the law.</u>

10. Mr. Borhanuddin then raised a noble and unique contention that section 30 of the Customs Act which deals with the fixation of value and rate of duty in respect of a consignment for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other charges do not have any manner of applications in the instant rules inasmuch as supplementary duty is imposed pursuant to section 7 of the Act and not under the Customs Act.

11. Now let us examine if there is any substance in this submission. In sub-section (2) of section 7 of the Act it has been laid down that the value of the goods for the purpose of assessment of supplementary duty would be the value which is determined under section 25 or 25A of the Customs Act plus the customs duties. Now let us turn to the provisions of section 6(1) of the Act. Sub-section (1) of section 6 clearly lays down that the value added tax will be realised from an importer at the time of importation and in the manner in which the customs duties are realised and that would be subject to that Act and any other duties and in case of VAT or supplementary duty that would be governed by the provisions of the Customs Act subject to the rules, orders and direction issued under the VAT Act. Therefore section 6(1) postulates that VAT will be realised at the time and in the manner as is done in case of customs duties and other charges and so far it relates to VAT or supplementary duty the same will be governed by the provisions of the Customs Act and any notification, rule or order issued there under provided the provisions of the Customs Act, notification, rule or order does not conflict with the VAT Act, that is, in other words subject to the provisions of the VAT Act and any notification, order, rule framed there under the provision of the Customs Act will be attracted in the matter of imposition and realisation of VAT as well as supplementary duty. Therefore, it clearly indicates that whenever the question of imposition and realisation of VAT and/or supplementary duty arises the provision of section 25 of the Customs Act is automatically pressed into service, that is, the provisions of section 25 is attracted if there is nothing contrary in the VAT Act and the VAT Act itself in sub-section (1) of section 6 provides that the provisions of the Customs Act will apply in the matter. Then comes the provisions of section 4 which relates to the rate of duty which is the issue in these rules. Here there is no dispute between the parties on the value of the goods or on the quantum of VAT and other charges. Only dispute that centers round the parties is the imposition or supplementary duty at the rate of 5% and if it is collectable or not. Now let us see what is the provision in the Act relating.to the rate of VAT. In sub-section (1) of section 4 it has been stated that in case of vatable items or vatable service VAT will be realised pursuant to the provisions of sub-section (2) and (3). Sub-section (2) says that in case of importation VAT will be realised when the goods are released for home use under the provisions of the Customs Act and the relevant date would be the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry and the rate of duty would be the rate which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry. The corresponding provisions in the Customs Act is section 30 which similarly provided that in case of import of goods the rate which is in force on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry will be the rate at which assessment will be made. In the instant case section 6 of the Act provides that in case of release of goods for home consumption the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the bill of entry will be applicable. So, here in this sub-section, in fact, the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act has been incorporated so far it relates to the assessment of VAT. Section 6(2)(Kha) of the Act incorporates the corresponding provisions of section 104 of the Customs Act. In sub-clause (Kha) it is expressly and in an unambiguous term laid down that in case of release of goods from the warehouse for home consumption as is done under section 104 of the Customs Act the rate of VAT would be the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the Bill of Entry not the rate which was either prevalent on the date of issuance of the Bill of lading and/or opening of the letter of credit. Therefore, this sub-clause (Kha) of sub-section (2) of section 4 says that if goods are kept by in bonding the same on importation the consignee is under the legal obligation to pay the VAT at the rate which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry for ex-bonding the goods, that is, for release of the goods for home consumption. In this connection it may also be mentioned that at the relevant time there was section 109 in the Customs Act which provided that in case of in bond goods when they are released subsequently and if there be any alteration in the rate of duties the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry for release of the goods for home consumption would be relevant and section 109, therefore, clearly indicates that it is a provision which is attracted in the special circumstances for releasing in bond goods when there is in the meantime change of rate of duties before presentation of the bill of en-try for home consumption. In the instant case we need not fall back to the then provisions of section 109 of the Customs Act in view of the provisions of sections 3, 4, 6, 7(2)(Kha) and (3)of the Act. Section 3 of the Act is the charging section. There also it is clearly indicated that in case of ex-bond or in bond of any goods or service into Bangladesh provisions of Customs Act, 1969 shall be applicable but subject to the provisions of the VAT Act and/or any notification, rule or order passed thereunder which we have already indicated. We have already indicated that for determining the value for the purpose of realisation of supplementary duty the value is which is determined under section 25 or section 25A plus import duties. Therefore, the value which is determined for the purpose of calculation of customs duties and other charges is lesser than the value which is taken into computation for realisation of supplementary duty because in the value import duties are also added to other costs of the goods. Therefore, we get a clear indication as to the value on which supplementary duty is to be imposed and in section 7 it has been indicated at what stage the supplementary duty is to be realised from different categories of persons. Section 7(2)(Kha) clearly indicates that supplementary duty in case of an importable item will be levied and collected at the time when the import duties are realised by the customs department. We need not advert to other sub-clause, of sub-section (2) since in these rules we are confronted with the situation where the imposition of supplementary duty at the import stage is in dispute. Therefore, it can be said without hesitation that section 30 is applicable in case of calculation and realisation of supplementary duty as provided by section 7(2)(Ka) of VAT Act. In this connection it may further be mentioned that for these consignments letters of credit were opened before June, 1999 and the in bonds were also done in 1999 but the goods were ex-bonded in April, 2000 when there was SRO No. 44 dated 14.2.2000 re-imposing supplementary duty on these items at the rate of 5%. The fate of the ratio decidendi of the two decisions namely — Hannan's case and Ahmed Hossain's (42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199) have been nullified by the Parliament by incorporating section 30A to the Customs Act and section 30A of the Customs Act was inserted by Act 12 of 1995. Therefore, when the letter of credits were opened in these rules section 30A of the Customs Act was very much there in the Statute Book and on top of that section 7 is also there right from the introduction of the Act in 1991 and it is not a new introduction or added to subsequently. All through section 7 is in the Act as there are sections 3, 4 and 6. Therefore, whenever a trader or an importer opens a letter of credit for the importation of goods he knows it well that the existing law is that as and when necessary government may issue notification under the relevant sections of the VAT Act, that is section 14(1) of the Act granting exemption and section 7(1) of the Act for imposition of supplementary duty on different goods from time to time. Mr. Borhanuddin in the course of his argument frankly admitted that when VAT Act was enacted by the Parliament these goods figured in the third schedule of the Act and at that time the rate of supplementary duty was 10% but subsequently by amending the law by the Finance Act of 1999-1999 these two items were excluded from the third schedule which has subsequently been added. Therefore it is the Parliament and not the Government which has imposed supplementary duty. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the instant case imposition of supplementary duty is contrary to the provisions of Article 83 of the Constitution. Rather 'it is pursuant to the provisions of an act of Parliament which clearly makes provision for imposition of supplementary duty on the goods in question. It is true there was no supplementary duty on the goods when the letter of credit was opened and also when the bill of entry was submitted for registration for in-bonding the goods but nevertheless the importer knew it very well that section 7 is there and at any time there can be a notification for re-imposition of supplementary duty on the items in question and by the SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 the supplementary duty on the goods have been re-introduced not at the original rate of 10% but at a concessional rate of 5%. It is now well settled in all the jurisdictions that there cannot be any estoppel against a Statute, that is, an Act of Parliament and everybody is under the legal obligation to abide by the provisions of an Act of Parliament. In the instant case the Act clearly provides for imposition of supplementary duty and the Parliament has delegated their authority to the government only in respect of fixing the rate of supplementary duty from time to time by publishing necessary SRO pursuant to the provisions of section 7 of the Act and in the instant case SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 has been so issued pursuant to the authority delegated to the Government for the purpose. Therefore, in the instant case supplementary duty has been imposed and assessed pursuant to the provisions of the VAT Act in accordance with law. Any benefit given by way of concession or exemption to a citizen does not create a vested right nor the doctrine of promissory estoppel comes into play. In this connection it may be noted that the principle of law laid down in 42 DLR(AD) 1$7 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 has been done away by the parliament by adding a new section namely section 30A to the customs Act which has brought about a qualitative change in the law. Thus the rate of duty as indicated in section 30 of the Customs Act would be the rate of duty which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry notwithstanding the fact that there was no supplementary duty at the time of opening of the letter of credits in question.

12. In this connection we may further say that Mr. Borhanuddin half heartedly relied on the observations given by the Appellate Division in Mizanur Rahman's case and submitted that had it been a case of customs duty the question of vested right or promissory estoppel would have been available. This appears to best passing remark and not a ratio decidendi of the decision. In saying so we are not oblivion, of the fact that even a ratio decidendi of the Appellate Division is binding on us as good law but in view of the position of law as it stands to day i.e. after introduction of section 30A in the Customs Act no one can come before this Court and invoke either the doctrine of vested right or promissory estoppel in the event of an express provision as contained in the Act as there cannot be an estoppel against the law. Therefore, in view of the provisions as contained in the Act we are led to the conclusion that in the instant case the petitioners are liable to pay supplementary duty pursuant to the provisions of SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 and also pursuant to the then provision of section 109 of the customs Act. The provisions as contained in section 7(1), (2) and (3) of the VAT Act read with the then section 109 of the Customs Act which was in force at the relevant time, It appears that the duty which was prevalent on the date of submission of bill of entry for clearing in-bond goods for home consumption rate of duty is the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the bill of entry for ex bond. Here we may further mention that by in-bonding the goods in the warehouse the importer does not acquire any vested right to get the goods cleared at the rate which was prevalent on the date of in-bonding the goods because on that date the goods were not cleared for home consumption and question of payment of duties and charges. arises when an importer and /or consumer releases the goods for home consumption and in case, of ware-housed goods the goods are release for home consumption when bill of entry is submitted for that purpose under section 104 of the Customs Act. Therefore, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and of the legal provisions which we have discussed earlier leads us to the irresistible conclusion that there is neither any force nor any substance in the submissions made by Mr. Borhanuddin and we find it difficult to subscribe to his submission.

13. In the result, all these rules are discharged. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

এ, এফ, এম, আবদুর রহমান, বিচারপতি- অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তটির ওপর ইস্যুকৃত রূলটি নিষ্পত্তির জন্য মাননীয় প্রধান বিচারপতি মহোদয়ের দফতর হইতে প্রেরিত হইয়াছে।

২। অত্র আদালেতের দেওয়ানী রিভিশন মোকদ্দমা নং ৩২৬৬/১৯৯২ এর পতিপক্ষ অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্ত দ্বারা উক্ত রিভিশন মোকদ্দমাটিতে অত্র আদালত কর্তৃক বিগত ১৩-৭-২০০২ তারিখে প্রদত্ত রায় আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে দায়ের করা হইয়াছে।

৩। রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারীর নিবেদন হইতেছে এই যে রিভিউ দরখাস্তের প্রতিপক্ষ জনাব আলী বাদী হইয়া মোকাম কুমিল্লার ৩য় মুনসেফী আদালতে দেওয়ানী ৬৩৫/১৯৭৯ নং মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করিযা নালিশী সি এস ও এস এ প্লট নং৬৮৮ অধীন ১.২৮ শতাংশ ভূমির ৫ ভাগের ২ ভাগ অংশ তথা ৫১ শতাংশ ভূমিতে খরিদমূলে নিজ মালিকানা দাবী করিয়া সহ শরিকদের বিরুদ্ধে বন্টন প্রার্থনা করেন। উক্ত মোকদ্দমাটি পরবর্তীতে দেওয়ানী ৩৬/১৯৮৫ নং মোকদ্দমায় পূনঃ নম্বরকৃত হইয়া বিচারিক আদালতে বিগত ৩১/৩/১৯৮৫ তারিখে ডিক্রি প্রদত্ত হইলে উহার বিরুদ্ধে রিভিশন দরকাস্তকারী জেলা কুমিল্লার জেলা জজ আদালতে দেওয়ানী আপীল নং ৮৮/১৯৮৫ দায়ের করিলে উক্ত আপীলটি মোকাম কুমিল্লার সাব জজ ১ম আদালতে বিগত ৩১-৩-১৯৯৫ তারিখের রায় দ্বারা মঞ্জুর হইয়া বিচারিক আদালতের রায় ও ডিক্রি বাতিল হইয়া মুল দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা নং ৩৬/১৯৮৫ মোকদ্দমাটি ডিসমিস করা হইলে রিভিশন দরখাস্তকারী প্রতিপক্ষ জনাব আলী অত্র আদালতে দেওয়ানী বিভিশন মোকদ্দমা নং ৩২৬৬/১৯৯২ দায়ের করেন এবং ১-১২-১৯৯২ তারিখে রুল অর্জন করেন। উক্ত রুলটির প্রেক্ষিতে রিভিশন মোকদ্দমার প্রতিপক্ষ তথা অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষে বিজ্ঞ আইজীবী জনাব আব্দুল কুদ্দুস মিয়া ১(এ) হইতে ১ডি নং প্রতিপক্ষদের পক্ষে ওকালতনামা দাখিল করেন। কিন্তু মোকদ্দমাটি বিগত ১৭-১২-১৯৯৬ তারিখ শুনানীর জন্য প্রস্তুত হইলেও তদাবধি উহা কোন বেঞ্চে শুনানীর জন্য তালিকাবদ্ধ হয় নাই। পরবর্তীতে বিগত ৯-৭-২০০২ তারিখে অত্র আদালতের তৎকালীন বিচারপতি জনাব মোঃ ফজলুল হক মহোদয়ের বেঞ্চে তাহা শুনানীর জন্য তালিকাবদ্ধ হইলে ঐ দিনই রিভিশন দরখাস্তকারী প্রতিপক্ষের অনুপস্থিতিতে তাহা শুনানী হইয়া পর দিবস ১৩-৭-২০০২ তারিখে রায় প্রচারিত হয় এবং তদ্বারা দেওয়ানী রিভিশন মোকদ্দমার রুল এবসলিউট করা হয় এবং তর্কিত আপীল আদালতের মোকদ্দমা ডিসমিস হওয়া সংক্রান্ত রায়টি বাতিল করিয়া বিচারিক আদলত প্রদত্ত রায় ও মোক্দ্দমায় প্রদত্ত ডিক্রিটি পুনঃবহাল করা হয়।

৪। ইহার বিরুদ্ধে অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারী বিগত ৮-১-২০০৩ তারিখে মাননীয় প্রধান বিচারপতি মহোদয় বরাবরে অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তটি দাখিল করিলে অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তের উপর অত্র আদালত কর্তৃক বিগত ২৮-১-২০০৩ তারিখে রুল প্রদত্ত হয়।

৫। আমরা রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষে বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবী জনাব এম এ কুদ্দুস মিয়া এবং রিভিউ প্রতিপক্ষ পক্ষে বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবী জনাব আব্দুল বারেক চৌধুরী কে শুনানী করিয়াছি এবং নিম্ন আদালতের নথী সহ পক্ষগনের উপস্থাপিত বাচনিক ও দালিলিক সাক্ষ্য প্রমানাদি পুঙ্খানুপুঙ্খরুপে পর্যালোচনা করিয়াছি। আমরা বিজ্ঞ আইজীবি গনের মুল্যবান বক্তব্য যথার্থভাবে অনুধাবন করিয়াছি।

৬। রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষে বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবি জনাব এম এ কুদ্দুস মিয়া রিভিউ দরখাস্তটির সংরক্ষনীয়তার স্বপক্ষে বক্তব্য প্রদানকালে নিবেদন করেন যে তিনি ২৪-৫-১৯৯৫ তারিখে দেওয়ানী রিভিশন মোকদ্দমা নং ৩২৬৬/১৯৯২ এ ১ নং প্রতিপক্ষের ওয়ারিশগনের পক্ষে ওকালতনামা দাখিল করিয়া মোকদ্দমাটি শুনানী করবার জন্য প্রস্তুত ছিলেন। কিন্তু ১৯৯৫ সাল হইতে শুরু করিয়া মোকদ্দমাটি শুনানীর জন্য প্রস্তুত হইলেও উহা ৯-৭-২০০২ তারিখের পূর্বে আর কখনোই অত্র আদালতের কোন বেঞ্চেই শুনানীর জন্য তালিকাভুক্ত হয় নাই এবং ৯-৭-২০০২ তারিখে উহা পুর্নাঙ্গ শুনানী গ্রহনক্রমে ১৭-৭-২০০২ তারিখে রায় প্রচারিত হয়। বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবি জনাব এম, এ, কুদ্দুস মিয়া নিবেদন করেন যে তিনি মোকদ্দমাটি হঠাৎ করিয়া মাননীয় বিচারপতি জনাব মো: ফজলুল হকের আদালতে তালিকাভূক্ত হওয়ার বিষয়টি জ্ঞাত ছিলেন না এবং ঐ কারনেই উক্ত মোকদ্দমাটি একতরফাভাবে শুনানী সম্পন্ন হয়। তিনি নিবেদন করেন যে তিনি মোকদ্দমাটি তালিকাভূক্ত হওয়া সংক্রান্ত বিষয় জ্ঞাত থাকিলে অবশ্যই প্রতিপক্ষ পক্ষে মাননীয় বিচারপতি মহোদয় সম্মুখে কারন সমূহ ও যুক্তিতর্ক উপস্থাপন করিতেন এবং এইরুপে প্রতিপক্ষগনের যুক্তির্তক উপস্থাপিত না হওয়ায় প্রতিপক্ষের পক্ষে ন্যায় বিচার নিশ্চিত হয় নাই। ফলে অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তটি মজ্ঞুরযোগ্য বটে।

৭। অপরদিকে বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবি জনাব আব্দুল বারেক চৌধুরী দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইন ১৯০৮ এর ৪৭ আদেশের ১ বিধির উপর নির্ভর করিয়া নিবেদন করেন যে রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারীর পক্ষে এমন কোন কারন প্রদর্শিত হয় নাই যা দ্বারা রিভিউ দরখাস্তটি শুনানী করা যাইতে পারে। তিনি নিবেদন করেন যে দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইন ৪৭ আদেশের ১ বিধিতে যে সমস্ত বিধান অন্তর্ভূক্ত আছে রিভিউ দরখাস্তকারি তাহার কোনটিই নির্ভর অত্র আদালতে রিভিও দরখাস্ত দাখিল করেন নাই। ফলে অত্র রিভিউ দরখাস্তটি মঞ্জুরযোগ্য নহে।

৮। দেও্রয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইন ৪৭ আদেশের ১ বিধিটির বিধান নিম্নরুপ;

দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইন ১৯০৮

আদেশ ৪৭, রুল ১:

Rule:1:- (1) Any person considering himself aggrieved—

(a) by a decree or Order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred,

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed or
