full_judgment:
F.R.M. Nazmul Ahasan, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 29.04.2012 passed by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur in Title Appeal No. 36 of 2008 reversing those dated 21.07.2008 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Madaripur Sadar, Madaripur in Title Suit No. 40 of 2005 decreeing the suit should not be set-aside.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of title along with further declaration that the order dated 28.02.1974 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. XIII-3137/M-1005/1972-73 and the order dated 06.01.2006 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. XIII-B-14/2003-04 by the office of the defendant No. 15 are illegal and inoperative with further declaration that the Mutation Case No. IX-P-I-254, M.P.R/2001- 02 of the plaintiffs is still in force as well as another declaration that the deed dated 03.04.1974 being No. 2679 of the defendant No. 1 is forged, inoperative and void.

3. The plaintiff's case; in short, is that the scheduled land to the plaint belonged to the tenant A. Wahed Howlader who proposed to sell out the suit land with an agreement to re-convey the same. The predecessor of the plaintiffs, A. Aziz Mollah agreed to purchase the suit land. Accordingly, the suit land was sold out by a registered deed of sale dated 11.02.1965 being No. 673 with a registered deed of re-conveyance for a period of 7 years. The said period was expired on 11.02.1972 as A. Wahed Howlader did not take back the suit land by any registered deed repaying the consideration money for which the deed of sale dated 11.02.1965 being No. 673 became an out and out deed of sale. While enjoying the possession of the suit land, Aziz Mollah died leaving one son Shahjahan Mollah who died leaving the plaintiffs as his heirs. The plaintiffs have been enjoying the possession of the suit land by paying rents after getting their names mutated. The defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case against the said mutation before the office of the defendant No. 15 stating for the first time about the result of the Miscellaneous Case No. XIII-3137/M-1005/1972-73 filed before the erstwhile C.O. (Revenue), Madaripur now Assistant Commissioner (Revenue), Madaripur Sadar, Madaripur. The plaintiffs knew nothing about the said case before that occasion. The order dated 28.02.1974 passed in the aforesaid case was obtained ex-parte in collusion with the process server showing the service of summon of Aziz Mollah being hanged. The deed of sale dated 03.04.1974 being No. 2679 fabricated by the defendant No. 1 is nothing but a mere paper transaction as A. Wahed Howlader had no saleable interest in the suit land. The order dated 06.01.2005 passed by the defendant No. 15 canceling the mutation of the plaintiffs is illegal, void and inoperative. Thus, the defendant No. 1 denied the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land on the basis of his aforesaid created documents.

4. Hence, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the suit.

5. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint contending inter alia that the suit reveals no cause of action and it is bad for defect of parties and barred by limitation. The further case of the defendant No. 1, in short, is that A. Wahed Howlader mortgaged the suit land to the predecessor of the plaintiffs. Accordingly, a deed of sale with a deed of re-conveyance got registered. A. Wahed Howlader requested Aziz Mollah to execute the return deed of sale after repayment of the consideration money but Aziz Mollah denied. Thereafter, A. Wahed Howlader filed Miscellaneous Case No. XIII- 3137/M-1005/1972-73 before the C.O (Revenue), Madaripur and Aziz Mollah contested the case by filing written objection. Ultimately, the said case was allowed on 28.02.1974 and Wahed Howlader took over possession of the suit land on 11.04.1974 and sold out the same by a registered deed of sale dated 03.04.1974 being No. 2679. Aziz Mollah instituted Title Suit No. 324 of 1974 before the 1a Court of Munsif Adalat, Madaripur and the said suit was dismissed. The defendant No. 1 has been enjoying the possession of the suit land by paying rents after getting his name mutated. The suit land was recorded in the present survey in the name of the defendant No. 1. Hence, the suit instituted by the plaintiffs is liable to be dismissed with cost.

6. The plaintiff’s side examined as many as 3 witnesses and on the other hand, the defendant side examined as many as 4 witnesses to prove their respective cases. The trial Court on perusal of the evidences on record and examination of the materials on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.

7. The defendant No. 1 being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment, and decree passed by the trial court preferred Title Appeal No. 36 of 2008 before the Court of District Judge, Madaripur who transferred, the some to the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur for hearing and disposal, the appellate court allowed the appeal upon reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate court, the plaintiffs-petitioners preferred revisional application before this court and obtained the present rule.

9. At the time of hearing Mr. Mesbahul Islam (Asif), the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners. On the other hand, no one appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

10. Mr. Mesbahul Islam (Asif), the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is not a proper judgment of reversal in accordance with the provisions as laid down under Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the learned Judge of the trial court rightly and properly decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs with the findings that the suit is not barred by limitation as the defendant No. 1 fraudulently obtained the orders and deeds in question; that the deed of sale as well as deed of re- conveyance dated 11.02.1965 in question for 7 years expired on 11.02.1972 long before the promulgation of Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 dated 03.08.1972 under P.O. 44 of 1972 which is not applicable in the present suit; that A. Wahed Howlader had no saleable interest in the suit land after the said 11.02.1972 for which the deed dated 03.04.1974 being No. 2679 is inoperative and he had no possession of the suit land on 11.04.1974. The appellate court without adverting the aforesaid findings of the trial court improperly reversed the same and thereby committed an error of law which occasioned a failure of justice.

11. He further submits that the trial court after framing proper issues and on considering the evidence of both the parties rightly and properly decreed the suit assigning proper reasoning's but the appellate court without considering the correctness of reasoning's by which the trial court took decision in favour of the plaintiffs-petitioners improperly set-aside the same without assigning proper reasoning's thereof Thus, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court cannot be sustained in law.

12. He next submits that the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners had been able to prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence before the trial court but the defendant could not prove his case stating in the written statement by adducing oral and documentary evidence that he has any possession in the suit land. Thus, the trial court on considering the evidence of the respective parties and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the relevant provision of law rightly and properly decreed the suit of the plaintiff but the appellate court without proper perusal of the evidence on record and on misreading the evidence on record, misconstrued the fact and thereby arrived at a wrong decision by setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court which occasioned a failure of justice. Thus, he prayed for set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court.

13. At the time of hearing, the learned Advocate for the petitioners filed a supplementary affidavit dated 21.05.2015 annexing the latest survey and submits that the B.S. record of right has been prepared in the name of the petitioners which reveals that the petitioners are in possession in the suit land.

14. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioners and perused the revisional application along with the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court as well as the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and examined the papers annexed with the revisional application and also the exhibits. I have also perused the lower court records.

15. For proper disposal of the Rule, let as examine the trial court judgment at first. The trial court on considering the pleadings of the respective parties framed as many as 6 issues in the suit-

I) Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

II) Whether the suit is barred by limitation?

III) Whether the suit is barred by defect of parties?

IV) Whether the plaintiffs have title and possession in the suit land?

V) Whether the Miscellaneous Case No. 1005/1972-73 dated 28.02.1974 and Miscellaneous Case No. 14/2003-2004 dated 06.01.2005 is illegal and in effective?

VI) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for?

16. While deciding the issues, trial court examined 3 P.Ws and 4 D.Ws. The trial court at first discussed the issue No. 3 and found that though the defendant in his written statement stated that the suit is barred by defect of parties but he did not specifically mentioned the names of the respective persons and also at the time of cross-examination there is no such allegation made out by the defendant as such the trial court decided that the suit is not barred by defect of parties.

17. The trial court next discussed the issue No. 2 and found that the defendant side in their written statement stated that the grand-father of the plaintiff Abdul Aziz Mollah being aware of the Miscellaneous Case. Thus, the plaintiffs have no locus standi to file the suit after long laps of time but the plaintiff’s side claimed that they had no knowledge about the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case and the title suit mentioned by the defendant. The plaintiffs claim is that they Caine to know about the deed in question on 06.01.2005, when the defendant denied the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land.

18. The trial court considered the exhibit-6 and believed the evidence and the argument advanced by the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs that if the order dated 28.02.1979 was an illegal order and obtained by fraud then there is no question of limitation as claimed by the defendant. Thus, the suit is not barred by limitation.

19. The trial court, thereafter, decided issue Nos. 1, 4, 5 and 6 and found that admittedly Abdul Wahed Howlader was the original owner of the suit land and R.S. and S.A. Khatian was rightly prepared in their names exhibit-1 series. Abdul Wahed Howlader sold 0.50 acres of land to the predecessor of the plaintiffs Abdul Aziz on 01.02.1965 vide registered deed No. 673 exhibit-4 of the same date Abdul Aziz Molla executed and registered an Ekrarnama in favour of Abdul Wahed Howlader for 7 years exhibit-(Ka).

20. It is the case of the defendant that Abdul Wahed Howlader within the time limit asked to return the kabla but the predecessor of the plaintiff Abdul Aziz Molla refused.

21. The trial court found that there is no such evidence in support of the aforesaid claim on behalf of the defendant and after expiry of 7 years on 11.02.1972, the predecessor of the defendant failed to perform his duty to pay the consideration money and returned the same.

22. The trial court also considered the P.O. 49 of 1972 promulgated on 03.08.1972 and the provision of Section 95(Ka) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and also considered the decisions in the case of Bangladesh vs. Haji Abdul Gani Biswas and others report in 32 DLR(AD) 233 and found that the decision is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present suit and deed No. 673 dated 11.02.1972 became out and out a sale deed and after the expiry of the aforesaid deed dated 11.02.1972, the predecessor of the alleged defendant had no right and title in the suit land and the subsequent order passed by the Revenue Officer vide CO. Revenue Officer Miscellaneous Case No. 1005/1972-73 is illegal and the subsequent deed on the basis of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case vide deed dated 03.04.1974 on the basis of the aforesaid Revenue Case is also illegal and ineffective and the defendant No. 1 has got no right, title and interest by the aforesaid deed.

23. The trial court also decided that as the deed dated 03.04.1974 is an ineffective deed and no right, title and interest accrued by the defendant and the deed dated 11.02.1972 is not M existence and the plaintiffs have right, title and interest by inheritance and the order of cancellation dated 06.01.2005 is also illegal which was passed improperly against the plaintiff.

24. The trial court then discussed about the possession in the suit land and found that the defendant No. I claimed that the deed is executed and registered on 03.04.1974 but it is claimed that Abdul Wahed Howlader obtained possession on 11.04.1974 through Court which is impossible and contradictory as the defendant No. 1 was not a party in the Miscellaneous Case. So, this contention of the defendant is not believable at all.

<u>25. On the aforesaid discussions trial court arrived at a decision that as the right, title and possession of the plaintiffs is established by the evidence, the plaintiffs are entitled to get relief as claimed and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>26. On its turn the appellate court while considering the claim of the defendant considered the exhibit-I and 1(Ka) and Exhibit-4 deed dated 11.02.1965 and also the Ekramama dated 11.02.1965 exhibit-(Ka).</u>

27. The appellate court also discussed the claim and counter claim of the respective parties. The appellate court also considered the certified copy of the order sheet of exhibit-Kha from which it appears that Abdul Wahed Howlader filed redemption case on 29.06.1973 under section 95(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The opposite party appeared on 26.11.1973 and prayed for time. On the next date on 06.12.1973 written statement was submitted on behalf of the opposite parties. Thereafter on 28.02.1972 redemption case was allowed. From exhibit-Kha-2, the appellate court found that Shahjahan Molla son of Abdul Aziz Molla filed a review case on 12.04.1974.

28. The appellate court also found the process server Abdul Latif went to the place of occurrence for execution of the possession to the decree-holder. The alleged deed was registered on 03.04.1974 in favour of the defendant No, 1 (exhibit-Gha). From the certified copy of the Miscellaneous Case (exhibit-Cha) and Title Suit No. 324 of 1974 filed by Abdul Aziz Molla on 02.12.1974 wherein Abdul Wahed Howlader was defendant and it was dismissed on 15.01.1975. The appellate court also considered the rent receipt filed by the defendant (exhibit-Chha series). The appellate court also considered the rent receipt filed by the plaintiff side, D.C.R. Exhibit-3 series. From where it appears that the plaintiff side paid Tk. 30/= for mutation on 24.07.2002 and paid rent for the year of 2003 and 2004. The appellate court also found that the predecessor of the plaintiff Abdul Aziz Molla or Shajahan Molla did not mutate their names and paid any rent more than 30 years to the Government

29. The appellate court also discussed the evidence of the P.Ws. 2 and 3 and found that they have deposed suppressing the facts. The appellate court also considered the evidence of the D. Ws. 1, 2, 3 and 4 and found that there is no contradiction in the evidence of the defendant witnesses. The appellate court also discussed about the redemption case which was allowed in favour of Abdul Wahed Howlader and the possession given to the predecessor of the defendant Abdul Wahed Howlader on 0904.1979.

30. On considering the aforesaid evidence, the appellate court found that the plaintiffs could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence. On the other hand, believed the evidence of the defendant side and also found that the defendant No. 1 purchased the land on 03.04.1974 before obtaining possession by the seller Abdul Wahed Howlader and thereafter, after registration of the deed, delivered the possession to the defendant No. 1. The appellate court also disbelieved the contention of the evidence of P.Ws. that Abdul Aziz Molla had no knowledge about the Miscellaneous Case and title suit. It was created by false personification.

31. The appellate court also disbelieved the full contention of the plaintiff witnesses and found that the defendant No. 1 is in possession of the suit land. The appellate court also considered the provision of Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the decision referred to by the plaintiff-appellant reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 and also considered the decision reported in 34 DLR 237 wherein transaction passed and closed principle was set-aside.

32. The appellate court found that on 11.04.1974, according to order in redemption case dated 28.02.1974, possession was given to Abdul Wahed Howlader before that i.e. on 03.04.1974 Abdul Wahed Howlader, sold the suit land to the defendant No. 1 and handed aver possession. On that time the principle of transaction passed and closed, was not established by the Court. It was published in the year of 1980 after obtaining possession by the defendant No. 1.

33. The appellate court also found that the plaintiff's side did not file the suit within 6 years from the aforesaid decision "Principle on transaction passed and closed" and did not file the suit within 12 years from the dispossession by the defendant. The plaintiff side failed to prove that they are possessing the land and so the suit is barred by limitation.

34. The appellate court further found that though the deed dated 11.02.1965 was within the purview of principle transaction passed and closed but the plaintiff being out of possession have lost their title in the suit land, and the appellate court with the aforesaid findings and observations set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

35. It appears from the judgment and decree passed by the courts below that the trial court framed proper issues in the suit and decided those issues on considering the evidence of both the parties and the relevant provision of law and fact and decreed the suit.

36. The appellate court reversed the same with the contention mainly that the suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiffs have no possession in the suit land. Though, the appellate court admitted that the alleged deed of the defendant No. 1 executed and registered on 03.04.1974 by Abdul Wahed Howlader but possession was given to him on 11.04.1974 from which it reveals that while he was not in possession i.e. the plaintiffs were in possession and if the plaintiffs were not in possession and there was no question of possession through process server on 11.04.1974 and before obtaining possession how he transferred the land on the same date i.e. 03.04.1974. The appellate court did not consider this factual aspect at all and believed that the defendant is in possession, is not a proper appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case. The next point is that the appellate court found that the plaintiff did not file the suit within 6 years from the publication of the judgment by the appellate court after principle transaction passed and closed and also did not file the suit within 12 years of dispossession. This, findings is not also a proper finding's of fact.

37. The appellate court further found that the predecessor of the plaintiffs did not mutate their name and long after 30 years, the plaintiffs have mutated their names and paid rent to the Government.

<u>38. From the aforesaid contention it cannot be concluded that the right and title cannot be brushed aside by not mutating the name or names by the plaintiffs.</u>

39. On the aforesaid facts and circumstances, it appears that the appellate court wrongly held that the suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiffs have no possession in the suit land. It is evident from the evidence of the P.Ws that P.Ws. 2 and 3 corroborated the evidence of P.W. 1 that they are in possession in the suit land long before and they have paid rent to the Government and from the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioners, it appears that the B.S. record has prepared in the name of the plaintiffs.

40. From where, it is presumed that the plaintiffs are in possession in the suit land. It appears from the evidence on record that the defendant side produced some certified copies of the order of Revenue Officer and the subsequent orders but in support of their claim they could not prove by adducing proper evidence that those are genuine and passed in accordance with law. Rather, it reveals that it was obtained fraudulently by practicing fraud upon the Court. Thus, the existence of the aforesaid proceeding can be questioned at any time and there is no limitation in the facts and circumstances prevails in the suit before this Court. The reasoning's given by the appellate court of filing suit out of time is not proper and not based upon the fact and law relevant to the suit.

41. The learned Advocate for the petitioners also referred to some decisions in the case of Mahadeb Chandra Mondal and another vs. Dulal Chandra Mondal and other reported in 25 BLD (AD) 233 wherein it is held, "State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950-Section 95A-As the date of re-conveyance expired before the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 came into force, the transaction in question could not be treated as a usufructuary mortgage transaction and the appellant was no entitle to get back the case land on the basis of Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act."

<u>42. In the case of Abdus Salam Sheikh and others vs. Puspa Rani Shil and others reported in 16 BLD (AD) 299 wherein it is held, "State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950-Section 95A-The clear legislative intent of Section 95A is that cases of sale attended with agreement for re- conveyance whether registered or unregistered would come within the ambit of complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of 7 years and provisions of section 95(4) (5) would apply to such transfer. A contrary view would apply to such transfer. A contrary view would clearly make the provision of Section 95A nugatory and frustrate its purpose."</u>

43. And in the case of Bangladesh vs. Haji Abdul Gani Biswas and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 wherein it is held, "Transactions subsisting when P.O. 88/72 was promulgated are hit by Section 95A save and except those which were not alive when P.O. 88/72 was promulgated being transactions past and closed."

44. From the discussions made above and on considering of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and the decision referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioners, I am of the view that the appellate court without considering the evidence on record and the relevant provision of law, arrived at a wrong decision and illegally set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and thereby committed an error of law which occasioned a failure of justice. Thus, the rule succeeds.

45. In the result, the rule is made absolute.

46. The judgment and decree dated 29.04.2012 passed by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur in Title Appeal No. 36 of 2008 is hereby set-aside.

47. The judgment and decree dated 21.07.2008 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Madaripur Sadar, Madaripur in Title Suit No. 40 of 2005 is hereby restored. The suit is decreed.

48. The order of stay granted earlier by this court is vacated.

49. Send down the lower court records along with a copy of this judgment to the trial court at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J: This Appeal, by leave, is directed against the impugned judgment and order dated 24.03.2002 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4985 of 1999 discharging the Rule.

2. The case of the appellants, in brief, is that the pre-emptor-appellants filed pre-emption Case No. 8 of 1996 in the Court of the Additional Senior Assistant Judge, Mymensingh under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948 for pre-emption of 12-1/3 acres of land against the pre-emptee-respondent on the allegation, inter alia, that 14 acres of land of ROR Plot No. 274 appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 131 was recorded in the name of Md. Shahed Ali who died leaving behind the pre-emptor-petitioners, Md. Shahidul Islam and others as heirs; that the pre-emptor Nos.1, 2 and 3 are the 2nd wife, a son and a daughter respectively of the said Md. Shahed Ali respectively and the said Md. Shahidul Islam is a son of the said Md. Shahed Ali; that by amicable partition amongst the heirs of the said Md. Shahed Ali, the pre-emptor-petitioners and the seller Md. Shahidul Islam got the said 14 acres of the case plot No. 274 by inheritance and they had been on joint possession of 14 acres in the case plot; that while the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam, son of the pre-emptor-petitioner No.1 and brother of the pre-emptor-petitioner Nos.2 and 3 had been owning and possessing 14 acres of land of the case plot in ejmali along with the pre-emptee respondent, a stranger to the case plot by a sale deed dated 03.07.1995 of TK. 60,000.00 without the knowledge of the pre-emptor-petitioners and that the pre-emptor-petitioners are co-sharers by inheritance in the case plot and as such they filed the pre-emption.

3. The pre-emptee-respondent contested the pre-emption case by filing written objections contending, inter alia, that the Md. Shahed Ali, predecessor of the pre-emptor-petitioners and seller, Md. Shaidul Islam, had 14 annas share and Saheran, mother of the said Md. Shahed Ali had 2 annas share in 14 acres of the case plot and accordingly S.A. Khatian No. 131 was finally published; that afterwards the said Shaeran died leaving behind son, Md. Shahed Ali, by amicable partition amongst the heirs of the said Md. Shahed Ali, the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam got the entire 14 acres of the plot and had been in possession of the same; that the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam requested the other co-sharers of the said Md. Shahed Ali to purchase the case land but all of them refused. Thereafter the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam requested the pre-emptee-respondent to purchase the case land who purchased the case land by a sale deed dated 03.07.1995 and he has been in possession of the case land since his purchase. Moreover, the pre-emptee-respondent made construction in the case land before the receipt of notice of the case.

4. Leave in the appeal was granted to consider the submissions of Mr. Abu Bakar Siddique, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants that 14 acres of land of ROR Plot No. 274 appertaining to S.A. Khatin No. 131 marked exhibit-4 was recorded in the name of Md. Shahed Ali who died leaving behind the pre-emptor petitioners, Md. Shahidul Islam and others as heirs and this fact is admitted by the pre-emptee-respondent and that the learned Trial Court after scrutiny and on examination of the documents marked exhibit Nos. 1-4, held that the pre-emptor-petitioners are co-sharers in the case land and the petitioners proved their claim but the learned Judge of the High Court Division was totally wrong in not holding that the petitioners are co-sharers by inheritance in the case land. Mr. Sidduique further submits that the pre-emptor petitioners and the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam were in joint possession of 14 acres in the case plot and in the absence of any partition either amicable or by registered deed amongst the pre-emptor-petitioners and the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam and the pre-emptee-respondent having been failed to prove that the seller got 14 acres of the case plot in any way the pre-emptee case fails. Lastly Mr. Siddique submits that the pre-emptee-respondent O.P.W. No.1, Md. Matiur Rahman having stated in examination in chief that the dispute land by way of partition was obtained by Md. Shahidul Islam, son of Shahed Ali but in cross examination he totally contradicted himself by deposing that he cannot say how much land the pre-emptors got. Thereafter, he cannot also say in which plot Shahidul Islam got the land; further that he cannot say where and in what date the amicable partition took place and he will not be able to produce any paper and such a statement of the opposite party, O.P.W-1 having not been corroborated by any witness whatsoever or by circumstances of the case, the case of the pre-emptee fails. And the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division totally ignored and did not discuss the evidence of such material witness O.P No.1 resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice to the serious prejudice of the petitioners-appellants.

5. Mr. Abu Baker Siddique, learned Advocate, for the appellants strenuously supported the submissions which are the grounds for allowing the leave.

<u>6. Mr. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate-on-record, appearing for the respondent submits that the learned Single Bench of the High Court Division after thorough analysis and assessment of pleadings, the evidences adduced by both parties found that the pre-emptor appellants are Locoparente with the pre-emptee-respondent and they played a definite role in signing about the disputed transaction and as such the appellants have lost their right of pre-emption by their estoppel and acquiescence. In support of this decision reported in 14 BLD (AD) 30, 50 DLR, 1998 HCD 616, 38 DLR 361. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge, after proper consideration of the evidence, facts and circumstances of the case, found amicable partition in between the parties and thus correctly allowed the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 115 of 1997 and set aside the judgment and order dated 29.05.1997 passed in pre-emption case No. 8 of 1996 by the Senior Additional Assistant Judge, Mymensingh. Mr. Ali lastly submits that it reveals from observation and findings of Single Bench of the High Court Division that the prayer for pre-emption is barred by principle of estoppel and acquiescence.</u>

7. It appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that "Assuming that Shahidul has not disposed of the whole of the .14 acres of land of the case holding it can make any difference in establishing whether the petitioners co-sharers of the case holding. I say no, Shahidul has claimed exclusive ownership over the entire .14 acres of land of the case holding. The portion of land of the case holding which has not been disposed of by Shahidul my well remain with him exclusively. The effect of the partition would be that the other members of the family would not have any interest in land which has been apportioned to Shahidul by amicable partition."

<u>8. From the evidence on record it appears that said .14 acres of land was the property of late Md. Shahed Ali and after his death it descended upon his heirs. But it is the admitted case that the wives and children of late Md. Shahed Ali have amicably partitioned the land amongst themselves. The petitioners have not succeeded in proving by material evidence that they are co-sharers in the case holding. It is evidence that Md. Shahed Ali claimed excusive ownership over the entire .14 decimals of case land.</u>

9. In view of the above discussion and reasoning, we find no substance in the appeal.

10. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11.04.1985 passed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 375 of 1979.)
full_judgment:
Amirul Kabir Chowdhury J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the plaintiff is against the judgment and order dated 11.04.1985 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench in Second Appeal No. 375 of 1979. 

2. Predecessor of the plaintiffs, late Moulvi Joynal Abedin purchased the suit land in revenue sale held on 11 July 1942. The judgment debtor namely, Haralal challenged the sale by filing Title Suit No. 48 of 1942 but lost it at all stages and finally in second appeal which was dismissed on 3 August 1948. Joynal Abedin mutated his name and paid rent all through till his death in 1960 and his name was recorded in the preliminary Record-of-rights. But after his death the heirs of his brother Dr. Abdul Halim in collusion with Revenue Officers got their names recorded in the finally published khatian in respect of 8 annas share of the suit land, putting up the claim that the revenue sale was benami transaction in that Dr. Abdul Halim younger brother of Joynal Abedin, had purchased 8 annas share in the land and that there was threat of dispossession of the plaintiffs from half of the land. Hence the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 502 of 1975. 

3. Defendant respondents contested the suit denying the allegations and claiming that Joynal Abedin admitted the joint purchase and relinquished his claim to the extent of 8 annas share by a registered Nadabipatra dated 21 June, 1945 in the basis of which the finally published khatian recorded their 8 annas inter-est. The suit was decreed by the trial court. Both the trial court and the lower appellate court concurrently found that the Nadabipatra was forged document, copy of which was produced for the first time after the death of Joynal Abedin, that the finally published khatian in favour of joint purchase got no basis and on those findings decreed the suit. In second appeal - S.A. No. 375 of 1979 a learned Single Ridge of the High Court Division observed that the concurrent findings were not sustainable in law as the courts below wrongly shifted the onus of proof of the benami purchase and the Nadabipatra upon the defendants. 

4. The learned Single Judge by the impugned judgment and order allowed the appeal setting aside the judgment and decree of the courts below and sent back the suit on remand to the trial court to adjudicate the matter afresh in the light of the observation made in the body of the judgment. 

5. Hence is this appeal 

6. Leave was granted to consider the submissions made on behalf of the appellants that the order of remand is improper in that concurrent findings of the trial court and the lower appellate court are based on evidence and that the onus to prove the benami purchase to the extent of 8 annas share of the suit land is upon the defendant and that presumption in favour 
of nadabipatra Ext.0 has been rebutted by the plaintiffs and therefore there was no room of the High Court Division to send the suit on remand. 

7. Mr. Abdul Quiyum, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants reiterated the aforesaid submissions made earlier. 

8. He thereafter submits that on the basis of evidence both the courts below came to con-current conclusion that the nadabipatra produced on behalf of the defendant respondents was not a genuine document and without adverting to the materials on record the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment on remand. There being cogent evidence indicating that the nadabipatra was not a genuine document and there being concurrent conclusive finding to the effect by both the courts below the High Court Division com-mitted error in sending the suit again on remand. 

9. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel opposes the appeal. 

10. We have considered the submissions and perused the materials on record. 

11. It appears that the High Court Division in consideration of the materials on record observed, inter-alia, 
"Oral evidence with regard to possession, as have been claimed by both the parties in respect of the disputed land, seems to be very much balanced. The courts below could not find any direct contradiction among the witnesses of the defendants side, who were examined to prove their possession. But upon making certain aspersion on the character of the D.Ws. The courts below have believed the evidence of P.Ws. in arriving at a finding of possession. I have already mentioned that payment of rent for long time is also a piece of evidence regarding possession but the courts below without considering such evidence, specially exhibit-A series, have found possession in favour of the plaintiffs upon taking into consideration only the oral evidence of Borgaders notwithstanding the fact that P.W.2 Daiya Gazi appears to be a partisan witness as one of his son has purchased some land out of the disputed property from the plaintiffs. 

12. As a matter of fact, the courts below have abruptly held that exhibit-C is a gorged document. Thus, in my opinion, non-consideration of exhibit-A series by the courts below has caused a serious error in the decision of the case merit and that the courts below have also committed an error in procedure by shifting the onus upon the defendants to prove that exhibit-C is a genuine document. I have already observed that the plaintiffs did not take any stop to prove their case that during his life time Joynal Abedin got his name mutated in the relevant register in pursuance of exhibit-1 and did not also produce any rent receipt in support thereto. In the interest of justice a chance should be given to the plaintiffs to prove their case by producing any evidence in support thereto if there be any." 

13. In view of above mentioned observation we are of the view that the High Court Division did not commit any error in sending the case on remand to adjudicate the matter afresh in accordance with law giving the parties opportunity to adduce further evidence in support of their respective claims in addition to the evidence already on record. The order does not put any bar upon the plaintiffs to adduce evidence to prove their claim. 

14. We are at a loss to understand as to what prompted the plaintiffs to prefer this appeal. 

15. In view of the discussion made above we do not find any substance in this appeal. 

16. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed. 

17. Parties do bear their respective costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Rais Uddin, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 18.9.2008 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Tangail in Title Appeal No.22 of 2006 dismissed the appeal and affirmed those dated 23.2.2006 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Madhupur, Tangail in O.C. Suit No.111 of 2002 dismissed the suit, should not be set-aside.

2. The relevant fact giving rise to this Rule, in short, is that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit praying for permanent injunction contending, inter-alia, that the original owner of suit land was Ananta Baishnabi, Kedernath Karmakar and Loknath Karmakar who sold the suit land to Join Uddin Q Joinal Abedin and handedover the possession of the suit land to Joyenuddin and thereafter several transfers were made through kabala deeds and ultimately the predecessors of plaintiff No.1-3 Nurul Islam became the owner of the suit land who died leaving behind plaintiff Nos.1-3 as his heirs. One Mokter Hossain became the owner of the 9 decimals of suit land died leaving behind plaintiff No.4-8 as his heirs and thereby the plaintiffs filed the suit praying for permanent injunction against the defendants who are given threat to disposes the present petitioners from the suit land wherein the present petitioners have been possessing the suit land by constructing dwelling but and living there in and some houses have been possessing by giving rent to the tenants.

3. The defendants contested the suit by filing joint written statements denying material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter-alia, that the suit land was acquired by the Road and High ways in the year 1940 and it was published in Gazette and prepared L.A. map. The suit land had no possession, right, title of any others except the Road and High ways. The defendants further slated that no notice was served upon the plaintiffs for demolitions their establishment and on 2.11.2002 there was announcement through mike from the authority of Road and High ways to demolish of illegal establishment from the Government land.

4. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 6(six) witnesses and the defendants examined 2(two) witnesses in support of their respective cases.

5. On conclusion of trial the learned Judge of the trial court after hearing the parties and considering evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 23.02.2006. Against the said judgment and decree the plaintiffs preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Tangail. On transfer it was heard and disposed of by the teamed Additional District Judge, 2nd Court who after hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court by his judgment and decree dated 18.09.2008.

6. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree the plaintiffs as petitioners moved this court and obtained the instant Rule.

7. Mr. Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has placed the Revisional Application, pleadings, evidence, judgment and decree of the courts below and other materials on record before this court and submits that the trial court failed to discuss the evidence of the plaintiffs and the defendants, moreover in his finding found the possession of the plaintiffs. He submits that the appellate court on discussion of the evidence both oral and documentary in his finding found the possession and prima facie title of the plaintiffs but dismissed the appeal on misconception of law, fact and circumstances of the case on the ground that the suit land is not specified by mentioning boundary in the schedule of the plaint which is not sustainable in law. He lastly submits that finding and observation of the courts below are not based on evidence and materials on record and as such judgment and decree of the courts below are not sustainable in law and he prayed for to make the rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree of the courts below.

8. In support of his contention he has referred the decisions, reported in: (1) 8 BLC (AD) 72, (2) 16 BLC 727, (3) I1 BLT (AD) 124, (3) 56 DLR (AD) 22.

9. Mr. Swapan Kumar Das, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the Opposite-parties opposed the rule and submits that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title by producing original deed. He submits that in the Suit there are 8 plaintiffs with separate holding has not been mentioned in the plaint. He submits that plaintiffs filed S.A. Khatian but failed to submit any deed in support of their, Khatian which is not acceptable and sustainable in law. He submits that in the plaint there is no specification of the boundary under Order VII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that the plaintiffs failed to make any statement in the plaint about the original via deed. He lastly submits that concurrent finding of facts reached by the courts below and there is no misreading and non-consideration of the evidence and as such there is no reason to interfere by this court in revision and he prayed for discharged the rule.

10. In support of his contention, he has referred the decisions reported in: (1)21 BLD 163, (2) 12 BLC (AD) 36, (3) 64 DLR (AD) 133.

11. In order to appreciate the submission made by the learned advocates for the parties, I have gone through the revisional application, pleadings, evidence, exhibits, judgment and decree of the courts below and the relevant provision of law very carefully.

12. Now the question calls for consideration whether the learned Judge of the courts below has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decisions occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree.

13. On perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiffs brought the suit for permanent injunction against the defendants. The plaintiffs claimed the suit land by purchase.

14. In support of their claimed submitted two deeds marked as exhibit-4 and 4Ka, Khatian exhibit-I, Trade license exhibit-2, 2Ka, electric bills, rent receipts, holding taxes, receipt of Pour taxes marked as exhibit-3 series, Mutation Purcha exhibit-5, Dakhila exhibit-5Ka, electricity bill of the houses marked as exhibit-9 series, Mutation Khatian of Khatian No.822 exhibit-10.

15. The learned Judge of the trial court considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit with the finding-

“বাদীদের পূর্ববর্তীদের নামে নালিশী জমি বাবদ এস, এ খতিয়ান প্রদঃ ১(খ) প্রস্তুত হওয়া দ্বারা নালিশী জমিতে বাদীদের পূর্ববর্তীর স্বত্ব ছিল এটা প্রতিষ্ঠিত বা প্রমানিত হয় না কারণ খতিয়ান দ্বারা কোন জমিতে খতিয়ান প্রস্তুত কালে খতিয়ানে উল্লেখিত ব্যক্তি দখলে ছিলেন (পৃষ্ঠ নং-৯) এটাই প্রমানিত হয়। বাদীপক্ষ নালিশী জমিতে দখলে থাকার সমর্থনে খাজনার দাখিলা প্রদঃ ৫ সিরিজ হিসেবে দালিলিক সাক্ষ্যরূপে দাখিল করেছে এবং পি,ডব্লিউ-২ থেকে পি-ডব্লিউ-৬ পর্যন্ত সকল মৌখিক সাক্ষ্যরা নালিশী জমিতে বাদী পক্ষের দখলে থাকার স্বপক্ষে পরস্পরকে সমর্থন করে সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করেছে এবং বিবাদীপক্ষের সাক্ষী পি-ডব্লিউ ১ ও তার দেয় সাক্ষ্যের জেরায় স্বীকার করে যে, নালিশী জমিতে বাদীপক্ষ দখলে আছে। তবে যেহেতু বাদী পক্ষ নালিশী জমিতে তাদের আপাতঃ স্বত্ব (prima facie titel) এর দাবী প্রমানে ব্যর্থ হয়েছে সেহেতু নালিশী জমিতে বাদীপক্ষের দখল আইন কর্তৃক সমর্থিত দখল নয়।”

16. It further appears that the learned Judge of the appellate court considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court with the finding-

“ইহা স্বীকৃত যে, নালিশী সম্পত্তি সি,এস ৪৪ ও ৪৫ খতিয়ানভূক্ত। উক্ত সম্পত্তি সি,এস রেকর্ডীয় মালিকদের ওয়ারিশগন বাদীগনের পূর্ববর্তীদের নিকট বিক্রয় করেন মর্মে দাখিলী কাগজাদী হতে পরিলক্ষিত হয় এবং তাদের ওয়ারিশদের নামে এস,এ ১০০ খতিয়ানে রেকর্ড হয় মর্মে দেখা যায়। বিবাদীপক্ষ ইহা স্বীকার করেন এবং বাদী ও বাদীগনের পূর্ববর্তীদের নিকট হতে খাজনা আদায় করা হয় ইহাও স্বীকার করেন। ফলে নালিশী সম্পত্তির রেকর্ড সংক্রান্ত বিষয়ে কোন অসামঞ্চস্যতা নাই। কিন্তু বিবাদী পক্ষ দাবী করেন যে, নালিশী সম্পত্তি ১৯৪০ সনে সড়ক ও জনপথের জন্য অধিগ্রহন করা হয়েছে। এই মর্মে গেজেটের অংশ সত্যায়িত দাখিল করেন। কিন্তু দীর্ঘদিনের মধ্যে কেন তাদের নামে অধিগ্রহন কৃত সম্পত্তি রেকর্ড হলো না ইহা আদালতের নিকট বোধগম্য নয়। এখানে উল্লেখ্য বাদীর আরজীর তপশীলে নাঃ সম্পত্তি ১৮ শতক মর্মে দাবী করেন। জবানবন্দী দৃষ্টে দেখা যায় ৮ জন বাদী ৮টি দোকানের মালিক মর্মে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে। উক্ত দখলকৃত সম্পত্তির পরিমান সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে উল্লেখ করেন নাই। তদুপরি বাকী সম্পত্তি কিভাবে কোথায় আছে সে সম্পর্কে কোন সাক্ষ্য আদালতে উপস্থাপন করে নাই। ফলে নালিশী সম্পত্তি সুনির্দিষ্ট ও সুস্পষ্ট নয় মর্মে প্রতীয়মান হয়। বাদীগনের বায়াদের বিষয়ে যে সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করেছেন অর্থাত মালিকানার দলিল সম্পর্কে জাবেদা নকল দিয়েছেন কিন্তু মূল দলিল সম্পর্কে কোন ব্যাখ্যা নাই। ফলে নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদীদের স্বত্ব সুস্পষ্ট নয়।”

<u>17. In a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiffs shall have to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land in order to get decree. The court may incidentally enquired into prima facie title of the parties and the court need not enter into disputed title unless the possession of the plaintiffs is clearly established by evidences of the plaintiffs. The courts below have dealt mainly on the point of title of the plaintiffs which should not have been the consideration in a suit for permanent injunction. The findings of the courts as to possession of the suit land on the basis of evidence on record.</u>

18. In the instant case both the courts below concurrently found exclusive possession of the plaintiffs but the trial court observed that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title in the suit land. The learned Judge of the appellate court found possession as well as prima facie title of the plaintiffs with the finding-

“উক্ত সম্পত্তি সি,এস রেকর্ডীয় মালিকদের ওয়ারিশগণ বাদীগণের পূর্ববর্তীদের নিকট বিক্রয় করেন মর্মে দাখিলী কাগজাদী হতে পরিলক্ষিত হয় এবং তাদের ওয়ারিশদের নামে এস,এ ১০০ খতিয়ানে রেকর্ড হয় মর্মে দেখা যায়। বিবাদীপক্ষ ইহা স্বীকার করেন এবং বাদী ও বাদীগনের পূর্ববর্তীদের নিকট হতে খাজনা আদায় করা হয় ইহাও স্বীকার করেন। ফলে নালিশী সম্পত্তির রেকর্ড সংক্রান্ত বিষয়ে কোন অসামঞ্জস্যতা নাই।”

19. The learned Judge of the appellate court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the suit land was not specified in the schedule.

20. In this connection I feel it necessary to put the relevant provision of law under Order VII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the relevant portion of the plaint in the schedule which as under:

21. Order VII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure-

"Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers."

22. The relevant portion of the plaint in the schedule

তফশিল

জেলা- টাংগাইল, থানা- মধুপুর, মৌজা-মধুপুর।

সেঃমেঃ খং নং	আর,ও,আর খং নং	দাগ নং	শ্রেণী	পরিমান

৪৪	১০০	২০৮	বাড়ী	.১০ শতাংশ

৪৫	“	২০৮/৭০৬	কান্দা	মোট .১৮ শতাংশ

চৌহদ্দি

যাহার উত্তরে- প্রতাপ সিংহ

দক্ষিণে- জোয়াদ ডাঃ এর স্ত্রী

পূর্বে-সি,এন্ড বি রাস্তা

পশ্চিমে- জেলা বোর্ডের রাস্তা

এই চৌহদ্দির মধ্যে .১৮ শতাংশ ভূমি যেখানে বাদীপক্ষের ইউপেটার্নের টিন সেট বিল্ডিং ১টা, এল পেটানের টিন সেট বিল্ডিং ১টা, ল্যাট্রিন ৩টা, ইসলামিয়া গেস্ট হাউজ ১টা একতলা বিশিষ্ট, টিপটপ কনফেকশনারী আশা ফাষ্টফুড এন্ড কনফেকশনারী ১টা বাংলাদেশ বই ঘর ১টা, সেলুন ৩টা, বীজ ভান্ডার ১টা, বলকানাইজিং ও ওয়র্কশপ১টা, হোন্ডা এবং টেম্পুর পার্টের দোকান ২টা, গ্রীল ওয়ার্কশপ ১টা অবস্থিত।

23. From a plain reading of the above quoted portion of the plaint of the schedule and relevant provision of law it is clearly and specifically stated the schedule of the land by giving plots number as well as boundary compliance of the mandatory requirement of law in giving description sufficient to identify the suit land and as such the appellate court on misconception of law and misinterpretation of the schedule of the plaint arrived at the wrong decision which are not sustainable in law.

24. Now, let me see the legal position of the case in the light of decisions cited from the Bar.

25. The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, reported in:

(1) 8 BLC (AD) 72, wherein their lordships held-

"The suit for permanent injunction is essentially a suit for possession. Though the title may be incidentally gone into but in a suit for permanent injunction the Court need not enter into disputed question of title except to the extent as it would help in finding which of the parties have possession. The plaintiff could not bring home their possession in the suit land for a decree for a permanent injunction."

(2) 11 BLT (AD) 124, wherein their lordships held-

"All the Courts below have considered the legality or otherwise of the award by which the plaintiffs claim title to the suit land but without considering the evidence on record as to possession both the trial court and the Court and the Court of appeal below decreed the suit for permanent injunction. The High Court Division as well without considering the evidence as to possession dismissed the suit for permanent injunction. The suit being a suit for permanent injunction in which the question of title may be gone into incidentally but decision of title in a suit for permanent injunction ought not to have been the guiding principle. The Court cannot disentitle the plaintiff of a decree for permanent injunction if he can prove possession and in thin view the plaintiff could not be evicted with force if continues to be in possession unless in due process of law and could exercise his right of possession restraining everybody including the real owners. In a suit for permanent injunction the Court need not enter into disputed title except to the extent that it would help the Court in finding which of the parties have prima facie title and exclusive possession.

26. The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties, reported in:

(1)21 BLD 163, wherein their lordships held –

"Although the S.A. Khatian stood in the name of Hasina Jamil but the S.A. Khatian cannot confer any title in respect of any landed property to anybody. The learned Judge Found that the suit property as per schedule of the plaint is 1.29 acres of land which appertains to plot No.38 of C.S. Khatian No. 179 but unfortunately, the said property was not found in C.S. Khatian No. 179. The learned Judge also found from Ext. I the sale deed normally registered on 30.3.1939 and he purchased the property of C.S. plot No.28 and not C.S. Plot No.38 of S.A. Khatian No.179. Accordingly the learned Judge dismissed the suit and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court, upon a reading of C.S. Khatian Ext. 3(a) not Ext. 3 as the learned Judge referred the C.S. Khatian No.179 and the hal khatian No. 422, dag As stated as 38 but quantity of land measured 1.29 acres of land was sold. The learned Judge termed the discrepancy as simple anomaly."

(2)12 BLC (AD) 36, wherein their lordships held —

"Plaintiff for the purpose of success in his suit and thereupon to have the relief sought in the suit is required first, to establish that the suit as framed is maintainable and that when the Court finds that the suit is maintainable then goes for consideration of the claim of the plaintiffs in respect of the subject matter of the suit and that while the claim made in the suit is being established by legal evidence, the Court passes a decree in favour of the plaintiff and if it is otherwise then dismisses the suit. Thus, the plaintiff is to establish first for having the relief in the suit instituted by him that his suit as framed is maintainable and if same is not established then generally the Court is not required to go for adjudication of other contentions making which relief has been sought in the suit"

(3) 64 DLR (AD) 133, wherein their lordships held-

"When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immuned from interference by the revisional Court except there is non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record. The High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact. It is concerned with the questions as to whether the appellate court in giving a particular finding has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice as such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law or there is misreading or non-consideration of material evidence in arriving at such finding."

27. The law 'is now Well settled that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate court is binding on High Court Division, as a revisional court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non, consideration or misreading of the material evidence and misinterpretation of law which affect the merit of the case.

28. In the instant case both the courts below found the possession of the plaintiffs and the appellate court also found the prima facie title of the plaintiffs but dismissed the appeal on the ground that the suit land is not specified in the boundary which is misinterpretation and misconception of law as stated above. The plaintiffs having complied with the mandatory requirement of law in giving description by numbers and boundaries is quite identifiable and not vague and as such suit property can be identified by boundaries and numbers. The appellate court on misconception of law and misinterpretation of the schedule of the plaint arrived at the wrong decision which are not sustainable.

29. In view of the discussions, decisions and reasons stated above, I am lead to hold that the judgment and decree passed by the courts below cannot be sustained in law and are liable to be set aside. Thus, 1 find merit in the rule.

30. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree of the courts below are set aside and the suit is decreed.

31. There will be no order as to costs. The order of status-quo granted earlier by this court stand vacated.

32. Let the Lower Court Record along with the judgment and decree be sent to the court below at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 21st August, 2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1815 of 1997).
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: Delay of 7 days is condoned.

2. This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the Judgment and order dated 21.08.2002 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 1815 of 1997 discharging the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated 10.10.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Second Court, Kurigram in Other Class Appeal No. 321 of 1995 allowing the appeal upon setting aside those of dated 19.04.95 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Razar Hat, Kurigram in Other Class Suit No. 37 of 1994 decreeing the suit in preliminary form.

<u>3. The petitioners filed the above suit praying for partition after declaration of their title in the suit land contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to C.S Khatian No. 117 measuring 2.01 acres originally belonged to Sharbananda Das and Matinath Das in equal shares and their names were recorded in the C.S. Khatian and out. of the above 2.01 acres of land one decimal of land was acquired for the road; Sharbananda, who got 1.00 acre of land in his share, he died leaving behind one daughter the defendant No.1 and one son the plaintiff No.2, the plaintiff No.1 was possessing the suit land as her life estate; that plaintiffs have homestead in the western side of Plot No. 227 and they, without partition, were facing inconvenience to possess the suit land and hence the suit for partition. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to C.S, Khatian No. 116 is under Khatian No. 117; Sarbananda Das and Matinath Das were the korfa tenants of the suit land and they having defaulted in paying the Rent Suit No. 3485 of 1940 was filed which being decreed Rent Execution Case No. 807 of 1941 was filed in which Purnamayee, the mother of defendant No.1 auction purchased the same on 10.9.1941 and got possession; Purnamayee being in possession of the suit land since her auction purchase S.A. Khatian was prepared in her name and she duly paid rents and after her death her son, the defendant No.1 is in possession of the same and the plaintiffs were no longer in possession of the suit land after the auction sale.</u>

<u>4. The trial court decreed the suit in preliminary from holding that suit land appertains to C.S. Khatian No. 117 and both parties admitted that Sarbananda and Motinath Das were the tenants in the said C.S. Khatian No. 117; Sarbananda was predecessor of the plaintiffs and Motinath was the predecessor of the defendant No.1; the lands of C.S. Khatian No. 117 were not auction  sold and the defendants could not prove that Purnamayee, the mother of the defendant No.1, got the land of C.S. Khatian No. 117 on the basis of auction purchase and as such preparation of S.A. Khatian in the name of Purnamayee has no basis at all; the documents filed by the defendants show that it is only the lands of C.S. Khatian No. 116 which were auction sold and as such plaintiffs title and possession in respect of eight annas share in respect C.S. Khatian No. 117 as described in the schedule Ka of the plaint being proved the plaintiffs are entitled to get a preliminary decree.</u>

<u>5. The defendant No.1 then preferred Other Class Appeal No. 31 of 1995 and the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Kurigram, after hearing, allowed the appeal holding that the certified copy of the C.S. Khatain No.116 shows that C.S Khatian No. 117 is an under tenure Khatian of C.S. Khatian No. 116 and so after the lands of C.S Khatian No. 116 were auction sold the title and possession of the Korfa tenants under C.S. Khatian No. 117, which is the under tenure Khatian of C.S Khatian No. 116, automatically extinguished; the trial Court ought to have found that Poyatu Barman was the tenant of C.S. Khatian No. 116 and Sarbananda and Motinath were the korfa tenants of C.S. Khatian No. 117 which is the under tenure Khatian of C.S Khatian No. 116; according to the provisions of section 48(C) of the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 if the land of tenant is auction sold, the possession of korfa tenant is extinguished and so after such auction sale there is no necessity to file any case against korfa tenants after issuing any notice upon them, the plaintiff No. 1 claimed portion of the suit lands on the basis of her life estate and if her claim is accepted then how her son, plaintiff No.2, during her life time can get the land as per provisions of the Hindu Law. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in civil Revision 1815 of 1999 and the High Court Division after hearing discharged the Rule holding that admittedly the suit land appertains to C.S. Khatian No. 117 and the total land in the Khatian is 2.01 acres and Sarbananda and Motinath were the korfa tenant under Puyatu Barman and Harakanta Barman in equal sharers, the C.S. Khatian No.117 has been marked exhibit Ka(1); Exhibit Ka is the C.S. Khatian No. 116 in which it is found that C.S. Khatian No. 117 was the under khatian of khatian No. 116 as such 2.01 acres of land was also mentioned in that khatian; the papers and evidences filed show that 2.01 acres of land was auctioned sold in Rent Execution Case No. 807 of 1941 and Purnamoyee auctioned purchased the same through Court and Ext. Gha is the sale certificate showing the area of auctioned land as 2.01 acres; Ext. Ga is the S.A. Khatian where the name of Purnamoyee has been recorded in respect of the land auction purchased by her and there are good number of rent receipts which has been marked exhibit Kha series showing payment of rent by Purnamoyee which prove the continuous possession of the defendant No.1; the plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses among them P.W.1 is the plaintiff No. 2 the son of plaintiff No.1 and P.Ws.2 and 3 are the neighbours and P.W.4 is the plaintiff No.1, the mother of plaintiff Nos. 2; P.W.4, in her cross-examination stated that she does not know whether the suit land has been auctioned sold or not and she is also not aware of the S.A. record of the suit land; she never paid rent of the suit land and can not say the khatian and plot number of the suit land and her son has instituted the suit; the above statement of P.W.4 on oath goes against the case of plaintiff as she herself did not file the suit and it is only her son, plaintiff No.2, instituted the present suit during the life time of his mother and so plaintiff No.2, has no locus standi to file the suit. The High Court Division in its judgment referred to the case of Rai Krishna Shaha vs. Md. Matleb Ali Pramanik and others reported in 34 DLR (HCD) 179 where it has been held:-</u>

<u>"Considering the aforesaid provisions of sub-sections (1) and 3 of Section 3 of the Hindu Womens Rights to the Property Act (XVIII of 1937) it clearly appears that during the period of her life time a Hindu widow is a complete owner and co-sharer of any property or holding in question with the right to claim partition and consequently having the right to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In this connection it may be mentioned that it has been represented that Mostafa Kamal, J. sitting single in another Bench has held the same view in Civil Revision Case No. 98 of 1978 by his judgment dated 4th February, 1982".</u>

6. The High Court Division, considering decision in the above reported case held that the plaintiff No.2 has no locus standi to file the suit but his mother deposed that her son instituted the suit and so the above statement supports the auction sale and the continued possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land and accordingly the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), did not commit any error in observing that during the life time of plaintiff No.1 has son the plaintiff No.2 is not entitled to any relief.

7. We have heard the learned counsel of the petitioner and perused the evidence and materials on record. The learned counsel could not show any misreading or non-consideration of the evidence and the materials on record. Accordingly there is no cogent reason to interfere with the decision of the High Court Division.

8. The petition is dismissed.

End.
