Mr. Md. Alim Hossain, Advocate ------- for the Petitioners. 
Mr. Md. Shahidul Islam, D.A.G. with Mr. Sukumar Biswas, A.A.G ------- for the Respondents.
parties:
Badsha Mollah being dead his heirs: 1(a) Meher Banu, wife of late Badsha Mollah and others
Vs.
The Chairman, First Court of Settlement, Segunbagicha, Police Station- Ramna, District- Dhaka & another
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J: This Rule has been issued on an Application under Article 102 (2) (a) (ii) of the Constitution of Bangladesh at the instance of the Petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 13.10.93 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka dismissing Case No. 87 of 1988 (Ka, SI.329, P.762(22), House No. 122, Block-D, Shershah Suri Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka), as evidenced by Annexure-S to the petition moved in Court today, should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no fugal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts in short, are that, the original Petitioner Badsha Mollah entered into an agreement on 2.5.1976 for purchase of house No. 122, Mohammadpur Colony, Block-D, Shershah Suri Road, Mohammadpur House Estate, Police Station-Tejgoan, at present Mohammadpur, District Dhaka with its owner Md. Ishaque, son of Late Gasit Khalifa who acquired the ownership of the said house on the basis of the allotment as per Memo. No. 490 (150)- Relf/1, dated 30.01.1957 issued by the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka on 31.01.1957. The original allotment letter having been lost the Petitioner obtained an attested copy of the same from the Ministry of Works. It was stipulated in the Deed of Agreement dated 2.5.1976 executed in between the Petitioner and Md. Ishaque that he would deliver physical possession of the house in question to the Petitioner on the date of agreement on payment of Taka 10,000.00 (Taka ten thousand) as advance out of total consideration of Taka 15,000.00 (Taka fifteen thousand) and the remaining balance of Taka 5,000.00 (Taka five thousand) of the consideration would be paid at the time of execution of the Sale Deed by Md. Ishaque in favour of the Petitioner within a period of three months from the date of knowledge of the procurement of the necessary papers by the owner Md. Ishaque. It is also stated that the original deed of agreement was filed before the Deputy Commissioner, Settlement, Ministry of Works as per Memo. No. 4440/DCS, dated 18.6.1976 issued by the Assistant Commissioner, Settlement. According to the terms of the deed of agreement for sale (Annexure-C), the Petitioner paid Taka 10,000.00 (Taka ten thousand) to the said Md. Ishaque on 2.5.1976 and obtained physical possession of the house in question from him and since then the Petitioner has been living in the said house with the members of his family without any objection from any quarter. Md. Ishaque was an employee of the Pubali Bank Limited till his death on 24.11.1988. The said Md. Ishaque approached the Petitioner for further advance of the consideration money to meet the expenses for procuring the necessary papers required for registration of the Sale Deed in question and the Petitioner gave a sum of Taka 4,400/- (Taka four thousand and four hundred) to said Md. Ishaque who received the said money by granting a separate receipt on 30.1.1977 and promised that he would complete the sale transaction within the shortest possible time. But Md. Ishaque failed to keep his words and delayed the execution and registration of the sale deed after receiving the balance of the consideration money. The Petitioner was compelled to file Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 against Mohammad Ishaque impleading the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Govt. of Bangladesh. The Suit was decreed ex parte on 27.1.1978 against the defendants in favour of the Petitioner as the defendants did not contest the suit. On the basis of the said decree a sale deed was executed and registered in favour of the Petitioner by the Court on 8.6.1978. Thereafter, the Petitioner mutated his name in the record of right and paid all Government dues and Municipal taxes as well. The Petitioner then applied to the Deputy Commissioner, Settlement under Ministry of Works requesting him to mutate the name of the Petitioner enclosing all the relevant documents. Having obtained no response from the Deputy Commissioner, Settlement, the Petitioner apprehending that the property in question might be included in the list of abandoned properties, filed Title Suit No. 1019 of 1981 before the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against Government officials and consequently, the same was also deemed ex parte in favour of the Petitioner on 28.2.1983. Subsequently the defendant Nos. 1-3 filed a Miscellaneous Case being No. 50 of 1986 for setting aside the said ex pane decree. In the said case Md. Ishaque, defendant No.4 in the suit, appeared and filed written objection stating that he has no interest in the property as the Petitioner got Sale Deed executed and registered through court. The said Miscellaneous Case was dismissed and after a long lapse of time the Petitioner came to know that the property in question has been enlisted in the "Ka" List in the Gazette published on 28.4.1986 as abandoned property. Thereafter, the said gazette notification was cancelled and a new Gazette was published on 23.9.1986. Thereafter the Petitioner filed Case No. 87 of 1988 before the Court of Settlement in which one Shafi Ahmed filed an application disclosing that the property in question was sold out by Md. Ishaque to one Shamsul Arefin in the year 1966 and subsequently the said Md. Ishaque entered into an Agreement for Sale with the Petitioner on 2.5.1976. Thereafter, the Court of Settlement called for the particulars of the said sale by its order dated 16.11.1992 from the office of the District Registrar, Dhaka. The District Registrar informed that Md. Ishaque executed a Sale Deed in favour of one Mahirunnessa on 9.6.1966 being Sale Deed No. 9336. Against the said order dated 16.11.1992 the Petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 494 of 1992 but that was rejected summarily. Thereafter, the learned Court of Settlement fixed 12.10.1993 for hearing of the case on which date the Petitioner filed an application stating that on thorough enquiry he came to learn that the alleged deed of 1966 was a forged one and the vendor Md. Ishaque did not execute the same and the Petitioner filed another Title Suit being no. 273 of 1993 before the First Court of Assistant Judge praying for declaration that the alleged Deed of Sale No. 9336 dated 9.6.1966 was forged, null and void and also prayed for keeping the proceedings of the case in abeyance till disposal of the aforesaid Suit. Refusing such prayer, the learned Court fixed 13.10.1993 for Judgment. On the date fixed the Court of Settlement delivered the judgment dismissing the case. At this juncture the Petitioner filed this Writ Petition challenging the judgment and Order dated 13.10.1993 and obtained the present Rule and stay.

3. The Respondent Government has contested the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition denying all the materials facts made in the application contending inter alia that the case property originally belonged to Md. Ishaque who sold it to one Mahirunnessa wife of Shamsul Arefin by a registered, Sale Deed being No. 9336 dated 9.6.1966. It is asserted that since such purchase, she had been possessing the same till 1971 and that she left the property and this country during the War of Independence for unknown destination and her whereabouts are unknown to the Government as such the property in question has been declared as abandoned property under The Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 (P.O. No.16 of 1972). The Respondent's contention is that since Md. Ishaque had no subsisting or saleable interest in the property in the year 1976 to transfer to the Petitioner, the Petitioner in fact has purchased the Case Property from a person who had no right, title and interest in the said property and by the purchase the Petitioner acquired no right, title and possession in the property.

4. Mr. Md. Alim Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the Petitioners (heirs of the original Petitioner Badsha Mollah, now deceased) submits that the original lessee Md. Ishaque was in possession, control and management of the property in question and he never left this country at any time and he was all along present in Bangladesh as a Bangladeshi national and was an employee of Pubali Bank till his death. While the said Md. Ishaque was in possession of the property he entered into an Agreement on 2.5.1976 for Sale with the deceased Petitioner Badsha Mollah for a consideration of Tk. 15,000/- out of which he paid Tk.10,000/- as earnest money. Mr. Hossain also submits that the original owner Md. [Masque refused to execute and register the Sale Deed demanding more money. Finding no alternative Badsha Mollah filed Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 for a decree of specific performance of contract against Md. Ishaque and making the Government as defendant in the Suit. The said Title Suit was decreed ex paste on 27.1.1978. Thereafter, the Petitioner got the Sale Deed registered through the Court on 8.6.1978 by filing Title Execution Case No. 16 of 1978. It is also argued that pursuant to Article 7 of P.O. 16 of 1972 and Section 5(1)(a) of the Abandoned Buildings (supplementary provisions) Ordinance, 1985 ("Ordinance") no notice was served upon the original Petitioner and the Government could not show any paper to the effect that the property had on any material date been taken possession of as an abandoned property and as such the listing of the case property in the "Ka" List is ex facie illegal and without lawful authority. It is also argued that the Petitioners claim to be in possession of the case property on the basis of an Agreement for Sale of 1976 and by virtue of a decree passed by the Civil Court in Title Suit No. 83 of 1976 and as such the possession of the Petitioner cannot be said to be unlawful. Mr. Hossain further submits that the Petitioner got the registered Sale Deed through Court by way of execution of a decree passed in Title Suit No. 83 of 1976 against the Government and as such the Government is legally estopped from raising the claim that the case property is an abandoned property. It follows, Mr. Hossain submits, that in view of the said decree the Government cannot claim that the property is an abandoned one and the Court of Settlement's judgment and order is submitted to be a perverse one and liable to be declared illegal and passed without lawful authority. It is also argued that the Petitioner filed another Title Suit being No. 1019 of 1981 against the Government for a decree of a declaration of title of the Petitioner in the case property which was decreed ex- parte on 28.2.1983. To set the said decree aside the Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1986 wherein the original lessee Md. Ishahque appeared and filed written objection denying the claim of the Government and admitting title and possession of the Petitioner. The said Miscellaneous Case was dismissed on contest on 16.11.1988 and no further step was taken by the Government against dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case. In these circumstances, the Petitioners submit, the property cannot be declared as on abandoned property and the very enlistment of the property in the abandoned buildings list as "Ka" List property is illegal and without lawful authority. It is also argued that the lessee Md. Ishaque claiming the property as not abandoned property filed an application before the S.D.O. South, Dhaka being Miscellaneous Petition No. 78 of 1974. In that proceeding the Officer-in-charge, Abandoned Property decided that the property in question is not an abandoned property and recommended a release of the some by his order dated 12.10.1974. In support of his submissions Mr. Hossain has referred to the cases of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Shahjahan reported in 2 ADC, P-411, Abdur Rashid Mollah-vs-Bangladesh and another reported in 2 ADC, 245, Bangladesh Vs. Chairman, Court of Settlement and others reported in 50 DLR (AD), 93, Feroz Ahmed Vs. Bangladesh reported in 13 BLD, 160. Facts of those cases are, however, found by this Court to be different and distinguishable from the case at band.

5. Mr. Shahidul Islam, learned Deputy Attorney General and Mr. Sukumar Biswas learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Government have submitted extensively on the facts and issues raised in the Affidavit-in-Opposition. They argued that the case property was legally enlisted in the "Ka" List of abandoned buildings under the relevant provisions of the Ordinance. They submit that the case property was originally allotted to Md. Ishaque on 31.1.1957. The said Md. Ishaque subsequently transferred the case property to one Mohirunnessa, wife of Shamsul Arefin by a registered Deed of Sale being No. 9336 dated 9.6.1966. The said Mohirunnessa left this country during the War of Independence leaving the case property uncared for. Resultantly, the case property was declared abandoned under the relevant provisions of law and the property vested in the Government under P.O. 16 of 1972. Consequentially, the said Md. Ishaque has had no right, title and interest in the said property to transfer to the Petitioner after 1966. It is also argued that the Agreement for Sale and the subsequent different proceedings in different cases and the decree thereof are collusive and created by the Petitioner only for the purpose of grabbing the property of the Government. For that reason the Petitioner has not acquired any interest, right, title and possession in the property.

6. Both the learned Deputy Attorney General and Assistant Attorney General also submit that the Suit for specific performance of contract remained barred under section 6 of the Ordinance and the Government is not bound by the said decree because it does not reflect a substantive determination of any issue regarding the abandoned character of the property. In this regard the ratio decidendi of the judgment in CQMH Md. Ayub Ali Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 47 DLR(AD)71 and Bangladesh Vs. A.T.M. Mannan and others reported in 1 BLC(AD) 8 are relied upon. It is also argued that the onus is on the claimant to prove that the property is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation to deny the fact alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of listing the property as abandoned property merely because the claimant disputed the same. Mr. Shahidul Islam also argued that, admittedly the possession of the case property was not delivered either by Md. Ishaque or by the Court to the Petitioner, therefore, the claim of the Petitioner to be in possession of the case property on the basis of bainanama and the registered Deed obtained through Court is absolutely false and unbelievable. It is also argued that enlistment of any property under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance is conclusive proof of fact that the property has been legally enlisted as an abandoned property in the Gazette and it is from him who claims the property as not an abandoned property to prove that fact and rebut the position taken by the Government treating the property as an abandoned one. It is also argued that the Court of Settlement has rightly observed in its judgment and order that the Petitioner has totally failed to prove his case by submitting relevant documents before it or indeed by otherwise establishing the presence of the original owner in this country on or before P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force and acquisition of title by his alleged vendor. It is further argued that in the absence of title of Md. Ishaque in the case property the Petitioner on the basis of Agreement for Sale and decrees in Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 and Title Suit No. 1019 of 1981 has not acquired any right, title and interest in the property.

7. Moreover, it is submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney General and Assistant Attorney General, the Government has not declared the property owned by Md. Ishaque as abandoned but the property owned by Mohiunnessa has been declared as abandoned as the said owner left this country before the promulgation of P.O. 16 of 1972 and her whereabouts were not known to the Government. It is also argued that the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement is legal and this Court cannot interfere with the findings of a Court of facts as a Court of Appeal in exercise of its Writ jurisdiction unless it can be shown that the Court of Settlement has acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material facts causing prejudice to the Petitioner or it has acted mala fide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In support of their submissions they have referred to the case of Bangladesh —vs- Md. Jalil and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10.

8. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, perused the Writ Petition, Supplementary Affidavits, Affidavit-in-Opposition and the annexures annexed thereto as well as the records called for from the Court of Settlement by this Court.

<u>9. The core issue for determination under the Rule Nisi pertains to the conclusiveness of the abandoned nature of the property that features in the list of abandoned buildings and as attaches automatically by operation of Section 5(2) of the Ordinance. The claimant made an Application under Section 7 of the Ordinance to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from the List on the ground that the building is not an abandoned property and has not been vested in the Government under P.O. 16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order. The onus, therefore, squarely lies upon the claimant to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the fad alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant.</u>

10. Now it is to be considered by this Court to what extent the Petitioner could prove his case and rebut the position taken by the Government.

<u>11. In the present case the Petitioner claims that the original lessee Md. Ishaque was the owner in possession of the property and through the said Md. Ishaque the Petitioner claims his title and possession of the property and also claims that the Petitioner on the basis of an Agreement for Sale entered into the possession of the case property and got the Sale Deed through Court in execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 83 of 1978. Thereafter, his title has been again confirmed by a decree passed in Title Suit No. 1019 of 1981. On the other hand, the definite case of the Government is that the property belonged to one Mohirunnessa by purchase from the said Md. Ishaque by a Deed of Sale being No. 9336 dated 9.6.1966 and as such the Petitioner has not acquired any right, title and interest in the property since he claims his title through Md. Ishaque who in fact had no right, title and interest in the property at the time of execution of the agreement in the year 1976. Therefore, he enlistment of the case property as abandoned one in the "Ka" List is legal, valid and lawful.</u>

<u>12. In view of the present situation and the question raised by the Government regarding title of said Md. Ishaque and Mohirunnessa, it appears that the Court of Settlement called for the Sale Deed dated 9.6.1966 from the Office of the Sub-Registrar's Record Room and examined one of the Office Assistants of the Record Room. In support of the Deed called for by the Court and upon examination the Court of Settlement found that the original allottee Md. Ishaque sold the case property to one Mohirunnessa in the year 1966 and therefore, he had no subsisting interest thereafter in the case property and observed that Md. Ishaque could neither enter into an agreement for sale of the property to the Petitioner nor have any other person on behalf of him sell the suit property and also observed that the decree for specific performance of contract passed in Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 as well as the decree passed in Title suit No. 1019 of 1981 is void ab initio and by the said decrees no title passed to the Petitioner. It is also observed by the Court of Settlement that the Petitioner was afforded sufficient opportunity to produce documents of the original lessee of the property and to depose before that Court. But the Petitioner repeatedly sought adjournments and utterly failed to produce any document in original to prove his case and also failed to produce Md. Ishaque before the Court. It is also observed that the Petitioner did not file the original allotment letter before the Court of Settlement but he filed an attested copy of the allotment letter instead of original one which led the Court to believe that the original allotment letter was delivered to Mohirunnessa by the original lessee Md. Ishaque.</u>

13. Moreover, from a perusal of the decrees passed in Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 and 1019 of 1981 it appears that there is no declaration in either decree that the building is not an abandoned properly or that it has not vested in the Government under P.O. 16 of 1972. Nor, is there any direction upon the Government to return the building to the Petitioner or release it from the List of abandoned buildings. The decrees do not require the Government to do anything. So, the aforesaid decrees do not come within the proviso of Section 5 of the Ordinance which runs thus:

"Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which........

"(a) Any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have [been] vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person".

14. In view of the quoted provisions of law enlistment of the property in "Ka" List cannot be pleaded as illegal. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner also argued that the Petitioner was not afforded opportunity to produce his documents and to adduce evidence before the Court of Settlement but the record shows that the Petitioner took several adjournments on various grounds, as is also reflected in the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement, but ultimately failed to produce any document in support of his claim. The Counsel for the Petitioner further argued that no notice was served upon the Petitioner before enlistment of the property in the "Ka" List.

15. From a perusal of the Agreement for Sale of 1976 and the decrees passed in Title Suit No. 83 of 1977 and 1019 of 1981 nowhere is it found that the possession was delivered to the Petitioner by Md. Ishaque or he got the possession through Court. The preamble of the Gazette published on 23.9.86 shows that the declaration by its own express terms permits of construction to the effect that the properties listed in the Notification have already been taken control of by the Government and that the Notification is predicated on that essential fact of control assumed over such property . Furthermore, this has to be read with Section 114, illustration (e) of the Evidence Act, 1872 that permits of a presumption of regularity to be attached to all governmental function discharged in due course. Furthermore, the Petitioner could not satisfy the Court of Settlement by producing any evidence that the vendor Md. Ishaque was in possession of the property in question at the time of execution of the alleged bainanama in the year 1976 or indeed before or after the P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force. From this it is to be deduced that the Notification as above records not only the listing of certain properties as abandoned properties but more importantly the fact of these having passed into the control, supervision and management of the Government at the material date in due course.

16. We have gone through the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and this Court finds that the Court of Settlement considered all the crucial questions raised before it and the Court of Settlement rightly decided the questions considering all the papers and evidences placed before it on the very day of the delivery of judgment. It is also this Court's view that subsequent to the judgment of the Court of Settlement the Petitioner obtained a decree in Title Suit No. 273 of 1993 filed against the said Mohirunnessa and the Government simply to forestall the judgment of the Court of Settlement. It is also found that the Petitioner on different dates by Supplementary Affidavits submitted some documents which were not produced before the Court of Settlement at the time of hearing of the case. Therefore, the Court of Settlement on the basis of the documents available before it considered the case as on the date of delivery of the judgment.

17. In view of the above facts this Court finds that the case of the Petitioners in its entirely is nothing but a castle in the air having no leg to stand and as such we find that the Court of Settlement committed no illegality and find no reason to interfere with the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement.

18. In the result, the Rule is, hereby discharged, without any order as to costs.

19. The Order of stay as initially granted is, hereby, recalled and stands vacated.

20. Send down the records received from the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka forthwith along with a copy of this Judgment.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 990 of 2006
lawyer:
Zahirul Islam, Advocated on Record ------ For the Petitioner 
Respondents ------ Not represented
parties:
M/S. Meghna Dairy and Food Products Ltd.   ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27-06-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3891 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Md. Hassan Ameen J : The petitioner seeks leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 27-06-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3891 of 1998 discharging the Rule.

<u>2. Short facts relevant for disposal of this petition are that the petitioner in course of his business opened and L.C. being N.864/L.C. 9800842 dated 04-08-1998 through Standard Chartered Bank Ltd, Dhaka for import of 199, 755 Metric Tons Full Milk Powder form Australia at the rate of U.S.$ 1210 per Metric Ton. After arrival of goods at the Chittagong Port, the Petitioner submitted the Bill of Entry being No. C-00142 dated 26-11-199 together with all necessary papers, for the purpose of assessment of duties and taxes on the basis of C & F value. But the respondent No.2 directed to assess on the basis of tariff value at the rate of U.S. 1875 per metric ton by giving an order of the back page of the Bill of Entry pursuant to Notification being SRO No 55/98/Shulka dated 19-08-1998.</u>

3. Being aggrieved, the petitioner move the High Court Division, submitting amongst others that the fixation of tar value was not fixed in conformity with the prevailing international market rate and that the authority had no basis for such determination of the tariff value and that the same was not fixed following the Rules framed therefore i.e. Valuation Determination (imported goods) Rules, 1997 and that the respondent had no authority to determine the tariff value and that the tariff value is arbitrarily and not based on any material and in violative of the provision of Section 2597 of the Customs Act and that there is no nexus between tariff value and the prevalent international rate for such item and that as per provisions of Section 30 of the Customs Act, the Assessing Officer was required to fix the valuation as per provision of Section 25(1) of the Customs Act since invoice value has been disputed by the Customs Authority.

4. In the instant case, it appears that the petition opened an L.C. on 04-08-1998 for import of Full Cream Milk Powder from Australia at the rate of U.S.$ 12010 per metric ton and after arrival of the goods at the Chittagong Port, he submitted Bills of Entry together with all relevant papers on 26-11-1998 for the purpose of assessment of customs duty, tax and other charges on the basis of C & F value. But the customs authority denied assessing on the basis of C & P value and directed to assess the goods on the basis of tariff value at the rate of U.S.$ 1810 per metric ton pursuant to notification No. 55/98/Cus dated 19-08-1998.

<u>5. The High Court Division found that the petitioner being well aware of the provision of Section 30 of the Customs Act, which provided that the valuation of the imported goods is to be fixed for the purpose of assessment of customs duty, on the basis of the normal value as contemplated The Lawyers by Section 25(1)(2) of the Customs Act or the tariff value as contemplated by Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, as may be the case is and as in force on the date of the Bill of Entry is submitted and accordingly, the petitioner's contention that he is entitled to pay customs duty, tax and other charges on the basis of invoice value not on tariff value is not acceptable in law. Further in the absence of any disclosure of the relevant and reliable materials to show that the fixation of tariff value on the imported goods are arbitrarily grossly inflated and does not reflected the fair value of the goods in the international market, the writ petition is not maintainable and is liable to be rejected in limini relying on the principle as has been settled in the case of Mostafa Kamal and another vs. Commissioner of Customs and other reported in 52 DLR (AD) page 1 Further the fixation of tariff value as alleged, is an official business of the authority, unless and until there being any proof to show that it has been fixed violating any provision of Rule or law is otherwise bad in the eye of law as per Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act. Hence, this leave petition.</u>

6. Mr. Zahirul Islam, the learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the petitioner, submits that the fixation of tariff value was not a discretionary matter of the Government rather it was subjected to compliance of provisions and procedures of Rules namely (i) formation of Advisory Committee according to the provision of rules and (ii) fixing the tariff. Value considering the normal price of the items in question as prevalent and in the instant case neither the Advisory Committee was constituted nor the normal price of the item in question had been collected and taken into consideration and as such the impugned fixation is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. He then submits   that the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the impugned tariff value to be fixed without constituting Advisory Committee and without find out the normal value of the Milk Power as such the impugned judgment is not sustainable   in the eye of law. He then submits that the impugned tariff value had not been fixed procedure as laid down in the শুল্ক মূল্যায়ন(আমদানীকৃত পন্যের মূল্য নির্ধারন) বিধিমালা-১৯৯৭ as such the impugned fixation of tariff value and imposition of said value on petitioner's consignment was without lawful authority and is of not legal effect. He lastly submits that the assessment on the basis of CRF certificate under Section 25A is not an unqualified fixation rather fixation of value under section 25A also same as fixation of normal value under Section 25(II) and as such in lieu of impugned assessment under tariff value, the petitioner was legally entitle to get assessment of the goods on the basis of normal value as fixed under Section 25(I) (II) and as such contrary assessment on the basis of tariff value was without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

7. We have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the materials available on record and reasons to believe that the findings and decisions of the High Court Division do not suffer from any illegality or legal infirmity and as such there being no substance in this Petition for leave to appeal. The same is dismissed.

End.

Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan instructed by ASM Khalequzzaman Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants.

parties:
Md. Motiruddin Mondal @ Matiar Rahman Mondal & others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Full Mohammed Mollah & others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23.08.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1998 of 1999)
full_judgment:
M.M. Ruhul Amin J.: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 23.08.2001 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1998 of 1999 making the Rule absolute.

2. Short facts are that the predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 1005 of 1984 for declaration of title in the first schedule land measuring 70 acres. The appellant and the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon were impleaded as defendant and proforma defendant respectively. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule suit land originally belonged to Raja Amiya Narayan Sannayal of Puria raj Estate. Khailash Chandra Mahantau and Ishwar Chandra Mahantu took pattan of the suit lands from the Putia Raj Estate.

<u>3. Subsequently they settled the suit lands in favour of the plaintiff respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and one Boyezuddin Mollah by way of korfa pattan on 15th Kartick, 1357 B.S. The S.A. and R.S. record of rights being S.A. Khatian No. 384 and R.S. Khatian No. 17 were, prepared and correctly published in the name, of the plaintiff respondent Nos.1 and 2 and Boyezuddin. Boyezuddin possessed the 'Kha' schedule land by cultivating it. After the death of Boyezuddin his heirs transferred the entire share to the plaintiff respondent Nos. 1 and 2 by a kabala dated 12.01.1977. The C.S. record of rights of the 'Kha' schedule land was prepared and published in the name of Mudhu Lal Bhowmick, Jadu Lal Bhowmick, Ram Ballav Bhowmick, Chandra Kumar Bhowmick and Jageswar Bhowmick as tenants under the landlord. They surrendered their land orally in favour of Zaminder long before the acquisition of Zamindary by the Government. The plaintiff respondent by way of korfa settlement and by kabala dated 12.01.1977 have been owing and possessing the land in exercise   of right, title and interest. On Magh 25, 1389 B.S. the defendants disclosed that the R.S. Khatian of 'Kha' schedule property was prepared in the name of their father and they wanted to take possession   of the land. Accordingly the plaintiff was constrained to file the present suit.</u>

4. The defendant's case is that the suit land of C.S. Khatian No. 422 belonged to Mudhu Lal Bhowmick and others who were C.S. recorded tenants and it was transferred in favour of Uzir Mondal, the father of the defendants by unregistered deed dated 11 Poush, 1353 B.S. Thereafter, the defendants changed the nature of the suit property by excavating a pond and have been in possession of the suit property for more than twenty years. But due to their illness they could not take step to have their names recorded in the S.A. record. After the death of their father the defendants inherited the suit land. The plaintiffs and Boyezuddin who never possessed the suit property collusively got their names recorded in the S.A. an R.S. records.

5. The learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Naogaon decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff respondents. The defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 184 of 1997 before the learned District Judge, Naogaon who by his judgment and decree dated 15.06.1999 allowed the appeal. Against the judgment of reversal the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No. 1998 of 1999 before the High Court Division and upon hearing the Rule was made absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court was set aside.

6. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division committed an error of law in reversing the decision of the appellate court in view of the finding of the appellate court that the plaintiff respondents failed to rebut the presumption of the R.S. record of rights which has been finally published in the names of the defendant and the further submission that the S.A. record of rights and R.S. Khatian No. 17 have been published in the names of the plaintiff respondents without any basis in view of the fact that the case of korfa settlement has not been proved  and hence the kabala executed by the heirs of one of the korfa tenants has not been acted upon and the further submission that the appellate court found that the S.A. record of right and R.S. Khatian No. 17 in the names of the plaintiff respondents have no basis but the High Court Division committed an error of law in reversing the decision of the appellate court in revisional jurisdiction.

7. We have heard Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the appellants and Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel for respondent Nos. 1-3 and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

8. It is not disputed that the suit land belonged to Modhu Lal Bhowmick and other under landlord Amiya Narayan Sannayal of Putia Raj Estate and C.S. Khatian No. 422 of Mouza Borpai, P.S. Manda was prepared and finally published accordingly. The plaintiff’s case is that Modhu Lal Bhomick and others surrendered their land orally in favour of the landlord and thereafter Khailash Chandra Mahantau and Ishwar Chandra Mahantu took settlement of the suit lands from the Zaminder. Subsequently Khailash Chandra Mahantau and Ishwar Chandra Mahantu settled the suit lands in favour of the plaintiff respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and one Boyezuddin Mollah by way of korfa pattan on Kartick 15, 1357 B.S. and the S.A. and R.S. record were correctly prepared and finally published in the names of the plaintiff respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and Boyezuddin. After the death of Boyezuddin his heirs transferred the entire share in favour of the plaintiff respondent Nos. 1 and 2 by a kabala dated 12.01.1977. The case of the contesting defendant is that their predecessor Uzir Mondal got the land by unregistered deed dated 11th Poush, 1353 B.S. from Modhu Lal Bhowmick and others and after their purchase they changed the nature of the suit property by excavating a pond and have been in possession of the suit property for more than twenty years. But due to the illness of their father they could not take step to have their names recorded in the S.A. record.

9. It is undisputed that S.A. record was prepared in the name of the defendant rather same was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs.

10. It is not disputed that A.S. Khatian No. 17 in respect of the suit land was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs earlier but later on R.S. Khatian No. 82 for the suit land was also prepared in the name of the defendants.

11. The trial court held that the plaintiffs could not file any pattan nama in their favour granted by Khailash Chandra Mahantau and Ishwar Chandra Mahantu on Kartick 15, 1357 B.S. The trial court accepted the contention of the plaintiffs that those were lost on the way while going to the Court from their dwelling house. G.D. entry was accordingly lodged by the plaintiffs at the local police station and the trial court accepted the contention of the plaintiffs that those papers were lost, so the plaintiffs could not file those. The trial court found that on the basis of the S.A. record prepared in the name of the plaintiffs   they paid rent to the Government and produced 17 dakhilas before the Court. The trial court further observed that if the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land there was no reason for preparation of S.A. and R.S. records in their names and there was also no reason for them to pay rent for the suit land by 17 dakhilas.

12. The trial court further held that the plaintiffs filed two dakhilas granted by the landlords in their favour. But in the dakhilas the plot number and khatian number were not mentioned but those were granted by the Putia Raj estate and there is no evidence on record that the plaintiffs were tenants in respect of other lands under Putia Raj Estate. The trial court did not believe the defendant's contention that during S.A. record their predecessor Uzir Mondal was ill and as such could not get land recorded in their names. The trial court found that defendant's two elder brothers, Mahir and Lahir were aged 28 and 20 at the time of S.A. operation. So according to defendant's own case if their father was ill at the time of S.A. operation the two elder brothers who were adult at that time could take step for recording their name in the S.A. Khatian.

13. The defendants' case is that his father got the suit land by unregistered deed of the year 1353 B.S. from C.S. tenants Modhu Lal Bhowmick and others. The unregistered document was lost from the Court and as a result the heirs of Modhu Lal Bhowmick and others subsequently on 25.11.1987 executed another document in favour of the defendant and from the recitals of the subsequent document, it appears that their predecessor-in-interest transferred the suit land in favour of Uzir Mondal, the predecessor of the defendant on 11th Poush, 1353 B.S. orally. The Court while disposing of an application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiffs held that unregistered document filed by the defendant was not reliable because there were several erasing and over writings in the document and the same was newly created for the purpose of the present suit.

<u>14. The trial court further opined that the unregistered document was removed from the Court's record and the presumption is that the defendant did it as by order dated 16.03.1986, the Court while disposing of temporary injunction matter remarked that there were several erasing and over writings in the document and the same was newly created for the purpose of the present suit and the above observations are against the defendant.</u>

15. It is the definite case of the defendant that after the purchase by his father by unregistered document they changed the nature of the suit property by excavating a pond in the suit land. From the C.S. Khatian No. 422, it is clear that Plot No. 442 was recorded as pond in the finally published C.S. Khatian.

16. Therefore, the question of excavating pond by the defendant after their purchase by unregistered deed (initially) and then oral purchase (the 2nd case) in 1353 B.S. is a math.

<u>17. The trial court further observed that the D.W.1, Md. Jahiruddin Mondal in his evidence stated that his father Uzir Mondal excavated a pond in the suit land in 1349 B.S. whereas in the written statement they claimed to have purchased by unregistered deed (initial, case) and subsequent case oral the suit land in 1353 B.S. So it is difficult to believe the so-called either by unregistered deed or oral purchase of the defendant in 1353 B.S. as because it has been claimed purchasing the land they excavated a pond in the suit land in 1349 B.S.</u>

<u>18. The trail court further held that the defendant produced only one dakhila of the year 1991 and they could not file any other dakhila. It appears that the appellate court while allowing the appeal did not reverse the findings of the trial court on material points. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute it appears took into consideration the material evidence on record including evidence of P.Ws. and 6 and D.Ws. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 and the relevant documents and held that the trial court took into consideration the documentary and oral evidence on record and recorded its reasoning in support of its findings and decision and the judgment of the trial court is well reasoned. On the other hand, the appellate court did not discuss the evidence on record properly and did not controvert the findings of the trial court with reference to documentary and oral evidence on record.</u>

<u>19. The High Court Division further held that the judgment of the Court of appeal suffers from defect of misreading of evidence and non-consideration of materials of materials on record.</u>

<u>20. In the circumstances, we are of the view that the High Court Division considered the materials on record in proper perspective and after assigning cogent reasons arrived at a correct conclusion and hence does not require interference by us.</u>

<u>21. The appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.
