case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13.07.2002 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No.235 of 2000 and Civil Appeal Nos.236-246 of 2000 and C.A.Nos.17, 29-42 of 2001.)
full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J: These appeals are Review by leave of the common judgment and order dated 13.07.2002 passed by this Appellate Division dismissing the Civil Appeal No.  235 of 2000 together with Civil Appeal Nos. 236-246 of 2000 and Civil Appeal Nos. 17 and 29-42 of 2001.

2. The aforesaid Civil Appeal Nos. 235 to 246 of 2000 and 17, 29-42 of 2001 by leave were preferred by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and others against the common judgment and order dated 18.02.1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in disposing of the Writ Petition Nos. 3052, 3077, 3099, 4148, 3226, 3230, 3228, 3050, 3051, 3108, 3683 and 3676 of 1997 and the common judgment and order dated 18.05.2000 passed by another Division Bench of the High Court Division in disposing of the Writ Petition Nos. 3085, 3086, 3427, 3428, 3429, 3430, 3431, 3432, 3433, 3434, 3435, 3436, 3606, 4756 and 3286 of 1997 and both the Benches on consideration of the facts and circumstances as well as materials on record of the respective cases made the Rules absolute.

3. The High Court Division while issuing the Rules in the writ petitions called upon the appellants (review petitioners)hereof, who were respondents in the writ petitions, to show cause as to why the respective orders passed by them on different dates directing to make assessment of Customs duties and taxes on the imported goods of the respective writ petitioners as per the tariff value fixed therefore, in view of the issuance of the notification being SRO No. 113-AIN/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997, by which the applicability of the scheme of CRF has been withdrawn from the imported goods in question, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

4. The case of the respective writ-petitioner-respondents were that they opened their respective letters of credit when the Preshipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996, issued under Section-25A of the Customs Act, 1969 vide SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996 (here-in-after referred to as SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 or the Rules, 1996) containing schedule-1 therein, was in force and the schedule-1 of the said Rules, 1996 contained a list of 12 importable items, which were kept out of the benefits of the CRF scheme. The respondents opened their respective letters of credit for import of items, not included in the schedule- I of the aforementioned SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, and as such the imported goods were entitled to the benefits of the CRF scheme. Accordingly after inspection of such imported goods at the loading port, the CRF Certificates were duly issued by the government approved Preshipment Inspecting Agency complying with the provisions of the Rules, 1996 prior to the date of issuance of the S.R.O. No. 113-Ain/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997, published in the Gazette on 13.05.1997 (hereinafter referred to as SRO No. 113 dated 13.05.1997), by which the imported goods in reference along with some other imported goods were included in the list of schedule- I of S.R.O. No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 and thereby the imported goods were barred from getting the benefits of the CRF scheme with effect from 13.05.1997, as the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 was published in the Gazette on 13.05.1997, and that the imported goods in reference were, however, saved and entitled to get the benefits of the CRF scheme, since the CRF certificates were issued in terms of the SRO Nos. 113 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 32.12.1996. The respondents hereof having opened the letters of credit long before the issuance of SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, which came into effect from 13.05.1997 as aforementioned, the writ petitioners acquired vested right to be assessed on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificate issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act, and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 could not take away such vested right of the importer-respondents in view of the principles as laid down in the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and also the judgment dated 11.05.1998 passed by this Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995.

5. Before the High Court Division on behalf of the writ respondents it has been submitted that in view of the provisions of Sections 30 and 30A read with Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969, the Government has power to fix the tariff value of the imported goods, and the imported goods were to be assessed on the basis of the tariff value prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry and that on behalf of the writ petitioners it has been submitted that with the introduction of Tariff value under Sections-25(7) and 30A of the Act the restriction put on by Section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969, for determining the normal value of the imported goods as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry has been relaxed and that the non obstante clause, as appearing in section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969, made its application overriding all other sections of the Customs Act, 1969 and that the writ petitioners opened the letters of credit relying on the declaration of the government made vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 issued pursuant to Section-25A of the Act, 1969, assuring release of the imported-goods, on payment of the Customs duty and other charges to be assessed on the basis of the value of the imported-goods verified and certified in the CRF Certificates issued by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspection Agents against payment of their required fees and charges, and that the importer-writ petitioners: got their goods inspected by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspection Agents (PSI Agents), on payment of their required fees and charges, as per SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and the Rules, 1996 framed and issued under Section-25A of the Act and that thereby the writ petitioners have acquired vested right to have the customs duty assessed on their imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificated value duly issued by the government approved PSI Agents.

<u>6. The High Court Division on due consideration of the submissions made on behalf of the contesting parties and relying on the principle laid down in the decisions given by Appellate Division in the cases of Collector of Customs Vs. A. Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167; Collector of Customs Vs. Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199; and Mostafizur Rahman Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40 made the Rules issued on the writ petitions absolute holding that the respondents thereof acted illegally, arbitrarily and without lawful authority in refusing to assess the Customs duty, tax etc. on the imported goods on the basis of the value mentioned in the CRF Certificates issued by the PSI Agents and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 could not affect the vested right accrued to the respondents on the issuance of the CRF certificates pursuant  to SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act.</u>

7. This Division in disposing of the said civil-appeals preferred against the aforesaid judgments passed in writ petitions by the High Court Division making the Rules absolute considered the submissions of the appellants that the imported goods in reference, subsequently being included in the list of schedule-1 of SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, were taken out from the benefit of CRF Scheme, and those not being case of withdrawal, reduction or exemption of the duty under section 19 of the Customs Act, the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 were not applicable in the appeals and that the High Court Division committed error of law in making the rules absolute relying on the aforesaid decisions, and that the imported goods having been excluded from the purview of the CRF scheme, introduced under section 25A of the Customs Act, vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, the value of the imported goods after said date i.e. 11.05.1997 were to be assessed in terms of section 25(1) and (2) read with Section-25(7) of the Customs Act as contemplated by the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act and as such the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the duty on the imported goods were to be assessed on the basis of CRF certificated value of the goods issued in accordance with law and that the appeals were fully covered by the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149.

8. Upon hearing the learned advocates of the contesting parties and considering the materials on record this Division was pleased to dismiss the appeals and the appellants being aggrieved filed the instant reviews by leave, which have been registered as appeals.

9. During admission hearing of the review applications it has been submitted by the learned Advocates appearing for the review-petitioners that on the issue involved in the review applications, conflicting decisions have been given by this Division and the decision of this Division being the law of the land it is necessary that this Court need reconsider the issue raised and lay down the correct exposition of the law to be followed by the Courts and Tribunals of the Republic and that this Division finding substance thereon was pleased to grant leave to review the issues involved in the appeals in the following terms:-

"We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and the contents of the petitioners. It has been submitted that the Appellate Division missed the question of law that the issue of effective date of value and vested right to such value was determined by the Appellate Division in the case of Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 wherein their Lordships held that the importer had no vested right so far value of import is concerned and that the said judgment was delivered by five Hon'ble Judges and that the Appellate Division comprising 3 Judges in effect overruled the said decision of 5(five) Hon'ble Judges and thus such overruling of the decision of a larger Bench is an error of law apparent on the face of the record.

Considering the statements made in the review petitions and the submissions of the learned Advocate, we find substance. It appears that in the decisions of the appeals, earlier disposed by this Division reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40, 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and 52 DLR (AD) 149 and in the decision given by this Division in disposing of the Civil Appeal No. 235 of 2000 (under review) some anomaly and contradictions surfaced, which required to the clarified/resolved. Accordingly, leave is granted to review the decisions given in the appeals in reference, on the following grounds:-

I. Because three member Bench of the Appellate Division cannot differ with the decision of five member Bench and as such the decision in the instant case given by three member Bench differing from the decision in 52 DLR (AD) 149 given by five member Bench, a review of the impugned judgment is appropriate and necessary to lay down the correct proposition which will be the law of the land.

II. Because there having been conflicting decision given by this Division, review of the impugned judgment is necessary and appropriate to determine which of the two views is correct and shall be treated as the law of the land.

III. Because manifestly and consistently with the decision of this Division reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199, 52 DLR (AD) 149 and unreported decision rendered on 24.04.2007 in Civil Appeal Nos. 55-80 of 2001, the matter of valuation of imported goods is covered by section 30 and 30A of the Customs Act which by necessary implication permits retrospective operation and as such the impugned decision is clearly inconsistent with the earlier decisions of the Hon'ble Court and therefore needs review."

10. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned advocate, and the learned Additional Attorney General made submissions in support of review of the judgment and order passed in the appeals and Mr. A. Razzak, learned advocate, made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order passed by the Appellate Division in dismissing the appeals.

11. In the (review) appeals the issue to be answered is whether the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) certificates issued, under Section-25 A of the Customs Act read with SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and S.R.O. No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, as were in force till the date of withdrawal of the benefit of CRF scheme from the imported goods in reference through inclusion of the said imported goods in the list of schedule-1 of SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996 along with some other items, vide SRO No. 113-Ain/971705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997 published in the gazette on 13.05.1997, thereby making the said SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 effective on and from 13.05.1997, and presented before the customs authority for the purpose of assessment of duty under Section-30 of the Act after 13.05.1997, are binding on the appellants hereof, since the importers relying on the declaration given by the government vide S.R.O. Nos. 316 dated 3.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 pursuant to Section-25A of the Act, 1969, opened their respective letters of credit incorporating therein the condition of obtaining CRF certificate as mentioned in the said SROs and procured the CRF certificates in accordance with law and thus acquired vested right, to get their respective imported goods to be assessed on the basis of the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 and whether the CRF certificate issued validly under Section-25A of the Act supersedes the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Act.

12. The learned advocates for the review-appellants submitted that in deciding the cases of (1) Abdul Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, (2) Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199, (3) Mostafizur Rahman reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and (4) Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 this Division has settled the law that the importers cannot claim any vested right on the value of the imported goods or the rate of duty thereon on the basis of the value of goods or rate of duty, as the case may be, prevailing on the date of opening of the letters of credit and that the provisions of Section-30 of the Customs Act, 1969 have to be followed for determination of the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Custom's duty, tax etc. It has been submitted that the value of the imported goods and the rate of duty as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry along with all required documents and papers before the Customs authority for assessment of the duty, tax etc., shall be the value of the imported goods and the rate of duty to he imposed on such goods as per Section-30 of the Customs Act and there is no confusion on this issue.

13. The learned Advocates referring to the judgment under review dated 13.07.2002 submitted that in fact the same has overruled the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 49 (judgment dated 01.06.2000) and that their lordships must have inadvertently overlooked the fact that the said decision, reported in 52 DLR,  has been passed by a Bench consisting of 5 Judges whereas the judgment under review is given by a Bench consisting of three Judges and that in the facts, and circumstances it was necessary to get the appeals under review heard and disposed of by a Bench consisting of at-least five Judges. The learned Advocates then submitted that in the instant case admittedly on the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry under reference, the imported items were taken out of the CRF Scheme vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 and therefore on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry the CRF certificates issued in respect of the imported goods had no legal binding .inasmuch as with the withdrawal of the benefit of the CRF scheme from the imported goods, those goods fell under the purview of Section-30 of the Act and the mere issuance of the CRF Certificate cannot put a bar as per the principle of estoppel, since there cannot be any estoppel against statue. Section 30 of the Customs Act provides the date for determination of the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Customs thirty and since the imported goods under reference were taken out of the purview of CRF scheme as far bad (on 13.05.1997, the importers are not entitled to ally benefit on the basis of the CRF certificates issued in respect of the consignments of which the Bills of Entry were submitted on 13.05.1997 or thereafter. The learned Advocates submitted that due importance should be given to the date mentioned in Section 30 of the Customs Act, the parent statute for determination of the "value of the imported goods and the rate of duty" to be imposed thereon. The value of the imported goods is to be determined as per Section-25(1) & (2) of the Customs Act, in the absence of existence of tariff value fixed as per Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, and that in terms of Section 30 of the Customs Act existing tariff value was to be treated as the value of the imported goods, on the basis of which customs duty was to be assessed, but their lordships in the judgment under review failed to consider this aspect of the law and the fact that with the withdrawal of CRF benefit from the consignments under reference, the binding force of CRF certificate ceased and the tariff value in force has to be taken into consideration for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty and thus their lordships arrived at an erroneous decision. The learned advocates referred to the judgment and order dated 26.04.2007 passed in the case of Commissioner of Customs Vs. Unita International (Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2001) heard and disposed of along-with about 374 appeals, on the same issue, by a Bench of this Division consisting of five Judges, wherein it has been held that the assessment of Custom duty, has to be made on the goods-imported in terms of normal value or tariff value, as the case may be, as per provisions of Section 30 read with Sections-25 (1) & (2) and 25(7) of the Customs Act and that though the L.Cs were opened prior to 13.05.1997 the importers cannot claim any vested right for assessment of customs duty on their imported goods, on the basis of CRF certificates issued after issuance of the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, and that the rejection of the CRF value by the Customs Authority has been made in view of existence of the tariff value, which is within the valid jurisdiction of the Customs Authority, and submitted that in view of the principles laid down in the said judgment dated 26.04.2007, and being the latest judgment on the issue, the judgment of the appeals under review cannot be sustained and is liable to be set aside.

14. On the other hand Mr. Abdur Razzaq, the learned Advocate appearing for the importer-respondents, submitted that the importers having opened their respective letters of credit incorporating the condition of obtaining CRF certificate relying on the declaration given by the government vide SRO No. 316-Ain/94/1568/Shulka dated 03.11.1994, and in terms of SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996, as were in force, and accordingly the importers having got their imported goods duly inspected and the required CRF certificates issued therefore, by the government approved PSI Agents, against payment of the prescribed fees and charges, in compliance to the said SROs, such importers acquired a vested right to get the assessment of the Customs duty and charges on the imported goods on the basis of the value mentioned in the CRF certificates, at least which were issued prior to issuance of SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997.

15. The learned Advocate also submitted that the date fixed for determination of the value of the imported goods mentioned in Section 30 of the Customs Act has been relaxed for two specific situations, one is when Tariff Value, fixed under Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, is in force and the other is when the verified and certified value of the imported goods is mentioned in the CRF certificates issued under the authority of Section 25A of the Customs Act complying with the provisions of the SRO Nos.  316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996. Section 25(7) of the Customs Act has provided for fixing an unified rate of value of any imported goods, to avoid the discrepancies in the determination of the customs duty having regard to the value of the goods imported from different countries with different rates of price prevailing at the relevant time, that is to say, that on any specific imported goods there may be different procurement prices in different countries on the same day and on importation of such goods procured at different prices will cause different valuation of the imported goods creating differences in the assessment of customs duty. The government in order to avoid the same, on collecting prices of the same goods imported from different countries, fixes a common price as value of such imported goods in terms of Section-25(7) of the Customs Act, for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty and such fixed common price is known as Tariff Value and that such Tariff Value, till modified or altered, is applied to all such imported goods without question as to the procurement price of the individual importers and such fixation of tariff value has facilitated and simplified the assessment process of Customs duty and clearance of the imported goods. Such Tariff Value superseded the provision of Section-30 of the Act, as was in force, at the relevant time.

<u>16. Thus the tariff value as fixed is not the contemplated value of the imported goods prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry as per Section-30 of the Customs Act. The tariff value though fixed at an earlier date but has been accepted as the value of the imported goods on the date of presentation of the relevant Bill(s) of Entry, provided such goods do not come within the purview of CRF scheme. The value of imported goods mentioned in CRF certificates has been made acceptable for the purpose of assessment of the Customs duty, provided such imported goods were not listed in schedule 1 of SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996.</u>

17. The learned Advocate then submitted that the CRF certificate scheme has been introduced by the government to have a check on the importation of proper goods by the  Government approved agents, who/which were authorized to inspect and certify the description, quality, quantity and value of the goods-imported at the loading port complying with the provisions of SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 and. the government has assured, declaring through said public notifications, that such CRF certificates shall be accepted for the purpose of determination of the value of the imported goods in assessing the customs duty. Such the CRF Certificated value supersedes the value mentioned in section 30 of the Customs Act inasmuch as Section 25A has been given an overriding force over all the Sections of the Customs Act, thereby the provisions of Section 25A overrides the provisions of Section 25(7) as well as Sections 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. It has been submitted that the assessment made by the PSI agents is also based on Section 25(1) and (2)of the Customs Act giving due importance to the price prevailing in the countries from which procured in certifying the value of the goods after being loaded in the vessel for import purpose.

18. The learned advocate pointedly submitted that the decision of the "Unita International" case referred above was based. on the grounds on which leave was granted i.e.

"to consider the submissions that the High Court Division erred in law making the Rules absolute ignoring that Section 25A of the Customs Act relates to the value on the basis of which the goods imported are to be assessed and it has nothing to do with exemption in the rate of duty and the CRF facilities under Section 25A having been withdrawn before the presentation of the Bills of Entry Provisions in Section 30 of the Customs Act were applicable and accordingly the customs authority rightly refused to assess the duty on the basis of Certificates and the High Court Division, without taking into consideration the provision of Section 25(1), 25(7), 30 and 30A of the Customs Act, erroneously held that the respondents acquired vested right on the opening of the letters of credit."

and their lordships in the said judgment (Unita case) have held that: "In the present cases, the respondents claim legal/vested right on the ground that at the time of opening the letters of credit they could get the imported goods assessed on the basis of CRF and subsequently by different notification the above privilege was withdrawn/cancelled but as it appears in 52 DLR (AD) 49, the Appellate Division held no vested right accrued even though at the time of opening of the letter of credit there was a notification (SRO) providing for lesser tariff value. So there is no question of acquiring vested right by the respondents merely on the basis of such SRO's relying on which they opening their letters of credit:"

19. and thus it appears that the decision in the "Unita International" case is based on the date of opening of the letter of credit, which is not the case in the appeals under review. Further the judgment under review has not been considered in deciding the said "Unita International" case.

<u>20. We have perused the impinged judgment and considered the submissions of the learned advocates of respective parties. It appears that though Section 30 of the Customs Act provides that the value of the imported goods to be the value prevailing as normal price as per Section 25 (1) & (2) of the Customs Act, on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty, yet the government has made relaxation in aforementioned two circumstances namely in case of existence of the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Customs Act and in case of furnishing CRF certificate issued pursuant to Section 25A of the Customs Act complying with SRO Nos. 316 dated 3.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996.</u>

21. In the instant cases after opening their respective LCs the importers complying with the terms of the LCs and provisions of the SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act, got the imported goods inspected by the duly approved Government PSI agents on payment of the prescribed fees and charges, and obtained the required CRF certificates, thereby as per the assurance given by the government vide S.R.O. Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 pursuant to Section-25A of the Custom Act, which is an independent promise of the government, the CRF Certificates issued in terms thereof became binding on the Customs authority, thereby such importers have acquired a right to get their imported goods assessed for payment of Customs duty On the basis of the value certified in the CRF Certificates.

22. It appears that their lordships in the judgment under review have analyzed the issue involved as under:

"It has been recognized by superior Courts of the sub-continent that specific assurance made by the government may give rise to equitable protection under promissory estoppel. The question is whether a notification under section 25A of the Customs Act gives rise to a vested right and protection under promissory estoppel. Section 25A amended till 1995 provides that the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved reshipment inspection agency will he accepted as the basis for assessment and the price under this section means the value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of Section 25. The respondents relying on the notification under this section acted to their detriment by having their goods inspected by inspectors appointed by the Government and by incurring expenses for such inspection. Would in such special circumstance of Government's assurance that the price so determined by the inspection would be accepted by them as the basis for assessment create a vested right? Would it be inequitable and unjust to allow the government to treat such inspection certificate as an idle exercise and a scrap of paper having no value at all? The promise of accepting the price having been made by the appellant under a law, should the Government by bound by such a promise when the other side has acted bonafide and to his detriment relying on that promise?"

23. And that their have lordships relied on the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of M. P. Sugar Mills Vs. State of U.P. reported in AIR 1979(SC) 621 in arriving at their decision. Their lordships quoted the following passage from the said Indian decision in the body of the impugned judgment:

"Doctrine of promissory estoppel has been variously called 'promissory estoppel' requisite estoppel, quasi estoppel and new estoppel'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppel', is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. The true principle of promissory estoppel seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or affect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken placed between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppel need not be inhibited by the same limitation as estoppel in the strict sense of the term. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason, logic or principle why promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action, if necessary to satisfy the equity."

24. We are in respectful agreement with the analysis as made by their lordships of this Division, in the body of the impugned judgment of the appeals under review, quoted above, and rely on the same for consideration of the issue on the certificated value.

25. It appears that at the relevant time the value of any imported goods could be determined in three different ways on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry i.e. (i) one being the value to be determined following the provisions of Section-30; (ii) the second one being the tariff value, fixed pursuant to Section 25(7) of the Customs Act; and (iii) the third one is the value certified in the CRF Certificate issued by a government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency following the provisions of SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued pursuant to section 25A of the Customs Act. Having regard to the non-obstante clause appearing in Section 25A of the Customs Act the CRF certificated value of the imported goods overrides all other modes for valuation of imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duty on such imported goods. The value of the imported goods certified in the CRF Certificate relates to the date of issuance of the CRF certificate, and not to the date of opening of L/C or the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry as per Section-30 of the Act.

26. It appears that in deciding the appeals under review their lordships have considered the application of CRF certificates having regard to the date of opening of letters of credit but not the date of issuance of the CRF certificates, (emphasis given) as contemplated by the provisions of Section 25A of the Customs Act and the declaration given by the government therefore vide SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996. The CRF Certificates have been issued against payment of fees/charges by the respective importers to the government approved PSI agents, who inspected the imported goods at the port of loading and issued the CRF certificates in accordance with law.

<u>27. The provisions of Section-25(7) of the Act for fixation of tariff value goes to show that the Government may fix a value of imported item(s) and until such value is altered or changed, though fixed at an earlier point of time, is accepted by Customs Authority as the value of the goods, in place of the value calculated as per Section 25(1)and (2) read with Section-79 of the Customs Act, as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry in terms of Section-30 of the Act, inspite of the fact that there may be differences in between the Tariff value in force, fixed as per Section-25(7) of the Act, and the value calculated as per Section 25(1) and (2) of the Act, prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, as per Section-30 of the Act. Similarly in view of the CRF scheme, the value certified in the CRF certificate on the date of issuance of the certificate is accepted as the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty in view of the declaration given by the government vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994. It is to be noted that the Bill(s) of Entry is/are naturally presented sometime after the date of issuance of the CRF certificate, since it takes time to reach the goods at the port of discharge, and the CRF certificate is issued on inspection of the imported goods at the port of loading before the vessel sails there from, and that the value of the imported goods may vary on the date of submission of the Bill of Entry in usual course. Since the importer has acted on the assurance and declaration given by the government under the CRF scheme vide SRO No. 316 dated 3.11.199.4 the value of the imported goods as mentioned in CRF Certificates has been accepted for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty by the customs authority on presentation of the Bill of Entry with such CRF certificate issued at an earlier date. The importers having acted upon the assurance of the government such CRF certificated value becomes effective for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty, no matter when the Bill of Entry with such CRF Certificate is presented. As per SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 the CRF certificate becomes effective once it is issued, provided on the date of issuance of the certificate the imported item comes under the purview of the CRF scheme and the law permits issuance of such CRF Certificate on such date. The Customs authority has accepted this position and acted accordingly and made assessments of Customs duty on the imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificate issued earlier to the date of submission of the Bill of Entry. Thus it appears that for the goods-imported covered by CRF scheme, the date of issuance of the CRF Certificates actually matters for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty and not the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry. Therefore even if the imported item is taken out from the purview of CRF scheme with effect from 13.05.1997, any CRF certificates issued prior to said date in accordance with law is valid and is binding on the Customs authority, no matter when the relevant Bill of Entry is presented for the purpose of assessment of duty. In the instant cases where the CRF certificates were issued prior to 13.05.1997 in respect of the imported items, not included in the list of schedule-1 of the SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 prior to 13.05.1997, those are not debarred from getting benefit of the CRF scheme. The SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 cannot affect the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 inasmuch as with the issuance of CRF certificate the transaction is complete and closed and is binding on all concern, since the parties concern have performed their respective obligations in the issuance of the CRF certificates.</u>

28. (২) পরিদর্শন সংস্থা কর্তৃক প্রত্যয়নকৃত পণ্যের মূল্য কমিশনারের নিকট অযৌক্তিক প্রতীয়মান হইলে তিনি প্রত্যয়নকৃত মূল্যের ভিত্তিতে সাময়িকভাবে পণ্য শুল্কায়ন ও খালাস করিবেন, তবে প্রত্যয়িত পণ্য মূল্য অযৌক্তিক প্রতীয়মান হওয়ার কারণ ব্যাখ্যাপূর্বক চালান খালাসের এক মাসের মধ্যে Customs Act, 1969 (IV of 1969) এর section 193 C এর বিধান অনুসারে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন এবং উক্ত ট্রাইব্যুনাল, প্রত্যয়নকৃত মূল্য বাতিল করিতে পারিবে।

(৩) উপবিধি (২) অনুসারে প্রত্যায়িত মূল্য আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল কর্তৃক বাতিল করা হইলে যে পরিদর্শন সংস্থা উক্ত প্রত্যয়নপত্র জারি করিবে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে বর্ণিত অসত্য ঘোষণার জন্য Customs Act, 1969 (IV of 1969) এর section 32 অনুসারে সংশ্লিষ্ট কমিশনার অব কাস্টমস উক্ত Act এর Section 156(1) এবং তৎসংঙ্গে পঠিতব্য Table 14 এ বর্ণিত শাস্তিমূলক ব্যবস্থা হিসাবে উক্ত সংস্থার বিরুদ্ধে পঞ্চাশ হাজার টাকা উর্দ্ধে নহে এমন দন্ড অথবা যে পণ্যের মূল্য অসত্য ঘোষণার কারণে অপরাধ সংঘটিত হইয়াছে উক্ত পণ্যের মূল্যের তিনগুন, যাহার অংক বৃহত্তর হইবে, এমন দন্ডে দন্ডিত হইবেন এবং উক্তরুপ পণ্য ও বাজেয়াপ্রাপ্তযোগ্য হইবে।

29. On a careful examination of the aforesaid provisions, quoted hereinabove, it appears that Section 25A has non-obstante clause by which the provisions of Section 25A overrides all other Sections of the Customs Act, thereby the provisions of Section 25A will prevail over all other provisions of the Customs Act, 1969 including those of Section 25(7) as well as Sections 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. It further appears that Section 25A provides that the Government may by notification in the official gazette, declare, amongst others, the price of any imported goods verified in the prescribed manner (i.e. mentioned in a CRF Certificate by an approved. Pre-shipment Inspection Agency) shall be accepted as the basis for assessment of Customs duty and pursuant to that provision of Section-25'A of the Customs Act, the government issued the SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994, quoted above, wherein the Government has categorically declared that the price of any imported goods verified and certified by an approved Reshipment Inspecting Agency shall be the basis for assessment of customs duty, subject to compliance of the provisions of the SROs i.e.-Clauses-1(Kha), 2(2),2(4) and 13 of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and Clauses; 79(Kha), (Uma), (Dha) of SRO No. 244, dated 31.12.1996. Such declaration of the government is independent of all other sections of the Customs Act. Thus it is clear from the aforesaid provisions of Section 25A read with those of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 that the value of any imported goods verified and certified by an approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency shall be the basis for assessment of the customs duty inspite of the existing provisions of Sections 25(7) (for fixing Tariff value) and Section-30 of the Customs Act and that there is no restriction as to the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry accompanying the CRF certificates issued for the purpose of assessment of custom duty or as to expiry of the validity or effectiveness’s of such CRF Certificate(s) once issued.

30. Section 25(7) provides for fixation of tariff value by the Government following the procedure laid down therefore and that such tariff value, as may be fixed, unless altered or modified, prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry, shall be the value of the imported goods, subject to the overriding provisions of Section 25A of the Customs Act read with SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 i.e. CRF certificates issued thereunder, for the purpose of assessment of customs duty.

31. The value of the imported goods certified and verified in the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) Certificate issued by 'the government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency under Section-25A of the Act shall be the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty and shall be binding on the customs authority superseding the Tariff value fixed under Section-25(7) of the Act and or the normal value, if any fixed under Section-15(1) &(2) read with Section-79 as per Section-30 of the Act. It further appears from the provisions of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 that such Clean Report of Findings Certificate is issued by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agencies only on payment of the required fees and after inspecting the goods at the port of loading certifying, amongst others, the value thereof and such CRF Certificate being issued as per the declaration made by the Government to the effect that "Section-25A তে প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে সরকার ঘোষনা করিল যে -----” and “------প্রদত্ত প্রত্যয়নপত্র শুল্কায়নের ভিত্তি হিসাবে গৃহীত হইবে।”  vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11:1994 pursuant to Section 25A of the Customs Act, such certified value becomes binding upon the customs authority to admit and accept the said value as the value of the thwarted goods, when the Bill(s) or Entry is/are presented, for assessment of Custom's duty. Thus once a CRF Certificate is issued by an approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency, complying with said SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 such certificate becomes binding on the authority for the purpose of assessment of the duty, etc. inasmuch as such CRF certificated issued under section-25A overrides the provisions of Section 25(7) and Section 30 of the Customs Act in view of the nature of the non-obstante clause appearing in Section-25A of the Customs Act.

32. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we do not find any substance on the submission of the learned Advocates appearing for the review petitioner that with the inclusion of the imported items in reference in the list of schedule-1 of S.R.0.244 dated 31.12.1996, vide S.R.0.113 dated 11.05.1997, such item(s) is/are not entitle to the benefit of CRF Certificate scheme if the relevant Bill(s) of Entry is/are presented after 13.05.1997 for assessment of customs duty. It is also submitted that in view of the principle that there is no estoppel against statute and the provisions. of Section-30 of the Customs Act has retrospective effect, the CRF certificates under reference have lost their effectiveness with the inclusion of the imported goods in schedule-1 of S.R.O.244 dated 31.12.1996 vide SRO 17, No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 with effect from 13.05.1997 and hence the orders as passed by the Customs authority refusing to accept the CRF certificates are in accordance with law. But in the facts and circumstances, said principle of estoppel is not applicable in the instant case, particularly in view of the overriding provision of Section-25A read with the declaration given, by the government vide S.R.O. No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and the importers having acted on such declaration of the government, the CRF certificates became effective on the date of issuance thereof and remains valid. There is no mention of any date in the law as to the expiry or validity of such CRF certificates.

33. The judgment of "Unita International" (being C.A. No. 55 of 2001) disposed of along with other 747 Civil Appeals; dated 26.04.2007 appears to be inconsistent with the provisions of Section-25A of the Customs Act as was in force. The words "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act" appearing in section 25A goes to show that the application of said Section-25A supersedes all other sections of the Customs Act and shall accordingly prevail over the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Act and also the provisions of Sections 30 and 30A of the Act.

34. The observations made in the aforesaid judgment and order dated 20.04.2007 passed in Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2001 to the effect that:

"Since the concept and definition of normal price and tariff value have distinct meaning with separate legal interpretation as to its aspects and application for the purpose of determination of value for assessment of duty of any goods under import, the customs authority on receipt of a Bill of Entry, first of all, is bound in law to ensure whether the goods having respective H.S. Code falls under prevailing tariff value notification and if it is so, as was found in many of the writ petitions, are to treat those goods as per section 25(7) because of the fact that tariff value supersedes the concept as well as application of normal price under Section 25(1) & (2) and 25A. So if any goods which fall under tariff SRO of a relevant period shall straightway attract the provision of Section 25(7). Therefore, only on items of import which does not fall under tariff value notification of a relevant period can be treated under Section 25A if it does not attract tariff value and this treatment of valuation implies pure and simple determination of normal price under Section 25(1) and (2) read with 25A as the case may be. Accordingly the determination of normal price and tariff value, as in the above writ petition, nullifies the pleas of the respondents for acceptance of CRF under section 25A. The cancellation of CRF value is done in pursuance to tariff SRO which is within the valid jurisdiction of the appellant. The claim of the writ petitioner respondents to the date of opening letter of credit has got no relevance arid, material footing in these cases of the writ petitioner respondents because if any consignment in question is subject to treatment under section 25(7) there lies no room for attracting the provision of section 25(1) & (2) read with section 25A whatsoever."

35. Goes to show that the tariff value fixed under section 25(7) of the Customs Act supersedes the CRF .value certified under Section 25A of the Customs Act but the law as discussed hereinabove is otherwise.

36. On careful perusal of Section 25(7) and 25A of the Customs Act reveals that Section 25(7) override of all other sub-sections of Section 25 of the Customs Act only, whereas Section 25A overrides all other Sections of the Customs Act and thereby the CRF value certified validly under Section 25A overrides any tariff Value fixed under Section 25(7). Therefore it cannot be said that only the items of import which do not fall under tariff value notification of a relevant period can be treated under Section 25A and that if any imported goods fall under tariff SRO of a relevant period shall straightway attract the provision of Section 25(7) Provisions of Section-25A of the Customs Act supersedes, the Provisions of Section-25, which includes Section-25(1) & (2), 25(7), 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. CRF; certificates issued validly shall get preference and the value certified therein shall supersede the value of the imported goods fixed under Sections 25(1) & (2) and or 25(7) of the Customs Act and shall be binding on the Customs authority. Thus the goods imported with CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 shall get the benefit of the CRF scheme and such goods shall be assessed for customs duty on the basis of the CRF certificated value.

37. Thus the Customs duty of the imported goods, the value of which have been duly verified and certified by the government approved by Pre-shipment Inspecting Agencies at the port of loading prior to 13.05.1997; the publication date of the SRO No. 113-Ain/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997 in the official gazette, should be assessed on the basis of such CRF certificated value and that Section 30 of the Customs Act will not affect the value of such imported goods certified in the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997, inspite of withdrawal of such goods from the benefit of CRF scheme effective from 13.05.1997 i.e. prior to the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry to the Customs authority, for assessment of Customs duty.

38. It thus appears that the out of 27 appeals under review 18 appeals being (1) Civil Appeals( on review) Nos. (1)339 of 2009 arising out of C.A. case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 7.12.1999 passed by the High Court Division in Company Matter Nos. 6, 47 of 1996 and 22 of 1997 respectively)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J. The above appeals, by leave, are directed against the common judgment and order dated 7.12.1999 of the High Court Division passed in Company Matter Nos. 6 of 1996, 22 of 1997 and 47 of 1996 allowing the applications filed by the respondents of the respective appeals under section 233 of the Company Act 1994 and declaring that the issuance of (a) 13790 debentures by Chittagong Cement Clinker Grinding Mills Limited, (CCCG) in the Matter No. 6 of 1996, (b) 2870 debentures by Kohinoor Chemical Company Ltd in Matter No.  22 of 1997 and (c) 12030 debentures by Eagle Box Carton Manufacturing Company Ltd in Matter No. 47 of 1996, all in favour of the appellants with interest @ 13.55 per annum are void and the respective Trust Deeds made in respect thereof are also void.

2. In Civil Appeal No. 171 of 2000 facts, in brief, are that the respondent Nos. 1-4 and 6-48 along with CCCG, the respondent No. 5, filed Matter No. 6 of 1996 seeking declaration that the issuance of 13790 debentures, each valuing Tk. 10,000/, issued by the company in favour of the appellant No. 1 with 13.5% interest as well as the trust deed in respect thereof being void are liable to be Cancelled on the averments That they, holding 1,29.729 shares, represent 10.50% share hold of the company; the factory of the above company was established at Chittagong in the year 1969 and the company was incorporated in the year 1979; in the year 1989 the appellants, while holding 100% shares of the company, sold their 49% of the shareholding in the company, 34% shares to the members of the public who are represented by the respondent Nos. 1-3 and 15% to its officers and workers who are represented by the respondent No. 4, before the above sale, the company issued prospectus dated 14.2.1989, wherein a sum of Tk. 7,21,34,931/-was shown as quasi-equity loan to the company from the appellant No. 1 with no mention of interest to be charged thereon; however in the balance sheet of the company, as of 30.6.92, Tk. 12,26,56,225 was shown as quasi-equity loan and in the balance sheet there was also no mention of interest on the said quasi equity loan; thereafter the appellants, by agreement S for sale dated 27.6.1993 sold their remaining 51% shares to T.K. Oil Refinery Ltd, the respondent No. 49, and before the sale of the above 51% shares on 27.6.1993 the appellants, holding 51% shares, had five directors in the Board of the Company and the purchasers who bought 49% shares had four directors; the respondent No. 49, after purchasing the balance 51% shares on 27.6.93, similarly had five directors and the purchasers who bought 49% shareholding also had four directors in the Board; the appellants, by virtue. of their majority in the Board of Directors, while selling the balance 51% shares, passed a resolution on 27.6.1992 for issuing 13790 debentures of Tk. 10,000/- each, payable with 13.5% and then the aforesaid debentures were issued and a trust deed was also created in respect of the said debentures and the respondent Nos. 50-54 were made trustees of the said trust deed and in that process a sum of Tk. 33,00,000/- was spent from the fund of the company although there . was no need to form a Board of Trustees as the said debentures were payable only to the appellant No. 1 and accordingly the appellants liable to pay back the said amount of Tk. 33,00,000/-to the company; while I3CIC, the appellant No. 2, took management of the company from 1982, the company started, incurring loss and upto  30.6.1988 the company incurred loss of Tk. 5,4616,579/- but the above loss was not deducted while fixing the amount of the quasi equity loan on the basis of profit made due to revaluation of the assets of the company; the appellants did not give any loan to the company to the tune of the amount as shown as quasi-equity loan and as such they were not entitled to any reimbursement for the said amount against the so called quasi equity roan and as such the issuance of the debentures is void.

3. The appellant's contested the above matter and filed affidavit-in-opposition contending that after the management of the company was placed with appellant No. 2 in the year 1982 it made a profit of Tk. 53.74 lacs in the year 1983-84, Tk. 74.52 lacs in the year 1985-86, Tk. 255.97 lacs in the year 1986-87, Tk. 832.90 lacs in 1987-88, Tk. 950.20 lacs in 1988-89, Tk. 771.07 lacs in 1989-90 and Tk. 741.30 lacs in 1990-91 and Tk. 774.10 lacs in 1991-92 and the company declared dividends of 20%, 30%, 35% and 40% in 1988-89, 189-90, 1990-91 and 1991-92 respectively; the appellant No. 1, before selling its 49% of shareholding, decided to make fresh valuation of the assets of the company as since its incorporation the value of the land, building, machinery and other movable and immovable’s of the company including the goodwill increased manifold and on revaluation Tk. 12,26,36,225.00 was found as the appreciated value but however since the company remained under its management and control, the appellant No. 1, without realizing the about amount of Tk. 12,26,36,225.00, allowed the said amount to be retained by the company in the form of quasi-equity loan and also did not charge any interest thereon till sale of the balance 51% shares and at the time of selling the balance 51% shares specifically claimed the above quasi equity loan with interest @ 13.5%; the value of the assets of the company having increased manifold and the company also earned profit of crores of Taka, the value of the shares of the company also increased manifold but the above 49% shares of the company were sold only at face value and so the purchasers of 49% shares to make huge gain, did not raise any objection to the creation of the said quasi equity loan; <u>8. The High Court Division, after hearing the applications analogously, by common judgment, allowed the applications and cancelled the respective debentures as being void holding, amongst others, that (a) A member has an interest in maintaining the value of his share and he may bring himself within section 233 if he can show that the value of its shareholding is seriously diminished or jeopardized by reason of conduct of those having defect control of the company which is unfair to the member concerned. A member has an interest in competent management of a company, its profitability, dividend policy which will have effect on his financial interest as a shareholder and on the value of his shares. The act or omission by the majority who are in defector control of the company affecting the interest of the share-holders generally including the petitioners as a minority shareholder is called in question in an application under section 233. (b) A company and is shareholder are two distinct and separate entitles. A majority shareholder cannot appropriate to them-selves money, property or advantages which belong to the company or in which shareholders are entitled to participate. Such conduct amounts to fraud on minority and cannot be anticipating; such conduct amounts to fraud on minority and cannot be ratified. A malafide exercise of powers by Directors affecting interest of the company as well as shareholders generally is not rectifiable. If the company is deprived of its assets because of the majority approving such decision, it would be in itself is fraud on minority. (c) It is permissible if a shareholder allows the company to retain an amount of the profit payable to him by way of dividend as loan to the company to retain an amount of the profit payable to him by way of dividend as loan to the company. A surplus of assets over liabilities share capital and capital reserved is treated as distributable profit. Such a surplus includes profits. Such a surplus includes profits obtained on the sale of fixed assets for more than their cost price or written down value. A company is prevented from paying dividend out of profit unless current profit is sufficient to write off earlier losses. (d) There cannot be any profit out of revaluation of any fixed assets without disposal of the same by sale or otherwise and that too without writing off the treading losses of earlier financial years. (e) A shareholder does not become automatically entitled to any part of the profit until resolution is taken and a dividend is declared by the company out of such profit. (f) The prospectus stated that the quasi equity loan was created out of an estimated profit arising out of increased value of the assets over the years since incorporation of value of the assets over the years since incorporation of value of the assets, over the years since incorporation of the company by revaluating the assets without disposal of the same and without any resolution declaring the dividend from such profit and that too without deducting the accumulated loss of Tk. 546 crore as is 30.6.1988. Even the Auditors opined that earlier losses ought to have been deducted from the said quasi equity loan. (g) A shareholder cannot claim the increased amount in the value of any asset of the company without realising the same by disposal of the asset as it would offend the principles of company law. His interest confirm to by shareholding in the company. Appreciation of value of fixed asset is also a fixed capital of the company and such increase in the fixed capital enhances share value. Such increase cannot be considered profit. Therefore, the quasi equity loan in question is not tenable in law and is not repayable to GOB: (h) If the company is made to repay the quasi equity loan, it would amount to diminishing the value of the shares of the company which could prejudice the interest of the shareholders including the petitioners, and it would also affect the interest of the company. (i) It appeared from the minutes of AGM on 10.6.93 and EGM on 12.9.93 that the minority, opposed the creation of debenture and repayment of quasi equity loan, but majority voting power wrongfully created quasi equity loan and approved the same in the Board and General Meeting. The said quasi equity loan is harsh, burdensome and wrongful to the petitioners, minority shareholders and the Board and General Meeting resolutions are oppressive and prejudicial.</u>

Shahidul Huq Bulbul, the respondent No. 3 who spoke for the minority shares was as follows:-

সরকার কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত হারে (১৩.৫%) সুদসহ সরকারের বিবিধ পাওনা কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন পরিশোধ সম্পর্কে আলোচনা ও মতামত গ্রহন:

মাননীয় চেয়ারম্যান উপরোক্ত আলোচ্যসূচীর উপর কোম্পানির অন্যতম পরিচালক জনাব মির্জা আবদুল মতিনকে উপরোক্ত প্রস্তাবটি সভায় উপস্থাপনের আহ্বান জানান। জনাব মতিন কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও সরকারের অন্যান্য পাওনাদি বাবদ সর্বমোট ১৩,৭৯,০৬,৭০৫/- টাকা পাওনার বিবরণ ও তার প্রেক্ষাপট সম্পর্কে সকলকে অবহিত করেন। এই কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও অন্যান্য পাওনা বিগত কয়েক বৎসরের নিরীক্ষিত স্থিতিপত্রে অন্তর্ভুক্ত করা হয়েছে এবং কোম্পানীর পরিচালকবৃন্দ ও শেয়ারহোল্ডার বৃন্দ কর্তৃক বিগত সকল সাধারণ সভায় তা অনুমোদিত হয়েছে। জনাব মতিন আরো উল্লেখ করেন যে, সরকার ৫১% শেয়ার বিক্রির মাধ্যমে তার মালিকানা স্বত্ব ত্যাগ করছেন। এমতাবস্থায়, নিরীক্ষিত হিসাব মোতাবেক অত্র প্রতিষ্ঠানের নিকট কোয়াজি ইকুইটি ও অন্যান্য খাতে সরকারের পাওনা কোম্পানীকে ঋণ হিসাবে গ্রহণ করতে হবে। সমুদয় দাওনার উপর সরকার কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত ১৩.৫% হারে সুদ পরিশোধ করিতে হবে। প্রসঙ্গতঃ তিনি উল্লেখ করেন যে, ৫১% শেয়ার বিক্রির টেন্ডার ফর্মে শতকরা ১৩.৫% সুদে উক্ত ঋণ গ্রহণ সাপেক্ষে কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও কর্পোরেশনের অন্যান্য পাওনা পরিশোধের সুস্পষ্ট বিধান রয়েছে। তিনি আরো উল্লেখ করেন যে, ��রকারের মোট পাওনা ১৩.৭৯,০৬,৭০৫/- টাকা যা ১৯৯১-৯২ অর্থ বৎসরের নিরীক্ষিত হিসাব মোতাবেক স্থীতিপত্রে কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন খাতে ১২,২৬,৩৬,২২৫/- টাকা বৈদেশিক ঋণ খাতে ২৫,৬৫,০৩০/- টাকা এবং অন্যান্য দেনার তালিকাভুক্ত এডিপি ঋণের উপর অপরিশোধিত সুদ খাতে পাওনা ১,২৭,০৫,৪৫০/- টাকার উল্লেখ আছে। এ বিষয়ে মাননীয় চেয়ারম্যান ও শেয়ারহোল্ডারদের নিকট বিশদ বক্তব্য রাখেন। পরিশেষে আনুষ্ঠানিকভাবে শেয়ারহোল্ডারদের মতামত গ্রহনের জন্যে জনাব মতিন মাননীয় চেয়ারম্যানকে অনুরোধ জানান। অতঃপর চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয় সরকারের কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও অন্যান্য পাওনার বিপরীতে নির্ধারিত হারে সুদসহ ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যু সম্পর্কে হাউসের মতামত আহ্বান করেন। এ পর্য্যায়ে নিম্নোক্ত পরিচালক ও শেয়ারহোল্ডারগণ বক্তব্য রাখেন।

পরিচালক জনাব এ,এস, শাহদুল হক বুলবুল:

জনাব বুলবুল এ বিষয়ে আলোচনার সূত্রাত করে বলেন যে, ৪৯% শেয়ার বিক্রয়ের সময়ে প্রসপেক্টাসে কোন সুদের কোন উল্লেখ ছিল না। কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও সরকারের অন্যান্য পাওনা সম্পর্কিত ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যুতে তাদের কোন আপত্তি নেই, তবে সুদসহ ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যু তাদের নিকট গ্রহনযোগ্য নয়। সরকার কর্তৃক আরোপিত ১৩.৫% সুদ অগণতান্ত্রিক ও অগ্রহনযোগ্য বলিয়া তিনি উল্লেখ করেন। এ পর্যায়ে জনাব বুলবুল জনৈক রেজাউল করিম কর্তৃক লিখিত একটি পত্র সভায় পাঠ করে শোনান এবং সুদসহ সরকারের দেনা পরিশোধ অনীহা প্রকাশ করেন।

জনাব রুহুল আমিন, ফলিও নং-১৪১০৭:

আলোচনায় অংশগ্রহণ করে জনাব রুহুল আমিন কোয়াজি ইকুইটি সম্পর্কে জনাব শাহুদুল হক বুলবুলের বক্তব্য সমর্থ করেন এবং এ কোয়াজি ইকুইটি অগণতান্ত্রিক বলে আখ্যায়িত করেন। তদুপরি কোনরূপ অগণতান্ত্রিক সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ হতে বিরত থাকার জন্যে তিনি পরিচালক মন্ডলিকে অনুরোধ জানান। এ ব্যাপারে কোনরূপ অগণতান্ত্রিক পদক্ষেপ নেয়া হলে তারা আইনগত ব্যবস্থা গ্রহন করবেন বলে তিনি হুশিয়ারী উচ্চারণ করেন।

জনাব এনামুল হক চৌধুরী ফলিও নং-০০৩২৭:

জনাব এনামুল হক চৌধুরী কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন সম্পর্কে জনাব শাহুদুল হক বুলবুল ও জনাব রুহুল আমিনের সহিত একমত প্রকাশ করেন এবং সুদসহ ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যুর বিরুদ্ধে তার মতামত ব্যক্ত করেন।

জনাব মোঃ মহিউদ্দিন, ফলিও নং- ০০৯২৫৫:

জনাব মোঃ মহিউদ্দিন, সুদসহ ডিবেঞ্চার গ্রহনের ব্যাপারে ৩৪% শেয়ারহোল্ডারদের পক্ষ হবে আপত্তি প্রকাশ করেন। এ পর্যায়ে ৫১% শেয়ারহোল্ডারদের পক্ষ হতে বিসিআইসির প্রতিনিধি পরিচালক জনাব মির্জা এ, মতিন কোম্পানীর চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয় এর নিকট কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও অন্যান্য পাওনার বিপরীতে প্রস্তাবিত হারে সুদসহ ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যুর বিষয়টি নিষ্পত্তির জন্য আবেদন জানান। চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয় বিষয়টি নিষ্পত্তি করলার্থে পরিচালক মির্জা এ, মতিনের আবেদন গ্রহণ করেন এবং ইলেকশন কমিশনার জনাব কাজী ইকবাল হোসেনকে ভোট গ্রহন কাযক্রম পরিচালনার জন্যে আহ্বান জানান।

ভোট গ্রহনের অব্যবহিত পূর্বে পরিচালক এ,এস শাহুদুল হক বুলবুলকে আহ্বানে অধিকাংশ শেয়ারহোল্ডার তাদের স্বস্ব আসন ত্যাগ করে সভাকক্ষের খালি জায়গায় দন্ডায়মান হন এবং ভোট দানে বিরত থাকেন। এ পর্যায়ে ইলেকশন কমিশনার আনুষ্ঠানিকভাবে ভোট গ্রহন শুরু করেন ভোট গ্রহন শেষে তিনি সভার সামনে ব্যালট বক্স খুলেন এবং ভোট গণনা করেন।

ইত্যবসরে শেয়ারহোল্ডারগণ তাদের স্ব স্ব আসনে ফিরে আসেন। তখন ইলেকশন কমিশনার ব্যলট পরীক্ষান্তে ঘোষণা করেন যে, প্রস্তাবটির পক্ষে ৪,৩৮,৬০০টি ভোট (অর্থাৎ উপস্থিত ভোটারদের শতকরা ৭৭.২% ভাগ) পড়ে এবং বিপক্ষে কোন ভোট পড়ে নি।

সিদ্ধান্ত : ইলেকশন কমিশনার কর্তৃক এ ভোটের ফলাফল ঘোষণার প্রেক্ষিতে চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয় এ মর্মে ঘোষনা করেন যে, ১৩.৫% সুদে সরকারের কোয়াজি ইকুইটি লোন ও অন্যান্য পাওনা মোট টাকা ১৩.৭৯,০৬,৭০৫.০০ এর বিপরীতে ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যু সংক্রান্ত বিষয়টি সংখ্যাগরিষ্ট ভোটে অনুমোদিত ও গৃহীত হলো।

20. Regarding Civil Appeal No. 172 of 2000 which arose out of Matter No. 22 of 1997, it appears that the authorised capital of the company was Tk. 50,00,00,000.00 divided into 50,00,000 ordinary shares of Tk. 100 each out of which 5,00,000 shares were fully paid up and the appellant No. 1, having decided to keep, 2,55,000 shares, i.e A Group shares representing 51 % shares, decided to sell 49% that is 2,45,000 shares i.e 13 Group shares, out of which 34% i.e, 1,70,000 shares to public and 15% i.e- 75,000 shares to the officers employees; the value of the assets of the company having increased manifold. before sale of 49% shares, the assets were revalued by the Chartered Accountants as on 31.3.1988 and Tk. 10,27,99,818.00, the appreciated value of the assets, being not realized by the appellant No. 1 from the company, was shown as quasi equity loan to the company; at the time of creation of the above quasi equity loan, the appellant No. 1 was the owner of 100% shareholding of the company and it is only on 14.2.1989 that prospectus was issued for sale of 49% shares and thereafter the purchasers subscribed for 49% shares and so at the time of creation of quasi equity loan and/or on 142.1989, when prospectus was issued for sale of 49% shareholders there was no minority shareholders of the company and accordingly the purchasers of 49% shareholding, not being shareholders of the company at the time of creation of quasi equity loan, the question of keeping them in the dark/or misleading/misinforming them as to any act of the company and also committing fraud upon them by the creation of the above quasi equity loan did not arise. Further in the prospectus issued on 10.5.1988 for sale of 49% shareholding of the company and in the above appreciated value of assets or profit of Tk. 10,27,99,818.00 was shown as quasi equity loan to the company and in the above prospectus under the heading "Financial Forecast" it was mentioned that the company made a net profit of Tk. 49,15,088 (before tax) during nine monthly ending on 31.3.1988 and the accumulated profit, after making sufficient provision for income tax and other as on 31.12.88, stands at Tk. 2,86,12,245.00 and the company, was also a profitable concern, further, the appellant No. 1, on consideration that the company would remain under its management and control till balance 51% share are sold, allowed the company to retain Tk. 10,27,99,818.00 as quasi equity loan and also did not demand any interest on the same and the purchasers of the 49% shareholding, with-out raising any objection to the creation of quasi equity loan, purchased 49% share-holding as by the deal they made huge gain as though the actual value of its shares was much more than the face value but the above 49% shares were sold at face value; then at the time of sale of balance 51% shares decision was taken by the Board of Directors/or issuance of debentures bearing interest @ 13.5% repayable within 10 years against the quasi equity loan; Article 44 of the Articles of Association of the company also authorised creation of such debentures by the Board of Directors then resolution was also taken in the extra ordinary general meeting of the company held on 11.4.1993 approving issuance of debentures with interest; further the Controller of Capital Issues by its memo dated 10.4.1993 also approved the issuance of debentures; there is also nothing on record to show that in the Board Meeting and/or in the extra ordinary general meeting of the company the respondents or any other shareholder did raise any objection to the creation of quasi equity loan and/or issuance of debentures. It further appears that in the Balance Sheet of the years 1986-1987 there was no mention of any "quasi equity loan" as the said balance sheet was prepared before the revaluation of the assets and liability of the company. Further earlier, on consideration that the actual value of the assets of the company increased manifold and the company was a profitable concern and accordingly the value of the shares were more than the face value but the 49% shareholding of the company was sold at face value, the purchasers of 49% shareholding, without raising any objection to the creation of quasi equity loan, purchased the shares and Mr. Obaidul Karim, the respondent No. 7, the buyer of 51 shareholding, on consideration that the assets of the company became valuable and the company is also a profitable concern, apart from agreeing with terms of the Public Notice that the intending purchasers of 51% shareholding will have to acknowledge the liability of the company to issue debentures with 13.5% interest against the quasi equity loan, purchased 51% shares, i.e 2,55,000 share of 11.100 each, at Tk. 7,97,00,00,000.00, which is many times more then the face value, and in the sale Agreement dated 15.12.94 executed by him the above term regarding the issuance of 90350 debentures by the company with interest @ 13.5% was incorporated.

21. Regarding Civil Appeal No. 173 of 2000 it appears that the authorised capital of the company was Tk. 10,00,00,000.00 divided into 1,00,00,000/-ordinary shares of Tk. 10/-each out of which 5,00,000 shares were fully paid up. The appellant No. 1, having decided to keep 2,55,000 shares, i.e A Group shares representing 51% shares decided to sale 49% that is 2,45,000 shares i.e B Group shares, out of which 34% i.e, 1,70,000 shares to public and 15% i.e 75,000 shares, revalued the value of assets of the company as in the meantime the same increased manifold and in the Revaluation Report given by the Chartered Accountants as on 30.6.88 and Tk. 5,75,33,742.00 was shown as the appreciated amount after revaluation was shown as quasi equity loan to the company; in the prospectus issued on  for sale of 49% shareholding of the company the above appreciated amount of Tk. 5,75,33,742.00 was also shown as quasi equity loan; the actual value of the assets of the company having increased manifold and the company was also a profitable concern, the actual value of the share was also much more than its face value but 49% shareholding were sold merely at face value only and moreover, the appellant No. 1, at the time of selling 49% shareholding, on consideration that the management and control of the company would remain under its control till sale of the balance 51% shareholding, without realizing they said amount of Tk. 5,75,33,742.00, which is the amount due to appreciation of the value of the assets from the company, allowed the company to retain the same as quasi equity loan as reflected in the prospectus; further considering that the value of the shares was much more then its face value 49% shares were oversubscribed.

22. Further when the quasi equity loan of Tk. 5,25,33,743.00 was created, the appellant No. 1 was the owner of 100% share-holding of the company and the purchasers of 49% shareholding did not yet become the minority shares. So admittedly at the time of creation of the above quasi equity loan, the appellant No. 1 being the owner of 100% shareholding of the company, there was no minority share-holders of the company and accordingly the purchasers of 49% including the respondents, not being shareholders of the company at the time of creation of quasi equity loan, the question of keeping them in the dark/or misleading/misinforming them as to any act of the company and also committing fraud upon them by the creation of the above quasi equity loan did not arise specially the purchaser of 49% of the shareholding, anticipating huge gain, without raising any objection to the creation quasi equity loan, purchased their shares. Further on the above consideration the 49% shares as offered, were oversubscribed. It also appears that the above quasi equity loan was not shown in the balance sheet of 1987-1988 because the said balance sheet was prepared before the revaluation of the assets of the company.

23. It also appears the Board of Directors of the company in its 44th meeting held on 25.4.1994 took decision to pay the quasi equity loan by furnishing bank guarantee but as the said decision could not be implemented as five banks; who were approached, did not respond to the requests of the company to provide bank guarantee and so the Board of Directors, in. its 76th Meeting, took decision that the dues of the appellants would be paid by issuing of debenture with interest @ 13.5% per annum and in the above meeting representative of the minority share-holders only opposed to the payment of interest on the debentures. It also appears that Article 44 of the Articles of Association of the company provided for creation of such debentures. It also appear that the shareholders of the company in the extraordinary general meeting of the company held on 7.2.1993 also approved the decision to convert the quasi equity loan of Tk. 5,25,33,743 to 5253 debentures of Tk. 10,000 each with interest @ 13.5%. It also appears that an amount of Tk. 6,77,23,372.00 was given by the appellant No. 2 to the company from time to time by taking loan from the different banks and the loans were granted by the banks with interest and so it was quite natural that the above amount of Tk. 6,77,23,372.00 was payable to the appellant No. 2 by the company with interest and accordingly in the said meeting decision was taken to convert the above loan of the appellant No. 2 into 6777 secured debentures with 13.5% interest. Further the Securities and Exchange Commission by its Memo dated 21.7.94 also approved the issue of above debentures. The respondents having not raised any objection to the creation of quasi equity loan and also the decision for issuing debentures the question of fraud by the appellants upon the minority shareholders did not arise. Further the respondents are not entitled to any relief in view of the principle of waiver estoppel and acquiesce.

24. It also appears that in respect of all the three companies, the appellant No. 1 decided to dis-invest its 51% shares and the terms of tender as contained in all the Public Notices issued by the Ministry of Industries it was provided, amongst others, that the intending purchasers of 51% shares will have to agree that the dues of the respective companies against quasi equity loans of the appellant No. 1, will have to be repaid by the respective companies and in the said Public Notice it was specifically provided that ১৩.০৫% সুদ সম্বলিত হস্তান্তরযোগ্য ১০(দশ) বৎসর মেয়াদী ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যুর মাধ্যমে পরিশোধের ব্যবস্থা করিতে হইবে। কোম্পানীর বর্তমান বোর্ডের সিদ্ধান্ত মোতাবেক ইস্যুকৃত এই ডিবেঞ্চারের দায়িত্ব কোম্পানীতে অব্যাহত থাকিবে। ইহা গ্রহণে ৫১% শেয়ার ক্রেতার কোন আপত্তি থাকিবে না মর্মে বিক্রয় চুক্তিতে শর্ত থাকিবে” and the successful the buyers of the 51% shares of the respective companies participated in the bids on giving consent to the above conditions and their bids, being found highest, were accepted and thereafter the Ministry of Industries, as per decision of the National Economic Commercial issued Letters of Intent in favour of the successfully bidders notifying them that their bids have been accepted and then the successful bidders, in terms of the Letters of Intent, also furnished respective undertakings stating that they had accepted the liabilities of the respective companies including that of quasi equity loans and would pay those to the concerned person or the authorities on behalf of the respective companies and then in the extraordinary general meeting of the respective companies decisions were also taken to the effect that against the dues of the appellant No. 1 against quasi equity loans, the respective companies would issue debentures bearing interest @ 13.5% repayable within 10 years and then series of debenture were issued in respect of quasi equity loans of the appellant No. 1 and also in some cases in respect of the dues of the appellant No. 2; for management of the debentures Trust Deeds were executed; agreements for sale were also executed between the appellant No. 1 and the respective companies on different dates and clause 2 & 3 of the said Agreements of Sale provided as follows:-

“ক্রেতা উক্ত কোম্পানীর যাবতীয় দায়-দেনা, যেমন: সরকারের কোয়াসী ইকুইটি লোন, বাংলাদেশ কেমিক্যাল ইন্ডাষ্টিজ কর্পোরেশনের পাওনা, বাংলাদেশ শিল্প ব্যাংক, বাংলাদেশ শিল্প ঋণ সংস্থা অথবা অন্য কোন অর্থলগ্নী প্রতিষ্ঠান বা কোন বাণিজ্যিক ব্যাংকের পাওনাদি এবং শ্রমিক ও কর্মচারীদের বেতন মজুরী, চাকুরীর অন্যান্য সুবিধাদি, ভবিষ্যত সম্ভাব্য দায় (Contingent liability) ও অন্যান্য দায়-দেনাসহ সকল প্রকার সুনির্দিষ্ট দায়-দেনাসমূহ কোম্পানীর দায়-দেনা প্রচলিত নিময়/শর্ত মোতাবেক পরিশোধ করবেন। ক্রেতা সরকারের কোয়াসী হুকুইটি লোন ও কর্পোরেশনের পাওনা (প্রয়োজনীয় সমন্বয় সাপেক্ষে) ১৩.৫০% হারে সুদসহ বাৎসরিক কিস্তিতে ১০(দশ) বৎসরের মধ্যে নিম্ন বর্ণিত ডিবেঞ্চার ইস্যুর মাধ্যমে পরিশোধ করবেন।

25. It thus appears that the purchasers of 49% shareholding, including the respondents of the respective appeals, being not shareholders of the respective companies at the time of creation of the quasi equity loans, the question of keeping them in the dark and/or misleading/misinforming that as to the creation of quasi equity loan and also committing fraud upon minority does not arise and further the purchases of 49% shareholders of the companies including the respondents even knowing about the quasi equity loans as shown in the respective prospectus, in order to make huge gain, subscribed the shares without raising any objection to the creation of quasi equity loans and in fact the above shares were oversubscribed; further after about. 4 years, the purchasers of 51% shareholding, apart from acknowledging the liability of the companies to issue debentures with 13.5% interest against the above quasi equity loans, purchased the shares at a price which is many times more than the face value at which the purchasers of 49% shareholding, including the respondents, purchased the shares.

<u>26. Accordingly we are of the view that the purchasers of the 49% shareholding of the respective companies including the respondents, who earlier made huge gain by purchasing their shares at face value, cannot claim relief sought for in view of the principles of limitation, estoppel, waiver and acquiescence.</u>

<u>27. Further, in terms of the provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act, relief can be sought in the following circumstances</u>

<u>(a) the affairs of the company are being conducted or the powers of the directors are being exercised in a manner prejudicial to one or more of its members or debenture holders or in disregard of his or their interest; or</u>

<u>(b) The company is acting or is likely to act in a manner which discriminated or is likely to discriminate the interest of any member or debenture holder;</u>

<u>(c) a resolution of the members, debenture holders or any class of them has been passed or is likely to be passed which discriminates or is likely to discriminate the interest of one or more of the members or likely to debenture holder;</u>

<u>28. Accordingly we are also of the view that the provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act 1994 are not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the present appeals. Accordingly the decisions cited by the learned counsel of Civil Appeal No. 172 of 2000 are also not applicable in the present appeals as the facts and circumstances are different.</u>

29. In the result the appeals are allowed. The judgment and order dated 7.12.1999 passed in Company Matter Nos.  6, 47 of 1996 and 22 of 1997 are set aside. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
