case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 29.01.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 504 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J.:- This Civil Appeal, by leave granted in Civil Review Petition No. 16 of 2008, has arisen from the judgment and order dated 29.01.2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 504 of 2001 making the rule absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 17.09.2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 218 of 1992 affirming those dated 25.06.1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 72 of 1992 dismissing the suit.

<u>2. Mohammad Humayun-the predecessor of the present plaintiff-respondents herein, as plaintiff; instituted Title Suit No. 224 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of the Sub-judge, Dhaka which was subsequently transferred to the court of Sub-judge and 4th Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 72 of 1992, for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession and for further declaration to the effect that the expert decree passed in Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff.</u>

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Hazi Abdul Wahab. Hazi Abdul Wahab transferred the suit property in favour of his second wife-who adopted Islam as religion from Hinduism and took the name Nurjahan Begum. The said Nurjahan Begum expressed her desire to take Abdur Rouf, a son of the plaintiff, as her son and Hazi. Abdul Wahab gave his consent to it. When said Abdur Rouf became adult he married a girl of a family of Tongi Area without the knowledge of his father and started living at the residence of his father-in-law and in the meantime Nurjahan Begum died in Dhaka Medical College Hospital on 28.08.1978 without any issue. As a result the heirs of Abdul Wahab got the suit property by the law of inheritance. But Abdur Rouf claimed the suit property on the ground that Nurjahan Begum before, her death, made a gift of the suit property in his favour for which the plaintiff Md. Humayun instituted Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 for partition Abdur Rouf also filed Title Suit No. 165 of 1975 claiming the suit property which was subsequently dismissed for default. The Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 filed by the plaintiff was decreed on compromise on 01.03.1999 and the plaintiff got the suit land in his shaham by the said compromise decree.

4. That Abdur Rouf-the proforma defendant No. 2 entered into an agreement for sale of the suit property with the defendant No. 1, on 09.02.1977 and subsequently the defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 for specific performance of contract against Abdur Rouf and that suit was decreed ex-parte and the defendant No. 1, by filing execution case, got the kabala deed executed and registered through court on 05.02.1979 Thereafter, the defendant No. 1 filed a suit for permanent injunction, that since the decree for specific performance of contract was passed during the pendency of Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 the said decree was barred by the principle of lies-pendency, moreover since the defendant No. 2 had no right, title and interest in the suit property, the defendant No. 1 also could not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit property by that decree That the defendant No. 1 dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit property in the middle of 1979 and hence the plaintiff has filed this suit

5. The defendant No 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint His defence case was that Abdul Wahab transferred the suit property in favour of Nurjahan Begum by executing a deed of lease and as Nurjahan Begum had no issue she brought up the proforma defendant No. 2-who had been living with' Nurjahan Begum in the suit property and Nurjahan Begum thereafter transferred the suit property by way of gift in favour of the proforma defendant No. 2 on 20.08.1970 and confirmed that oral gift by executing a written instrument on 23.08.1970 and subsequently died on 28.08.1978. That the plaintiff was fully aware of this fact and he attempted to dispossess the proforma defendant No. 2 from the suit property. The proforma defendant No. 2 then filed Title Suit No. 165 of 1975 for permanent injunction which was subsequently dismissed for non-prosecution. That the proforma defendant No. 2 executed a bainapatra in favour of the defendant No. 1 on 09.02.1977 by taking Tk. 50,000/- out of stipulated consideration of Tk. 80,000/- and handed over possession of the suit property to the defendant No. 1. But since the proforma defendant No. 2 failed to execute the sale deed as per bainapatra the defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 for specific performance of contract and got decree and also the sale deed executed and registered through court and got possession also through court. That as the plaintiff attempted to dispossess the defendant No. 1 from the suit land the defendant No. 1 filed a suit against the plaintiff and obtained an order of temporary injunction. That the plaintiff filed a suit for partition and though all the defendants except the present proforma defendant No. 2 filed compromise petition in that suit but this proforma defendant No. 2 did not sign that compromise petition. That the plaintiff has no right, title interest and possession in the suit property and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

6. The trial court, on consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties, dismissed the suit. The appellate court below affirmed this judgment and decree of the trial court. The plaintiff then moved the High Court Division in revision being Civil Revision No. 504 of 2001 and obtained rule. A Single Bench of the High Court, ultimately, made that rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree of the courts below and decreed the suit.

<u>7. The defendant No. 1 then moved the Appellate Division with a petition for leave to appeal being No. 502 of 2006 and by the judgment and order dated 18.11.2007 the Appellate Division dismissed that leave petition. Thereafter, the defendant-petitioner filed an application for review of the said judgment and order dated 18.11.2007 and the Appellate Division, after hearing both the parties, allowed that review petition and granted leave on consideration of the submission of the learned Counsel for the leave petitioner to the effect that both the courts of facts concurrently found that the plaintiff was never in possession of the suit property and could not prove his possession and alleged dispossession from the suit property and failed to establish his possession in the suit property within 12 years prior to the institution of the suit and as such the suit was barred by Limitation and rightly dismissed the suit but the High Curt Division acted in excess of its revisional Jurisdiction in decreeing the suit without reversing the concurrent findings of fact of the courts of facts on the question of limitation and without considering the provisions of law.</u>

8. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate for the defendant-appellant has made submissions to the effect that in this suit the plaintiff has totally failed to prove his possession in the suit land within 12 years prior to institution of the suit and as such the suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession was barred by limitation, that both the trial court and the appellate court below, on thorough examination of the evidence adduced by both the parties, rightly found that the plaintiff could not prove his possession in the suit land and also alleged dispossession therefrom and, therefore, rightly dismissed the suit; that the High Court Division acted in excess of its revisional jurisdiction in decreeing the suit without reversing these concurrent findings of the courts of facts on finding of any misreading or non-reading of the material evidence on record. The learned Counsel for the defendant-appellant has made submissions to the effect also that Civil Revision No. 504 of 2001 was decided by the High Court Division in the absence of the present appellant who was the present appellant-who was opposite party No. 1 in that civil revision; that no notice of that civil revision was served on the opposite party No. 1 of that civil revision and consequently the opposite party No. 1 (the present appellant) did not get any opportunity to contest the rule issued in that civil revision and as a result the High Court Division could not take the right decision and consequently made the rule absolute most unjustly; that the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is not sustainable in law in view of the fact that the High Court Division did not advert to or reversed the concurrent findings of both the courts of facts. The learned Counsel has contended that both the courts of facts, on proper evaluation and appreciation of the evidence adduced by both the parties rightly found that the plaintiff could not prove his possession in the suit land within 12 years prior to the institution of the suit, but the High Court Division without taking into consideration these concurrent findings of the courts of facts made the rule absolute most unjustly and arbitrarily.

9. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel has argued that the very defence case that the suit property was transferred to Nurjahan Begum by its original owner Abdul Wahab by deed of lease dated 19.03.1958 is not acceptable at all that this alleged lease deed is void because it was created after 16th December, 1955 which is hit under section 75 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate has contended that the said lease deed was a mere paper transaction only which was never acted upon; that the proforma defendant No. 2 Abdur Rouf also could not acquire any right, title or interest in the suit property by virtue of the alleged oral gift made by Nurjahan Begum in his favour. The learned Counsel has argued also that the plaintiff of the present suit filed Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 for partition of the suit property and that suit was decreed on compromise by a competent court of law and so long this decree stands the defendants of the present suit cannot claim any right, title and interest in the suit land. The learned Counsel has argued also that the plaintiff has proved by sufficient evidence that the defendant No.1 dispossessed him from the suit land forcibly after obtaining the decree for specific performance of contract in Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 and as such this suit is not barred by limitation at all. The learned Counsel has contended that both the trial court and the appellate court below committed wrong in making assessment of the evidence adduced by the parties and thus arrived at a wrong findings and decision that the High Court Division assessed the evidence on record and other facts and circumstances properly and thus came to the correct decision.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also those of the courts below.

11. Admittedly, the suit land originally belonged to Hazi Abdul Wahab. It is also an admitted fact that Hazi Abdul Wahab transferred the suit land to his second wife Nurjahan Begum by a registered lease deed dated 19.03.1958. The plaintiff, in his very pleadings, has stated this fact and did not raise any question as to the validity of this lease deed. The plaintiff in his plaint, rather, has stated to the effect that since Nurjahan Begum died childless the suit property devolved upon the heirs of Abdul Wahab after her death. The plaintiff, admittedly, did not raise any question as to the validity of this lease deed before any court-either in the present suit-or in any other earlier suits. In this present appeal before this Division, for the first time, the plaintiff has raised this question as to the validity of the lease deed in favour of Nurjahan Begum. However, this is a question of law and as such we entertain this question and hold that this lease deed being created after 16th December, 1955 is hit under section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such is not a valid one.

12. Now the question is whether Nurjahan Begum acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession on the basis of this invalid lease deed. It is plaintiff’s case that Nurjahan Begum was in possession of the suit land after having this alleged lease deed executed and registered in her favour on 19.03.1958 and remained in possession of the suit land till her death in the year 1978. Both the trail court and the appellate court below, on proper assessment of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances, found that Nurjahan Begum was in possession of the suit property by exercising her own right and title thereon on the basis of this alleged lease deed till her death in the year 1978. So, Nurjahan Begum acquired title in the suit land by virtue of adverse possession for more than 12 years. The plaintiff himself has admitted in his very pleadings that Hazi Abdul Wahab the original owner of the suit land transferred the suit land to his 2nd wife Nurjahan Begum by a registered lease deed dated 19.03.1958 and after the death of Nurjahan Begum the heirs of Abdul Wahab got the suit land by virtue of inheritance. These very statements of the plaintiff himself prove sufficiently that Nurjahan Begum possessed the suit land by exercising her own right, title and interest thereon on the basis of this registered lease deed dated 19.03.1958 and in the circumstances Nurjahan Begum acquired title in the suit land by virtue of adverse possession for a long period of about 20 years. The plaintiff has claimed that after the death of Nurjahan Begum he along with other heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab inherited the suit land. But this claim of the plaintiff is not acceptable at all. The plaintiff or other heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab are not the heirs of Nurjahan Begum. So, at the death of Nurjahan Begum the question of acquisition of the suit property by the heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab does not arise at all The present appellant, as defendant No.1, in the original suit, pleaded a case that Nurjahan Begum before her death gifted the suit land to Abdur Rouf a son of the plaintiff whom Nurjahan Begum adopted as a son. The plaintiff himself also has pleaded that Nurjahan Begum with the consent of her husband Abdul Wahab Look Abdur Rouf as her son and reared up him. The plaintiff though has pleaded a case that subsequently Abdur Rouf, after attaining his marriageable age, married a girl of Tongi Area and started levity in his father-in-law's house at Tongi, but this case of the plaintiff has not been substantiated. Rather we find that there are sufficient evidence to prove that Abdur Rouf used to reside with Nurjahan Begum till her death. However, admittedly the defendant No.1 filed a suit for specific performance of contract being Case No. 231 of 1977 against Abdur Rouf and got an ex-parte decree and in execution of that ex-parte decree he got the kabala deed executed and registered through court and also got delivery of possession of one of the rooms of the suit property through court. The contesting defendant has adduced some evidence to prove that Nurjahan Begum gifted the suit property to Abdur Rouf orally and Abdur Rouf used to possess that suit property on the basis of oral gift and Abdur Rouf subsequently transferred the possession of the suit land excepting one room only on the basis of bainapatra executed by him in favour of the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 1 has also proved by adducing necessary papers that after getting the kabala deed executed and registered through court in respect of the suit property he mutated the suit land in his name and paid rent to the government and got rent receipts and he has constructed also a 7 storied building on the suit land.

13. The plaintiff though has claimed that he was in possession of the suit property within 12 years prior to institution of the suit, but this claim of the plaintiff even if taken as true, does not entitle the plaintiff to get the decree as prayed for. Because according to the own case of the plaintiff Nurjahan Begum was possessing the suit land till her death in 1978 and this suit was filed in 1984. So, the plaintiff, if at all, took possession of the suit property after the death of Nurjahan Begum he possessed the same only for 5/6 years before filing of this suit. Since we have already found that at the death of Nurjahan Begum the plaintiff could not acquire any right, title or interest in the suit property the alleged possession of the plaintiff in the suit property for 5/6 years only does not entitle him l to get a decree in this suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession.

14. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali. the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent has argued also to the effect that since the plaintiff- respondent got a decree for partition in respect of the suit land in Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 from a competent court of law his claim of title in the suit property cannot be brushed asides. But we are unable to accept this argument also of the learned Counsel. We have already I found that Nurjahan Begum acquired valid title in the suit property by virtue of long possession of more than 12 years on the basis of an invalid registered lease deed. So, the plaintiff or other heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab had no right, title and possession in the suit land. The Partition Suit being Title Suit No. 167 of 1975 was filed among the heirs of Abdul Wahab and it was decreed on compromise. The pro-forma defendant No. 2 Abdul Roof though was made a defendant in that partition suit, but admittedly, he was not made a party in that compromise petition and he did not sign that compromise petition. However, where the suit property belonged to Nurjahan Begum this Partition Suit No. 167 of 1975 filed among the heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab and the decree thereof arc not of any value at all, rather this compromise decree is a nullity. On the basis of this compromise decree the plaintiff or any other of the parties of that compromise acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property and this compromise decree is not binding on Abdur Rouf also-who did not sign the compromise petition.

15. However, on careful scrutiny of the evidence on record we find that the trial court and the appellate court below, on correct evaluation and appreciation of the evidence on record, rightly found that the plaintiff never had/has any right title and possession in the suit land. The trial court, therefore, rightly dismissed the suit and the appellate court below rightly affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court.

<u>16. The High Court Division has committed wrong in decreeing the suit of the plaintiff setting aside the concurrent findings and decision of the court of facts. The High Court Division appears to have decreed the suit holding it as not barred by limitation. The High Court Division made observations to the effect that according to the own case of the contesting defendant No.1 he got possession of the suit land partly in the year 1977 when the bainapatra was made and got possession of the rest of the suit land in the year 1979 through court in execution of the decree in Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 and that the present suit .was filed in the year 1984 and as such it was not barred by Limitation. Obviously, the High Court Division did not take into consideration at all the admitted fact that Hazi Abdul Wahab-the original owner of the suit land transferred the suit land to Nurjahan Begum by a registered deed of the year 1958 and since then Nurjahan Begum was in possession of the suit land by exercising her own right and title thereon and thus acquired good title in the suit land by virtue of adverse possession for about 20 years till her death and as such at the death of Nurjahan Begum the heris of Hazi Abdul Wahab including the plaintiff could not acquire any right, title arid interest in the suit land. Nurjahan Begum admittedly, died in the year 1978 and as such the plaintiff though adduced some evidence to prove that he possessed the suit land for some period after the death of Nurjahan Begum in the year 1978 but this fact does not entitle him to get a decree for declaration of title and khas possession. The High Court Division took into consideration the alleged sloe decree passed in Partition Suit No. 167 of 1975 and opined that by virtue of this decree the plaintiff has got the suit property in his share ignoring the fact altogether that the plaintiff and the other heirs of Hazi Abdul Wahab did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land at the death of Nurjahan Begum-who acquired valid right, title and interest in the suit land by virtue of long possession for more than 20 years on the basis of a registered lease deed, though invalid. The High Court Division's further findings that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 231 of 1977 for specific performance of contract is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act since it was obtained during pendency of the partition suit-also is not correct. Since the decree of the Partition Suit No. 167 of 1975 is a nullity, doctrine of lis-pendency will not hit the decree passed in Title Suit No. 231 of 1977.</u>

17. However, from the above discussion it is evident, that the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division has been erroneous and as such cannot be sustained in law.

18. In the circumstances this appeal succeeds.

19. Hence ordered that the appeal be allowed on contest against the respondent No. 1 and ex-parte against the rest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division he set aside and those of the appellate court below and the trial court be affirmed.

End.

parties:
Collector of Customs and others ------ Appellants
Vs
TK Oil Refinery Ltd and 22 others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J : The above appeals, by leave, are directed against the common judgment and order dated 18-8-1998 of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition Nos.704, 2304, 2305, 1935, 1564, 1172, 1155, 1536, 1391, 1561, 1583, 2105, 1425, 1562, 2112, 1163, 1730, 1429, 1845, 2014, 2296, 2297, 2012 and 2015 of 1994 making absolute the Rules obtained impugning the Circular dated 3-7-94 issued by the Controller, Customs Valuation Division, the respondent No.4, fixing the value of Crude Degummed Soybean Oil, CDSO, and also Crude Palm Oil, CPO, as shown in the above circular and also impugning the order, dated 28-11-94 and 29-11-94 issued by the appellant No.1 imposing duty based on the enhanced value of US$ 574.50 per metric tonne in terms of the above Circular dated 3-7-94 in disregard of the invoice value.

2. The respondent in Civil Appeal No. 8 of 2002 filed Writ Petition No. 2304 of 1994 on the averments that they opened L/C dated 25-4-94 for import of 1000 metric tonnes of CDSO at the rate of US $ 443 per metric tonne C & F Chittagong as shown in the invoice and after arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port they, through their Clearing and Forwarding Agent, submitted bill of entry of 22-8-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other taxes and charges on the basis of invoice value but the appellant No.1 directed the respondents to declare the value of the imported goods @ US$ 574 per metric tonne fixed as the indicative value of the goods by the Memo dated 3-7-1994 and also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

3. The respondents in other appeals filed respective writ petitions challenging similar orders on the averments which are more or less similar.

4. The common contentions of the respondents in the above writ petitions were that the above circular and orders (a) are contrary to the provisions of Customs Act, (b) the impugned orders made by the Customs authority in different Nathies for the purpose of assessment of customs duties were arbitrary (c) there was no objective basis of fixation of the value of CDSO and CPO, imported by the respondents for the purpose of assessment of customs duties (d) the customs officials acted illegally in giving direction to the respondents to declare value at a value which the authorities fixed at their level without notifying the same in the Gazette, (e) the National Board of Revenue, the appellant No.2, as well as customs officials, are not legally authorised to fix value of a particular imported merchandise in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties, (f) the appellant No.2 as well as the customs officials acted in a colourable manner in fixing the value in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties which in other way was nothing but the tariff value and, as such, the value so fixed, having not been notified in the official Gazette, the action of the customs authority of taking the predetermined value as per circular dated 3-7-94 is illegal; (g) there being no law authorising the appellant No.2 as well as customs officials to fix value of any imported merchandise as indicative value in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties, the action of the appellants in making direction to the respondents to declare the said indicative value is violative of Article 31 of the Constitution.

5. The appellants filed affidavits-in-opposition in some of the writ petitions, which were used in all the writ petitions, contending that by the SRO dated 9-6-1994, the tariff value on CDSO and CPO were deleted and even after the deletion of the tariff value the customs authority, in the absence of tariff value, was competent to fix normal price of the imported goods prevalent in the national and international markets under section 25(1) of the Customs Act and in fixing the normal value by the Tax Assessing Agency and the price shown in the invoice was not binding upon the said agency and the said circular dated 3-7-94 is an internal communication and the Customs Authority, being empowered by the provisions of section 25(1) of the Act. has fixed the normal price in advance; it is not correct that the current price of CDSO ranged from US$ 438 to 442 per metric tonne and for the purpose of determination  of normal price of CDSO and CPO the appellants through their agencies, particularly through Bangladesh Embassy in Malaysia, collected price of CDSO which was at US$ 574 per metric tonne and taking into consideration the international market price and the interest of the importers, business communities and consumers, the Customs authorities fixed the indicative value of CDSO at US$ 575 per metric tonne and that when the bills of entry were submitted there was no tariff value and accordingly, the appellants did not commit any illegality in giving the directions to the respondents to declare the value of CDSO and CPO as mentioned in the order made on the body of the bills of entry; the object of fixing the price through the Circular dated 3-7-1994 was to prevent under invoicing of' the value of the imported goods and accordingly, in fixing the price circulated by the Circular dated 3-7- 94 the appellants acted quite fairly and reasonably in exercise of their statutory power; further, it is also not correct that the respondents were not aware of the above Circular dated 3-7-94 as they, against the above circular, made representations to the appellant No.2 for reconsidering the value of CDSO and CPO so fixed and they in their above representations admitted that they imported some quantity of CDSO at the rate of US$ 580/585 per metric tonne and, as such, it was very much clear that the price fixed by the appellant No. 2 was the prevalent price of the CDSO and CPO in the international market; the association of the respondents also had dialogue with the appellants in connection with the fixing of the price of the imported goods and they, by their letter dated 16-7-94, represented to the appellant No.2 to reconsider the matter of lowering the value of CDSO and CPO as shown in the Circular of 3-7-94 and to allow the respondents to take delivery of the oil imported by them on assessment of customs duty on the basis of tariff value in respect of imports where letters of credit were opened prior to the deletion of the tariff value.

6. The respondents filed affidavit-in-reply contending that the Government is not competent to fix any price like the indicative price and whatever price is fixed by the Government for the purpose of assessment of customs duties the same is required to be notified through official Gazette; the price that has been fixed as indicative value by Circular dated 3-7-94 has no nexus to the international market price of the CDSO and CPO; the Circular dated 3-7- 94 being merely internal communication has no legal sanction for assessment of customs duties at a rate different from the invoice value or at a value higher than the prevalent tariff value; the appellants have obtained the price of CDSO from the countries which are not regular exporting countries and, as such, fixation of the price on the basis thereof can- not be considered as a dependable basis; the respondents imported the CDSO and CPO at a price which was quoted by their exporter and the appellants have not obtained the price of CDSO and CPO prevalent in the countries like Brazil and Argentina where from the respondents imported the CDSO and CPO and, as such, the price that has been relied upon in the fixation of price of CDSO and CPO as circulated through the Circular dated 3-7-94 has no nexus and bearing in the matter of fixation of the value of CDSO and CPO imported by the respondents; further, the respondents opened the letter of credit prior to the fixation of the indicative value and, as such indicative value fixed subsequent to the opening of letters of credit is in no way applicable to the matter of assessment of customs duties of the oil imported by the respondents.

7. The High Court Division, after hearing, made the Rules absolute.

8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney- General appearing for the appellants in support of the leave granting order, submitted that though the appellants could not substantiate assessment on the basis of indicative value as not being contemplated under the Customs Act, but in terms of the provisions of section 25(1) of the Customs Act in case of disagreement with the invoice value the authority was entitled to determine the normal price of the imported goods and the High Court Division erred in law in not giving direction to assess the customs duties and other taxes on the basis of normal price to be determined in accordance with law considering the prevalent market price at the country of origin with an opportunity to the importers to produce any paper or documents in support of their invoice values, inasmuch as the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act are applicable in respect of both the value as well as rate of duty to any imported goods on the date on which bill of entry is presented under section 79 of the Act and, as such, the direction of the High Court Division to make assessment on the basis of the prevalent tariff value on the date of opening of letter of credit, which stood deleted long before the date of filing of the bill of entry, instead of assessment of normal value of the import is not sustainable and the finding of the High Court Division that the respondents by opening of letter of credit when tariff value was prevalent, acquired a vested right of assessment on the basis of tariff, is contrary to the principles as laid down in Mizanur Rahman's case, 52 DLR (AD) 149 and further the Government has authority to determine the normal prices and realise duty thereon at the rate prevailing on the date of submission of the bill of entry.

<u>9. The learned Counsel for the respondents submitted that section 25 of the Customs Act, 1969 does not authorise the appellants to issue the circular dated 3-7-1994 and the same has been issued arbitrarily and without lawful authority as section 25 envisages determination of normal value under section 25(1) or fixation of tariff value by notifying through Gazette under section 25(7) and does not provide for determination of any "indicative value" as done in the present case and the appellants did not also make an attempt to determine normal value under section 25(1) of the Act based on any authentic contemporary evidence upon notifying the importer; further, since the points as raised in the leave stage had not been taken before the Court below, the appellants cannot raise such new points now; after the bills of entry were presented considerable time has already elapsed in the meantime and, as such, the prayer of the appellants made at this belated stage to allow them to determine normal value of the goods would amount to giving the appellants highest latitude though they, all along, acted in violation of law and tried to extract money from the respondents by fixing "indicative value" which is a foreign and unknown terminology; the invoice value/C&F value of the goods imported by the respondents being US$ 354 per metric tonne, the customs duty and other taxes thereon should be assessed on the basis of invoice value since there was no tariff value on the date of presentation of the bills of entry; the Circular dated 3-7-1994 and orders dated 28-11-1994 and 29-11-94 have been made without lawful authority, inasmuch as the value sought to be fixed for assessment of customs duties and other taxes on the said imported goods is arbitrary and without lawful authority and there is no authority conferred by section 25 to determine any 'indicative value' by a circular as has been done in the present case and section 25 of the Customs Act did not authorise the appellants to issue the impugned circular, inasmuch as section 25 only authorises to fix tariff value to be determined and fixed by Gazette notification under section 25(7) and does not provide for any authority to determine the value of imported goods by any circular.</u>

<u>10. As it appears, the High Court Division made the Rules absolute holding that a reading of the provisions of section 25(1)(2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Customs Act show that the Customs Authority is authorised to assess customs duties of imported goods at the value prevalent on the date when the bill of entry is presented for assessment of customs duties but, in the present case, the Customs authority fixed the indicative value for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO and CPO imported by the respondents long before the presentation of the bill of entry and accordingly, "indicative value", that has been fixed by the circular dated 3-7-94, cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of section 25(1)(2) and (3) of the Customs Act and that in terms of the above section the Customs Authority, in appropriate cases, no doubt, is competent to fix normal value of imported goods upon rejection of the invoice value or the declared value but in such a case the Customs authority would be required to notify importers informing them that the Customs authority is not accepting the invoice value or declared value as the basis for the purpose of assessment of customs duty and is going to fix the normal price of the imported goods for the assessment of customs duties and the customs authority would also be required to afford an opportunity to the importers to place their cases, if any, in support of their claim that the invoice value, in fact, is the normal price of the imported merchandise for the purpose of assessment of customs duties or that as against the invoice/ declared value of the imported goods the customs authority is going to tax the normal price of the goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duties but, in the instant case, that has not been done by the customs authority and the Customs authority fixed, through internal circular, certain prices of CDSO and CPO for the purpose of assessment of customs duties terming the same as "indicative value" but under the Customs Act, the revenue realising Authority or the Customs Authority is authorised to fix tariff value under section 25(7) of the Act at a prior date through Gazette notification for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and the indicative value that has been fixed later on and circulated through Circular dated 3-7-94 was admittedly not notified in the official Gazette; the learned Attorney-General submitted that the fixation of normal value in every case of imports upon notifying the individual importer would be an impossible task and, as such, for the sake of convenience, the revenue authority has fixed the value of the imported merchandise at a prior date through the Circular dated 3-7-94 for making the same as the basis for assessment of the customs duties in disregard of the invoice value, but the above submission cannot be accepted because in fixing the citizen with the liability of payment of tax, the concerned authority is required by strict compliance of law authorising it to fix a citizen with the liability of payment of tax and the plea of impossibility of fixation of the normal value of the imported merchandise in the case of each individual importer upon hearing him or that upon affording him an opportunity to place his case, if any, in support of the invoice value, cannot be accepted and the respondents, under the law, cannot be allowed to resort to the practice of pre-fixation of the value of the imported goods for assessment of customs duties in that the Government or any other agency authorised by the delegated legislation can- not act in a manner which is not authorised or provided in the law or by the law; further, the affidavit of the appellant does not show that price to the CDSO and CPO at which those were sold by the countries wherefrom import was made by the respondents, being not taken into consideration at the time of fixing the "indicative value", the statement of the appellants in Annexure-2 to the affidavit-in-opposition to the effect that the price of CDSO in the international market at the relevant time was at about US$ 580/585 per metric tonne and, in that state of the matter, the appellants were quite correct in fixing the value of the goods in question at the amount circulated through the Circular dated 3-7-94, cannot be accepted and in no way it can be said that the invoice value of the respective imports did not reflect the value prevalent in the international market and, be that as it may, the fact remains that appellants, by law or under the law, are not authorised by an internal circular to fix any value like indicative value of any imported merchandise in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties. The High Court also did not accept the submissions of the learned Attorney-General that, in terms of the principle laid down in PLD 1988 Karachi 99, the matter of assessment of customs duties of the goods in question be sent back to the customs authority for making assessment after hearing the respondents as the facts of the above case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant cases.</u>

11. As it appears, at the conclusion, the High Court Division directed that the customs authority is to assess the customs duties of the goods in respect of which the letters of credit were opened prior to the deletion of the tariff value by the SRO dated 9- 6-1994 on the basis of tariff value prevalent at the time of opening of letters of credit and in other cases taking the invoice value but the above order of the High Court Division to the extent that "in other cases taking the invoice value" is modified to the extent, that if the invoice value as shown by the respondents are not acceptable to them the Customs Authority will be at liberty to fix normal price in terms of the provisions of section 25(1) of the Customs Act in accordance with law and then assess customs duty and other duties on the basis of normal price so fixed.

All the appeals are dismissed with the observation as made above.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2178 of 2009
lawyer:
Garib-E-Newaz, Advocate instructed by A.K.M. Shahidul Huq Advocate on Record ----- For the Petitioners 
Respondents ----- Not represented
parties:
Kadbanu Bibi and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Wazed Ali Sikder and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 25.05.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3610 of 1995)
full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J.:- Instant application under Article 103 of the Constitution is directed against the judgment and order dated 25/05/2009 passed by the High Court Division discharging the rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3610 of 1995 thereby affirmed the judgment and decree dated 18/06/1995 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal, dismissing the Title Appeal No. 30 of 1992 affirming the judgment and decree dated 28/01/1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mehendigonj, Barisal, decreeing the Title Suit No. 26 of 1990 declaring that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mehendigonj, Barisal, as illegal, collusive and void.

<u>2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the instant petition are that the respondent No. 1 hereof as plaintiff filed the suit against the petitioner, as principal Defendant, and others contending, amongst others, that the schedule property in the suit belonged to petitioner No. 1 hereof, who entered into an agreement for sale of the same to the plaintiff-respondent hereof in 20.03.1989 on receipt of Tk. 1200/- as advance out of the consideration money and the possession was also delivered and thereafter on receipt of the balance of the consideration amount on 14.04.1985 required sale deed was duly executed and registered and accordingly the plaintiff got his name mutated in the records of right and have been paying the land revenue to the Government and that on or about 08.04.1990 the plaintiff came to know that the defendant-petitioner No. 1 hereof filed Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 without adding the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 hereof as a party in the suit and accordingly the plaintiff filed an application for adding him as a defendant in the suit, which was rejected on 09.04.1990 upon hearing the parties, and that on the same day a sole decree was passed in Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 on the basis of a compromise petition. The defendant No. 1-petitioner hereof claimed that he got the suit land by way of gift vide a registered heba-bil-ewaj deed dated 10.12.1981 from his minor son but the said minor son transferred the suit property along with other properties to the plaintiff prior to execution of the said heba deed and thus the heba deed was fraudulent, collusive and void document also being made without consideration and therefore the said son could not subsequently inherit the suit property from his mother the defendant No. 1, after her death, and that the decree in Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 was obtained on the basis of a solenama and that too by practicing fraud upon the Court and therefore the impugned decree is void, illegal, without jurisdiction and liable to be cancelled.</u>

3. The defendant No.1 petitioner hereof contested the suit by filling written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit property belonged to Azid Ali Bepari and that the defendant No. 1 was the wife of Azid Ali Bepari and that the said Azid Ali Bepari gifted the suit land in favour of the defendant No. 2, son of defendant No. 1 on 10.12.1981, who at the relevant time was a minor and delivery of possession was received by the defendant No. 1 on behalf of her minor son, the defendant No. 2, and accordingly they were enjoying usufructs from the suit land on payment land revenue and that the gift was genuine and that there was no act of fraud in the transfer through the heba deed and that the defendant No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 547 of 1983 for setting aside the heba deed and that by suppressing the service of summons of the case and playing fraud upon the Court obtained an exparte decree against the defendant No. 1 on 09.06.1986 and that thereafter for setting aside the said exparte decree the defendant No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 and that the defendant No. 1 though entered into a 2nd marriage yet used to visit her first husband's house regularly and she possessed the suit property along with other properties through her brothers. Azid Ali Bepari being defendant No. 1 in the said suit (Title Suit No. 76 of 1989) filed a solenama and accordingly the Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 was decreed on the basis of said solenama setting aside the decree passed in Title Suit No. 547 of 1983 and that the plaintiff was not made a party in said Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 and that the defendant No. 2 denied to have entered into any agreement with the plaintiff or executed any baina patra in respect of the said property and that the possession of suit property was never handed over to the plaintiff and that the sale deed dated 14.04.1985 is a collusive, void, antedated and illegal one and that the baina patra dated 20.03.1980 was a created document to undo the heba deed dated 10.12.1981.

4. On consideration of the materials and evidence on record and the submissions of the learned Advocate appearing for the respective parties, the learned Assistant Judge, decreed the suit on contest against the defendant-petitioner No. 1 hereof and exparte against the rest setting aside the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 declaring the same to be void, illegal, collusive, without jurisdiction and nullity.

5. Being aggrieved, the defendant-petitioner No. 1 hereof filed Title Appeal No. 30 of 1992 before the learned District Judge, Barisal, and the said appeal, on transfer, was heard and dismissed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal, and that in the appeal the petitioner Nos. 2 and 3 were added as appellant Nos. 2 and 3 claiming to have become owners in some part of the suit property by purchase from the defendant-petitioner No. 1 hereof and that being aggrieved by such dismissal the defendant-appellant-petitioners hereof moved the High Court Division in civil Revision No. 3610 of 1995 and upon hearing, the Rule, issued therein, has been discharged by the High Court Division by the judgment and order impugned in the instant civil petition.

6. We have perused the leave petition and the judgments of the Courts below as annexed to the petition as well as the provisions of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and considered the submissions of the learned Advocate.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that the suit being a suit for declaration simplicitor is not maintainable as per provisions of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as in the prayer portion of the plaintiff in the suit land and that the Appellate Division in several cases has held that a suit in which title of the plaintiff has been disputed by the defendant, a declaration of title and possession is necessary and in the absence of a prayer for such declaration such suit is not maintainable in view of the provision to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and hence the decree as passed is illegal and not maintainable.

8. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that specific issue was framed being issue No. 4. “বাদীর নালিশী জমিতে স্বত্ত্ব দখল আছে কি? and that the contesting parties in the suit have contested the said issue with evidence and that the trial Court on consideration of the materials and evidence on record as well as the submissions made by the learned Advocates of the contesting parties found the title and possession of the plaintiff on the suit land and further it appears that though in the prayer portion such specific prayer for declaration title and possession was not made but in the body of the plaint the title and possession of the plaintiff was claimed and that since the question of title and possession was made an issue in deciding that suit and contesting the parties without raising any objection contested the same being issue No. 4 quoted above and the trial Court on consideration of the materials and evidence on record found the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit, the defect as alleged was cured, more so when no objection was raised against such defect in the suit and when no objection was raised against the framing of said issue No. 4. It seems that the trial Court on its wisdom to adjudicate the case property, on consideration of the pleadings of the parties, framed the said issue No. 4 in accordance with law.

<u>9. We are of the view that the decisions of the Appellate Division on the point of maintainability referring to Section-42 of the Specific Relief Act, as submitted by the learned Advocate, are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and that in fact the contesting parties were given due opportunity to contest the issue framed to decide the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. It further appears that the appellate Court below also considered the issue of title and possession of the plaintiff respondent No. 1 hereof on the suit land and found that the impugned gift deed to be a void document since the recipient was minor at the relevant time and had no occasion to purchase any 'jainamaz' and deliver the same as consideration for the gift, as alleged, and that the Appellate Court below in detail discussed the case as well as the evidence available on record and dismissed the appeal with cost affirming the judgment of the trial Court. It also appears that the High Court Division has considered all aspects of the cases, including the issue No. 4 framed and decided by the trial Court, in the following manner:</u>

<u>"On appeal, it appears, the learned Appellate Court also considering the evidence and materials on record came to the finding that the plaintiff acquired title in the suit land by registered kabala dated 24.04.1985 executed and registered by Aid Ali and that the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land since then and that Kadbanu or Kadam Ali did not acquire any title in the suit land by heba-bil-ewaj dated 10.12.1981 and that Kadam Ali being minor at the relevant time had no capacity to give Jainamaj and Tasbih' in exchange of the gift and that no possession was handed over to Kadbanu Bibi or Kadam Ali and that the defendant did not produce the original heba-bil-ewaj deed in the Court, but produced the certified copy of the same and that Azid Ali knew to give his signature but he has executed the heba-bil-ewaj deed by putting thump impression and that the heba-bil-ewaj deed was not acted upon. On these findings the learned appellate Court dismissed the appeal. It appears, the present suit is a suit for declaration that the decree dated 09.04.1990 passed in Title Suit No. 76 of 1989 is void, fraudulent and not binding on the plaintiff as he was not made party in the said suit though he claims to be the owner of the suit land by registered deed dated 14.04.1985. Both the Courts found that the present plaintiff was a necessary party in the said suit, but he was not made party and that his application for addition of party was rejected by the trial Court. The case of the defendant is that the suit as framed is not maintainable. According to the learned Advocate for the petitioner the defendants having challenged the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the present suit, the plaintiff ought to have prayed for declaration of his title in the suit land along with the prayer for declaration that the decree dated 09.04.1990 is void. According to the learned Advocate in the present suit no prayer for declaration of title having been made, the present suit for declaration that the decree dated 09.04.1990 is void is not maintainable. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the decision of Ratan Chandra Dey and others Vs. Jinnator Nahar and others reported in 13 MLR (AD) 168 and the decision of Md. Jashimuddin (Kanchan) Vs. Md. Ali Ashraf reported in 11 BLD (AD) 101 wherein there lordships of the Appellate Division held that when the defendant in his written statement claim title and possession in the suit land, a simple suit for declaration that a decree or a deed is void is not maintainable, without first establishing his title to the suit land. The proposition of law as has been decided in the said 2 decisions are not disputed, but in the present case both the Courts correctly found that the plaintiff was able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. It may be noted that the trial Court framed issue No. 4 to the effect that whether the plaintiff has got right, title and possession in the suit land and the trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record specifically found that the plaintiff has got title and possession in the suit land. Since in the present suit an issue has been framed as to the title and possession of the plaintiff and both the Courts found that he got right, title and possession in the suit land, in my opinion, further declaration regarding title of the plaintiff is not essential in the present suit land as such in the absence of such prayer for declaration of title, the present suit as framed in also maintainable. Thus it shows that the facts of the present case is distinguishable from the facts of the above reported eases and as such, in my opinion those decisions are not applicable in the present case."</u>

<u>10. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and as the contesting parties contested the issue No. 4 as to the title and possession on the suit land, having had all opportunities, we do agree with the findings and decision of the High Court Division and further we are of the view that the objection as raised by the learned Advocate referring to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act at this stage do not merit any consideration in the facts and circumstances of the case, discussed hereinabove.</u>

11. Accordingly no interference with the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is called for.

12. Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1262 of 2005
lawyer:
Md. Maqbul Ahmed, Advocate, instructed by A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record. ----- For the Petitioners.

VS
Md. Hafezur Rahman and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3.8.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4479 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J : This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 3.8.2005 passed a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4479 of 1995 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and order dated 19.8.1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd court, Chittagong, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 219 of 1991 reversing those of dated 20.8.1991 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Raozan, Chittagong, in Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1988 allowing pre-emption.

<u>2. The respondent No. 1 instituted the above miscellaneous case for pre-emption of the case land measuring 9½ decimals of land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or in the alternative under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949, on the averments that the above land originally belonged to Yunus Mia Chowdhury, the opposite party No.2, who sold the same to Amina Khatoon, the predecessor of the opposite party No.1 by registered sale deed dated 27.7.87 which was entered in the volume on 23.2.88; Amina Khatoon is a stranger to the case jote; the notice of the above sale deed being collusively suppressed, the pre-emptor, a co-sharer of the case jote, had no knowledge of the above transfer and he came to know about the same only on 3.4.88 and thereafter on 11.4.1988 he filed this miscellaneous case.</u>

3. The pre-emptee petitioner contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations and contending that the pre-emptor not being a co-sharer the case for pre-emption is liable to be rejected.

4. The learned Assistant Judge, after hearing, allowed the pre-emption holding that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court Chittagong, after hearing, allowed the appeal holding that the pre-emptor is' not co-sharer. The respondent No.1 then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 4479 of 1994 and after hearing, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that B.S. Record, Ext.3, and the sale deed Ext. 5 (Ka) by which the pre-emptor purchased his land in the case jote, clearly show that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case jote and the finding of the appellate Court to the effect that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case jote being not based on correct assessment of the evidence on record can not be sustained.

5. The learned counsel for the pre-emptee petitioner submits that the High Court Division fell in error in not considering that the deed dated 27.7.87, against which pre-emption is sought, is not in fact a transfer deed as in the same value of the case land was shown at merely Tk. 98/- and further the possession of the land covered under the above deed was also not delivered and so the above deed may be termed as a deed for protection of possession of the pre-emptee petitioner against which a pre-emption case is not maintainbale; the appellate Court correctly found that the pre-emptee is not wholly a stranger in view of the fact that her husband Ranju Miah was one of the co-sharers in the R.S. Khatian No. 2480 and further as the B.S. Record was not correctly prepared and for that the recorded tenant executed and registered the above deed dated 27.7.87 for removal of that mistake and the said deed as is in fact not a sale deed; the High Court Division having had failed to take notice that the pre-emptee petitioner was not a stranger to the case jote and that she has been possessing the case land and residing in the homestead situated therein for long time and if the pre-emption case is allowed the paternal homestead of the petitioner will go into the hand of the pre-emptor.

<u>6. As it appears the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that the pre-emptor purchased a portion of the case jote by Ext. 5(Ka) and his name was recorded in the B.S. record, Ext.3, in Khatian No. 54 and the rent receipts Ext.4 series, also show that he, after purchasing the said land, mutated his name and paid rents regularly and he, as co-sharer, is in possession in the case land and the B.S. Khatian which has been published finally does not contain the name of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptee has also not challenged that preparation of B.S. Khatian in the name of the pre-emptor and so prima facie the pre-emptor appears to be a co-sharer and further the title of the pre-emptor in the case land can be challenged by the pre-emptee only in a properly constituted title suit.</u>

7. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the evidence and the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. The learned counsel could not point at any illegality or infirmity in the decision of the High Court Division so as to call for any interference.

8. The petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1431 of 2009
lawyer:
Md. Shardur Abul Hossain, Advocate, (appeared with the leave of the Court) Instructed by Md. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 11.05.09 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 57 of 2003)
full_judgment:
B. K. Das J. This application for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and, order dated 11.5.09 of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division making the rule being Civil Revision No. 157 of 2003 absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree of the courts below and decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. 

2. The respondent Nos. 1-8 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 18 of 1997 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Kasba, Brahmanbaria, impleading the present petitioner as defendants and respondent nos. 9-22 as other defendant and respondent no. 23 as Preformat defendant, praying for declaration of title to the suit land and for recovery of Khas possession there-in alleging, inter alia, that the suit plot No. 638 and 639 along with on non suited plot no. 643 measuring 39 decimals of land originally belonged to Samena Bibi which was finally published in her name in C. S. Khatian and that the said Samena Bibi died leaving behind her only daughter Amena Khatun and thereafter Amena Khatun died leaving behind her daughter Malekernessa alias Melaka. While Melaka was owning and possessing the said plots she transferred the entire land of plot no. 643 by executing and registering deed of sale no. 3219 dated 26.4.62 and 07 decimals of land from the suit plots by executing and registering another deed of sale bearing no. 4967 dated 6.12.72 to the plaintiff no. 4 Abdul Sobhan alias Sobhan Miah. After purchase he mutated his name and got Jama separated in separation case no. 22483-84 by ' creating a separate Khatian no. 982 and took a loan from the Janata Bank, Brahmanbaria branch by mortgaging the said 07 decimals of land. Thereafter Maleka Begum died leaving behind one son Abdul Hossain, father of plaintiff no. 5, who died leaving behind plaintiff nos. 3-5 as his sons and daughter and thus the plaintiff nos. 1-4 became the owners of .27 decimals of land in the suit plot by way of purchase and by inheritance. It is further stated that in S.A. operation the suit property along with the property of plot no. 643 has been wrongly recorded in the name of one Aderjaman and other, predecessors of the defendants in khatian no. 117. The plaintiff learnt about the wrong record in the S. A. khatian on the basis of so-called partition suit no. 172 of 1929. The defendant no. 5 with the help of other defendants forcibly entered into the land of plot no. 638 on 30.9.96 and constructed two ducal tin shed and 3 chouchala tin shed defying the objection raised by plaintiff no. 3. 

3. The defendant no. 5 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suit plot no. 638 and 639 along with non suited plot no. 643 measuring an area of .39 decimals of land belonged to Samena Bibi and her name was rightly recorded in C. S. Khatian. Samena Khatun subsequently defaulted to pay rents and the Talukder was going to file a suit for realization of rent when Samena Bibi executed Istafanama deed dated 06.06.1920 and surrendered the property in favour of the landlord who settled the property to Munshi Mia son of Nawaj Ali on 10.09.1921 and thus Munshi Sheikh became the sole owner of the land of the said 3 plots and has been in possession of the said land and prayed for dis-missal of the suit. 

4. The Mal Court took necessary evidence both oral and documentary and on hearing the parties by the impugned judgment and decree dated 19.04.49 dismissed the suit. 

5. Being aggrieved thereby the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal no. 74 of 1999 before the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria, and that the 1st Court of the Additional District Judge, Brahmanbaria by judgment and decree dated 23.7.2002 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the decision of the trial Court. 

6. Being aggrieved thereby the plaintiff as petitioner moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision no. 57 of 2003 and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the rule absolute, set aside the judgment and decree of the courts below and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. 

7. Being aggrieved thereby the defendant as petitioner filed the instant petition seeking leave to appeal before the Appellate Division. Mr. Sharder Abul Hossain, the learned Advocate appears with the leave of the court for the petitioner while Mr. Mazibur Rahman, the learned-on-record appears on behalf the of respondent nos. 1-4 and 7.

8. We have heard the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and all other evidence on record. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in disturbing the findings of facts arrived at by both the Courts below and on misreading of the evidence on record committed an error of law in holding that the plaintiffs did not mention the date of cause of action and the date of dispossession and also gave perverse finding upon non-consideration of the findings of facts recorded by the lower appellate Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned judge of the High Court Division committed an error of law in holding that the suit is barred by limitation and also in finding that the plaintiffs did not adduce any direct evidence to prove alleged dispossession. 

9. The grounds and submissions appear to have merit. 

10. Accordingly, leave is granted. 

11. Security of Tk. 1,000/-is to be deposited within 1(one) month. 

12. The petitioners are permitted to pre-pare the paper book out of court in accordance with the Rules. 

13. The order of stay granted earlier, by this Division shall continue till disposal of the appeal. 

End.
