case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 8.8.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3667 of 1993.)
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha J. This appeal by leave is directed from a judgment of the High Court Division in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. The suit out of which this appeal arises is for partition filed by the respondents.

2. Their claims are that the suit Jama recorded in C.S. Khatian Nos.  84, 69 and 47, described in schedule Nos.  1,3 and 4 was owned and possessed by Karful Bewa and the Jama in the C.S. Khatian Nos. 120, 53 and 16 of Mouza Jamalpur now Palisha Indrakuchi and Pakhalia described in schedule Nos. 2, 5 and 6 was owned and possessed by Karful Bewa and Barandi Mondal in equal share. Barandi Mondal died leaving 4 sons, the defendant No. 5 Azijatullah Mondal, Shahed Ali Mondal, Alimuddin Mondal and Jabbar Mondal and 4 daughters, Nekjan, Sokina, Sakiran and Atarjan. Shahed Ali died leaving behind one son Baitullah and 3 daughters, the defendant No. 7, Most. Hinduri, Zahiran and Ahiran. Zahiran died leaving her husband the defendant No. 8. Ohiran died leaving 4 sons, defendant Nos. 9-12. Alimuddin died leaving the defendant No. 13 and 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 17-19 and Haziran. Haziran died leaving her only son, the defendant No. 20. Abdul Jabber died leaving Sons and daughters, the defendant Nos. 21-31, Nekjan Bewa died after the promulgation of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance,1961 leaving son Khamir Master and the defendant Nos. 24- 31 and son Jasim Uddin. Khamir Master died Leaving 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 25-27 and 3 daughters, the defendant Nos. 38-30. Jasimuddin died leaving behind wife, the defendant Nos. 30 and 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 33-35 and 2 daughters, the defendant Nos. 36 and 37, Sakina died leaving 2 sons, the defendant Nos. 38 and 39 and 2 daughters, Sahera and Rahima and husband Nazar Master Ralunan and the defendant No. 50. Naser Master died leaving daughter, the defendant No. 41. Atarjan died leaving behind her husband, the defendant No. 42 and 2 sons, the defendant Nos. 43 and 44, and 4 daughters, the defendant Nos. 45-48. Julekha died leaving the defendant No. 49. Karpul Bewa died leaving 2 brothers, Samir Mondal and Sadar Mondal. Samir Mondal died leaving wife Asimon and son Abdul Mondal. Sadar Mondal died leaving son Taison Ali and daughter Tambiton Bewa. Ahdul Mondal sold 2.76 acres of land by Kabala deed dated 11th September, 1961 to the plaintiff No. 1. Taison and Asimon sold 3.30 acres of land to the plaintiff No. 2 by Kabala dated 1st September, 1961. Taison, Abdul and Asimon Bewa transferred 2.85½ acres of land to Fulzan by deed of exchange. Fulzan died leaving behind her son the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 daughters, the defendant Nos. 2-4, Plaintiff No. 2 sold .30 acre and .45 acre of land out of his purchased and inherited land to the plaintiff No. 1 by two Kabalas. Plaintiff No. 2 transferred some land to his wife, Keni Bibi, and Rahimuddin sold .75 acres of land to the plaintiff No. 3. Thus plaintiffs possessed 7.32 acres of land in the suit Jama and claimed saham in respect of the same on the ground that the suit Jams was never partitioned. The defendants refused to partition the suit land.

3. Some of the appellants who are defendant Nos. 6-12 and their predecessors contested the suit jointly. Their case in short is that the suit land under C.S. Khatian Nos. 84 and 120 belonged to Barundi Mondal alone. Karful Bewa had no share in the same. The name of Karful Bewa was wrongly recorded in the Khatians. Neither she nor her heirs ever possessed the suit land. The heirs of Borundi Mondal were in possession of the land in CS, Khatians exclusively. The suit jama which was recorded in c.s. Khatian Nos. 69, 47, 53 and 16 of Mouza Pathatia was under possession of Sadi Mondal, who died leaving widow Karful Bewa and brother Barundi Mondal. His widow Karful Bewa inherited 4 annas share in the property left by Sadi Mondal. Borundi possessed 12 annas share. After his death the heirs have been in possession of the property. Karful Bewa had no issue, she had adopted Naimuddin, predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 1-2 and she made a Hiba-bil-ewaz in respect of some property out of the suit khatians to him. There arose dispute between the sons of Borundi Mondal and Naimuddin. Thereafter on 2nd Paush 1337 a deed of relinquishment was executed in respect of the said lands. Tasirudden, the only son of Sadar Mondal executed a Nadabi Patra on 17th January, 1935 in favour of the sons of Borundi Mondal.

4. Defendant Nos. 1-4 and 46 prayed for separate saham. Defendant Nos. 1-4's claim is that their predecessor Fulzan got 2.85 acres of land and died leaving one son, the plaintiff No. 1, and two daughters, the plaintiff Nos. 2-4, Defendant No. 46 stated that Karful Bewa had right, title and interest in the suit jama as described in schedule Nos. 1, 3-4. Burundi and Karful owned and possessed the suit jams described in schedule Nos. 2, 3-5 in equal share. Burundi died leaving 4 Sons and 4 daughters. Sakina died leaving behind husband Nazar Master, brother Azitullah, and sister Atarjan. Nazar Master got 8 annas share of Sakina who died leaving daughter Full Bibi alias Fazilatunnessa. Atarjan died leaving sons the defendant Nos. 39-44, daughters, the defendant Nos. 45-48 and husband Abdur Rahman, who died leaving son and daughters, Abdus Samad, the defendant No. 43, the son of Atarjan Phull Bibi sold .14 acre of land to the defendant No. 46 by Kabala dated 24th December, 1975. Defendant No. 47 sold out .03 acre of land to this defendant by a Kabala and besides, the defendant inherited .07 acre of land in the suit jama and the defendant No. 46 has been in possession of .24 acre of land.

5. The trial court decreed the suit in preliminary   form. On appeal from the said decree, the court of appeal below reversed the judgment. Plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division a revision petition which restored those of the trial court. The High Court Division observed that Karful Bewa was the sole recorded tenant in respect of land in schedule Nos. 1, 3 and 4 and she was also owner of 8 annas share in respect of the land in schedule Nos. 2, 5 and 6 with Borundi Mondal; that the plaintiffs proved that Karful Bewa was the owner in respect of those lands; that exhibits 1(a), 1(b) and 1(e) show that Karful Bewa was a tenant in respect of the suit land; that the court of appeal below misread exhibit series and in view of section 103(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, there is presumptive value about Karful Bewa's title in respect of those land and that the court of appeal below had committed error of law in reversing the judgment of the trial court.

<u>6. Question that calls for consideration is whether the presumptive value that the C.S. khatian can be rebuttable by the S.A, khatian prepared under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the absence of any other evidence. Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that since the S.A, khatian was prepared after hearing objections of the plaintiffs, the High Court,. Division has committed fundamental error in giving the presumptive value to the S.A. Khatians over the S.A. Khatian. In support of his contention he has referred the case of Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal, 17 DLR(SC) 392. The second point raised by the learned counsel is that the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the judgment of the court of appeal below without reversing the findings of fact arrived at by the final court of fact on the question of record of rights.</u>

7. There is no dispute that out of 6 khatians, 4 khatians were prepared showing Sadi Mondal's jote and in respect to two khatians Borundi Mondal's jote was recorded. Of the 6 khatians, Karful Bewa was shown to have exclusive possession in respect of 3 khatians and in respect of other 3 khatians, Karful Bewa had 8 annas share and Borundi Mondal 8 annas share. This Borundi Mondal is the brother of Sadi Mondal. In paragraph 7 of the written statement the defendant Nos. 6 and 21 admitted that Karful Bewa had sixteen annas possession in respect of C.S. Khatian No. 84 and that she had 8 annas share in respect of C.S. Khatian No. 120. It was held in Promatha Nath (supro) that The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record-of-right represents the correct state of affairs on the date it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter, therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof."

<u>8. With due respect I am unable to endorse the above views that after a presumption attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 such presumption diminishes progressively with the lapse of time and that the older the record the less is its presumptive value. H, Rahman, J, did not cite any authority basing upon which he has arrived at such conclusion. An entry in a record-of-rights under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act is presumed to be correct until the contrary is shown. (Anup Mahto V. Mite Dusadh, 59 CLG 147 (PC). It was concluded by the judicial committee that 'therefore all the courts have to do with the Record is to apply this presumption as directed by the section. It is because such record-of-rights was prepared with considerable formality and the proceedings of the Revenue Offices were conducted with publicity after hearing objections against draft record. The Revenue Officers heard and decided disputes following the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure, It is true that no finality attached to them and it was open to the parties to reopen the questions decided in the ordinary civil courts. Until a civil court decides the dispute, a presumption of correctness shall continue. This presumption being statutory one is not taken away merely by an allegation by a party that the entry was not correct. The presumption under this section may be rebutted by either evidence external to the settlement proceedings or evidence of matters apparent on the face of those proceedings.</u>

<u>9. A presumption is a rule of law that courts shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact or from particular evidence unless and until the truth of such inference is disproved. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court from a particular circumstance. A presumption of law is always obligatory being expressed in the, form of an imperative rule of law and therefore, the court is bound to act according to the rule and cannot refuse to draw the presumption. This presumption may or may not be rebuttable. When rebutted it is called rebuttable presumption of law and is indicated in the Evidence Act by the expression 'shall presume'. This presumption occurs in sections 79-85, 89 and 105. When not rebuttable it is called "irrebuttable presumptions of law" or "conclusive proof". Three instances of such presumptions are mentioned in sections 41 and 112. Presumptions are rebuttable, as their evidentiary effect may be negative by contrary proof. They are indicated in the Evidence Act by the expression 'may presume' and are mentioned in sections 86-88, 90 and 114. When a presumption operates in favour of a party, the burden of proof is on the opponent. It is true, a presumption of law in favour of the accuracy of the entry in the record-of-rights cannot arise when the point in issue has already been decided on evidence between the parties by a decision of the civil court.</u>

10. To rebut such presumption the defendants have filed only a khatian, the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, 1950. Except the said khatian, they have failed to produce any other evidence. The court of appeal below held that since the record-of-rights was prepared in the name of the defendants after a contested hearing before the Revenue Officer under section 19(3), the defendants have been able to prove their title in the suit land. There is fallacy in the opinion. The court of appeal below erred in holding the above view for, a record-of-rights prepared under Section 19(3) of the Act of 1950 cannot confer title upon person in whose favour it was prepared. Even the record-of-rights prepared   under the repealed section 143A cannot be the basis of title to the land. It may be used for collateral purpose of possession.   If the views taken by the court of appeal view are accepted, no litigant will be required to take shelter to the civil court for establishing the right, title and interest in the suit land.

11. Section 19 is included in Part IV, Chapter IV under the heading preparation of 'record-of-rights' The said Chapter contains sections 17 to 31 Section 17 provides for preparation of record-of-rights prepared or revised of the interests of all rent-receivers as are liable to be acquired under the provisions of the Act of 1950 with a view to the assessment of compensation payable for all such interests including the interests which have already been acquired under. Chapter II It was held in the Province of Province of East Pakistan V Muhammad Hossain Mia, 16 DLR(SC)667 that the notification contemplated under section 17(3) of the Act was a notification giving notice to the intention of Government to take up preparation of new record-of-rights for the assessment of compensation payable for the interests acquired under the Act, and has a conclusive evidence that the order has been made for the preparation or revision record-of-rights.

12. Section 18 says, the particulars should be recorded in the record-of-rights. When a draft record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 19(1) containing particulars referred to in section 18, the publication of the draft is with a view to receive and consider any objection that may be made as regards any entry in the record-of-rights. The finality referred to in sub-section (3) of section 19 which shall have conclusive evidence is for the purpose of payment of compensation and the court cannot draw any presumption other than that There is no presumption of possession of land in respect of record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) like the one under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Reference in this connection are the cases of Halima Begum V. Syed Ahmed, 21 DLR 854, Chan Mahmood (Md) V. Md. Hossain Ali, 3 BLC 364, Abdul Kader Bari V. Kaiser Ahmed Howlader, 4 BLC 17, Ahmed Meah V. Abdul Majid, BLD 1985 (HCD)47, Md. Naimuddin Sarder V. Abdul Kalam Biswas, 39 DLR(AD) 237. In Halima Begum the preemptor claimed pre-emption as co-sharer on the strength of record-an-right prepared under the Act of 1950. It was observed that record-of-right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to C.S. record of right is not certainly available with regard to State Acquisition Khatians, There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians.... I add here that certainly there will he presumption of the correctness of the B.S. Khatians prepared or to he prepared after a thorough survey which is under process.

13. In Akrab Ali V. Zahiruddin, 30 DLR(SC) 81 relates to presumption as to the entries in the settlement records. The settlement khatian was recorded as 'jote Aftab Uddin Sarkar occupant Faizuddin Haji by purchase at Rs. 50'; In the column of the tenancy it has been described as the and  right of a settled raiyat d in the column 'rent', a remark has been made to the effect 'fit for rent but no transaction The C.S record-of-rights was finally published in the district of Dhaka before the amendment   of Bengal Tenancy Act, when any transfer of an occupancy raiyoti holding or a part thereof was compulsorily registerable, irrespective of the fact whether the consideration was above or below Rs 100 Before such amendment, in view of section 17 of the Registration Act, only those transfers which were for Rs 100 and above were compulsorily registerable The purchase of the land appertaining to C S Plot No 1873 by Foizuddin Haji from Aftab Uddin Sarkar for Rs 50 did not require under the law a registered instrument It was made orally Faizuddin Haji got into occupation of the land by virtue of his purchase from Aftab Uddin, who was a settled raiyat of the village but no rent appeared to have been fixed The name of Faizuddin Haji was recorded as an occupant by purchase arid the class of tenancy was stated to be that of a settled raiyat and in the remark column for rent, it was assessable to rent but no amount of rent was mentioned as there was no transaction The question which was raised was whether from such entries a presumption of the recorded person can be made. This Division held that the presumption as the correctness of the said entries necessarily arose by virtue of subsection (5) of section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act.

14. Section 31 of the Act of 1950 provides that the government may, instead of proceeding under section 17, by notification, in official gazette, order that a compensation assessment roll be prepared under Chapter V in respect of any particular district, part of a district or local area on the basis of the record-of-rights last prepared and finally published under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 or Chapter IX of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 without any revision or after revising or recording only such particulars in such record as may be specified in the notification. The repealed provision of section 143A has presumptive value of the record-of-rights cannot be equated with a record-of-rights prepared under section 19 of Act of 1950.

15. Under the repealed provision it was provided in sub-section (2) that an application filed under subsection (1) shall be deemed to he a plaint and order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under Code of Civil Procedure No such language is used in section 19(3) or in section 143B of the Act of 1950. Even a record-of-rights prepared under section 143A which has presumptive value does not confer any title to a litigant on the basis of such record because it is not a suit for declaration of title but it is a proceeding for rectification of mistake of the record-of-rights prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. So the scheme of the section showed that if a record-of-rights was prepared in pursuance of a decree of a civil court in exercise of powers under section 143A, there is presumption as regards possession of the said land. Reference in this connection are the cases of Assistant Custodian V. Bholanath Ghua and 36 DLR (AD) 79, Riazuddin V. Jatindra Kishore, 37 DLR (AD) 202. Therefore, under no stretch of imagination it can be inferred that by reasons of the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) the defendant have acquired title in the land as held by the court of appeal below.

16. Next question is whether there was extinguishment of title of the plaintiffs' predecessors in pursuance of the deed of relinquishment (মুক্তিপত্র) exhibit A(1) The court of appeal below held that since Naimuddin admitted in this deed as the adopted son of Karful Bewa and relinquished his right, the plaintiffs could not claim title by way of inheritance and purchase of the property of Karful Bewa and that admittedly Naimuddin was not the legal heir of Karful Bewa. The defendants failed to adduce any legal evidence to prove the C.S. record-of-rights prepared in favour of Karful Bewa other than the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the Act of 1950. As observed earlier by this record-of-rights no presumption of title can be drawn as is available under section 103B. More so, the suit was remanded to the trial court enabling the defendants to prove মুক্তিপত্র dated 18th December, 1930, exhibit:-A(1) and the A deed dated 17th January, 1935 exhibit-A(2) a deed executed by Toisor Ali in favour of Alimuddin Mondal arid Jamir Ali Mondal. In this deed the executant admitted that the recipients were in possession of the lands over statutory period. The court of appeal below held that Naimuddin extinguished his title by executing these two deeds and therefore the plaintiffs cannot claim any title as heirs of Naimuddin. It misread ext-A(2) for, Naimuddin did not relinquish his title in the lands covered by the deed. This finding is self contradictory with its earlier finding, inasmuch as, Naimuddin being the adopted son of Karful Bewa, he did not inherit her property. More so, after the remand of the suit, the trial court held that though exhibit-B(1) (wrongly mentioned as ext-B(1). It would be ext-A(2) was exhibited but the contents of the deed having not been proved by the defendants in accordance with law, the contents couldn't be looked into; that in proof of exhibit-A (2), the defendants did not produce any in dependent witness and that despite giving opportunity to the defendants, they failed to prove enforceability of exhibit-A(2). It was further observed that the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 have been able to prove their title and. possession in the suit land, The court of appeal below has totally over-looked those findings and illegally took exhibits-A(1) and A(2) as the basis of title of the defendants and illegally held that the title of the plaintiffs' predecessor extinguished. In view of the above, the judgment of the court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal.

17. As observed above, in the C.S. khatian Karful Bewa's 16 annas possession in Schedule, 1, 3 and 6 had been recorded. Though the jote was shown in the name of Sadi Mondal, since this record has presumptive value in the absence of rebuttal evidence by the defendants that despite showing 16 annas possession of Karful Bewa the defendants' predecessor continued   possession in the said land have not established by them and also in respect of exhibit 1(a) she had 8 annas possession. What's more, in the absence of any evidence either oral or documentary that though Sadi Mondal's jote was noted in exts 1-1(b), whether the legal heirs of Sadi Mondal ever exercised the title and possession in the lands covered by those deeds, it is difficult to accept the defendants claim of ownership in those lands. There is no finding either in their regard. The onus lies upon the defendants to prove that despite such recording, Karful Bewa had no possession therein and that they have been continuing possession from the time of predecessors have not been established.

<u>18. Though the High Court Division has not discussed and assigned proper reasons in interfering with the judgment of the court of appeal below, it ought to have assigned reasons since there was judgment of reversal, the ultimate decision of the High Court Division that exhibit-1 proved Karful Bewa's status as 16 annas possession and in respect of exhibits-1(a) and 1(b), she had 8 annas with Borundi Mondal; that exhibit-B also proved that Karful Bewa was tenant in possession; that exhibit-1(a) and 1(d) proved her status of 8 annas occupant which proved her absolute ownership in respect of those recorded lands and that the court of appeal below wrongly disbelieved the plaintiffs' title and possession upon misreading of the pleadings and documentary evidence on record.</u>

19. There is no merit in this appeal. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to costs.

<u>26. As per provision of Section 103(B) (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, every entry in a record of right finally published shall be evidence of the mater referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it proved to be incorrect. The entry can be regarded as presumptive evidence of the matter referred to in the entry; as also of the condition things which existed at the time of record of right was prepared. The entry in the record of rights has only a probative value. We have seen that the lands of C.S. khatian No. 84 and 120 were of the Jote of Baramdi Monda and land recorded in C.S. khatian No. 69, 47, 53 and 16 were the Tote of Sadi Mondal. The term 'Dote" ordinarily means "holding" and a tenancy is described as 'jote' in general. In the case of Narendra Chandra Vs. Rajendra Chandra Chanda reported in AIR 1941 Cal 506 it was observed that 'Jote' is a perfectly general expression to mean tenancy of any kind. In the case of Sariatullah V. Joyenuddin AIR 1935 cal 462 it was held that the "jute simply means a tenancy". In the case of Upendra Kishore Sarker Vs. Khalii Fakir reported in 139 I.C. page 544 it was observed that "Jote may mean a raiyat, under raiyoti, or any sort of holding for the purpose bf cultivation. <u>27. On the other hand, the contesting defendants produced ext. 28. The plaintiffs in their pleading did not state any words about the source of title of Korpul Bewa. Mr. Quamrul Haque Siddique, relied on the upon the case Akbar Ali, and other Vs. Jahiruddin reported in 30 DLR (SC)81 and submits that since Korpul Bewa was occupation in the land in question and same was agricultural lands, so she was raiyot and accordingly after her death, the plaintiff predecessor inherited the same. That is, in the cited case holder of the Rote transferred the land to the person in occupation orally which was accepted as valid transfer. But in the case, in hand, I do not find any pleading or evidence to the effect that the Jote owners Sadi Mondal or Baramdi Mondal had transferred the land under partition, in any way, to Korpul Bewa. Admittedly, Korpul Bewa was the wife of Sadi Mondal, that is, she was the family member of Sadi Mondal and after his death she inherited 1⁄4th  share of the property left by him, since they had no issue. In absence of any pleading and evidence it is difficult to hold that except as wife of Sadi Mondal Korpul Bewa acquired entire holding otherwise. An adverse entry, will not per see constitute actual dispossession. Moreover, there is nothing in the pleadings of the plaintiffs that tenancy of Korpul Bewa was created by long and continuous occupation and the landlords received any rent accepting the tenancy of Karpul or, in any other way, her exclusive tenancy had been established or tenancy of Sadi Mondal, and after his death, his other heirs, had been extinguished.

29. In view of the circumstances as discussed above, I find substance in the appeal.

30. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. Consequently, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside.

31. A.H.M. Shamsuddin Choudhury J. I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha and Hasan Foez Siddique, JJ. I agree with the judgment prepared by my learned brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, J.

COURTS ORDER

The appeal is dismissed by majority decision.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11th of September, 2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1589 of 2013)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 11.09.2014 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1589 of 2013 discharging the Rule.

2. Facts of the case, in brief, are that the petitioner and the proforma-respondent Nos. 21- 24 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 05 of 2002 in the Court of Joint. District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka praying for a declaration that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 by the Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka on 28.05.1960 was not binding upon them. They stated, inter alia, that the land of Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 was part of C.S. Plot No. 67 under C.S. Khatian No. 174 and the total area of C.S. Khatian No. 174 of Mouja Dhanmondi, former Keranigonj Police Station and at present Dhanmondi Police Station was 60.13 acres and the superior landlords were Nezabot Ali Kha, Abdul Hakim and others. The land of the C.S. Plot No. 67 was owned and possessed by one Gopeswar Paul, son of late Bhubaneswar Paul as tenant under the superior landlord and C.S. record-of-rights was finally published in the name of tenant Gopeswar Paul. C.S. Plot No. 67 comprised   an area of 38.48 acres. Said Gopeswar Paul while owning and possessing the said land died leaving behind two sons, namely Nilkanta Paul and Harekrishna Paul as his heirs. Subsequently, Harekrishna Paul died leaving behind only son Debraj Paul as his heir. Said Nilkanta Paul and Debraj Paul while possessing the said land, sold 4 bighas of specific chala land out of total 38.48 acres of land of C.S. Plot No. 67 to one Sreejukta Kiron Chandra Bandapadhaya, son of late Binod Chandra Bandapadhaya vide registered deed No. 1845 dated 14.07.1933 and delivered possession to him. Thereafter, Kiron Chandra Bandapadhaya sold his entire purchased 4 bighas land, equivalent to 1.33 acres with trees standing thereon to Md. Shahjahan Bhuiyan, son of late Moulvi Mohammad Abdul Wahab Bhuiyan, predecessor of the present petitioner and opposite party Nos. 21-24 vide registered sale deed No. 4623 dated 18.08.1948 and handed over possession to them and they are in possession of the said land jointly. The Government, for the construction of the residence of Government employees, acquired 16.75 acres of land including 1.33 acres of C.S. Plot No. 67 owned and possessed by Md. Shahjahan Bhuiyan vide Land Acquisition Case No. 06 of 1948-49 and compensation was prepared in his name for an amount of Tk. 3,976.11. But the Government did not take possession of the entire acquired land including the land owned and possessed by the predecessor of the petitioner as the said land was not needed for the purpose for which acquisition proceeding was started, and the said land is a small unspecified part of a bigger plot. The compensation was not withdrawn by the predecessor of the petitioner and the said amount was deposited in the Government Revenue Accounts. Since possession of 1.33 acres of land owned and possessed by the predecessor of the petitioner was not taken over by the Land Acquisition Department, the said land remained in the possession of the petitioner's predecessor Md. Shahjahan Bhuiyan who died on 18.02.1982. On the recommendation of the Ministry of Works and Housing, the then Prime Minister directed release of the unused acquired portion of land of the owners in possession on 18.03.1974, and also directed to take back the compensation money from those awardees who had taken compensation, and further directed to publish Gazette Notification immediately in that regard. But the said direction was not acted upon. Ultimately, in the year 1984 decisions were taken by the Government for implementation of the earlier decision. Mrs. Salma Bhuiyan, mother of the petitioner on 19.06.1989 filed an application to the Minister, Ministry of Land for releasing the said property form L.A. Case No. 06 of 1948-49 and he directed the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.) Dhaka to submit report after inquiry. Accordingly, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.), Dhaka after inquiry submitted report on 26.06.1989 to the Ministry of Land. In the said report it was clearly stated that the petitioners were in possession of the said property by constructing structures. The petitioner's property not having been released, they filed Title Suit No. 133 of 2001 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the Government for declaration of their 16 annas right, title and interest in the said ; 1.33 acres of land and the said suit is pending for disposal. The opposite party Nos. 1-18 or their predecessor got their names recorded in respect of 50 decimals of land out of total 1.33 acres of the aforesaid land ; of C.S. Plot No. 67 at the field level in the recent Dhaka City Survey and they filed appeal under Rule 31 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Rules, 1955 framed under State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and from the said case record, the petitioner found photocopy of the certified copy of the judgment and decree dated 28.05.1960 passed in Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 of the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka and the petitioner came to know that the opposite party Nos. 1-18 or their predecessor, suppressing the facts of the earlier title deed, possession of the petitioner's predecessors as well as acquisition proceedings, obtained a decree in respect of unspecified 50 decimals of land out of total 38.48 acres of land. The petitioner does not claim any interest in the suit land of the Title Execution Case No. 32 of 1962 but claim different land by way of earlier title document because of the question of the identity of the suit land. The said judgment and decree has cast cloud upon the right, title, interest and possession of the suit land of the petitioner because of identity of the suit land and the decretal land. As the heirs of late Md. Shahjahan Bhuiyan, they filed Title Suit No. 05 of 2002 before the District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka against the opposite party Nos. 1-18 and prayed for declaration that the judgment and decree passed on 28.05.1960 in Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 of the 3rd Court of Munsif, Dhaka is not binding upon the plaintiffs of the present suit.

3. During pendency of the Title Suit No. 05 of 2002 with a view to pre-empt the possible judgment of the suit, the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-18 forcibly tried to dispossess the petitioner from the suit land and as such, the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 21-24 on 18.05.2009 field an application under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4. Respondent Nos. 1-11 as defendants of the suit filed written statements stating, inter alia, that their predecessor purchased the land measuring an area of 50 decimals of C.S. Plot No. 67 out of total 38.48 acres of land vide registered deed No. 3075 dated 21.5.1953 from Debraj Paul and that on the same day A.M. Nur Meah and 2 others purchased 46 decimals of land from the same Debraj Paul and the said land is situated on the northern side of the land purchased by them. On 05.12.1955 aforesaid A.M. Nur Meah and others dispossessed the decree-holder opposite party Nos. 1-18, consequently, they filed Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 in the Court of Munsif and that suit was decreed in favour of the predecessors of the opposite party Nos. 1-18.

5. After hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge by his order dated 14.11.2012 rejected the application field under Order 39, Rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction.

6. Against the said order passed by the Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, the plaintiffs preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 317 of 2012, which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, who by his judgment and order dated 05.05.2013 dismissed the appeal.

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order of the appellate Court the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No. 1589 of 2013 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which was discharged by the impugned judgment and order. Hence, the petitioner has filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

8. Mr. Md. Ashad Ullah, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the petitioner and proforma respondent No. 20 to 24 claimed title to the property by way of inheritance and are in exclusive possession of the suit land since 18.08.1948 and hence, the High Court Division erroneously upheld the order of the lower Courts rejecting the application for injunction. He further submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the land concerned in Title Suit No. 152 of 1957 and the suit land are not the same and also that the petitioner was not party to the said title suit and hence, the result of the suit is not binding upon the petitioner. Finally, he submits that the High Court Division and the Courts below failed to notice that in view of the long standing exclusive possession of the petitioner in the suit land and title by way of registered deed dated 18.8.1948 balance of convenience and in-convenience is in favour of the petitioner and hence, the High Court Division erred in discharging the Rule.

9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-10 made submission in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and other connected papers on record.

<u>11. It is an admitted fact that the suit land was acquired in L.A. Case No. 06 of 1948-49 and although steps have been taken for release of the land from acquisition, the applicants have not succeeded in getting the land released. According to section 5 (7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 the land having been duly acquired and compensation paid, vests absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. Hence, the title in the property is no longer with the petitioner. We note from the plaint that the petitioner has not included any prayer for declaration of title and hence, in any event, the prayer for temporary injunction is not sustainable.</u>

12. In the impugned judgment the High Court Division observed that as per the admission of the plaintiff-petitioner the suit land of Title Suit No. 05 of 2002 was acquisitioned vide L.A. Case No. 06 of 1948-49 and that the plaintiff-petitioner is yet to be successful in releasing the said suit property from the list of acquisition and requisition and that his right to the suit land is yet to be established. It was further noted that there is no record of rights in respect of the suit land in the name of the plaintiff-petitioner and that there is no rent receipt to show that the plaintiff-petitioner is in physical possession in the suit land. The High Court Division concluded that the plaintiff-petitioner is yet to establish his right, title and possession in the suit land by way of releasing the suit land from the list of acquisition and requisition. So long the plaintiff-petitioner is unable to establish his title and possession in the suit-acquired land he cannot get any relief of temporary injunction

13. In the light of the discussion above, we find that the impugned judgment does not suffer from any illegality or infirmity and does not call for any interference. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 6.5.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for leave to appeal No.1359 of 2009).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This application for review arises out of the judgment and order 6.5.2010 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1359 of 2009 rejecting the same and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 13.05.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 13.05.2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.  59 of 1994 decreeing the suit.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this petition for leave to appeal, in short, are:

<u>3. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein filed Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 and Money Suit No. 2 of 2002 both in the Court of the Subordinate Judge (Joint District Judge) Second Court, Dhaka. Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 was for declaration of title to the suit land and for a further declaration that the plaintiffs were not bound by the judgment and decree dated 15.11.1979 passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 by the Subordinate Judge, third Court, Dhaka and also for declaration that the kabala executed through Court on 27.02.1980 in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka was fraudulent, collusive, illegal and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The suit land measuring an area of 0568 ajutangsha, originally belonging to Khiroda Shundari Daishya, was put to auction for arrears of rent in Certificate Case No. 660  of 1952-53 and was purchased by Ali Ahmed @ Dr. Monjurul Hoque on 20.06.1953. The sale was confirmed on 24.08.1953 and the sale certificate was issued in favour of said Ali Ahmed on 19.11.1953. Possession of the auction purchased land was delivered on 20.01.1954 through Court. Ali Ahmed being in possession of the auction purchased land for more than 12 years got his name mutated in the government record and paid rents accordingly. S.A. Khatian No. 197 and R.S. Khatian No. 1248 were accordingly prepared in his name. He died intestate on 18.06.1975 leaving behind a widow, namely, Khatibunnessa, who inherited the entire suit property as sharer of 4 annas share as his wife and the remaining 12 annas share as per the Doctrine of Return. While owning and possessing the suit property, Khatibunnessa died on 10.02.1978 leaving behind her only full brother Abdul Mannan, who inherited her entire property including the suit property and by a registered heba-bil-ewaj deed dated 29.11.1979, he transferred the same in favour of the plaintiffs. Thus the plaintiffs being the 16 annas owners of the suit property were in peaceful possession i thereof. Defendants created forged papers and tried to take possession of the suit property forcibly but owing to the intervention of respectable people of the locality, they failed in their illegal attempt. On 06.07.1980, the defendants along with a process server of the Court and police tried to take over the possession of suit land but the plaintiffs by showing decree of the court resisted them. After making inquiry from the bailiff of the Court the plaintiffs father, Abdul Majid, came to know that the defendants obtained a fraudulent decree on 15.11.1979 in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, and that the defendants entered into an agreement with one Rasheda Begum for purchase of the suit property on the basis of the said fraudulent decree. Rasheda Begum acquired no title to, and possession in, the suit property and therefore, the defendants did not acquire any title to the suit property on the basis of the bainapatra. The defendants got a kabala executed and registered in their names through Court in execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979. Neither the plaintiffs nor their predecessor were made parties in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979. Therefore, the decree passed therein was not binding upon them the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the defendants for permanent injunction, which was decreed on 28.03.1984 on contest. Against by the said decree, the defendants filed Title Appeal No. 196 of 1984 before the District Judge, Dhaka, which, on transfer, was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka, who allowed the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 24.01.1987 and dismissed the suit. Feeling aggrieved the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 76 of 1987 before the High Court Division, but the rule was discharged on 27.05.1992 and against which the plaintiffs filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.  297 of 1972 before the Appellate Division, and the same was dismissed.</u>

4. On 27.10.1993, the plaintiffs filed an application under order 21 Rule 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure for dismissing the Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980, arising out of the  decree passed in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979, and the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 29.01,1994 rejected the application. Though the defendants failed to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit property through the said execution case, they were telling the people of the locality that they would soon dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit property. The cause of action for the suit arose on 21.10.1993 when the defendants along with the bailiff of the Court asked the plaintiffs to hand over vacant possession of the suit property to them and the same was continuing in view of the claim of the defendants. While the suit was at the stage of peremptory hearing, the defendants along with 20/25 terrorists being armed with dangerous weapons entered into the suit property forcibly on 16.09.1997 and evicted the plaintiffs and their men therefrom. They looted away the household articles worth Tk.6,00,000/-, and also looted away the goods from 10(ten) family rooms and 13 (thirteen) shops in the suit property and took possession thereof. The defendants deprived the plaintiffs of getting rent from the tenants of the said family rooms and shops to the tune of taka 26,000/- per month. After the incident Mr. Abdul Majid, the father of the plaintiffs, lodged an First Information Report (FIR) with Lalbagh Police Station under Section 144/447/44 and 380 of the Penal Code. On behalf of the tenants one Wazir Ahmed also lodged an FIR with the said police station which was registered as Lalbagh P.S. Case No. 940 dated 16/09/1997. Subsequently the defendants by putting threat on the life of the plaintiffs as well as their father Abdul Majid and also by applying force got a white paper signed from them with the writing to the effect ‘‘১৬,৬০,০০০/- টাকা বুঝিয়া পাইলাম" though they received no money from the defendants. The defendants demolished the one storied building and the shop rooms standing on the suit land causing a loss of taka 20 lacs to the plaintiffs. From the semi pucca family quarter and the 13 (thirteen) shops the plaintiffs were earning Tk. 26,000/-per month; so they are entitled to get mesne profit at the said rate from that date. In the premises the plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 2 of 2002 claiming Tk.28,71,900/- with interest And cost.

<u>5. The petitioners herein contested the suits by filing written statements. Their case, in short, is that the suit property known as No.  1 Atash Khana Lane, along with other property owned by Khiroda Shundari Daishaya by purchase from (i)Binodini Daishaya by a registered kabala being No. 2892 of 1899 (ii) Shayam Chandra Shaha by a registered kabala being No. 3070 of 1899 and from Rai Mohan Shaha vide kabala No. 3430. Khiroda Sundari Daishaya purchased a portion of C.S. Plot No. 40 of C.S. Khatian No. 237 from Radha Ballav Shaha by a registered kabala dated 04/03/1932 and thus she remained in possession thereof as  the rightful owner. Khiroda sold the entire suit property to Salimunnesa by a registered kabala dated 27/03/1953 and delivered possession thereof to her. While in possession of the suit property by paying rents, Salimunnesa transferred her 8(eight) annas share to Rasheda Begum and the rest 8(eight) annas to Mohammad Ilias on 15/06/1959 who later by a registered deed of gift transferred his said 8 (eight) annas share to Rasheda Begum and delivered possession thereof to her. Thus Rasheda Begum became the 16 (sixteen) annas owner and possessor of the suit property. One Munjurul Hoq was a tenant in a portion of the suit property and as he defaulted in paying rent Rasheda Begum filed Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 in the Court of the then Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka for the realization of arrear rents. In the same court Rasheda Begum also filed House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 for eviction of said tenant, Doctor Manjurul Haque @ Ali Ahmed, and that the tenant forging signature of Rasheda Begum filed two applications for compromise in the name of Rasheda Begum and Khatimunnesa respectively in the said money suit and the house rent case and obtained compromise decrees. When Rasheda Begum came to know about the same, she filed Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 in the Court of Munsif 3rd Court, Dhaka praying for cancellation of the deed of agreement dated 16/11/1959 as well as the applications for compromise filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959. Rasheda Begum claimed that the owners of No. 1 Atash Khaha Jane, the suit property, were Khiroda Sundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Dash, who sold the said property to Salimunnesa on 27/05/1954. Defendant No. 2, Khatimunnesa of the said suit was the wife of Doctor Munjurul Haque @ Ali Ahmed, a tenant under Khiroda Sundari Daisyha and Lalit Mohan Dash and thus after the transfer of the suit property she became a tenant under Salimunnesa. Thereafter Salimunnesa sold her eight annas share to Rasheda Begum and the rest 8 (eight) annas share to Md. Bias along with the tenancy right of Khatimunnesa, and as she defaulted in paying the house rent, Rasheda Begum filed Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif 3rd Court, Dhaka for realization of the arrear rent and Md. Bias filed House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 for eviction of Khatimunnesa. Monjurul Hoque filed false complaints before the Anti-Corruption Department and the Martial Law News-Centre. Rasheda Begum was a pardanishin lady. At the ill advice of Manjurul Haque, the then-in-charge of Martial Law News Centre, Major Sharif, obtained the signatures of Rasheda Begum on two agreements and the compromise applications by coercion without disclosing the contents thereof. As the said agreements and the applications for compromise were created against the will of Rasheda Begum, she filed Title Suit No. 221 of 1964, in which Khatimunnesa and Doctor Manjurul Haque appeared and filed written statement claiming that they purchased 7(seven) annas share of the suit holding in auction on 20.06.1953. Title Suit No. 221 of 1964 was decreed on 25.12.1965 in favour of Rasheda Begum declaring that the registered agreements being Nos. 6904 and 6905 dated 16.11.1959 were void and ineffective and that the two compromise applications filed in Money Suit No. 50 of 1959 and House Rent Case No. 598 of 1959 were void. Against the judgment and decree Doctor Manjurul Haque and his wife Khatimunnesa filed Title Appeal No. 50 of 1966 before the District Judge, Dhaka, which on transfer was headed by a Subordinate Judge, who dismissed the said appeal by his judgment and decree dated 19.07.1966 affirming those of the trial Court. Doctor Manjurul Haque and his wife filed Second Appeal No. 1095 of 1966 before the then High Court and the appeal was also dismissed. Thus the right, title and possession of Rasheda Begum in the suit property was confirmed. While in possession of the suit property, Rasheda Begum entered into a contract with the defendants to sell the same at a price of Tk. 45,000/- and on receipt of a sum of Tk.15,000- as advance executed a bainapatra on 12.08.1972. As Rasheda Begum was avoiding execution and registration of the required kabala, the defendants filed Title Suit No. 62 of 1979 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The slat was decreed on 15.11.1979 and the defendants got the kabala executed and registered on 27.02.1980 through Court in Title Execution Case No. 03 of 1980. After the registration of the kabala when the defendants went to take possession of the suit property through Court, the plaintiffs resisted and the bailiff of the Court returned the 'writ of delivery' without executing the same with the prayer for police help. Meanwhile, the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 329 of 1980 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for permanent   injunction and obtained a decree; which was sot aside by the Appellate Court on 24.01.1987 in Title Appeal No. 1969 of 1984 filed by the defendants. The decree of the Appellate Court was upheld in Civil Revision No. 76 of 1987 by the High Court Division discharging the Rule as well as in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 297 of 1992 by the Appellate Division dismissing the petition. After disposal of the said Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal, the defendants prayed for police help to execute the decree and the Court allowed the prayer. The plaintiffs filed an application under Order XXI, Rule 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure just to block the further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980. The application was rejected on 23.01.1994 on contest. After that, the plaintiffs filed the instant suit making false and frivolous allegations just to continue with their illegal possession in the suit property depriving the defendants of the enjoyment of the fruits of the aforesaid decree. They further denied the claim of the plaintiffs that they were dispossessed by them by force from the suit property on 16.09.1997 and also denied the fact of looting away the goods from the suit property including from the tenanted rooms and shops causing financial loss of Tk. 20,00,000/- (twenty lacs) and the facts of getting rents from the tenants to the tune of Tk. 26,000/- per month. When Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1980 was revived the plaintiffs filed an application for staying further proceedings of the same but their prayer was rejected on 29.01.1994. Against the said order, the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 465 of 1994 before the High Court Division, but the rule was discharged on 27.08.1997 with a direction upon them to hand over the possession of the suit property to the defendants within 30(thirty) days. After getting possession of the suit land and the other adjacent lands, the defendants demolished the kucha and semi pucca rooms standing thereon. By investing lacs of taka they completed major portion of works for construction of a multistoried building and the remaining work was also under process. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 hereof filed Money Suit No. 73 of 2000 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for realisation of compensation of Tk.28,71,900/-(Twenty Eight lacs Seventy One Thousand and Nine Hundred) along with interest of Tk.15% till realisation and the said suit was transferred to the Subordinate judge (Joint District Judge)  Second Court and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 2 of 2002.</u>

6. These petitioners contested the said money suit by filing written statement denying the claim.

7. Both the title suit and the money suit were heard analogously.

8. The learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, vide his judgment and decree dated 21.03.2004 decreed Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 and the Money Suit No. 2 of 2002. Against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994, these petitioners filed First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 and against the judgment and decree passed in Money Suit No. 2 of 2002 these petitioners filed First Appeal No. 180 of 2004 in the High Court Division and the learned Judges of the High Court Division vide judgments and decrees dated 13.05.2008 dismissed both the First Appeals. Hence these petitions.

9. Against the judgment and decree passed in First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 defendants moved this Court by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 135 of 2009 and by the impugned judgment and order, this Court dismissed the leave petition on 6.5.2010.

10. After that, the defendants preferred this petition for review.

11. Perused the petition seeking review and the impugned judgment and order and other papers on record.

12. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel for the review petitioner, submits that by the Gazette notification dated 2nd April 1956 Memo 4024 L.R and LR 4836 LR respectively under section 3 of State Acquisition as amended by E.B. Ordinance 111 of 1956, the rent receiving interest vested in the government on 02.04.1956 and exhibit-1 shows Khiroda Sundari held a Mrish Ijara interest under a private landlord and it conclusively proves that the Certificate Case Number 660 of 1952-53 issued by L.R. government acquired estate is a manufactured paper and exhibits-2 and 2(Ka) are also forged papers and the claim of title of the plaintiffs falls through.

13. The learned Counsel further submits that the finding that the certificate case was filed by the Government for arrears of rent in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 while exhibits 2 and 2(Ka) show that certificate case was filed by R.L Government Acquired Estate against the provision of Section 4 of Public Demand Recovery Act is a mistake apparent on the face of record and in the circumstances judgment dated 06.05.2010 calls for review.

14. Mr. M.I. Faroqui, learned counsel for the respondent, submits that the petitioners miserably failed to make out any case for review of the impugned judgment.

15. The above submissions made on behalf of the petitioners merit consideration.

<u>16. Leave is granted to consider the following points:</u>

<u>I. Whether the Gazette notification dated 2nd April 1956 Memo 4024 LE and LR 4836 LR respectively under section 3 of State Acquisition as amended by E.B. Ordinance 111 of 1956, the rent receiving interest vested in the government on 02.04.1956 and exhibit-1 shows Khiroda Sundari held a Mrish Ijara interest under a private land lord and it conclusively proves that the certificate case Number 660 of 1952-53 issued by L.R. government acquired estate is a manufactured papers and exhibits-2 and 2(Ka) are all also forged papers and the claim of title of the plaintiff falls through.</u>

<u>II. Whether the finding that the certificate was filed by the Government for arrears of rent in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 while the exhibits; 2 and 2(1(a) show that certificate was  filed by R.L Government Acquired Estate against the provision of Section 4 of Public Demand Recovery Act is a mistake apparent on the face of record and in the circumstances, judgment dated 06.05.2010 calls for review.</u>

17. The petitioner is permitted to prepare the paper book out of Court in accordance with the Rules.

18. Further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 09 of 2010 and Money Execution  Case No. 03 of 2010 of the court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka both arising out of Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 be stayed till disposal of the appeal.

End.
