parties:
Messrs Bengal Steel Works Limited  ------- Petitioner. 
Vs. 
Chairman, National Board of Revenue, Govt. of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others  ------- Respondents
case_source: (In the matter of an application under Article 102 read with Article 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.)
full_judgment:
This Rule issued on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against an order dated the 27th July 1973 communicated by a Secretary to the National Board of Revenue, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for refund of a sum of Taka 4,71,912.74 paisa which is alleged to have been paid by the petitioner as excess duty in respect of certain consignments imported on behalf of the petitioner.

<u>2. The petitioner's case is that the petitioner imported during the months of 1971 a large quantity of M. S. Billets for their re-rolling factory on free list on the then Government Import Policy, but the billets arrived at a time when the country was involved in the War of Liberation. The petitioner duly made entry of those goods by executing proper bills of entry and assessment was made under the law by the Custom Authority at Chittagong. Payments were made to the foreign consignor and the billets were warehoused. There were five bills of entry in respect of the said goods for which separate bonds were executed being A-1 to A-5. The assessment aforesaid was made in normal course and delivery also was taken in respect of parts of the warehoused goods under bond Nos. A-1 and A-3. Exchange rates of Bangladesh currency in relation to foreign currencies were devalued on the 2nd January, 1972 and after such devaluation of the Bangladesh currency, measures were adopted by Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 to realise increased duty by re-assessing the value of the goods at the new exchange rate. It is stated that since there was an urgent necessity for the billets for the purpose of keeping the Mill running so as to save the industry from collapse and also to satisfy the workers, the petitioner took delivery of the consignments under protest on payment of the duty as reassessed on the basis of the new exchange rate, and in consequence of this increased assessment they have had to pay an excess amount of Taka 4,71,912.74 as shown in Annexure 'A' to the petition.</u>

3. The petitioner thereafter wrote to the First Secretary, Customs, National Board of Revenue on the 22nd April, 1972 and also on the 30th May, 1972 stating the details of the bills which were taken under protest by paying duty under the new rate of exchange and requesting the National Board of Revenue to pass an order for refund in respect of the excess duty paid by them. A representation also was made to the Member of Customs, National Board of Revenue, Government of Bangladesh through the lawyers of the petitioner on the 6th of July, 1972 explaining, in detail, the circumstances under which the excess payment of duty was made and suggesting that as it involved an interpretation of law it might be referred to the Ministry of Law for necessary clarification. Thereafter the petitioner received a letter from the Secretary, National Board of Revenue dated the 7th July, 1972, in reply to the petitioner's earlier letter dated the 22nd April, 1972 in which it was stated that the stand of the Customs House as to conversion of the assessable value at the new rate of exchange was correct in law and therefore the request to allow the assessment of the warehoused goods at the old rate of exchange could not be accepted.

4. Thereafter a representation was sent to the Ministry of Finance to the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh by a letter dated the 18th August, 1972 referring to rejection of the prayer by the National Board of Revenue and praying for clarification of the legal position of the basis of section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969. There having been no response to the said representation a reminder was sent by the petitioner's lawyers on the 11th December, 1972. The petitioner also in the meantime wrote a letter dated the 2nd September, 1972 to the Collector of Customs praying for an order for refund of the amount paid in excess. The petitioner received a reply from the Collector of Customs, Chittagong dated 9.1.73 in which the Collector of Customs stated that the rate of exchange applicable to the warehoused goods was the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the bills of entry and that the petitioner was entitled to refund of the excess amount paid provided that the petitioner filed the claim in time. Thereafter there was a further communication on behalf of the petitioner to the Collector of Customs, Chittagong in which it was submitted that the time-limit provided in section 33 of the Customs Act was applicable only in case of payment made either inadvertently or due to error or under misconstruction and as such the time-limit as provided in the said section had no application in the case of the petitioner in as much as the payment made by the petitioner was under compulsion and protest. On the 4th of May, 1973 the Collector of Customs appears to have written a letter to the First Secretary of the National Board of Revenue, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh stating that the billets imported by the petitioner were warehoused on the 26th of June, 1971 but at the time of actual removal of the billets from the ware-house duty was reassessed at the new exchange rate, instead of the old exchange rate prevalent on the date the bills of entry for warehousing were presented at the Customs House, either in haste or as a measure of safeguarding revenue but as the legal claim had not been filed within the time prescribed under section 33 of Customs Act, the Customs authority was technically handicapped in the matter and a request was made therein by referring to a ruling of the Central Board of Revenue dated the 16th of October, 1937, that the Customs authority might be authorised to allow refund in such case on the basis of the common law position, that money should not he retained by the Government to which the Government had no just claim.

5. Thereafter in a letter dated the 20th June, 1973 addressed to Assistant Collector of Customs for refund, it was pointed but by the petitioner that according to the Customs Manual Orders, a protest made concurrently with the payment of duty was regarded in practice as a claim that the duty had been paid as a result of misconstruction of the law by the assessing officer and was therefore treated as a claim for the purpose of section 40 of the Sea Customs Act (same as section 33 of the Customs Act). In reply to the aforesaid letter the petitioner was informed by Assistant Collector of Customs (Refund) by a letter dated 28.6.73 that the matter had already been referred to the National Board of Revenue for their consideration. Thereafter the petitioner's lawyers received a letter dated the 27th July, 1973 from Second Secretary, National Board of Revenue, Government of Bangladesh in which it was maintained that the goods had been correctly re-assessed under section 109 of the Customs Act on the basis of the revaluation of the goods in terms of the new exchange rate prevalent at the time of the removal of the said goods from the warehouse and the petitioner was informed that the National Board did not find any reason to interfere with the matter.

6. The contention of the petitioner, however, is that the assessment having been made fully and properly at time of the warehousing of the goods on the basis of the prevalent rate of exchange and the relevant documents having been retired by the petitioner's Bander, any re-assessment made on the ground that a new rate of exchange has come into existence as a result of devaluation of the currency of the country is wholly unauthorised and on the 26th August, 1973 they served a notice by a telegram upon Respondent No.1 demanding justice by cancelling, withdrawing or rescinding the letter dated the 26th July, 1973 and thereafter the application under Article 102 of the Constitution was moved, whereupon the present Rule has been issued.

7. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondents in which it has been asserted that the representation of the petitioner has been rightly rejected by the Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh as the duty charged on the goods was found to be quite in accordance with law. The definite case made out in the said affidavit is that according to the provision of the Customs Act the rate and amount of duty applicable to warehoused goods shall be the rate and amount assessable at the time of actual removal of such goods from the warehouse for home consumption, that not only the rate but also the amount of duty is to be determined with reference to the date on which the goods are cleared from the warehouse and that as the amount of duty depends on the assessable value the invoice value quoted in foreign currency is to be converted at the rate prevalent on the day the duty and other taxes are paid.

8. Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that having regard to the various provisions of the Customs Act, it is clear that the Customs Authority has power of reassessment of duty in respect of the goods imported in the country only under section 109 of the Customs Act (Act 1 of 1969) and the exercise of power under the said provision is permissible only when the rate of duty leviable on such goods has been altered under a legislative enactment. In the present case there having been no alteration of the rate of duty, the purported reassessment on the ground of devaluation of the currency of the country is wholly incompetent.

9. Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Asstt. Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents however maintains that the provision of section 109 is attracted also in a case when the amount of duty leviable on certain goods undergoes alteration as result of the change in the value of the goods purchased in a foreign currency in consequence of devaluation of the national currency. The substance of the contention of the learned Government lawyer seems to be that the value of the imported goods shall have to be ascertained again at the time when the goods are to be delivered from the warehouse on the basis of the rate of exchange prevalent at the time and if that is done it will be clear that the amount of duty leviable on the goods has been altered and in such a case reassessment is perfectly lawful according to section 109 of the Act.

10. The only question which calls for determination in this case is whether there shall be reassessment of customs duty on the imported goods which have been purchased in foreign currency and have already been assessed at the time of the delivery of the bill of entry on the basis of the value of the said goods expressed in accordance with the rate of exchange prevalent at the time on the ground that at the time of delivery of the said goods from the warehouse a different rate of exchange has come into force as a result of devaluation of the national currency in the meantime.

<u>11. Section 18 of the Customs Act provides that custom duties shall he levied at such rate as may he prescribed under the Tariff Act, 1934 or under any other law for the time being in force on goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh. Section 25 enacts that the value of any imported goods shall he taken to be the normal price, that is to say, the price which they would fetch, at the time the bill of entry is delivered under section 79, on a sale in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. Section 30 relates to the date for determination of rate of import duty and it provides that the rate and amount of duty applicable to any imported goods shall he the rate and amount chargeable on the date of the delivery of bill of entry to the appropriate officer and if such goods, have been warehoused under the Act the rate and amount of duty applicable thereto shall be the rate and amount chargeable at the time of the actual removal of such goods from the warehouse for home consumption. The next relevant provision is section 79 which lays down provision for the making of a bill of entry and according to the said provision the owner of the imported goods shall make entry of such goods for home-consumption or warehousing or for any other approved purpose by delivering to the appropriate officer a bill of entry thereof in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct. Section 80 contains the provision for assessment of duty, which provides that on the delivery of the bill of entry referred to in section 79, the goods or such part thereof as may be necessary may, without undue delay, he examined or tested and thereafter the goods shall be assessed to duty, if any, and the owner of such goods may then proceed to clear the same for home-consumption or warehouse them subject to the provisions contained In sub-section (2) with which we are not concerned at present, the only other provision which requires consideration in this context is section 109 to which a reference has already been made and the text of the said section is as follows :</u>

<u>'If any goods have been entered for ware-housing and assessed under section 80 but the duty leviable thereon is subsequently altered, such goods shall be reassessed on the basis of the altered duty and a new bond shall he executed by owner in accordance with the provisions of section 86 to replace the bond originally executed by him.'</u>

<u>12. On an examination of the aforesaid provisions it is clear that as soon as the imported goods arrive, a bill of entry is to be prepared according to section 79 of the Act and then assessment is to be made under section 80 of the Act, and for the purpose of assessment, a step is to be taken under section 25 of the Act for ascertaining the value of the imported goods. According to the said section, the value of any imported goods has been stated to be the normal price which the said goods would fetch, at the time of the delivering of the bill of entry under section 79, on a sale in the open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. In sub-section (2) and (3) of the said section various particulars have been mentioned which are to be taken into consideration for the purpose of determination of the normal price of the imported goods. The provision of the said section appears to be the only provision for determination of the value of the imported goods and it fixes a point of time with reference to which the value of the goods, in other words, the normal price of the goods, is to be ascertained. Section 30 of the Act also refers to a particular date for the purpose of determination of the rate and amount of duty and this is referable in case of warehoused goods to the date of the actual removal of the goods of the warehouse.</u>

13. The learned lawyer for the Government has tried to make a distinction between the two words "rate" and "amount" as have been mentioned in the said section 30. The learned lawyer has argued that the word "rate" does, no doubt, refer to the rate of duty which may be declared from time to time by the appropriate authority in exercise of the power granted by the relevant enactment but the word "amount" does, definitely, refer to the value of the goods which are sought to be charged under the taxing statute and this value of the goods is liable to fluctuate in consequence of various factors and that in case of the imported goods purchased in foreign currency the rate of exchange is certainly one of the causative factors for alteration of the value of the goods. The learned Assistant Attorney General has submitted that in section 109 of the Act under which a reassessment of the duty has been authorised neither the word "rate" nor the word "amount" has been used, but only the word "duty" has been and as such an alteration of the amount of duty consequent of a change in the value of the goods due to a chance in the rate of exchange is also contemplated in the said section.

<u>14. It appears to us that the interpretation which has been sought to be given to this provision by the learned Asstt. Attorney General is not consistent with the clear provisions of the statute nor he principle underlying the same. Although section 30 provides that the rate and amount of duty applicable to any imported goods which have been ware-housed, shall be the rate and amount chargeable on the date of the actual removal of the goods from the warehouse but from section 25 it is clear that the ascertainment of the value of the goods is referable to a particular date, namely, the date of delivery of the bill of entry under section 79 of the Act. The value of the goods has therefore to be ascertained on the basis  of the rate of exchange which was in force on that particular date. The provision as contained in section 25(1) relating to determination of the normal price on a sale in the open market on a particular date excludes the possibility of bringing in any concept of further determination of the value on the basis of a normal price in the market on some other date. We do not think that there is any scope for any doubt as to the real import of section 109 of the Act. The alteration of duty which has been referred to in the said section clearly indicates that the alteration contemplated therein is on the basis of the altered rate of duty. This view of section 109 which we are taking is in consonance with the principle under lying the statute enacted for realisation of taxes from a certain category of persons. So far as the consignee is concerned they have paid the value of the goods in the national currency equivalent to the price in the foreign currency on the basis of the then prevalent rate of exchange. They cannot be changed with a higher tax on the basis of the price of the goods which they have never paid nor the seller has ever received. According to sub-section (1) of section.25, it is clear that the value of the goods is the normal price at which the seller shall sell and the buyer shall purchase on the date of the delivery of the bill of entry. Such a value being, by definition, confined to a particular date, is not liable to fluctuate and cannot but been invariable amount. Long after the transaction had been completed and closed, the entire matter cannot be reopened and the buyer cannot be made to pay a higher amount, unless there is a positive statutory provision justifying such an increase. We therefore do not think that the Customs Authority was right in exercising their power under section 109 of the Act and reassessing the duty on the basis of the new valuation of the goods calculated at the rate of exchange coming into force long after the bill of entry had been delivered to the appropriate officer, namely, on the second January, 1972. It may he mentioned that some of the warehoused goods were delivered to the petitioner on payment of duty, assessed on the basis of the old rate of exchange.</u>

15. In construing the provisions of sections 30 and 109 of the Customs Act, we have been mindful of the principle applicable in case of interpretation of a taxing statute, as has been laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Nawabzada Muhammad Amir khan Vs. The Controller of Estate Duty and other reported in 13 D.L.R. (S.C.) page 105 in the following words :

"The provision relating to imposition of tax are to be strictly construed in favour of the subject so that if there be any substantial doubt it has to be resolved in his favour. But the machinery sections are to be liberally construed. If the incidence of tax be clear, the machinery sections should be so construed as to make the realization of the proper tax possible. They should not be so construed as to defeat the intention of the legislature and to prevent the realization of the tax that is in fact due."

<u>16. We are of the opinion that the intention of the legislature as has been expressed in the various provisions of the Customs Act is clearly to the effect that the occasion for reassessment, as is contemplated in section 109, arises only when there has been an alteration of the rate of duty declared by the appropriate authority at the time of taking delivery of the warehoused goods.</u>

17. The Rule is therefore made absolute. The impugned order dated the 16th July, 1973 as embodied in Annexure 'L' is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the total amount of Taka 4,71,912.74 paisa as has been realised by the Customs Authority as excess amount shall be refunded to the petitioner. The respondents shall pay costs of the petitioner, the hearing fee being assessed at 30 Gold Mohars.

Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.-I agree.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.638 of 2004
lawyer:
For Petitioners: Mr. Subhash Chandra Saha, Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-oh-Record
For Respondents: Not represented.
parties:
Md. Serajul Islam & another ------ Petitioners
Versus
Md. Abdul Latif & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. M. M. Ruhul Amin, J:- This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 05.01.2004 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 1444 of 2004 summarily rejecting the application. 

2. Short facts are that the pre-emptor filed Pre-emption Case No.41 of 1991 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Pirganj, Rangpur under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption against the preemptees and others stating, inter alia, that the land measuring 66 decimals of Plot No.381/628 of C,S. Khatian No.2, S.A. Khatian No.115 originally belonged to Naresh Chanara Basu and Indu Prava Basu in their raiyati right. The C.S. Khatian was accordingly prepared and finally published in their names. Before R.S. Khatian the said Naresh Chandra Basu and Indu Prava Basu after transferring the said land including the case land left for India. Md. Akbar Ali, Munsur Ali, Hosen Ali and Hosen Ali got the case land on the basis of lease. As per the deed of exchange dated 27.12.1986 Md. Akbar Ali transferred 161/2 acres of land to the pre-emptor. In this way the preemptor became a co-sharer in the disputed holding. The pre-emptor has got his homestead in the western portion of the case land. The opposite party No.3 of the pm-emption case sold the case land to the pre-emptee Nos.1 and 2 by a kabala dated 03.04.1991 beyond the knowledge of the preemptor. No notice of the kabala under pre-emption was served upon the pre-emptor. The pre-emptees are stranger purchasers in the case holding. The cause of action of the .case arose when the kabala under pre-emption was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act. 

3. The pre-emptees contested the case by filing written objection stating, inter alia, that the case is not maintainable in its present form and manner. It is barred by the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984. The pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case holding. The pre-emptees have homestead in the case land and they have no other land except the case land to construct their homestead and have been living therein. The pre-emptees spent Tk.1,000/- by cutting mud in the southern portion of the case land for making a bhiti for constructing a dwelling but by spending Tk.2000/- and spent of Tk.200/- for constructing a cow shed and also constructed a bamboo fence at a cost of Tk.500/-. The pre-emptee No:2 also spent Tk. I 000/- for constructing a dwelling but in the northern portion of the case land. So the pre-emption case is liable to fail. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge, Pirganj Rangpur upon hearing the learned Advocates for the parties and consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties allowed the pre-emption case. The pre-emptees preferred appeal and the appellate court allowed the appeal in part and modified the judgment of the trial court to the effect that pre-emptor would pay Tk.4000/- to the pre-emptees as cost of improvement. 

5. The pre-emptor moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction against the order of cost of improvement and obtained Rule. The High Court Division upon hearing the learned Advocates for the parties and consideration of the materials on record rejected the revisional application summarily. 

6. We have heard Mr. Subhash Chandra Saha, the learned Counsel for the petitioners and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers. 

7. It appears that the trial court and the appellate court concurrently held that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by way of exchange in the case holding and the pre-emptees are stranger purchasers and the pre-emption application was within time and also not bad for defect of party. The pre-emptees did not take any exception against the above concurrent findings of the trial court and the appellate court. 

8. It appears that the trial court allowed Tk.1200/- as improvement of cost whereas the appellate court allowed Tk.4,000/- as cost of improvement and the pre-emptor moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction against the cost of improvement of Tk.4000/- as awarded by the appellate court. 

9. Mr. Saha submitted that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer. In our view this argument of the learned Advocate cannot be accepted as it is the concurrent finding of the trial court and the appellate court that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer and the pre-emptees are stranger purchasers. Mr. Saha next argued that under section. 6 of Land Reform Ordinance, 1984. the pre-emption case is barred. 

10. The High Court Division held that the provisions of section 6 of the Ordinance, 1984 are not attracted in the pre-emption case and the pre-emption case is quite maintainable. 

11. For ready reference let us reproduce below section 6 of Land Reform Ordinance. 1984: 
"Any land used as homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be exempted from all legal processes, including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer, Court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted there from by any means; Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to the acquisition of such homestead under any law." On perusal of section 6 of the Ordinance, we are of the view that if section 6 is read with the proviso it lands to the conclusion that the same is not attract in a pre-emption proceeding. 

12. In the circumstances, we find no substances in the submissions of the learned Counsel. 

13. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed. 

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Ozi Ullalh, Advocate ------ For the petitioner 
Mr. Abdur Rahman, Advocate ------ For the respondent No.4
parties:
Md. Rabiul Haque ------ Petitioner
Versus
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Rural Development and Co-operative Division, Ministry of Local Government Rural Development 
and Co-operatives and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J: On application at the instance of the petitioner as rule Nisi has been issued to show cause as to why they should not be directed to regularize/absorb the service of the petitioner serving as Data Entry operator of the Development Project namely RLP of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) to the Revenue Budget of the BRDB under the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of his joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of SRO namely “উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের ও নিয়মিতকরন ও জ্যেষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” contain in Memo SRO No. 182/Ain/2005/ Somo/Bidhi-1/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 (Annexure-G) issued by the office of the respondent No.2 under by the Order of the Hon'ble President of the Republic which they are permitted/required by law to do and/or such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Relevant facts for disposal of the rule are that the petitioner is law abiding permanent citizen of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. He has been serving various development project of BRDB Data Entry Operator. The petitioner was firstly appointed under Development Project of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board as BRDB to the posts namely Data Entry Operator vide office Memo No. বাপউবো/পদপএ/ডাটা-এন্ট্রি/নিয়ো/প্রশা-৮৭/৯৪/১৫৫০ dated 05.12.1995. 

The petitioner has been serving the jobs to the BRDB since his appointment with the satisfaction of all concerned. Particularly the Office of the BRDB and also the Office of the Respondent No. 1. As a result the petitioner was transferred from one project to another the petitioner was lastly appointed under the project namely RLP of the BRDB vide office Memo No. বাপউবো/পদপএ/ডাটা-এন্ট্রি/নিয়ো/প্রশা-৮৭/৯৪/১৫৫০ dated 31.7.2013.  

3. Some of the employees of BRDB filed a writ petition being writ petitioner No.7484 of 2009 for regularizing them in revenue head from Development budget. The Division Bench comprising by their Lordships Ms. Justice Naima Haider and Mr. Justice Farid Ahmed vide their judgment and Order dated 17.01.2012 made the rule absolute. The present respondents being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the High Court Division filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division but it was dismissed upholding the judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

4. The petitioner stands on the same footing with the employees of BRDB who were earlier absorbed in the revenue head from development budget vide memo NO. বাপউবো/প্রশা/পার/নিয়োগ-১৯৪(১)/২০০০/৭৬২৬ dated 28.7.2005.  

5. The service of employees of various project under the various Ministers were absorbed earlier in the revenue head such as employees of 14 projects under the Ministry Of Social Welfare were absorbed in revenue head. 
6. It is stated that as fresh advertisement of certain employees was published in Daily Samokla dated 10.09.2013 without absorbing the petitioner. It was narrated in that circular that as many as 20 persons would be directly appointed in the revenue budget of the BRDB in that appointment schedule certain educational qualifications were enumerated in that appointment schedule. The petitioner having the same educational qualification as narrated above have been serving in the development project for more than 19 years. The appointment notice had been published instead of absorbing the petitioner in the revenue head in order to deprive the right and legitimate expectations created by the passage of time. It is reveled from the very publications of appointment notice that a lot of posts remained as vacant wherein the petitioner may step in. 

7. There is a Gazette notification issued by the Ministry of Establishment by the order of the Honb'le President of the Country namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” such notification was contained in Memo SRO No.182 Ain/2005 /somo/Bidhi-1S-9/2009 certain Rules were enumerated in that notification by which the employees of the development project are to be transferred to the revenue budget. After absorption their seniority are to be counted from the date of joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of the SRO. 

8. It was seen the respondents were reluctant to count the joining date of the petitioners not from the joining date of the development budget. In such a situation certain persons who earlier absorbed in the revenue head filed a writ Petition No.8983 of 2011 praying for direction to count their joining date form the date of joining in the development budget. The High Court Division initially issued a Rule Nisi and after hearing made the Rule absolute vide judgment and Order dated 14.05.2012. The writ respondents thereafter filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.308 of 2013 against the judgment of the High Court Division. The Appellate Division on 10.03.2013 after hearing was pleased to reject the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal upholding the judgment and Order of the High Court Division. 

9. The petitioner is not challenging the direct appointment process to the post namely Data Entry Operator under the revenue head of the BRDB. But at the same time it is asserted with full knowledge from the Head Office of the BRDB, to the effect that a huge number of the desired posts under the revenue head are vacant. Since the petitioner possessing all the qualifications as required by the BRDB to the appointment to the posts, the petitioner most humbly pray before this Hon'ble Court to pass a direction upon the Office of the respondent No.3 and 4 to keep 1 post vacant till disposal of the Rule. And such claim has already been accepted by some of the employees of the development project of BRDB who filed the writ. petition No.11522 of 2013 and at the time of issuing the Rule such type of Order as prayed in the present writ petition was passed by the High Court Division vide order dated 18.11.2013 in writ petition No.11522 of 2013 and the rule is fixed for hearing on 26.02.2014 for final disposal by this Hon'ble Court. 

10. On perusal of the application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh this Hoh'ble Court issued a rule Nisi. 

11. Mr. Md. Ozi Ullah learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner and Mr. Abdur Rahman appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4. 

12. Mr. Md. Ozi Ullah learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that some employees of the LGRD were absorbed from development budget to revenue budget and the petitioner stands on the same footing with them but he was not taken into the revenue head as such  the respondents adopted the policy of pick and choose and such exercise is illegal, malafide and not tenable under the law as such a direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

13. Learned Advocate next submits that the petitioner has been serving for over 19 years and there was a clear promise from the respondents that the petitioner would be taken into the revenue head and declining such promise is not fair and the petitioner had clear legitimate expectation and such right was sufficiently clear and unambiguous and expressed thus the petitioner must be taken into the revenue head but he was denied by the respondents hence a directions seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required and/or permitted by law to do. 

14. He further submits that Article 27 of the Constitution clearly speaks the equality of all the citizens and are entitled to equal protection of law while Article 31 provides the right to protection of law and they must be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law and such is the inalienable right and in the present context the petitioner was not treated in accordance with law and he did not get equal protection of law as because the other employees of the BRDB standing on the same footing with the petitioner were absorbed in the revenue budget from the development budget as such a direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

15. The learned Advocate further submits that the respondents being the public authority must act fairly and justly and not in violation of the law and equity and in the present case the petitioner was the worse victim of the misuse and abuse of the power by the respondents and he was not treated in accordance with law and the petitioner was supposed to be absorbed in the revenue budget but the respondents declined to do so therefore direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

16. He also submits, a lot of employees of development project of LGRD, Ministry of Education and Jubo Unnayan Adhidoptor were absorbed in the revenue head and furthermore some of the colleagues of the petitioner was absorbed in the revenue head as such a legitimate expectation has not only been created but also matured through various verdicts of the Highest Court and also the Office Memo of the respondent No.4 hence it is seriously required direction is seriously from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 
17. He lastly submits that there is a Gazette notification issued by the Ministry of Establishment by the order of the Hon'ble President of the country namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” in which Rule 6 enumerated that the joining date of absorbed employee would be counted the date of initial joining in the development project but such direction was denied hence a writ petition was filed being writ petition No.8983 of 2011 was filed and High Court passed the affirmative decision which was upheld by the Appellate Division in C.P. No.308 of 2013 the said Rule 6 was tested by both the Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as such along with direction of taking the service from development to revenue head another direction is required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of their joining in the development project which they are permitted and/or required by law to do. 

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention refers the case of Chief Engineer, The Local Government & Engineering Department and others Vs. Kazi Mizanur Rahman & 8 other respondents reported in 17 BLC Appellate Division page 91. 

19. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner perused the application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the annexure thereto. In order to arrive at a proper finding it is very much pertinent to refer the case of the Chief Engineer of Local Government and Engineering Department and others Vs. Kazi Mizanur Rahman and 8 others reported in 17 BLC AD page 91 where our Apex Court explained the principle of Legitimate Expectation very elaborately. 

"The doctrine of legitimate expectation is a concept which is akin to that a promissory estoppels and this concept has been developed in the European Community of Law. According to the doctrine where a person is a victim of an unfavorable decision taken by a public authority this may amount to an infringement of that persons legitimate expectation, where for example the decision contradicts an earlier promise or course of conduct on the part of the public authority concerned. Therefore this doctrine is circumscribed by certain limitations and expectations. The first and foremost consideration is that there must be a foundation in the petition claiming legitimate expectation and secondly there must be a promise or a representation on the part of the public on the claim of the person aggrieved by the decision. In this connection it will be very much pertinent to reiterate an observation of the Supreme Court of India in the case of National Building Construction Corporations Vs. Raghunathan reported in AIR 1998 SC page 2779 held that: 

"Incidentally in this case what question of 'legitimate Expectation' and not raised in the petition and foundation was laid in the pleadings for such a plea advanced before the Court. Strangely the High Court allowed this plea at the stage of argument and allowed the petitions only on the ground of Legitimate Expectation without least realizing that there was hardly any legitimacy in the claim of the respondents. In the absence of pleading and the affidavit of the respondents and support thereof the whole exercise done by the High Court cannot be but be termed to be speculation." 

Supreme Court of India in Food Corporation of India -Vs- Kamdhanu Cattle Food Industries Ltd. reported in 1 SCC page 71 observed: 

"The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a citizen in such a situation may not by itself by a distinct enforceable right but, failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary and this is how the requirement of due consideration of a legitimate expectation forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate expectation is as relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. Whenever, the question arises it is to be determined not according to the claimant perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bonafide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judiciary scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent." 

Similar views were taken by our Apex Court in the case of Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury, reported in 7 MLR AD page 265 which runs as follows:-

"In the case under our consideration no case has been taken made out from the side of the respondents that there was any act on the part of the Government that could have given rise to a legitimate expectation in the respondents to have the enterprise denationalized in their favour. It has already been mentioned that there is nothing in the Gazette notification of September 27, 1982 wherefrom it can be said from the side of the respondents that the same could give rise in the mind of ordinary prudence expectation of some kind including legitimate expectation of having the enterprise denationalized in their favour. The respondents have not been able to make out a case that in rejecting their representation for having the enterprise denationalized they were not treated fairly or in other words they were not treated equally along with others placed in a situation like that of them. The learned Counsel in support of his submission of absence of case of legitimate expectation on the part of the respondents has placed reliance upon the observation and the ratio of the case reported at AIR 1999 (SC), wherein it has been observed: 

"The principle is at the root of the rule of law and requires regularity, predictability and certainty in government's dealing with the public. The rule of law enforces minimum standards of fairness both substantive and procedural."

In this case this Division approved the views taken in the case of Hindustan Development Corporation. The Court will not interfere on the ground of procedural fairness to a person whose interest based on legitimate expectation might be affected. 

On due and proper consideration and the principles as laid down in the case of LGED—vs- Mizanur Rahman, our Apex Court has laid down certain guidelines on the principle of Legitimate Expectation after reviewing all previous judgment and rules in order to settle the principles of law as regards Legitimate Expectation which sum up under: 

I)	Whenever any vacancy in LGED is created in the revenue set up it shall consider for absorption of employees or officers of the development projects within the meaning of Section 2(ga) of the Rules, 2005 if the project in which she/he is working is completed subject to the condition that such employee or officer has requisite qualification for the said post. 

II)	Whenever a vacant post is created in the revenue budget, the LGED shall absorb/transfer any employee or officer form the development project mentioned is Clause (i) to fill up that post in accordance with Rules of 1985 and the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008. 

III)	An officer or employee shall be absorbed if she was appointed in the development project within the meaning of rule 2(Ka) of Rules, 2005 in accordance with the procedures prescribed for appointment in public employment. 

IV)	An officer or employee must have requisite qualifications for the post in which he is seeking absorption. 

V)	An officer or employee must have continuity service in the project in which he is working. 

VI)	An officer or employee must have satisfactory service record before his case is considered for regularization in the revenue budget. 

VII)	If an officer and employee whose rank and status does not relate to the posts advertised by the impugned notifications on the day of its publications, such officer or employee would not be eligible for consideration for absorption. 

VIII)	The employees and officers who have been working in the development projects mentioned in Clause (I) on monthly pay basis would only be eligible for consideration for I" absorption in the revenue budget. 

IX)	Unless and until vacancies in the revenue budget in the LGED are created the employees and officers of the development project mentioned in clause (I) cannot claim as of right to be absorbed in the revenue budget. 

X)	While considering and selecting an employee or officer of the development project for absorption in the revenue budget, the appointing authority shall maintain strictly the prevailing quota system for employment in the public employment being followed by the Government. 

XI)	The LGED shall consider the case of those working on master roll basis for absorption in the revenue by phases if they have requisite qualifications subject to the availability of vacancies according to their seniority."

	20. On the similar point our Apex Court in the case of Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) represented by its Director General Vs. Md. Mahbub Alam Khan and others held that the High Court Division came to a finding that in order to facilitate absorption of the personnel of development project the Government promulgated SRO No.182-A i n/2005/S homo/Bidhi 1/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 making clear and specific provisions to absorb all the personnel of development projects which started between 9th April, 1972 to 30th June, 1997. In the instant case, the project of the writ-petitioners started in July, 1993 and they are entitled to be absorbed under the revenue budget pursuant to the provisions of that SRO. The High Court Division further held that the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) at its meeting dated 31.12.2001 had taken decision to transfer all the personnel of the development projects expeditiously to the revenue budget and that the decision was circulated by the Planning Division by the memo dated 10.01.2008 asking all concerned to take necessary steps to transfer all completed development projects to the revenue budget. 

	21. The High Court Division considered the case of Bangladesh Vs. Mr. Abul Hossain (2003) BLD (AD) 129 in which this Division held that once a privilege is given to a person on condition of doing any act and if such condition is fulfilled and continues to be fulfilled, such privilege or right cannot be taken away or cancelled without giving a chance of being heard. Therefore, the High Court Division directed the leave-petitioners to absorb or regularize the writ-petitioners in the regular set up of the Local Government and Rural Development and Co-operatives under the leave-petitioners in permanent post as and when vacancy would arise subject to the condition that they are not otherwise disqualified.  

22. In the case of Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs. Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury and others reported in 22 BLD (AD) 2002, page 199 which runs as follows:-

It is held that "an expectation could be based on an express promise or representation or by established past action of settled conduct. The representation must be clear and un-ambiguous. It could be a representation to the individual or generally to a class or persons". 

"Every such legitimate expectation does not be itself fructify into a right and therefore it does amount to as right in the conventional sense." 

The High Court Division in arriving its decision in the instant case relying the decisions reported in 1 WLR page 1482, 2 AC 629 and number of reported decisions of All England Reports. 

In the case of Bangladesh Soya Project Ltd. Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief reported in 22 BLD (HD) 2002, page 378 which runs as follows:

"Government is always under an obligation to act fairly and reasonably even where the other party has no legal right in the conventional sense. This is so even in the case of a contract where the Government is one of the contracting parties.

"In the case of Asab Khan and others Vs. The Court of Settlement reported in 23 BLD (HCD) 2003, page 7 which runs as follows: 

"Legitimate expectation is a concept of administrative law which means that an administrative authority cannot abuse its discretion by disregarding undertaking or statement of its intent. Where an action of the administrative authority adversely affects legal right of an individual, duty to act fairly and reasonably is implicit." 

In the case of North South Property Development Ltd. Vs. Ministry of Land and others reported in 52 DLR (2000), page 7 which runs as follows: 

"A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice amount expectation which it would be within its power to fulfill". 

In the case of Rabia Basri and another Vs. Bangladesh Biman and another reported in 52 DLR (2000) page 308 which runs as follows:-

"The petitioner's expectation of being absorbed in the service after satisfactory completion of five years’ service cannot but be said to their legitimate expectation and in all fairness they should be absorbed in their service." 

In the case of M.P. Sugar Mills Vs. State of U.P. reported in AIR 1979 (S.C.) page 621 which runs as follows:-

"Doctrine of promissory estoppels has been variously called 'promissory estoppels; `requisite' quasi estoppels' and 'new estoppels'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppels', it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppels. The true principle of 'promissory estoppels' seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct, made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealing which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not." 

"This observation of Lord Denning clearly suggests that the parties need not be in any kind of legal relationship before the transaction from which the promissory estoppels takes it origin. The doctrine would seem to apply even where there is no pre-existing legal relationship between the parties, but the promise effect a legal relationship which will arise in further". 

"The true promise of promissory estoppels, therefore, seem to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowledge or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it." If it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealing which have taken place between the parties and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppels need not be inhabited by the same limitation as estoppels in the street same of the term. It is equitable principle evolved by the Courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason in logic or principle of promissory estoppels should also not be available as a cause of action it necessary to satisfy the equity. 

In the case of Commissioner of Customs Vs. Monohar Ali reported in 8 BLC (AD) 2003 which runs as follows:-

"The importers having acted on the promise made by the appellants under Section 25A of the Act to accept the price determined by the Government appointed inspectors, the appellants cannot go back on that promise as it was meant to be binding on them". 
In the case of Nurunnessa Vs. Bahar Ali Bepari reported in 1981 BLD (AD) page 91 which runs as follows:-

"Promissory estoppels-Government making promise-promises acting on the promise-No lack of power of the Government to make the promise-Government bound by the promise."

In the case of Central London Property Trust Ltd. Vs. High Tress House Ltd. (i) Denning J. considered the effect of an arrangement made by the parties and concluded. 

"Where parties enter into an agreement which is intended to create legal relation between them and in pursuance of such arrangement one party makes a promise to the other which he knows will be acted on and which is in fact acted on by the promises, the Court will treat the promise as binding on the promisor to the extent that it will not allow him to act inconsistently with it even though the promise may not supported by consideration in the strict sense." 

In another case of Secretary ,Ministry of Industries Nationalized Industries Division Vs. Saleh Ahmed and another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs. Saleh Ahmed and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) page 91 where our Apex Court held that:-

"The Government took the decision on agreement to release the mill in question lack of power on the part of the Government so to do is not the plea, rather a belated plea was taken that the decision has been revised by the Government although no such case was made out. Hence applying the aforesaid principle the least that can be said is that the respondents cannot allowed to act inconsistently and the decision to release the mill remains binding on them. The High Court by the writ has enforced this decision "to complete the formalities for transfer of the mill to the petitioner" 

The same principle as settled in 17 BLC (AD) case has been adopted and followed in the case of Golam Kibria (Md) Vs. Bangladesh by the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division held that:- 
"The doctrine of Legitimate Expectation is only an aspect which does not give rise to an enforceable right but only provides that the action taken by the authority while dealing with the citizen is not arbitrary. The applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expectation arises when an administrative body by reason of representation of by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way."

The aforesaid decision of the High Court Division has been reported in 65 DLR (2013) page 148. In another unreported case of Md. Mahbub Alam Khan and others vs. Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government Rural Development and Co-operatives, the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court Division while deciding the Writ Petition No.7484 of 2009 on 17.01.2012 held that the petitioners cannot be discriminated and the respondents cannot adopt a pick and choose policy. By working for a reasonable period time the petitioners have all acquired, skills and expertise and can legitimately expect that they will be absorbed. Having served for long years and in view of the past practice the petitioners can reasonably expect that they will be absorbed in the revenue budget. In this connection reliance is placed on the case of Attorney General of Hong Kong -Vs- Ng Then Shik 2 AC 629 a leading case on the doctrine of Legitimate Expectation wherein Lord Fraser said:-

"When a public authority has promised to follow a certain procedure it is in the interest of good administration that it should act fairly and should implement its promise so long as the implementation does not interfere with its statutory duty." 

The doctrine of legitimate expectation and its impact in the administrative law has been considered by our court. Explaining the nature and scope of doctrine of legitimate expectation in the case of Bangladesh -vs-Md. Abdul Hossain reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 129. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh held that once a privileged is given to a person on condition of doing any act and if such condition is fulfilled such privilege or right cannot be taken away or cancelled without giving a chance of being heard. 

23. Another aspect which needs to be addressed is that as a result of the petitioners continuance in service for substantial period of time have also become over aged and at this stage they are not in a position to complete with others or seek re-employment in some other establishment. The petitioners who are serving for long spells and have the requisite qualification for the job should not be thrown out but their services should be regularized as far as possible. 

24. The respondents are directed to absorb/ regularize the petitioner serving as Data Entry Operator of the Development project namely RLP of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) to the Revenue Budget of BRDP under the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of his joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of SRO namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫”contained in Memo SRO  No.182/Ain/2005/ somo/Bidhi-I/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 (Annexure-G) issued by the Office  of the respondent No.2 under by the Order of the Hon'ble President of the Republic which they are permitted/required by law to do vacancy arise subject to the condition that they are otherwise not disqualified. 

25. In view of the observation as made above the rule is disposed of without any order as to cost. 

26. Office is hereby directed to transmit a copy of this judgment to the concern authority at once.

End.

Mr. Sadananda Rana, Advocate ------ For the petitioners 
Mr. A.B.M. Bayezid, Advocate ------ For the Opposite party Nos.1-9
parties:

full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M.  Abdul Hakim, J:- This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-9 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 04.10.2003 passed by the Additional District Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No.351 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26.10.1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court No.2, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.248 of 1991. 

2. The opposite party Nos.1-9 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.86 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Bagerhat which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court No.2, Sadar, Bagerhat and renumbered as Title Suit No.248 of 1991 impleading the predecessor of the present petitioners as defendant Nos.1 and 2 praying for declaration of title and partition in respect of 5.79 acres of land as described in schedule to the plaint. 
3. The plaintiff's case, in brief, are that the suit land comprising C.S. Khatian No.14 under Mouza Dhansagar measuring an area of 7.02 acres originally belonged to Tasenuddin Shaikh which was correctly recoded in his name; that Tasenuddin Shaikh died leaving only son Abdul Aziz, daughters, Asiya Khatun and Sona Bibi as widow; that Abdul Aziz died leaving two sons, namely, Ruhul Amin Shaikh and Nazrul Islam Shaikh, three daughters, namely, Raushanara Khatun, Peyara Begum, Zarina Khatun and widow Majeda Khatun; that during his life time Tasenuddin sold .33 acres of land to defendant No.2, Mohabbat Ali Howladar. He further sold 1.82 acres to defendant No.1, Abdul Karim Farazi on 08.04.1953 on condition for re-conveyance. Subsequently, after taking further amount from defendant No.1, relinquish his claims for re-conveyance by a registered deed of Ekrarnama dated 20.03.1964; that Tasenuddin Shaikh said also sold 3.30 acres land to Hasenuddin by two registered deed dated 11.07.1953 and 24.08.1954. He further sold .66 acres to Kashem Ali Farazi and Momen Uddin Hawladar by a registered kabala dated 24.12.1960; that subsequently, Abdul Karim Farazi purchased .66 acres of land from Kashem Ali Farazi and Momenuddin Hawladar. This Abdul Karim Farazi acquired 2.48 acres of land in the suit Jama; that Abdul Karim Farazi, defendant No.1 sold 2.24 acres of land to Tasenuddin Shaikh by a kabala dated 20.03.1964 accordingly Tasenuddin got 3.15 acres of land in the suit Jama but due to inadvertence of the Moharar Dag No.1005 was wrongly inserted in place of Dag No.1075 in the aforesaid kabala dated 20.03.1964. The plaintiffs got their homestead on plot No.1075; that Hasenuddin Hawlader sold 3.30 acres (which he purchased from Tasenuddin Shaikh) to Abdul Aziz, predecessor of the plaintiffs by a kabala deed dated 09.08.1956 and Abdul Aziz sold .66 acres of land to Mahabat Ali Hawladar (defendant No.2). The plaintiff Nos.1-7 have been in possession of the land according to their shares; that plaintiff Nos.8-9 namely, Abdul Hannan Hawladar and Abdul Mannan Hawladar claimed to have purchased .72 acres from Sona Babi, wife of Tasenuddin and thus plaintiffs are entitled to get 5.79 acres of land in suit Jama; that it may be noted here that plaintiff Nos.1-7 filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat, being Title Suit No.40 of 1986 which was renumbered as 379 of 1986 and withdrawn due to some defects; that during recent settlement operation some portion of the shares of plaintiffs have been erroneously recorded in the names of the defendants which is requires to be corrected; that as some of the defendants having been co-sharers in the disputed Jama and some of them being the claimants of shares on vague deed, the co-sharers cannot arrive at a common platform for payment of rent for the same as there was no amicable partition amount the co-sharers and as defendant Nos.l-3 illegally want to retain the jama property in their possession, a partition by metes and bounds among the co-sharers is required with a view to removing all the aforesaid problems. The plaintiffs requested the defendants for partition but they refused to do so on 24th Agrahayan, 1394 B.S. corresponding to 11.12.1987 and hence the suit. 

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the lands of the suit Jama belonged to Tasenuddin Shaikh and he sold 1.82 acres of land to defendant No.1 by a kabala deed dated 08.4.1953 on condition of its re-conveyance on payment of the consideration amount and the defendant No.1 executed an Ekrarnama in favour of (Tasenuddin Shaikh) to that effect. He did not return the consideration amount in pursuance of the condition of the Ekrarnama; that Tasenuddin Shaikh subsequently sold .66 acres of land by a registered deed dated 24.12.1960 to Kasem Farazi and Momenuddin Molla both of whom sold out the same to defendant No.1 by a kabala dated 27.11.1962 and thus defendant No.1 acquired title to 2.48 acres of land of the suit Jama by purchase and he had been in possession of the same since purchase but Nine Annas and Eighteen Gandas equal to 3.89 acres have been recorded in the name of defendant No.1 in the Revisional Survey and the State Acquisition Khatian concerned; that although defendant No.1 did not put any claim over the excess land recorded in his name yet his heirs may claim it in future and although the conditional sale deed executed by Tasenuddin in favour of defendant No.1 became out and out a sale deed for non-compliance of the conditions of the said Ekrarnama yet he did not forego his claim in writing and it may create problems in future and in apprehension of the aforesaid facts and circumstances it was settled between Tasenuddin Shaikh and defendant No.1 that Tasenuddin would execute a deed foregoing his claim of re-conveyance and defendant No.1 would execute another deed to the effect that he would not put any claim over the excess land recorded in his name. Accordingly, two deeds were executed and registered on 20.03.1964 one by Tasenuddin and another by defendant No.1; that Tasenuddin executed `Na-Dabi' deed dated 20.03.1964 foregoing his claim stating that upon peculiar circumstances did not permit him to take back the land measuring 1.82 acres sold to the defendant No.1 on condition of re-conveyance; that Tasenuddin in connivance with the deed writer, identifier and witnesses got a sale deed written in respect of 2.24 acres of land and executed by defendant No.1 giving him an impression that it was a deed of `Na-Dabi' Patta. The deed, in question, was registered by practicing fraud. It was not read over to defendant No. 1. It was a fraudulent deed without any consideration. Tasenuddin did not disclose about it nor did he claim and possess land by virtue of that fraudulent deed. 

5. Defendant No.2 in his written statement stated that Tasenuddin transferred .33 acres of land to this defendant by a registered Patta. After his death, his son Abdul Aziz sold .66 acres of land by a kabala deed dated 22.02.1963. Tasenuddin gave settlement of .40 acres of land to Arab Ali Shaikh who made an oral gift of the same in favour of his son Kadam Ali; defendant No.2 in the name of his son Abdul Hoque Hawladar purchased .14 acres of land from Kadam Ali Shaikh by a registered kahala deed dated 20.05.1957; that Kadam Ali died leaving two wife's namely. Bibijan and Zarina Bibi sold .10 acres of land from Dag No.1067 to defendant No.2 by a kahala deed dated 13.03.1958 and this kabala deed was taken in the name of his son Abdul Jalil Hawladar. The Water and Power Development Board acquired .16 acres of land from co-sharer of Kadam Ali. The plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree as prayed for. 

6. In the suit, plaintiff examined 3 PWs on the other hand defendant examined 4 DWs to prove their respective cases. 

7. The learned Assistant Judge upon hearing and considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 26.10.1992, on the findings that suit is bad for defect of parties and plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their title and possession on the suit land by producing any documents and further failed to produce the kabala dated 20.03.1964. 

8. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No.35I of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Bagerhat. Consequently appeal was transferred to the. Court of Additional District Judge, Bagerhat, who by his judgment and decree dated 04.10.2003 allowed the appeal and decreed the suit and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. 

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment of the appellate Court, the defendants moved this Court in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule. 

10. Mr. Sadananda Rana the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners submits that the suit is bad for defect of parties since in the suit, plaintiffs did not implead the heirs of Kadam Ali and R.S. recorded tenant Arab Ali Shaikh but the appellate Court erroneously found that suit is not bad for defect of parties and decreed the suit. In this connection learned Advocate cited a decision reported in 37 DLR(AD) 216. Learned Advocate further submits that the appellate Court did not at all reverse the findings of the trial Court in respect of the Exhibit-4(F) and plaintiffs failed to produce the original deed in support of their claim. The appellate Court completely failed to appreciate and consider that the documents filed by the plaintiffs in the list of documents dated 10.03.1988 which is not tally with the documents filed by the Firishti dated 30.10.2012. He next submits that the judgment of the appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this respect learned Advocate referred 3 decisions reported in 1 MLR (AD) (1996) 430, 3 BLC (AD) 38 and 55 DLR (AD) 20. He also submits that the appellate Court totally misread and misconstrued the evidence and materials on record and also the judgment of the trial court and accordingly prayed that the rule should be made absolute. Further, in reply to the submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties, Mr. Sadananda Rana, submits that the plaintiffs have ample opportunity to produce/proves their documents in the appellate court but plaintiffs was totally negligent in filing those documents of title. Since sufficient materials and evidence are already on the suit should not sent back on remand as prayed by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. In this respect of the learned Advocate cited two decisions reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74 and 47 DLR (AD) 162. 

11. On the other hand, Mr. A.B.M. Bayezid, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties submits that the plaintiffs claimed their title in 1.82 acres through his father who transferred the said to defendant No.1 dated 08.04.1953 by registered sale deed dated 03.04.1953 coupled with registered Ekrarnama dated 08.04.1953 and confirmed- the sale by registered Ekrarnama dated 20.03.1964. The learned Advocate for the Opposite-parties further submits that certified copy of those documents are filed in court by the list of documents (Firishti) dated 13.10.2012. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties next submits that the plaintiffs exhibited series of documents to prove their title in the suit land by exhibiting C.S. and S.A. Khatian and rents receipts. Thus the plaintiffs were able to prove their title and possession in the suit land. Learned Advocate for the opposite-parties also submits that the judgment of the appellate court is a proper judgment of reversal and the appellate court on consideration materials and evidence on record rightly reversed the decisions of the trial Court, as such same cannot be interfere in the revisional Court. He lastly submits that the appellate court after considering the evidence of DW2 rightly found that suit is not bad for defect of parties. 

12. It appears that the trial Court on consideration of evidence and materials on record clearly found that suit is hard for defect of parties since the heirs of Kadam Ali and R.S. recorded owner Arab Ali Shaikh were not made parties in the present suit. The learned trial court on consideration of Exhibit-3 categorically found that Arab Ali Shaikh was R.S recorded tenant and main party in the present suit and co—share in the suit land but without impleading Arab Ali, the present suit for partition was field. In a partition suit, the established principle of law is that all co-sharer should be impleaded and failure implead any co-sharer render the suit liable for dismissal on the ground of maintainability. In this respect reliance may be place in the case of Mobinnessa and others Vs. Khalilur Rahman and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 216. 

13. It further appears that the trial court specially found that the documents filed by the plaintiffs are all certified copies and those were not marked as exhibits as per Order XIII rule 4(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this respect learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-opposite parties admits that although the documents were filed by the plaintiffs but those were not marked as exhibit. In this connection the learned Advocate for the opposite parties tried to submits since the documents are already on record the plaintiffs may be given chance to prove the same as per law. In reply learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners submits that although the plaintiffs hand an opportunity to produce the said documents in the appellate court but in this respect the plaintiffs did not taken any steps in the appellate Court. So, there is no scope to send back the case on remand to fill up the lacuna of the plaintiffs as it appears apparently that the plaintiffs were extremely negligence in this respect. Moreover, it appears that there is no misreading and non-consideration of any materials evidence on record. Thus there is no scope to send the case back on remand. In this respect of our apex court has already settle the principle that remand as contemplated under Order XLI, Rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not of matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in the any party's pleading. 

14. It transpires that the father of defendant No.1 Abdul Karim Farazi purchased 1.82  acres of suit land from Tasenuddin, the predecessor of the plaintiffs by registered Kabala dated 08.04.1953. Thereafter, Tasenuddin also sold .66 acres of to Kashem Ali Farazi and Momin Uddin Howlader by registered deed dated 24.12.1960 and they sold out the same to defendant no.1 by a registered Kabala dated 27.11.1962. Thus defendant no.1 acquired title in 2.48 acres in the suit Jama by the aforesaid purchases. Subsequently, the plaintiffs claimed that their predecessor, Tasenuddin Shaikh purchased 2.24 acres of suit land from predecessor of the defendant no.1, Abdul Karim by a Kabala dated 20.03.1964 although the plaintiffs predecessor claimed that he purchased the suit land from the predecessor of the defendant no.1 by kabala dated 20.03.1964 but failed to produced neither the certified copy nor the original of the said Kabala. Rather the plaintiff’s field different Kabalas by filling a Frishti which was not tally with the documents filed with the frishti in the suit. 

15. It further appears that in the instant case the specific findings of the trial court have not been reversed by the lower appellate court exercising its power under Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court having considered of the materials on record rightly dismissed the suit with some specific findings which have not been reversed by the court of appeal below which is not a proper judgment of the reversal, appellate court thus committed error of law in reversing the judgment of the trial court. In this connection we can place reliance on the decision in the case of Hajarilal Mondal and others Vs. Md. Mozzaffar Bapari and others reported in 8 BLC (AD) 77, wherein it has been held that it is a settled principle of law that the lower appellate court being the final court of fact will have to discuss and reassess the evidence on record independently while either reversing or affirming the finding of the trial court. In case of reversal it is more incumbent upon the appellate court to reassess the evidence on record and to arrive at his own independent finding. 

16. It has also been well settled by our apex Court, the plaintiff in order to succeed must established the own case to obtained a decree and weakness of the defendant case is no ground in the passing of the decree in favour of the plaintiff. It appears that in the present case plaintiffs did not take any steps to prove their title in the suit land as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree of partition where they failed to prove their title in the possession in the suit land as co-hearer in the suit land. It is further evident from the appellate court judgment that the appellate court without considering the evidence and materials on record abruptly came to a finding that the plaintiffs had right, title and interest in 5.79 acres of land but decreed the suit only for a total area of 1.23 acres out of which plaintiff Nos.1, 2 and 16 will get .24 decimal, .85 decimals and .14 decimals respectively. Thus it is evident from the judgment of the appellate court that whether the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree of for 5.79 acres or 1.23 acres land. Thus it is apparent that the appellate court failed to apply the judicial mind in passing decree in favor of the plaintiffs. 

17. I therefore, find substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. In the aforesaid promises, I set-aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court and restored those of the trial Court. 

18. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. 

19. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated. 

20. Send down the Lower Court Records expeditiously with a copy of judgment for information. 

End.
