full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, J. :- This Rule Nisi was issued on an application under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order under Memo No. Bhu: Re: 6/2002/1471 dated 08.07.2002 passed by respondent No.2 contained in annexure-G to the writ petition purporting to constitute a committee to rehear .Appeal Case Nos.3 I 335 of 2001, 31336 of 2001 and 41105 of 2001 and the notice dated 14.7.2002 issued by respondent No.3 contained in annexure-H to the writ petition for rehearing of above 3 cases on 24.07.2002 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 
2. Facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi as follows: 
A holding of 7.51 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.528 of Mouja-Joar Sahra, JL No.271 under former police station -Tejgaon now under police station - Budda, Dhaka belonged to one Joy Durga Das who died leaving behind his daughter's son, namely, Krisna Chandra Debnath to inherit his all properties. While owing and possessing the said properties, Krisna Chandra Debnath sold out 7.51 acres of land by six deeds of sale to Moulana A.K.M. Fazhil Hafiz, Hazi Zohra Khatun and Begum Rahima Hossein, each getting 2.50 acres of the aforesaid land. Subsequently, Begum Rahima Hossain sold out 1.25 acres of land to Ms. Hena Khatun by a deed of sale No.4329 dated 04.10.1961. However, the names of Ms. Hena Khatun and other original heirs were recorded and published in S.A Khatian No.942, but their names were recorded separately during Revisional Survey (R.S. record). Subsequently, the mother of the petitioner, namely Begum Rahima Hossain transferred .1650 acres of land from R.S. Plot No.5306 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2100 corresponding to SA Khatian No.942 to the petitioner by a deed of Heba-Bil-Ewaj No.10327 dated 09.6.1994. The petitioner got his name mutated against the case land by Mutation and Separation Case No.443/96-97 and started paying revenue taxes to the Government. However, .1708 acres of ditch land from R.S. Plot No.5306 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2100 was recorded in the name of the petitioner's mother and .1200 acres of ditch land from R.S. Plot No.5305 appertaining to R.S. Khatian No.2537 was recorded in the name of respondent No.7. In this way, .2908 acres of ditch land was k recorded in the name of petitioner's mother and respondent No.7 in the present plot No.57227. During land survey in Dhaka City area, .1222 acres Of ditch land from Plot No.57277 appertaining to D.P. Khatian No.7507 was recorded in the name of the petitioner and .0486 acres of land from Plot No.57227 appertaining to D.P. Khatian No.12839 was recorded in the name of petitioner's mother. In this way, .1708 acres of ditch land was recorded in the name of the petitioner and his mother. 

3. It further appears from the writ petition that respondent No.7 and other purchased .24 acres of land from C.S. Plot No.1242 and .56 acres of land from C.S. plot No.1243 from aforesaid Hena Khatun and Abul Bashar by registered deeds of sale. Subsequently, respondent No.7 and others got their names mutated against the case land by Mutation and Separation Case No.3722/76-77. In the revisional settlement the names of respondent No.7 and others were recorded in plot No.5306 of R.S. Khatian No.2537, but in the Dhaka City Land Survey, only .12 acres of ditch land from plot No.57227 of D.P. Khatian No.2537 was recorded in their names.

4. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid draft record-of rights, respondent No.7 and others filed Objection Case Nos.4714 of 2000, 4715of  2000 and 12903 of 2000 before the . Revenue-Officer under Rule 30 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 (in brief, Tenancy Rules, 1955) against the Tashdik record of .1708 acres of land in Plot No.57227 in the name of the petitioner and his mother. The revenue Office, after hearing both the parties and considering their relevant papers and documents, rejected the objection Cases on 8.11.2000. 

5. Being dissatisfied with the aforesaid rejection order passed in objection cases, respondent No.7 and others filed 3 Appeal Case being Nos.3 1335 of 2001, 31336 of 2001 and 41105 of 2001 under Rule 31 of the aforesaid rules before the Settlement-Officer, who heard all the appeal cases together, examined the relevant papers and documents and dismissed the 3 appeal cases on 13.11.2001. 

6. Respondent No.7 and others, thereafter, filed an application under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 before the Settlement Officer who, on receiving the application and on considering the contents thereof, set aside the order passed under Rule 31 and formed a 5-member committee (Appeal Board) headed by a Charge Officer for hearing of the said 3 appeal cases. The said committee heard the parties, recorded their statements, examined the papers and documents, inspected to ascertain the possession of ditch land and unanimously came to a decision making a specific recommendation on 6.3.2002 for restoring the order dated 13.11.2001 passed by the Settlement-Officer in appeal cases. 

7. On 17.3.2002, the Settlement-Officer, by exercising his special power and authority under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, resorted the judgment and order passed under Rule 31 in the aforesaid appeal cases. 

8. For reconsideration of judgment passed in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, respondent No.7, thereafter, filed an application under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to the Director (land records and surveys) who, by his letter dated 10.06.2002 sent the same to the Settlement-Officer, Dhaka to reopen the aforesaid appeal cases and decide those afresh as per Rules. 

9. The Settlement-Officer, by his letter bearing Memo .No.12/257/-5(11/528-2075 dated 16.6.2002, informed the Director (land records and' surveys) that there in no scope for reopening the matter in view of the fact that the committee constituted for that purpose has already decided the matter. 

10. In spite of aforesaid facts and circumstances, the Director (land records and surveys) respondent No.2 by his order under Memo No. Bhu: Re: 6/2002/1471 dated 08.07.2002 passed an order purporting to constitute a committee headed by the respondent No.2 charge officer-3 to hold a fresh hearing in respect of 3 appeal cases and report by 31.07.2002. Respondent No.3, in consequence of above order, issued a notice fixing a date for hearing of 3 appeal cases on 24.07.2002. 

11. Being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 10.6.2002 contained in Annexure-G and notice dated 14.07.2002 contained in Annexure-H, the petitioner filed this writ petition and obtained this Rule Nisi. 

12. Respondent No.7 contested the Rule Nisi by filling an affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit-in-oppositions denying the contentions made in the writ petition and supplementary affidavit filed by the writ petitioner. The case of respondent No.7 as set up in the affidavit-in-oppositions, in short, is that respondent No.7 and others produced deeds of purchase in respect of .80 acres of land but the Settlement-Officer prepared record of rights in their favour only in respect of 0.5708 acres of land vide D.P Khatian No.4778. The committee constituted by the Settlement-Officer under rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 did not properly consider documents of title in support of their claim and recommended restoring the judgment and order of the appeal cases illegally and as such draft record-of-rights prepared and maintained up to the appellate authority under rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 can not be sustained in the eye of law and the same requires a fresh scrutiny for coming to a correct decision. In view of above facts and circumstances, respondent No.7 made a prayer to respondent No.2, Director (land records and surveys) who being satisfied on material irregularities ordered further scrutiny of the matter under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and as such the impugned order dated 08.07.2002 contained in Annexure-G to the writ petition for constitution of a committee as well as notice dated 14.7.2002 contained in Annexure-H to the writ petition are lawful and valid and as such the writ petition should be discharged. 

13. At the very outset, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate along with Mr. S.R. Khosh Nabish, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that since the appeal cases were decided by the appropriate authority under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the judgment passed in appeal cases cannot be. changed, altered and modified by respondent No.2 as Settlement Officer exercising his powers and authority under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, unless there is an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights and as such, the order passed by respondent No.2 constituting a committee for reopening the appeal cases earlier decided under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is without lawful authority. He next submits that thought the Rule 42A of the East Bengal Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 gave respondent No.2 as a Settlement-Officer an authority to hear the matter in respect of record-of-rights before final publication thereof, the fact remains that the Settlement-Officer has already exercised such powers and authority by constituting a committee and that the aforesaid forum of law has already been exhausted and as such the order dated 08.07.2002 contained in Annexure-G to the writ petition for constitution of a committee for rehearing of appeal cases is beyond the scope of law. He then submits that similarly, the notice of hearing of the appeal cases as contained in Annexure-H dated 14.07.2002 having been issued in pursuance of an illegal order dated 08.07.2007 contained in Annexure-G has also been issued without lawful authority and as such the Rule Nisi should be made absolute. Learned Advocate for the petitioner, in support of his submissions, relied upon the decision in the case of Md. Aftab Ali Sheikh Vs. Director Land Records, Directorate of land records and surveys, Tejgaon, Dhaka and others, 11 MLR (HC) (2006) 226. 

14. On the other hand, Mr. M. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.7, submits that the grounds taken in the writ petition are neither proper nor legal, that respondent No.2 rightly constituted a committee, that respondent No.3 rightly issued a notice for rehearing of the appeal cases, that respondent Nos.2 and 3 have not  committed any illegality in doing the same and as such, constitution of a committee and issuance of a notice are not beyond the scope of law and as such, the Rule Nisi should be discharged. He next submits that respondent No.7 and others purchased the case land from the co-shares of the holding, got their names mutated against the case land by Mutation and Separation Case No.3722/76-77 and enjoyed peaceful possession by making demarcation over the same and as such respondent No.2 rightly constituted a committee and respondent No.3, rightly issued a notice for rehearing of the appeal cases in order to resolve the dispute and as such the Rule Nisi should be discharge. He further submits that since respondent No.7 and others after purchase of the land got their names mutated and that since they are in possession over the case land by paying development taxes and rent to the Government, the constitution of a committee for rehearing of appeal cases and issuance of notice directing the parties to appear before the committee were rightly done and as such, the Rule Nisi should be discharged. 

15. Be that as it may, Mr. Razik-Al-Jalil, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing of behalf the respondent Nos. l and 2, submits that under Rule 44,of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the director of land records and surveys has been vested with the powers to discharge all the functions of a revenue officer under Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and, that he shall have all the powers of a settlement officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42A and 42B of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 and that he may correct the fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rule, 1955. 

He further submits that since the record-of-rights has not yet been finally published, respondent No.2, may pass an order for necessary correction and as such, respondent No.2 has not committed any illegality in passing the impugned order and similarly, respondent No.3 has also not committed any illegality in issuing the impugned notice in consequence of the order passed by respondent No.2. 

16. We have gone through the writ petition and tM materials annexed thereto and considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for both the sides. 
17. On a close perusal of the writ petition, it appears that respondent No.7 and others filed Objection Case Nos.4714 of 2000. 4715 of 2000 and 12903 of 2000 under rule 30 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rule, 1955 against the Tasdik record of .1708 of ditch land in Plot No.57227 in the name of the petitioner and his mother, The Objection Officer after hearing both the parties and considering the relevant papers and documents filed by them rejected the objection cases by an order dated 08.11.2000, and the aforesaid facts are evident from Annexure-A and A 1 to the writ petition. 

18. Writ petition further revels that respondent No.7 and others thereafter, filed 3 appeal cases Nos.31335 of 2001, 31336 of 2001 and 41105 of 2001 under Rule 31 of the aforesaid rule against the order of rejection passed in aforesaid 3 objection cases. On receipt of the said appeal cases, the Assistant Settlement-Officer and Appeal Officer after hearing the petitioner and respondent No.7 and others and on examining the relevant papers and documents filed by them dismissed the said 3 appeals on 13.11.2001. The aforesaid fact is very much evident from Annexure-B to the writ petition. 

19. Respondent No.7 and others thereafter filed an application under Rule 42 of the said Rules before the Settlement-Officer who, on consideration of the contents made in the application, set aside the order passed under Rule-31 of the said Rule and formed a 5-.member committee (Appeal Board) for rehearing of the 3 appeal cases. The committee heard the parties, recorded their statements, considered their papers and documents, inspected the actual possession of the ditch land and recommended restoring the judgment and order dated 13.11.2001 passed by the Appeal Officer and sent the record of the case to the Settlement-Officer to pass the necessary order on the basis of recommendation made by the aforesaid Committee. 

20. On receiving the record of the case, the Settlement-Officer scrutinized the entire proceeding and affirmed the judgment and order passed under Rule 31 in the said 3 appeal cases. Respondent No.7 and others again filed an application for reconsideration of the order passed in the said appeal cases before the Director (land records and survey), who sent the same to the Settlement-Officer, Dhaka requesting him to re-open the matter and decided the same afresh as per Rules. 

21. It is seen from the record of the case that the Settlement-Officer delivered judgment in 3 appeal cases by exercising his powers and authority both under rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 after hearing of both the parties. 

22. In order to dispose of this Rule Nisi, let us recapitulate the Rule 30, 31, 42, 42A, 42B and 44 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 and consider them in juxtaposition with each other. 
"30. Objection: Blank forms of objection shall be supplied free-of charge, and all objections shall as far as practicable, he made in such forms. Along with the original objection, the objector shall file a copy or copies of the same for service on all other persons who, in the opinion of the Revenue-Officer are materially interested in the case. The Revenue-Officer shall issue notice informing the objector and all other persons so interested of the date and place fixed for the hearing of the objection, and, with each notice to a person, other than the objector, he shall forward a copy of the objection. Objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue Officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and an abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties materially interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue-Officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned. 

31. Appeal: (1) Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Revenue—Officer on any objection made under rule 30 may appeal to the Revenue-Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement-Officer or to such Revenue-Officer appointed with the Additional Designation of Assistant Settlement Officer as may be empowered by him in this behalf, within 30 days from the date of the order appealed against. Every such appeal shall he in writing and shall state the grounds on which the appeal is based and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and a process fee, in court fee, stamp as specified below. (a) ------ 
(b)------ 
(2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. 

42. Special Power of Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement-Officer :- A revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement-Officer' may, at any time before the publication of final record-of-right, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district, or local area shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. 

42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights :- The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement-Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquires as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue—officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. 

42B. Correction of obvious clerical errors before final publication of record-of-rights :- The Revenue officer, with the additional designation of `Settlement-Officer' shall, have inherent jurisdiction to correct obvious errors e.g., arithmetical or clerical errors before final publication of the record-of-rights. The Settlement-Officer may delegate the said power to some other Revenue officer, with the additional designation of Assistant Settlement Officer, subordinate to him. 

44. Powers vested in Director of Land Records and Surveys :- In respect of all operations under Chapter XVII of the Act which have been placed under the administrative control of the Director of Land Records and Surveys, East Pakistan, he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue-Officer under the said Chapter and shall have all the powers of a Settlement Officer under rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42A and 42B. 

23. It is on record that on 17.06.2002, the Director (land records and surveys), respondent No.2 passed an order constituting a committee headed by respondent No.3 to hold a fresh hearing in respect of the aforesaid 3 appeal cases. In consequence of aforesaid order, a notice was issued directing the parties to appear before the committee for participating in hearing of appeal cases on 24.7.2004. 

24. Before entering into the merit of the case, let us consider the power and authority of a Director (land records and surveys) as a Revenue-Officer.as contemplated in Rule 44 and Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

25. Rule 44 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 provides that under chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Director of land records and surveys has been vested with the power to discharge all the functions of a revenue officer who shall have the powers of a settlement officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42B of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 including a power of direction under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in the records-of-rights before final publication of the same. 

26. From a bare reading of Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, it  appears that a revenue officer with the additional designation of settlement officer, on receipt of an application from the aggrieved person or an official report for correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in the record of rights before final publication, may direct the correction of the fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights after giving the parties concerned a hearing to that effect. 

27. In view of the propositions of law quoted above, the Director of land records and surveys is the administrative head of the department concerned, but he is not empowered either by any provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or by Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 to amend, correct, change, modify or set aside the judgment passed by the Settlement Officer in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is an allegation of fraudulent entry procured by fraud in the record-of-rights. 

28. We have stated above that after delivery of judgment by the settlement-officer, respondent No.7 and. others filed an application for reconsideration of appeal cases under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. The settlement-officer, on receiving the application and on considering the contents thereon, set aside the judgment passed in appeal cases and formed a five-member-committee for rehearing of the appeal cases. The aforesaid committee, on hearing the parties and on considering the papers and documents, recommended restoring the judgment and order passed in appeal cases under Rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, so it is crystal clear that the settlement officer, by exercising his power and authority under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, disposed of an application filed by respondent No.7 and others. 

29. Under the facts and circumstances of the case and the propositions of law, we have no hesitation in holding that since the appeal cases were decided by the settlement officer in exercise of his power under Rules 31 and 42 of the East Bengal and Tenancy Rules, 1955, there is hardly any scope for reopening the matter again by the Director as Settlement-Officer under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is any entry procured by fraud in the record-of-rights before final publication of the same. 

30. The aforesaid view finds support in the 4 decision in the case of Md. Altab Ali Sheikh Vs. Director Land Records, Directorate of Land Records and Survey and others, 11 MLR (HC) (2006) 226, wherein it has been spelt out as under :
"Director of Land Records and Survey has no authority to interfere with the judgment passed in appeal under Rule 31 except on the ground of fraud. Director of Land Records and Survey though is the administrative head of the department has no jurisdiction or power under rule 42A to 'amend or set aside judgment of the Settlement Officer passed in appeal under Rule 31 of East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 except on ground of any entry in the record-of-rights obtained by fraud." 

31. In view of above decision and discussion, it is clear that the judgment and order passed in appeal cases under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the same cannot be amended, modified, changed or set aside by the Director of Land Records and Survey under Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 unless there is an entry which was procured by fraud in the record-of-rights. Within the four corners of the writ petition and affidavit-in-opposition, we do not find that respondent No.7 has made out any case of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights, and as such, we are of the view that since the Settlement-Officer has already exercised his power under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Director of Land Records and Survey does not have the authority to interfere with the same in the absence of an allegation of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights. 

32. On the facts and in the circumstances of the case, and the discussion made above, we are of the view that the order dated 08.07.2002 passed by the respondent No.2 for constitution of a committee for reconsideration of the judgment passed by the settlement-officer under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 as well as the notice dated 14.07.2002 issued by respondent No.3 directing the parties to appear before the committee for reconsideration of the appeal cases were issued beyond the jurisdiction, and authority of respondent Nos.2 and 3 and those were issued in excess of their jurisdiction. 

33. Another important aspect of the case is that during pendency of objection cases, respondent No.7 and others filed Title Suit No.27 of 2001 before the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for permanent injunction in order to restrain the writ petitioner from disturbing peaceful possession over the case land claimed by respondent No.7 and others. However, the learned Assistant Judge, Dhaka, by his judgment and order dated 06.11.2002, dismissed the suit. Respondent No.7 and others, thereafter, preferred Title Appeal No.578 of 2002 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka who transferred the same to the Court of learned Joint District Judge, Court, Dhaka and the learned Appellate Court, by its judgment and order dated 01.3.2003, decreed the suit. The writ petitioner thereafter filed Civil Revision No.817 of 2003 before the High Court Division which made the Rule absolute on 17.6.2008. Respondent No.7 and others thereafter filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1714 of 2008 before the Appellate Division which heard the same on 24.3.2009 and dismissed the appeal. Respondent No.7 and others thereafter filed Civil Review Petition No.48 of 2009 before the Appellate Division which also dismissed the same on 23.8.2009, so it is crystal clear that the possession of the disputed land has been determined by the competent Courts of law. Accordingly, the judgment and order delivered by the competent Courts of law, so far it relates to the possession of the suit property is binding upon the parties. In view of the above judgment and order, the parties of the suit are not entitled to raise any question of possession afresh in any civil Court having jurisdiction, since the matter has already been decided by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. 
It is important to note that High Court Division cannot decide the disputed question of title to the suit land; rather the same should have been decided by the competent Civil Court of law. 

34. It is a settled principle of law that the proceeding under article 102(2) of the Constitution is a summary one and it is mainly decided on the statements and documents annexed to the writ petition and the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respective parties. In this summary proceeding, the High Court Division neither decides the complicated question of title nor the disputed question of fact. The aforesaid view finds support in a decision in the case of Province of East Pakistan Vs. Kshiti Dhar, 16 DLR (1964) (SC) 457, wherein it has been held: 

"The principle is now well settled that a proceeding in the writ jurisdiction is more in the nature of summary proceeding in which examination of disputed questions of fact of a complicated nature is not as a general rule undertaken nor investigations of title to property made. It provides a means of obtaining a speedy decision in a case where a clear disregard of a statutory obligation or duty has resulted in the infringement or denial of a legal right about the existence of which there is not any reasonable dispute or controversy." 
In the case of New India Tea Company Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh and others, 31 DLR (AD) (1979) 303, it has been decided as under : 
"There is a long line of decisions in favour of the view that the High Court should not enter into disputed questions of fact nor decide any question as to title which require investigation into facts and taking of elaborate evidence." 
In the case of Shamsunnahar Salam and others Vs. Mohammad Wahidur Rahman and others, 51 DLR (AD) (1999) 232, it has been settled as follows: 
"A writ Court cannot and should not decide any disputed question of fact which requires evidence to be taken for settlement." 
The similar view was reflected in the case of Province of East Pakistan V. Azim Rahman, 20 DLR (1968) (SC) 71; Fatema Khatun and others Vs. DC, Dinajpur, 3 MLR (1998) (AD) 71; Tasmina Chowdhury and others Vs. Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and 4others, 49 DLR (1997) 29. 

35. In view of above discussion and proposition of law, if the parties are dissatisfied with the title to the case land, they may approach the civil Court having jurisdiction to address their grievances if so advised. 

36. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that since the Settlement-Officer has already decided the appeal cases by exercising his power under Rule 31 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Director of land records and surveys. respondent No.2 has no right and authority to constitute a committee to rehear the appeal cases afresh without having any allegation of fraud in the entry of record-of-rights and similarly, respondent No.3 has also no jurisdiction to issue the impugned notice in consequence of above-order as the constitution of a committee and issuance of notice thereof is beyond the scope of Rules as contemplated in the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

37. Accordingly, in the light of the findings made above, we find merit in this Rule. 

38. In the result, the Rule Nisi is made absolute.

39. The impugned order under Memo No. B hu:Re:6/2002/147 I dated 08.7.2002 passed by respondent No.2 contained in annexure-G to the writ petition constituting a committee to rehear Appeal Case Nos.31335 of 2001, 31336 of 2001 and 41105 of 2001 and the notice dated 14.7.2002 issued by respondent No.3 contained in annexure-H to the writ petition for rehearing of above 3 cases on 24.07.2002 are declared to have been passed without lawful authority having no legal effect. 

40. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of Rule Nisi is, hereby, recalled and vacated. 

41. Let a copy of the judgment be communicated to the Respondents forthwith. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A.N.M. Bashir Ullah J:- This Rule, on an application under Section 115 (I) of 
the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the CPC) filed by the plaintiff-petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-15 to show cause as to why judgment and decree dated 06.01.2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2" Court, Faridpur, in Title Appeal No.201(A) of 2005 allowing the appeal and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 27.09.2005 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur, in Title Suit No.120 of 1998 decreeing the suit, should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. By this Rule the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 6.12008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd  Court, Faridpur, in Title Appeal No.201 of 2005 has been challenged. The said title appeal arose out of title suit no.120 of 1998 and the said original suit has been witnessing its fifth judgment after filing of the suit on 16.7.1998.The first judgment in the suit was pronounced by the trial Court decreeing the suit on 23.9.1999 and as against the said judgment title appeal being no.2I3 of 1999 was preferred and the appellate Court below by its judgment dated 23.10.2002 sent the suit back on remand for trial afresh and accordingly the suit was again decreed by its 3' judgment dated 27.9.2005 and against that judgment the contesting defendants preferred title appeal no. 201 of 2005 in the Court of District Judge, Faridpur and the learned Joint District Judge. 2' Court, Faridpur as appellate Court allowed the appeal dismissing the suit by its judgment dated 6.1.2008 (4i and impugned judgment). The plaintiff-petitioners against that judgment moved this Court and obtained the present Rule and thus in disposing the present Rule the suit has been witnessing its fifth judgment. 3r The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the present -petitioners 
as plaintiffs filed title suit no.120 of 1998 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur for declaration of their title into .29 acres of land. Later on through amendment the plaintiffs also sought the declaration that the ex-parte-decree dated 08.7.1993 passed in title suit no.629 of 1981 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur is illegal and non binding upon them averring inter alia that .14 acres of land appertaining to RS plot no.137, 200 and 203 of RS khatian no.35 and .l5 acres of land appertaining to RS plot no. 137, 200 and 203 of RS khatian no. 36 originally belonged to Akiluddin Molla and the said land has been correctly recorded in his name. The plaintiffs are the heirs and successive heirs of Akiluddin Mona. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land from the time of their predecessor of Akiluddin Molla and the defendants have no right, title, interest and possession into the suit land.

4. The plaintiffs are the men of simple and credulous nature and they are from a remote village of the country who have no up to date knowledge about the management and preparation of the record of right. Late plaintiff no. 1 Chand Molla was entrusted with the preparation of the record of right in the name of the plaintiffs in the SA record of right and to that end he gave the required data to the concerned officials and he was in believe that the SA record has been prepared and published in the name of the plaintiffs but at the Iln.il stage of the SA record of right the late plaintiff Chand Molla became sick and the other plaintiffs were not proper person to take care of the same. But while the plaintiffs were in peaceful possession of the suit land, all on a sudden in the first part of the month of the Boishakh 1405 BS, the defendant nos. 1 -5 denied the title of the plaintiffs into the suit and and also disclosed that the SA record of right has been prepared in the name of their predecessor, Nazir Sheik in SA khatian no.129 although the defendants had no right, title, interest and possessing into the suit land. 

5. The further case of the plaintiffs is that Akiluddin Molla did never orally settle the suit land to Nazir Sheikh on 15'1' Baishak 1354 BS and Akiluddin Molla did never receive rents on 30th Baishak of the same year from the said Nazir Sheikh the said Nazir  Sheikh was never inducted into the possession of the suit land. The defendant no.3 has no homestead on the land of plot no200 and the defendant no.11 also has no homestead on the land of plot no.203 and it is fact that the Union Parisad erected road taking earth from the suit land with the permission of the plaintiffs and there are roads on the suit land. 

6. The further case of the plaintiffs is that Akiluddin Mona did not exchange .16 acres of land of RS plot no.200 with Ansaruddin Molla, the predecessor of defendant nos.24- 28 (though in the plaint this defendants have been mentioned emmeously as defendant rios.29-33). Akiluddin Molla did not get .05 acres of land from plot no.204 of RS khatian no.42 and 43 and he did never give .16 acres of land from plot no.200 of RS khatian no.35 and 36 to the said Ansaruddin Molla. The plaintiffs had no any knowledge about the title suit no.629 of 1981 or its ex-parte-decree. The summons and the other process of the said suit were never served upon the plaintiffs or their predecessor in interest. The summons and process of the said suit have been suppressed upon the plaintiffs thereafter the plaintiffs of that suit obtained a fraudulent ex-parte-decree on 08.7.1993. So the said decree is not binding upon the plaintiffs. Since the defendants have denied the title of the plaintiffs into the suit land in the first part of the month of Boishak 1405 BS, hence the suit. 

7. The suit was contested by 2 sets of defendants. In one set there was the defendant nos.l-5 and 7-16 while in another set there was the defendant nos.24-28. The defendants no.1 -5 and 7-16 filing written statements denied the material allegation made in the plaint and also claimed that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the suit. The case of the these defendants, in short, is that all the plaintiffs named in the plaint did not file the suit. Md. Kalam Molla. the son of the late plaintiff no. 1 Chand Mollah at the instance of some enemy of the defendants filed the suit to cause harm and mischief to the defendants. The house of the plaintiff nos.1-9 and 13 are far away from the suit land. 

8. The further case of the defendants is that it is fact that Akiluddin Molla was the recorded tenant' of the suit land and his name has been correctly recorded in RS khatian no.35 and 36. Akiluddin Molla was a land and who settled the suit land to Nazir Sheikh. the predecessor of the defendants on 15th Boishak, 1354 BS and he received the rents from Nazir Sheikh on 30th, Baishakh of the same year executing dakhilas. Nazir Sheikh was inducted into the possession of the suit land and he has been cultivating the same by his own plough. Nazir Sheikh had his own land adjacent to the suit plot who died leaving the defendant nos.1-17. The defendant no.3 has homestead on the land of plot no.20 I now he has extended his homestead in to the land of suit plot no. 200 and for the last 16 years he has been possessing the same. The defendant no.11 has been possessing the land of plot no. 203 erecting but thereon. The defendants and the local union parisad have collected earth from the suit land creating some ditch thereon. The suit land has been correctly recorded in the name of Nazir Sheikh in SA khatin no. 129. So, the suit of the plaintiffs is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

9. The defendant nos.24-28 through their written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint averred that the land of RS khatian no. 35 and 36 originally belonged to Akiluddin Molla while .05 acres. of land of RS plot no. 204 of RS khatian no. 42 and 43 belonged to Ansaruddin Molla, the predecessor of the defendant nos. 24-28. Before the RS record of right Akiluddin Malta exchanged .16 acres of land of plot no. 200 with .05 acres of land of plot no. 204 belonged to Ansaruddin Molla and accordingly in the in RS khatian no. 35 and 36 and also in RS khatian no. 42 and 43 there is the reference of the said exchange. In the SA record of right the said land was not recorded correctly in the name of Ansaruddin Mollah and as such the present defendants filed title suit no.629 of 1981 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur and the said suit was decreed ex-parte on 8.7.1983. The defendants of that suit though were served with the notice and summons of that suit but they did not appear in the suit. The decree of that suit is not fraudulent. These defendants have been possessing the land of RS plot no. 200. So, the Rule is liable to be discharged with cost. 

10. Upon the above pleadings, the trial Court framed as many as 6 issues to dispose 
of the suit. The plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses while defendant nos. 1-5/7-16 examined 7 witnesses and the defendant nos. 24-28 examined I witness and the plaintiffs and the defendants filed some documentary evidences which have been duly marked as exhibits in the suit. The trial Court on considered of evidence and other materials on record decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession into the suit. The contesting defendant nos.I-5/7-16 being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the trial Court preferred title appeal no. 20I(A) of 2005 in the Court of District Judge, Faridpur which has been ultimately heard by the Joint District Judge. 2nd  Court, Faridpur who by his impugned judgment dated 6.1.2008 allowed the appeal setting aside the judgment of the trial Court. The plaintiff-petitioners being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the appellate Court below moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

11. Mr. Sash Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners supports the Rule. He submits that both the trial Court and appellate Court below concurrently found the title of the plaintiffs into the suit land. They very categorically and significantly held that Akiluddin Molla was the owner of the suit land and the suit land was correctly recorded in his name in RS khatian nos. 35 and 36 and Akiluddin Mollah did not settle the suit land orally to Nazir Sheikh in 1354 BS and Akiluddin Molla did not exchange .16 acres of land of plot no. 200 with Ansaruddin Molla, the predecessor of defendant nos. 24-28 and this concurrent findings of Courts below are based on the proper assessment of the materials on record. So this concurrent
findings and decisions of the Courts below did not call for any interference from this Court. 

12. He next submits that the trial Court on a meticulous perusal and scanning of the evidence on record found the possession of the plaintiffs into the suit land but the appellate Court below on some erroneous view found that the plaintiffs have no possession into the suit land. The appellate Court below mis-constructed the evidence of P.Ws 1, 2 and 3. Both the PWs 2 and 3 categorically asserted that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. PW 3 did not give any evidence that he did not know the suit land or he did not know as to who has been possessing the suit land but the appellate Court below on some misreading of evidence of PW 3 mis-constructed his evidence and thereby came to a wrong finding that the P.W 3 did not know the suit land and did not know as who has been possessing the suit land. Both the PWs 2 and 3 have homestead contiguous to the suit land and this fact has not been denied by the defendants at trial. So the PWs 2 and 3 are very much competent witnesses to prove the possession of the plaintiffs. 

13. He also submits that the DWs 2, 3 and 4 have deposed to prove the possession of the defendant nos. 1-17, but none of them could have stated from when the defendants have been possessing the suit land so their such evidence is not credible at all to prove the possession of the defendants. 

14. He also submits that it is fact that the defendants have their homestead adjacent to the suit land and the local witnesses being misconceived of the said fact considered their such possession as possession of the suit land. 

15. He also submits that both the defendant nos.1-17 and 24-28 have been claiming their possession into the suit land and this sort of claim is sufficient to hold that neither the defendant nos. 1-17 nor the defendant nos. 24-28 have been possessing the suit land, rather it is the plaintiffs who have been possessing the suit and continuously from the time of their predecessor-in-interest Akiluddin Molla. There is no case in the hands of the defendants to show that the plaintiffs or their predecessor were ever dispossessed from the suit land at any point of time. More so, the plaintiffs have the right, title and interest into the suit land, so the evidence of possession must be considered with the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs into the suit land but the appellate Court below on some erroneous view found possession of the defendants.

16. As to the Advocate commissioner's report he submits that the report itself reveals that the commissioner did not find any fixed pillar or point for an accurate measurement and thereupon he started his measurement at his own discretion from the plot 199. So this type of measurement cannot be considered as genuine and fair. So the Advocate commissioner's report is not acceptable at all. 

17. He lastly submits that the appellate Court below on the wrong assessment of the evidence and other materials or record held that the plaintiffs have no possession into the suit land but this findings is not based on materials on record, as such, he has committed an error of fact as well as law occasioning failure of justice to the plaintiff-petitioners. So, the judgment of the appellate Court below is liable to be set aside making the Rule absolute.

18. On the other hands, Mr. Md. Osman Ghani Bhuiya, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party nos. 1-15 opposes the Rule. He submits that the suit was not maintainable as the plaintiffs have no possession into the suit land. The appellate Court below relying on the materials on record came to a correct conclusion that the plaintiffs have no possession into the suit land. So the suit is hit under the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

19. He also submits that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession into the suit land while the defendants by sufficient and cogent evidence could have proved their possession. He referring the Advocate commissioner's report exhibit-A submits that the Advocate Commissioner found the structures and various trees on the suit land and those structures and trees belonged to the defendants. The Commissioner also found ditch in the suit land as the defendants collected earth from the said ditch. Since the suit land is not plain now, as asserted, by the plaintiffs there is no scope for them to cultivate the land as plain land and the commissioner's report have supported the defendant's case that they have been possessing the suit land making structures thereon and also planting various type of trees into the suit land and the appellate Court below on the proper assessment of evidence and other materials on record found the possession of the defendants and rightly dismissed the suit. So, the judgment of the appellate Court below did not call for interference from this Court. So the Rule is liable to he discharged with cost. 

20. I have considered the above arguments and submissions of the learned Advocates of 
Sheikh Sam. & Ors (A.N.M. Bashir Ullah, J)325 both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record. 

21. On going to the materials on record it is found that it is almost admitted that the land of RS khatian no.35 and 36 originally belonged to Akiluddin Molla, the predecessor of the plaintiffs. But the case of the plaintiffs is that Akiluddin Molla did never settle the suit land to Nazir Sheikh while the case of the contesting defendant nos. 1-5 and 7-16 is that Akiluddin Molla orally settled the suit land in the first part of Boishakh 1354 BS to Nazir Sheikh, the predecessor of these of defendants and took rents from the Nazir Sheikh executing the dakhila on 30, Baishak of [354 BS. 

22. The case of the another set of defendants namely the defendant nos. 24-28 is that Akiluddin Molla exchanged .16 acres of land from the land of plot no. 200 with Ansaruddin Molla, the predecessor of defendant nos. 24-28 and in the said exchange Akiluddin Molla got .05 acres of land from the land of plot no. 204 from Ansaruddin Molla. 

23. The trial Court and the appellate Court below concurrently found that the right, title and interest which was available in favour of Akiluddin Molla at the time of preparation of RS record of right has not been extinguished in any way and both the Courts below also concurrently found that Akiluddin Molla did never settle the suit land to Nazir Sheikh nor exchanged with Ansaruddin Mona. The relevant findings of the appellate Court below runs in the following manner: 
“এমতাবস্থায় আনজিন তপাসিল বর্ণিত নালিশী জমিতে অখিলউদ্দিন মোল্ল্যার স্বত্ব অটুট থাকা প্রতিষ্টিত হয় এবং তাহার নিকট হইতে উক্ত সম্পত্তিতে ওয়ারিশসূত্রে ও ক্রমওয়ারিশসূত্রে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব অর্জিত হইয়াছে মর্মে উপরোক্ত আলোচনার মাধ্যমে প্রতিপন্ন হয়। অর্থাত আরজির তপসিল বর্ণিত নালিশী জমিতে বাদীপক্ষের দাবীমত স্বত্ব অর্জনের বিষয়টি যথাযথ বলিয়া প্রমাণ হয়।”

" From the above findings, it appears that the appellate Court below found the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs into the suit land. The trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs finding the right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiffs into the suit land. In the case of Abdul Kader Vs. Noor Mohammad, 36 DLR(AD) 261 it has been held that the findings of the Courts below on the basis of no evidence is of no legal consequence and the finding, of the Courts below could be disturbed if there is any misreading of the evidence or misconstruction of the evidence. In the case of 16 BLD (AD) 197 it has been held that the revisional Court may interfere in the concurrent findings of the facts of the Courts below when there appears misreading of evidence, wrong appreciation of evidence, non-consideration of oral and documentary evidence by the Courts below and when the findings of the Courts below are found to be perverse and not based on the evidence on record which resulted in to an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In the Case of Abdul Gafur Vs. Md. Abdur Razzak 62 DLR (AD) 242 it was held that the revisional Court cannot reverse the concurrent findings of the Courts below based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. 

24. Now, the preponderant views emerged from the above referred decisions is that if the concurrent findings of the Courts below are based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record, the some cannot be disturbed, but if the concurrent findings are based on the misreading of evidence, wrong appreciation of evidence and non-consideration of oral and documentary evidence by the Courts below, the findings and decisions of the Courts below can be disturbed. Now, let us considered whether the concurrent findings of the Courts below as to the title of the plaintiffs into the suit land suffers from any misreading or non-reading and misconstruction of evidence. 

25. From the materials on record it appears that the I" set of defendants could not adduce any evidence in order to prove the oral settlement of Nazir Sheikh. They asserted in their pleadings that Akiluddin Molla received rents from Nazir Sheikh executing rent receipts. DW I Md. Samsul Hug in his cross-examination stated in the following ways:
“আমি মালেক প্রদত্ত দাখিলা্ আদালতে দাখিল করিয়াছি। আমার দাখিলী দাখিলায় কোন দাগ নম্বর খতিয়ান নম্বর এবং জমির পরিমান উল্লেখ নাই। দাখিলায় মৌজার নামও উল্লেখ নাই।”

For the reasons stated above the said dakhilas have not been marked as exhibit in the suit by the trial Court. But from the very nature of dakhila it appears that the same did not bear the plot and khatian number and the quantity of land. This type of dakhila cannot be the genuine dakhila to show the payment of rents. In fact the set of defendants could not adduce an iota of evidence in support of their such oral settlement. 

In the S.A. record of right, the suit land has been recorded in the name of defendants in S.A. khatian no.I29, but it is very much settled now that the record of right is not the document of title of any land rather the parties are to show the basis of the said record of right but the defendants could not show any basis of the said SA record of

26. On the other hand, the defendant nos. 24-28 in their written statements could not even mention the date of alleged exchange. There is nothing in the evidence of DW 8 as to the prove of the said exchange, as such, both the Courts below rightly disbelieved the settlement in favour of Nazir Sheikh as well as the alleged exchange between Akiluddin Motto and Ansaruddin Molla. In the result, I am of the sharp view that the findings and decisions of the Courts below as to the right and title of the plaintiffs into the said land are based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record which calls for no interference from this Court. 

27. The appellate Court below though found the title of the plaintiffs into the suit land but ultimately dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs have no possession into the suit and and the plaintiffs did not challenge the decree of title suit no.629 of 1981.

28. It is fact that in the prayer portion of the plaint there appears no prayer as against the said title suit but the plaintiffs amended the plaint seeking relief against the said title suit in following terms and condition. The plaintiffs amended the plaint (ding a petition in the trial Court on 16.9.2003 where the relief against the said title suit was sought for in the following manner: 
উক্ত ৬২৯/১৯৮১ মোকদ্দমার ৮/৭/১৯৯৩ তারিখের একতরফা রায় ও ১৪/৭/১৯৯৩ তারিখের একতরফা ডিক্রি সম্পীর্ন অবৈধ বেআইনী যোগাযোগী ও অকার্যকরী রুল এন্ড ভয়িড ও কাগজের কারবার হইতেছে মাত্র েএবং উক্তরুপ ডিক্রি দ্বারা এই বাদী পক্ষ আদৌ বাধ্য নহে।”

In my consideration this sort of prayer should have been incorporated into the prayer portion of the suit but the same has not been done at all, as such, the appellate Court below high lighting the wanting of the same into the prayer portion held that the plaintiffs did not seek any relief as against the decree of the former title suit. 

In the case of Zamiruddin Ahmed Vs. Ziaul Haque and other, 49 DLR 622 it was held that party must not suffer for the bad pleading of the mufussil Court. In the said case this Court observed in the following ways: 

"Hence I feel inclined to observe that the pleading is not happy but the party must not suffer for confused and bad pleading. Law is settled that it is the substance and not the form of the plaint which at is to be looked and considered and Mufussil Court's pleadings are to be construed liberally" 

The plaintiffs though sought the relief as against the decree of the former suit but the said was not incorporated in the prayer portion of the suit but for any reason the relief was sought for within averment of the plaint and same also should have not been over looked by the appellate Court below. 

29. The plaintiffs claimed in the suit that the summons and process of the former suit had not been served upon them and the plaintiffs of that suit had suppressed the process and summons upon the defendants (plaintiffs of the present suit) of that suit and they practicing fraud upon the Court obtained a fraudulent decree. But the defendant nos. 24-28 did not take any earnest effort to address this allegation and they did not try to prove that the summons and process of that suit were served upon the defendants of that suit and no fraud was practiced upon the Court in obtaining the decree in that suit. So, in my consideration the appellate Court 

30. Now, corning to the question of possession of the parties, it appears that the appellate Court below disbelieved the evidence of PW I in regards to the possession as he could not say the plot numbers of the adjacent land of the suit land. He also disbelieved the evidence of P.W2 as he said that the suit land is possessed neither by the plaintiffs nor by the defendants and the land is fallen vacant as un-cultivated land. He also disbelieved the evidence of PW3 as he could not say the name of the mouja of the suit land but at the same time from the judgment of appellate Court below it is found that he did not rely on the evidence of defendants to ascertain the possession of the defendants. 

31. It is very natural and probable that P.W1 as one of the plaintiff will assert their possession in to the suit land, but from the evidence of PW2 who has homestead adjacent to the suit land it is found that he categorically stated that he had borga cultivated the land of plot no. 200 but for the last 2 years the land has been fallen vacant uncultivated. In cross-examination he categorically stated that he has the homestead in the northern side of the land of plot no. 200. This evidence or fact has not been denied by the defendants. So, PW2 is a very competent witness to tell anything about the possession of the suit land. 

32. More so, from the materials on record it transpires that PW 2 has given very truth and genuine evidence in the trial Court as to the present position of the suit land. PW 2 stated that at present for the last two years the land remains uncultivated and the same fact has been described by the DWs 2. 3 and 4 who have come in the Court to prove the possession of the defendants. Now, if the suit land or a portion thereof remains uncultivated for the last 2 or 3 years, by this fact, the persons who have title and interest into the snit land cannot he said to be out of possession or has been ousted from the suit land. 

PW3 Sheikh Khali! testified that he has homestead contiguous to the suit land and plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. From the cross-examination of the defendants it appears that PW3 is the relation of the defendants but their appears no suggestion that for any internal clique or for any other reason he has deposed falsely. Since the PW3 is also a contiguous land holder of the suit land, so he is a competent witness to depose as to the possession of the parties into suit land. From the materials on record it appears that both the P.Ws 2 and 3 are independent and disinterested witnesses and there appears no earthly reason to disbelieve them or to discard their unblemished and noted evidence in the Court. Since the title of the plaintiffs were found into the suit land, so the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 as to their possession into the suit land is consistent with the findings of the title of the plaintiffs. In this regard I can also rely upon the decision of the case of Erfan Ali Vs Joynal Abedin Mia, 35 DLR (AD) 217, where in it has been held that possession generally follows the title. The title of the plaintiffs were concurrently found by the Courts below, so the legitimate, rational and judicious conclusion would be that the plaintiff have been possessing the suit land pursuant to their such title. 

33. The defendant 110n. 1-5 and 7-16 had asserted their title in to the suit land on the
basis of oral settlement which has been found as a down right false hood, so their possession can not be considered on the basis of the said oral settlement. The defendants could not assert their beginning time and the date of possession, that is, from when they started to possess the suit land. D.Ws 2,3 and 4 have deposed to prove the possession of the defendants but in cross-examination all of them said that they did not know from when the defendants have been possessing the suit land. In fact the evidence of DWs 2, 3, 4 in respect of possession of the defendants do not tally with the materials on record. 

34. In this suit there is a local investigation held by DW 7 Advocate S.M. Al Mamun Hossain. He testified that he held the local investigation of the suit land and he submitted a report, marked exhibit-A. On a careful scrutiny of the said exhibit-A there appears sometimes in the following ways:
“নালীশী দাগের পার্শ্ববর্তী কোন স্থানে নকশা বা সরেজমিনে কোন সীমানা পিলার না থাকায় পক্ষগণের সনাক্তমতে বেনালিশী ১৯৯ দাগের উত্তর-পশ্চিমের কোন হইতে পরিমাপ কার্য শুরু করি।”
 
From the above statements of the report it is clear that the commissioner did not find any fixed pillar for the starting point of the measurement and it is known to everyone that for an accurate measurement and also for an unerring location of the suit land, the measurement must be started from a fixed pillar. Since the commissioner could not ascertain any fixed pillar, the starting of measurement from a certain place cannot be considered as fair and genuine. If for the sake of argument, it is conceded for a moment that he found tress and machan of bottle gourd or other trees into the land of plot nos. 200 and 2003 that does not mean that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land. From the materials on record it appears that the suit land is very much adjacent to the land of the defendants. Both the defendant nos. 3 and 11 have been living in the adjacent land of suit plot no, 200 and 203 and as such it was easier for them to claim their possession into the suit land but the fact remains that there is no reason for them to possess the suit land. So, the appellate Court below on the wrong assessment and misconstruction of the evidence on record found the possession of the defendants and thereby came to a wrong conclusion that the plaintiffs have no possession in to the suit land. The appellate Court below was not at all justified to find the possession of the defendants relying on the evidence on record, as such, I find merit in the Rule. 

35. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment of the appellate Court below dated 6:1.2008 passed by the Joint District Judge 2' Court, Faridpur in title appeal no. 201(A) of 2005 is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree of the trial Court dated 27.9.2005 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur in title suit no.120 of 1998 is hereby restored with some modification that the title of the plaintiffs in to the suit land is hereby declared and decree of title suit no.629 of 1981 of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur is declared illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs so far as it relates to the suit land of the plaintiffs. Considering all I pass no order as to cost. 

36. Let a copy of this judgment and order along with the lower Courts record be sent down to the concerned Court for information and necessary action.

End.
