parties:
Md. Younus Mia being dead his heirs: Sohel Ahmed and others
Vs.
Illias Ali Chowdhury being dead his Heirs: Mubin Chowdhury
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J:-This appeal by leave is directed against the judgement and order dated 29.11.2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.259 of 2001 making the Rule absolute and setting aside the judgement and decree dated 29.11.1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge and Anti-Smuggling Tribunal, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.239 of 1997 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 20.10.1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge-in-Charge, First Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No.85 of 1995 dismissing the suit.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are that respondent Nos. 1-8 (heirs of the original plaintiff Irfan Ali Chowdhury, who had purchased the suit land from the original owners) as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.350 of 1968 in the Court of the Munsif, Sylhet Sadar for declaration of title, recovery of possession by removing structures and also for permanent injunction. On transfer to the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sylhet the suit was lastly numbered as Title Suit No.85 of 1995.

3. The plaintiffs stated, inter alia, that the suit land is situated at locality Roy Hussain known as Amberkhana, Sylhet town and the same belonged to Karamatullah and others. The said owners used to hold and possess the suit land through their tenants Amu Singha and Garuba Singha. Karamatullah and others sold the suit land to Md. Irfan Ali Chowdhury by registered kabala dated 28.02.1927 and made over possession to him. Said Irfan Ali Chowdhury was the original plaintiff of the suit and died during pendency of the suit and was substituted by the present plaintiffs. The suit land comprises plot No.2 and western part of plot No.1 as per the said kabala. Irfan Ali Chowdhury used to hold and possess the suit land through said Amu Singha and Garuba Singha. Subsequently, Amu Singha took settlement of the suit land from him for one year by registered kabauliyat dated 27.07.1927 and used to live there till his death in 1342 B.S.

4. It is the plaintiffs case that after the death of Amu Singha his sons abandoned the said land and left for Monipur, India. Wife of Amu Singha also surrendered her right by making over possession to the original plaintiff and shifted to the house of her son-in-law Sinda Singha. The original plaintiff in turn gave up claim for arrear rent. Then the original plaintiff held and possessed the suit land by growing vegetables in one part and by cutting trees and bamboos from the other part.

5. Further case of the original plaintiff is that he settled the suit land for one year from Baishakh 1344 B.S. to one Jayanta Singha who executed a kabuliyat dated 1st Bhadra 1344 B.S. and after expiry of one year Jayanta Singha made over possession to the original plaintiff on 1st Baishakh 1345 B.S. Subsequently, one Mrs. Rosemary Keymer and her husband Mr. W. C. Keymer took lease of the western part of the suit land from the original plaintiff for 10 years by registered lease deed dated 19.12.1944 and they having possessed the said land for 2 years surrendered possession to the original plaintiff.

6. Irfan Ali Chowdhury once mortgaged the suit land with Town Bank, Sylhet and the bank filed certificate case for mortgage money and he amicably paid the dues and the property was released from mortgage. At the initial stage of settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in Irfan Ali Chowdhury's name, but defendant No.2 subsequently fraudulently got it recorded in the name of Krishna Singha, son of Amu Singha beyond his knowledge. The original plaintiff then filed objection case No.33 of 1961 and order was passed on contest for recording the plaintiffs name. But defendant No.1 then got the name of the plaintiff changed and caused preparation of record of right in his own name beyond knowledge of the plaintiff.

7. Further case of the plaintiffs is that defendant No.2 announced in the locality that he inherited the suit land from Krishana Singha who according to him is dead. But in fact Krishna Singha is alive and he visited Sylhet with his children three years back. Krishna had no right or title and he did not put any claim after his father's death. Defendant No.2 created some collusive documents without consideration in support of his alleged claim. The defendants threatened to disturb the possession of the plaintiff once in 1965 and the original plaintiff had to file Title Suit No.301 of 1965 in the then First Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of his title and permanent injunction. The plaintiff did not have all his documents available at that time. Further, the defendants of the suit belonged to minority community and the suit could not proceed for want of permission under East Pakistan Ordinance I of 1964. By the time permission was obtained defendant No.1 in collusion with defendant No.2 dispossessed the plaintiff in Chaitra 1373 B.S. and raised a Kutcha shed in the western part of the suit land. So, the plaintiff had to withdraw the said suit with permission to sue afresh.

8. It is further stated that although the heirs of Amu Singha surrendered possession of the suit land to the original plaintiff in 1342 BS, it was wrongly referred to as 1362 B.S. in the plaint of Title Suit No.301 of 1966. Therefore, the plaintiff filed the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of vacant khas possession upon removing structure, mesne profit and permanent injunction restraining the defendant opposite parties from changing the nature and feature of the suit land.

9. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Amu Singha in fate right who took settlement from the original plaintiff by executing kabuliyat dated Ashar 1344 B.S. While Amu Singha was living therein, he died leaving his son Krishna Singha, who died unmarried leaving his only nephew (sister's son) defendant No.2 as his only heir. Accordingly, defendant No.2 held and possessed the suit land. During settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Krishna Singha noting the name of the original plaintiff as landlord. The plaintiff in collusion with the Objection Officer changed the record-of—right in his name. Defendant No.2 then filed appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was allowed on contest on 09.09.1961. The further case of defendant No.1 is that defendant No.2 was possessing the suit land partly as homestead and partly as chara bari (abandoned homestead) and then he transferred part of the suit land as noted in schedule II of the written statement by kabala dated 07.08.1965 to defendant No.1 and delivered possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing part of the suit land purchased by him as stated above by constructing but and planting trees. The plaintiff is cunning and he took defendant No.2 in his confidence with high hopes that he would buy the land at a high price. Defendant No.2 having decided to sell part of the suit land to defendant No.1 began to kill time and refused presentation of kabala for registration and defendant No.1 then presented the kabala dated 07.08.1965 for registration before the Sub-registrar. Defendant No.2 did not appear at the instance of the plaintiff. So defendant No.1 had to file appeal before the District Registrar and the kabala was registered on contest on 02.02.1966. The plaintiff and defendant No.2 are in collusion and under influence of the plaintiff, defendant No.2 is remaining silent.

10. After hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record the Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. Then the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.239 of 1997, which was dismissed on contest.

11. Against the judgement of the appellate Court the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No.259 of 2001 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was made absolute. Hence, the defendants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.229 of 2007 before this Division.

12. Leave was granted on the following submissions of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners:

"I. That that High Court Division committed error of law in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below in the absence of any legal infirmity in such findings.

II. That the Courts below came to the relevant findings upon consideration of the evidence on record and the High Court Division committed error of law in setting aside those findings on the ground of non-consideration of material evidence without mentioning which of the material evidence on record was not considered by the courts below."

13. Mr. Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further submitted that both the trial Court and the appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiffs-respondents could not prove by oral and documentary evidence surrender and possession in favour of the original plaintiff followed by dispossession, and thus the High Court Division committed error of law in reversing the concurrent finding of fact without adverting to oral and documentary evidence. He further submitted that the Courts below found that the record of right is correct and based on evidence and as such, the High Court Division could only reverse such finding by adverting to evidence on record, which it did not do.

14. Mr. Qumrul Hoque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.8 made submission in support of the impugned judgement-and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took into consideration the contents of Exhibit- `Ga'(sale deed in favour of defendant No.1-predecessor of the appellants) which shows that Gopendra Singha was in possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the original owner Irfan Ali Chowdhury. Subsequently, he claimed the property by inheritance from Krishna Singha, and thus the story of inheritance by Gopendra Singha from Krishna Singha is falsified. Hence, the High Court Division was correct in reversing the decision of the Courts below, even though their findings were concurrent. He further submitted that the wife of Amu Singha surrendered the land to the plaintiff. He further submitted that the Courts below failed to appreciate Exhibits 2 and 3 and did not consider the evidence of P.Ws 1 to 5, who unequivocally deposed that dispossession took place on Chaitra, 1373 BS after defendant No.2 executed the deed on 07.08.1965 in favour of defendant No.1 and wrongly held that the plaintiff failed to prove his dispossession. The learned Advocate also submitted that the Courts below failed to consider material facts on record showing that defendant No.2 was not a tenant under the original plaintiff nor was he the heir of Amu Singha, and hence no title passed to defendant No.1. He further submitted that the High Court Division correctly found and observed that defendant No. 2 illegally dispossessed the plaintiff in Chaitra, 1373 BS and defendant No.1 did not produce any rent receipt or any other papers to show that Krishna Singha was a tenant of the plaintiff. Moreover, Gopendra Singha did not come to support the claim of defendant No. 1. He lastly submitted that the original plaintiff was in possession of the suit land through tenants W.C. Keymer and his wife Rosemary by registered lease deed dated 1944. They handed back possession of the property to the original plaintiff after two years of the tenancy.

15. Mr. Mohammad Abdul Hai, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1,2 and 5-7 also made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division.

16. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

17. On a perusal of the judgement of the trial Court, we find that the trial Court observed that there was no independent witness to support the claim of the plaintiff that Krishna Singha's mother handed possession of the suit land back to Irfan Ali Chowdhury. On the other hand, the trial Court highlighted the fact that the plaintiff's witnesses deposed that after Krishna Singha, his nephew Gopendra Singha was in possession of the suit land and that Gopendra Singha sold the suit land to defendant No.1. The trial Court observed that the evidence of P.W.3 Tara Miah supports the fact that the mother of Krishna Singha did not hand back possession of the suit land to Irfan Ali Chowdhury and that Krishna Singha did not abandon the suit land to go to India. It was observed that there was no documentary or oral evidence supporting the claim of Irfan Ali Chowdhury that he took physical possession of the suit land in 1342 BS. The trial Court further observed that the plaintiff did not lodge any diary or case with the police with regard to his dispossession from the suit land. It was noted that P.W.3 Tara Miah admitted in his cross-examination that Gopendra Singha went into possession of the suit land after Krishna Singha and, thereafter, sold the same to Makhon Miah (defendant No.1). It was also noted that P.W.4 in his cross-examination admitted that Monipuri people have been living in the suit property since 1950.

18. With regard to the possession by the plaintiff through tenant W.C. Keymer, the finding of the trial Court is that there was no witness to support the claim that Rosemary and her husband ever went into possession of the suit land. P.Ws 2 and 3 stated in their cross-examination that they did not know Rosemary. P.W.1, though she stated that Rosemary remained in possession of the suit land for two years and then handed back possession to Irfan Ali Chowdhury, the trial Court noted that there was no evidence to show that possession was handed back nor that Rosemary took possession of the suit land from Krishna Singha or Gopendra Singha. The trial Court concluded that Rosemary did not get possession of the suit land and that her letter of settlement was only a paper transaction.

<u>19. The appellate Court affirmed the judgement of the trial Court finding that the documents prove that defendant No.1 purchased the suit property on 07.08.1965 and has been in possession since that time and that the plaintiffs-appellants do not have any right and title in the property.</u>

<u>20. The High Court Division observed that defendant No.2 Gopendra Singha did not come to support the case of defendant No.1 and defendant No.1 did not produce any rent receipt or other papers to show that Krishna Singha was a tenant. It was observed that Irfan Ali Chowdhury got possession of the suit land and all the P.Ws and even D.Ws supported this claim of the plaintiffs and that the Courts below committed serious error in not considering that the suit land belonged to the father of the plaintiffs by right of purchase evident by a deed which was more than 50 years old.</u>

21. We note that the High Court Division mentioned that the trial Court after hearing the parties, without considering the evidence on record, wrongly and illegally dismissed the suit. However, we note from the impugned judgement that the High Court Division did not specifically refer to any of the evidence and materials on record to show which evidence the Courts below did not consider. The deed, by which Irfan Ali Chowdhury got the suit property is indeed very old. However, subsequent events and documents relating to those later events tend to indicate that Irfan Ali Chowdhury was no longer in possession of the suit land. On the contrary the evidence of the witnesses shows that defendant No.2 and his predecessors-in-interest were all along in possession of the suit land. We note that Krishna Singha, the predecessor of defendant No.1 got his name recorded in the record of rights as tenant, which the original plaintiff got corrected. But thereafter, Gopendra Singha (defendant No. 2 who sold the suit property to defendant No.1) filed an appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and got his name recorded in the record of rights. Khodeja Akhter Chowdhury who is the daughter of Irfan Ali Chowdhury deposing as P.W 1 could not controvert such claim. She admitted that her father's challenge against the record of rights was not fruitful. She also could not say whether her father took the matter further on appeal under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We note that P.W 1 stated in her evidence that her father took possession of the suit land in 1342 BS (c.1935 AD), whereas PW4 stated that in 1950 Manipuri people lived on the suit land. Coincidentally, in Title Suit No.301 of 1965, Irfan Ali Chowdhury had claimed that possession of the suit land had been handed over to him in 1362 BS. (c.1955 AD). Moreover, we note that P.W1 stated in her deposition that 1362 BS was mistakenly written and that the correct date was 1342. This is clearly falsified by the evidence of P.W4.

22. The trial Court thoroughly assessed the evidence, and noted that P.W.3 Tara Miah admitted in his cross-examination that the plaintiffs' side neither were nor are in possession of the suit land. It was also noted that there is no evidence to show when Irfan Ali Chowdhury regained possession of the suit land and when he was dispossessed therefrom.

23. In view of the evidence of P.Ws 3 and 4 it is clear that the predecessors of defendant No.1 were in possession of the suit land in 1950, even according to the plaintiffs' own witness. Thus, about 15 years before defendant No.1 purchased the suit land, Monipuri people were in possession and there was no evidence that possession reverted to the original plaintiff at any time after 1950.

24. The learned Advocate for the appellant referred to the decision in the case of Amanatullah and others Vs. Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan and another reported in 17 BLD(AD)199. In the cited case it was held by this Division as follows:

"It cannot be gainsaid that a finding of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate court is binding on the High Court, as a revisional court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case."

25. The same view was expressed by this Division in the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another Vs. Niron alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) 294.

26. In the facts of the instant case discussed above, we find that the High Court Division has reversed the concurrent finding of facts of the Courts below without specifically identifying any evidence which was misread or not considered by the trial Court or the appellate Court. The reference to non-consideration of the deed in favour of Irfan Ali Chowdhury dating to 1927 is of little consequence in view of the fact that admittedly the defendants' predecessors were the tenants in possession of the suit land from the original owners, having jote right by way of registered kabuliyat, and the record of rights was in their names as tenants. Irfan Ali Chowdhury purchased the land with the defendants' predecessor in possession as tenant. The finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court is that the plaintiffs could not prove that Irfan Ali Chowdhury ever went into possession of the suit land.

<u>27. We find that the trial Court has given a very elaborate judgement discussing the evidence and materials on record, and came to a finding based on those evidence and materials. The High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction could only reverse those findings by specific reference to evidence and materials, which were not considered or were misread by the trial Court, which would have materially affected the decision had they been considered.</u>

28. In view of the above discussion, we find that the trial Court and appellate Court have not misread any evidence nor left any material evidence out of consideration. In our opinion the decision of the High Court Division is not in accordance with the law and accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgement and order of the High Court Division is set aside. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

Hamed Kazi Being Dead His Heirs: 1(A) Mohammad Kazi And Others
Vs.
Jitendra Nath Halder
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J:-This civil petition for leave to appeal arises out of the judgement and order dated 21.11.2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4915 of 2004 discharging the Rule.

<u>2. The predecessors of the petitioners 1(a)-1(f) and others as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.84 of 2000 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Nazirpur, Pirojpur against respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and other co-sharers in the suit property for a declaration that the judgement and decree dated 20.10.2000 in Title Suit No.217 of 1983 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Nazirpur was obtained collusively and fraudulently and not enforceable upon them and also for a separate saham in respect of their property. They contended, inter alia, that the suit property originally belonged to C.S recorded owners, namely Keduram Haider, Chutu Halder and Kashinath Halder, sons of Rain Krishna Halder in eight annas share and the remaining eight annas share was owned and possessed by their paternal uncle Dwarika Nath Halder. Kashinath Haider died issueless leaving wife Biddya Sundari, who inherited his share and Dwarika Nath Haider also died unmarried and his share devolved upon his two nephews, Keduram and Chutu Halder in equal share and thus Chutu Halder got 2 annas 13 gandas by inheritance in the paternal property and 4 annas from his uncle Dwarika Nath and thereafter Chutu Haider died leaving only son Amaresh Haider. While Amaresh Haider owned and possessed 5.09 acres of land, on 26.02.1953 he transferred 44 decimals to Afzal Kazi and Hamed Kazi and before that on 12.05.1952 Amaresh transferred 17 decimals of land to Rafiz Uddin Kazi and Hamed Kazi though Hamed Kazi paid the entire consideration money and was in possession of the said property, but he got the sale deed registered in Benami of one Asman Khan for the reasons best known to him. Amaresh again on 02.04.1956 transferred 1.00 acre of land to Hamed Kazi and Rafiz Uddin Kazi. Keduram Haider died leaving three sons, namely Shasti Haider, Ambika Haider and Jageshwar Haider who inherited their father's property and while they had been owning and possessing, they along with the aforesaid Biddya Sundari and Amaresh Haider transferred 2.69 acres of land to Jagesh Chandra Mondal, Rajendra Nath Mondal and Brajendra Nath Mondal. Thereafter, one of the purchasers Brajendra Nath Mondal died leaving two sons, Subhas and Ashim Mondal, who sold 27 decimals of land to Hamed Kazi on 09.02.1979 and put him into possession. While he had been owning and possessing his share in the suit property Rafizuddin Kazi died leaving wife Golapi Bibi, three sons, namely Jalal. Alal and Afzal and 3 daughters, namely Mohna, Zohra and Sahera to inherit his 582decimals out of which Sahera got 6 decimals which she transferred to petitioner No.2 by way of Heba. As such, the petitioners own and possess the `B' schedule land of the suit property described in the plaint, the extent of which is 1.88 acres. They use some portion as homestead, some portion for gardening and some portion for cultivation producing different crops. On 15.07.2000 opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 disclosed that they have obtained the homestead portion of the suit land by virtue of a decree obtained in Title Suit No.217 of 1983 from the Court of the Assistant Judge, Nazirpur, Pirojpur and when confirmed about the said disclosure from the Court, the original petitioner forthwith applied for certified copy of the judgement and decree on 20.07.2000 and obtained the same on 14.08.2000 and thereafter filed the instant suit.</u>

3. The principal defendant —respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein contested the suit by filing separate written statements refuting all the material allegations as unfolded in the plaint contending in a nutshell that previously the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed a suit for partition in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Nazirpur, Pirojpur being Title Suit No.217 of 1983 against respondent No.2 and others and thereafter the suit was dismissed on contest against which the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.126 of 1986 before the District Judge, Pirojpur and upon hearing the parties the appeal was allowed setting aside the judgement and decree and sending the suit on remand to the trial Court. After remand the suit was decreed, against which the principal defendant-respondent No.2 preferred Title Appeal No.15 of 1990 before the District Judge, who on hearing the parties allowed the appeal and again remanded the suit to the trial Court. At that stage respondent No.1 compromised the suit with respondent No.2, the suit was decreed on the basis of solenama, and as such the present Title Suit No.84 of 2000 is not maintainable.

4. After hearing the parties and considering the materials on record the Assistant Judge by his judgement and decree dated 23.04.2003 decreed the suit.

5. Against the aforesaid judgement and decree the defendant-respondent No.1 preferred Title Appeal No. 55 of 2003 before the District Judge, Pirojpur. The appeal was transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge, Second Court, Perojpur, who after hearing the parties allowed the appeal setting aside the judgement and decree of the trial Court by his judgement and decree dated 02.01.2004.

6. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No.4915 of 2004 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was discharged. Hence, the heirs of the plaintiff arc now before us having filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal.

<u>7. Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mondal, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submitted that the Assistant Judge on careful consideration and meticulous analysis of the evidence, both oral and documentary, was pleased to decree the suit, but on appeal therefrom at the instance of the defendant-respondent Nos.1 and 2 the appellate Court erroneousiy allowed the appeal setting aside the judgement and decree on point of limitation, court fees and question of maintainability and the High Court Division on hearing the civil revision without entering into the merits of the case erroneously discharged the Rule, which is not sustainable in law. He further submitted that the appellate Court manifestly erred in law in allowing the appeal without proper reasoning and the High Court Division also committed error in discharging the Rule merely as barred by estoppel under section 115 of the Evidence Act though the law does not say so, because of the fact that the compromise decree was secretly made and obtained at a time when the suit came back on remand for the second time and the compromise was made between only the plaintiff and defendant No.1 of Title Suit No.217 of 1983 and no other defendants were aware of the same. He also submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule without taking proper notice of the principle of estoppel as embodied in section 115 of the Evidence Act as it is a rule of evidence by which a person is not allowed to allege and prove a thing under certain circumstances, but it is well settled that before a party could be barred by the principle to estoppel, waiver and acquiescence it must be established that the opposite party respondent acted bona fide on the clear, definite and unambiguous representation made by their adversary and that the opposite party respondents have altered their position in pursuance thereof. Even a mere gratuitous indulgence shown to a party in not enforcing its legal right for the time being cannot constitute estoppel or waiver and as such the impugned judgement and order is not sustainable in law. He submitted that the plaintiff-respondent No.1 of Title Suit No.217 of 1983(partition), i.e. defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 of Title Suit No.84 of 2000 after remand for the second time made a compromise decree secretly which is tantamount to an ex parte decree against the plaintiffs-petitioners and other defendants and by compromise decree practicing fraud they tried to grab the petitioner's property and from the knowledge of the aforesaid compromise decree they filed the instant suit within statutory period, and upon hearing the trial Court decreed the suit. On the other hand, the appellate Court as well as High Court Division erroneously and arbitrarily dismissed the suit without proper analysis of the evidence as well as relevant laws. He submitted that the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division in passing the judgement totally failed to consider the ownership and possession of the petitioners in the suit property 1.88 acres which they have been owning and possessing and residing in some portion thereof by constructing houses for more than 12 years by valid purchase. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that the High Court Division arrived at an abrupt decision to discharge the Rule upholding the order of the appellate Court that the suit is barred by estoppel without proper appreciation of the relevant law, as such the impugned judgement and order is not sustainable in law.</u>

8. Mr. Shamsul Hoque, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the respective parties and perused the impugned judgement of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

<u>10. It appears from the evidence and materials on record that in the instant suit the plaintiffs sought a declaration that the judgement and decree dated 20.10.2000 in Title Suit No. 217 of 1983 was obtained collusively and fraudulently. The earlier suit was one for partition and was ultimately decreed on the basis of a solenama and the plaintiffs of the instant suit contested the earlier suit and also prayed for saham. We find from the order sheet of earlier partition suit that defendant Nos. 9 to 13 filed an application praying for saham but that application was rejected because the applicants did not sign the application, but the trial Court noted that the earlier suit was decreed giving more than the due share to the defendants, who were party to the solenama. The appellate Court, on the other hand, noted that the solenama decree was passed in the earlier suit on 13.10.1997 and after that defendant Nos. 9 to 13 of that suit, who are the plaintiffs in the present suit filed an application praying for saham which was rejected on 01.03.1998. Their application for saham was filed again and was again rejected on 15.04.1998 and the decree was made final upon receipt of the Advocate Commissioner's report. The appellate Court observed that there was neither any revision filed against the rejection of the application for saham nor any appeal filed against the preliminary or final decree. The appellate Court concluded that the plaintiffs could not prove that the earlier suit was decreed without their knowledge and consent. The appellate Court pointed out that P.W. 1 admitted in his cross-examination that they went into possession in accordance with the final decree of Title Suit No. 217 of 1983.</u>

11. The High Court Division also noted that the lower court record of Title Suit No. 217 of 1983 clearly reflected that the present petitioners contested throughout the proceedings and thereafter abstained from making any objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report and thereby they are barred by estoppel from making any objection against the same when the final decree was withdrawn on 10.10.1999 and after that through application before the same Court they have withdrawn their papers.

12. Perusal of the judgement of the appellate Court shows that there was elaborate discussion of all the material points raised, and the judgement and decree of the trial Court was reversed upon proper scrutiny of the evidence and materials on record. In our view the High Court Division has rightly upheld the judgement and decree of the appellate Court and has given adequate reasons for doing so.

13. In view of the above discussion we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgement and the same does not call for any interference. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Md. Rafique and Others
Vs.
Sayed Md. Abdul Quiyum being dead his heirs: Mst. Rokeya khatun and others
full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25.11.2014 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No.19 of 2013 disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 13.01.2013 and 20.01.2013 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dhamrai, Dhaka in Title Suit No.34 of 2011 should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original title suit being No.34 of 2011 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Dhamrai, Dhaka for declaration of title along with a prayer for cancellation of a deed and perpetual injunction contending inter alia, that the disputed property appertaining to Mouza Khilgaon in C.S. Plot No.10P was the property under the government as abandoned property and the government decided to settle the land in favour of private individual. Accordingly, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff Fakir Chand pursuant to his prayer for taking permanent settlement was obtained allotment of the suit properties which was in fact initially acquired by the government in L.A. Case No.47 of 1959-60 and 11 of 1960-61. The predecessor of the plaintiff Fakir Chand obtained allotment on 02.11.1961 in respect of 02(two) kathas 07(seven) chhatak land of plot No. A-627(F) and 628(P) from the office of the concerned Executive Engineer, Public Works Department (PWD) followed by an allotment latter being Memo No.8059 (RDD) dated 02.11.1961. That the possession was delivered in favour of allotment-holder on 08.11.1965. Fakir Chand under the terms and conditions of the latter of allotment for obtaining a lease deed erected a tin-shed but on the suit property in the year 1965 and used to possess that homestead as of his dwelling hut. The further case of the plaintiff is such that Fakir Chand possessed the property through his caretaker and expired before 24/25 years. At his death; his two sons the plaintiff No. l and 2 one daughter, the plaintiff No.3 and one wife the plaintiff No.4 and mother of plaintiff No. 5 and 6 Halima Khatun became the heirs. The father of the plaintiff No.5 and 6 namely Rustom Ali as caretaker of the property used to look after the property. Rustom Ali while became bed ridden due to his paralysis disease, his wife Halima Khatun along with other plaintiffs use to possess the same in ejmali. The further case of the plaintiffs is such that the father of the defendants No.1-4 Altaf Hossain who was very much familiar to Rustom Ali Khan was allowed to possess the suit property without rent after the death of Altaf Hossain. The defendants No.1-4 concealed the original papers of the plaintiff. The government on 25.02.1982 executed and registered a lease deed being No.4643 in the name of Fakir Chand when Fakir Chand was already expired. The plaintiffs requested the government officials to register the lease deed in favour of them; but the office of the defendant No.7 disclosed before them that the lease deed has already been executed and registered in favour of their predecessor Fakir Chand. On 07.03.2010 the plaintiffs finding a sign board in the name of the defendant No.5 in the suit property they inquired into the matter and came to learn that the mother of the defendants No.1-4 Umme Salma Akter Khatun as am-mokter of Fakir Chand transferred the suit property on 10.09.1995 in favour of the defendants No.1-4 by a transfer deed No. 5278. The defendants No.1-4 entered into a contract with the defendant No.5 to construct a multistoried building in the suit property and according to that contract; the defendant No.5 hanged a signboard, which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit.

3. The contrary case of the defendants in short is thus that Fakir Chand obtained the allotment of the suit property by an allotment letter No.8059 dated 02.11.1961 from the government. Possession was delivered in favour of the lease-holder on 08.11.1965. Subsequently; Fakir Chand transferred the suit property in favour of the father of the defendants No.1-4 on 10.11.1970. For execution and registration of the sale deed both Fakir Chand and Altaf Hossain entered into a deed of agreement on 12.01.1970. The consideration money was fixed at Taka 15,000/-. On the date of deed of agreement Fakir Chand after taking a sum of Taka 13,500/- from Altaf Hossain handed over possession of the property. On the same date Fakir Chand executed a power of attorney on his behalf in the name of the wife of Altaf Hossain namely Umme Salina Khatun in respect of the disputed property and it was clearly mentioned in the power of attorney that Fakir Chand entered into a deed of agreement to sale the property in favour of Altaf Hossain and his attorney is empowered to execute and register the sale deed in favour of Altaf Hossain. The further case of the defendants is such that Fakir Chand since 12.01.1970 never looked after the property and his attorney Umme Salina Akter used to manage everything on his behalf and accordingly the government of Bangladesh recognizing the attorney Salma Akter registered the lease deed No.4643 on 25.02.1982 A.D. and in the lease deed the signature of attorney Umme Salina Khatun was obtained. It was further case of the defendants that their father Altaf Hossain in the year 1981 died leaving behind his legal heirs. After the death of Altaf Hossain by amicable partition the defendants No.1-4 use to possess the suit property and accordingly the attorney Salina Khatun for want of making a registered sale deed in favour of the defendants No.1-4 filed an application to the concerned Ministry of Housing and Public Works. Accordingly, the concerned Ministry pursuant to their memo No. 6/L-95/2107/1(2) dated 08.08.1995 gave permission to the attorney Salma Khatun for transfer of the property in favour of the defendants No.1-4. Thereafter, Salina Akter Khatun transferred the suit land in favour of the defendants No.1- 4 by a registered sub-kabala No. 5278 dated 10.09.1995. The defendants No.1-4 subsequently mutated their names and paying rent regularly. During city survey the suit land has been properly recorded in the names of the defendants No.1-4 and the defendant-opposite parties No.1-4 are paying upto date gas bill, city corporation holding tax, electricity bill etc. Recently they have decided to construct a multistoried building in the suit property and for that necessity they made a contract with the defendant No.5 a developer company to contract a multistoried building therein and the developer company according to their construct have prepared to construct the same. The further case of the defendants is such that the plaintiffs having no manner of right, title, interest and possession in the suit property on the basis of false allegations filed the suit, which is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after examining 07 witnesses from the side of the plaintiffs and 03 witnesses from the side of the defendants evaluating the documentary and oral evidence produced from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest by his judgment and decree dated 13.01.2013.

5. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred a title appeal being No.19 of 2013 in the court of learned District Jude, Dhaka which was transmitted to the 2nd Court of learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka for hearing and disposal and the learned Additional District Judge by the impugned judgment and decree dated 25.11.2014 disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and dismissal decree passed by the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the plaintiff-appellants have preferred this revisional application under section 1 15(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained this Rule.

7. During hearing of this Rule Mr. Md. Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Md. Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned trial court as well as the lower appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed illegality resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that admittedly after the death of Fakir Chand the lease deed in the name of Fakir Chand was executed and registered by the admitted owner of the property; government of Bangladesh and on the basis of agreement for sale before the lease deed the defendants have claimed the property from their vendor the alleged power of attorney of Fakir Chand Umme Salma Khatun, but in fact; there is no legal basis to transfer the property in favour of anybody prior to the lease deed executed and registered by the government. The learned Advocate further submits that the papers in favour of the defendants are collusive and forged having no legal basis which is totally ignored by both the courts below. The learned Advocate also submits that the courts below erred in law in disbelieving the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses without any cogent reason as to the death of Fakir Chand. The learned appellate court below during deciding the fate of the appeal failed to assess the evidence on record in its true perspective and arrived at an erroneous decision that the plaintiffs to the suit failed to discharge their onus of proof by any trust worthy evidence while the defendants to the suit in respect of their respective case successfully proved that they have acquired right, title, interest and possession in the suit property. The learned Advocate argued that the positive contention as transpired from the pleading of the plaintiffs was not considered by the courts below during passing their judgment and decree, which is an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate in support of his argument referred some decisions of this Court and our Apex Court. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the basic documents of the defendants were not properly evaluated by the learned courts below in their observation and findings. Under the ambit of Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure there has been material omission with regard to the materials on record and there is a misreading and non-reading of evidence as well as non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning of failure of justice, which deserve interference of this Court.

9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the learned counsel for the petitioners and submits that there is no illegality or irregularity from the sides of the learned trial court as well as from the side of the appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned appellate court below during disposal of the appeal rightly assessed the evidence on record in its true perspective and there is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and both the courts below concurrently held on proper evaluation of the evidence on records that the plaintiffs to the suit have measurably failed to discharge their onus of proof and on the contrary the defendants by adducing sufficient tangible evidence from their side successfully proved their specific case as agitated within their pleading in their written statement. The learned Advocate also submits that the admitted owner of the property government' by their execution and registration of the lease deed in favour of Fakir Chand completed the process of their allotment in favour of allottee of the suit property, Fakir Chand and the entire proceedings of the allotment was ended by execution and registration of the deed of lease and the lease-holder Fakir Chand legally acquired his right to property in the suit holding and also obtained the possession therein. Both the courts below concurrently observed in their findings and decision that the documentary evidence produced from the side of the defendants makes it clear that the title of the property was properly acquired by the defendants and the series of papers goes to show that in the disputed property; the contesting defendants No.1-4 acquired their right, title, interest and possession which is admitted practically from the admission of the plaintiff ~s witnesses during their depositions before the trial Court. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the witnesses of the plaintiffs in fact proved the case of the defendants as a whole; and it is not the case of the plaintiff-petitioners that the witnesses have become hostile or biased in favour of the defendants. The official witnesses produced from the side of the plaintiffs also have totally proved the case of the defendants in toto in their testimonies which are already on records and properly evaluated by the learned courts below in their observation and findings and there is nothing on record to show that the trial court as well as the appellate court committed any wrong or illegality during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred some decisions of our Apex Court and lastly concluded his submissions stating that the civil Rule having no merit is liable to be discharged.

10. Considering the submissions of the learned Advocates I have gone through the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate court in Title Appeal No.19 of 2013 and the judgment and decree passed by the trial court in Title Suit No.34 of 2011 along with the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties; both oral and documentary. I have also perused the connected papers including the original plaint of the plaintiffs and the written statement submitted from the side of the contesting defendants.

<u>11. On perusal of the case records it transpires that admittedly the disputed property was the property of the government which was acquired by them pursuant to Land Acquisition Case No.47 of 1959-60 and 11 of 1960-61. It is also an admitted position that Fakir Chand as a deserving person prayed for taking lease of the property and the authority concerned being pleased gave him allotment letter followed by a Office Memo No.8059(RDD) dated 02.11.1961 in respect of the suit land measuring 02 kathas 07 chhatak. It is also an admitted position that the concerned department of the government i.e. Ministry of Housing and Public Works, Dhaka after their allotment letter handed over possession of the property in favour of Fakir Chand. The allotment-holder thereafter in the year 1965 erected a tinshed but in the suit property and started to reside therein. It is the case of the plaintiffs in their plaint that their predecessor-in-interest Fakir Chand died on 08.09.1981. But the fact remains that the lease deed was registered on 25.02.1982 wherein there is a signature of the Attorney of Fakir Chand Umme namely Salma Khatun and it is the specific case of the defendants that Fakir Chand during his life time for want of disposal of the property in favour of Altaf Hossain, the father of the defendants No.1-4 entered into a deed of agreement on 12.01.1970 and in the deed of agreement which was a registered instrument, the consideration amount was fixed at Tk.15,000/-; out of which on the date of agreement Altaf Hossain paid Tk.13,500/- in favour of Fakir Chand. The possession was delivered on the same date in favour of Altaf Hossain. It is found that the attorney Umme Salina Khatun who happens to be mother of the defendants No.1-4 and wife of Altaf Hossain was appointed the attorney by Fakir Chand on 12.01.1970 by virtue of a registered power of attorney in respect of disputed property and by dint of that power (authority) Umme Salma Khatun as attorney put her signature in the registered lease deed No. 4643 dated 25.02.1982.</u>

<u>12. Consulting the connected papers meticulously it further transpires that the attorney was entrusted to dispose of the property followed by the transfer deed in favour of Altaf Hossain, the father of the defendants and at his demise, the defendants No.1-4 along with his other  brothers and sisters became the heirs who amicably started to possess the property left behind Altaf Hossain and the suit property by that amicable partition was under the possession of the defendants No.1-4. The attorney Umme Salina Khatun decided to transfer the suit land in favour of the possession-holders defendants No.1-4 and for the legal necessity to execute and register the transfer deeds he filed an application to the government. On behalf of the government the Ministry of Housing and public Works pursuant to their office Memo No.6/L-95/2107/1(2) dated 08.08.1995 gave a permission in writing to the attorney of Fakir Chand, Umme Salma Khatun to transfer the property in favour of the defendant-opposite parties and accordingly after getting permission from the government; the attorney by a registered sub-kabala deed dated 10.09.1995 transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant-opposite parties No.1-4. It further transpires from the papers on records and the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties that the purchaser-defendants No.1-4 after mutating their names in the government sheresta regularly paying rent for the suit property and getting rent receipts. It also appears from the papers on records that in respect of the disputed property there is a holding number of City Corporation and there is a payment of Gas bill, Electricity bill etc. in the name of Altaf Hossain who is admittedly the father of the defendants No.1-4.</u>

<u>13. Having gone through the records 1 find that, both the parties to substantiate their case have adduced witnesses. P.W.1; the plaintiff No.4 Md. Solid Khan who has deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs No.1-4 and 6 as of their Attorney. This witness in his testimony testified at a stage of his examination-in-chief that on 08.09.1981 Fakir Chand who was their father died. This witness also testified at a stage of his deposition that their father for want of execution of a deed in favour of the predecessor father of the defendants No.1-4, Altaf Hossain in respect of the disputed property handed over all the original papers in favour of Altaf Hossain and after the death of Altaf Hossain the defendants did not hand over those papers to them (the plaintiffs). It was also testified by this plaintiff No.04 that their father paid all the dues in favour of the government. P.W.1 identified the lease deed No.4643 dated 25.02.1982. He further testified that on 07.03.2007 he found a sign board in the name of a developer company in the suit property. During his deposition P.W. 1 frankly conceded that the defendants applied for a plan to D.I.T. and also testified that the original lease deed, letter of allotment and original copies of chalan in respect of the disputed property lies in favour of the predecessor of the defendants, Altaf Hossain. In a reply to a question during his cross-examination from the side of the defendants, P.W.1 testified at a stage that Umme Salma filed an application to dispose of the property in favour of the defendants No.1-4 in the concerned Ministry of Housing and Public Works of the government and obtained permission from the government to dispose of the property in favour of the defendants No.1-4. It is also admitted from the side of the plaintiff No.4 that the predecessor of the defendant-opposite parties, Altaf Hossain used to reside in the suit property. As to the death of Fakir Chand P.W.1 in his cross-examination testified that on 08.09.1989 Fakir Chand died. Subsequently; the same witness, plaintiff No.4 stated that Fakir Chand in the year 1981 expired. He has conceded during his cross-examination from the side of the defendants that in the lease deed on behalf of Fakir Chand his attorney Umme Salina Akter put her signature. He has admitted in his testimony during his cross-examination that in the death certificate issued by the City Corporation; which was produced from their side, there is a recital to the effect that Fakir Chand died on 05.09.2007 and there is no paper showing their mutation, payment of rent, payment of gas bill, water bill and electricity bill in respect of the suit property and they have failed to produce any scrap of paper to that effect. P.W.1 at a stage of his cross-examination in reply to a question from the side of the defendants admits that in the deed of agreement dated 12.01.1970 being No.370 there is a signature of his grandmother Fakir Chand and in every page of this "bainanama" the name of Fakir Chand is visible.</u>

14. The witness No.2 of the plaintiff Md. Abdul Halim in his testimony testified that, he knows the parties and the suit property and he also knew Fakir Chanel. In the testimony P.W.2 testified at a stage that in the suit property the defendants use to reside and the mother of the defendants, Umme Salina along with her husband Altai Hossain in what basis started to reside in the disputed property-it is not known to him (P.W.2). He also does not know as to whether Fakir Chand on 12.01.1970 appointed Umme Salina Akter his attorney. This witness admits that Umme Salma died in the suit property.

15. P.W.3 Md. Abdul Matin, who is a government official deposed before this Court. This witness is a Sub-Assistant Engineer of Dhaka Public Works Department and this P.W.3 testified that the lease deed No.4643 dated 25.02.1982 stands in favour of the lease-holder Fakir Chand and in that deed Umme Salma Akter Khatun on behalf of Fakir Chand after putting her signatures accepted the deed, which has been marked as Exhibit-4. This witness also compared the certified copy of the deed No.5278 dated 10.09.1995 with its attested copy kept in the file and this deed has been marked as Exhibit-5. During his cross-examination P.W.2 gave his deposition in the following way,

“আমি গণপূর্ত বিভাগ ৪, সেগুনবাগিচা থেকে এসেছি। আমি জবানবন্দিতে যে মন্ত্রণালয়ের কথা বলছি এটা গণপূর্ত মন্ত্রণালয়। এ-৬২৭, ৬২৬-খুল, এ-৬২৮, পার্ট নং প্লট ফকির চাঁনকে বরাদ্দ দেয়া হয়েছিল। ৩৭১নং পাওয়ার অফ এ্যার্টনী নিয়োগ করে। এই ফাইল ৪৬৪৩ নং লীজ ডীড তাং ২৫/০২/৮২ ইং আছে। উক্ত লীজ ডীড লেসি হিসেবে ফকির চাঁন পক্ষে উম্মে সালমা আক্তার খাতুন লেখা আছে। ফকির চাঁন ৩৭১ নং দলিল বাতিল করেছে এ মর্মে কোন কিছু আমাদের ফাইলে নেই। সত্য নয় যে, উম্মে সালমা আক্তার এই প্লট বিক্রির জন্যে অনুমতি চেয়েছিলেন।

০৮/০৮/১৯৯৫ইং  তারিখ স্মারক নং শাখা ৬/এল৯৫/২১০৭ মুলে তাকে বিক্রির অনুমতি দেয়া হয়েছিলো। যাদের কাছে বিক্রির অনুমতি দেয়া হয়েছিলো  তাঁদের নাম ১।সৈয়দ আব্দুল কাইয়ুম ২। সৈয়দ মোনায়েম ৩। সৈয়দ আনায়ার হোসেন ৪। মোসাম্মৎ রোকেয়া।

আমাদের ফাইলে ৫২৭৮ নং দলিল তাং ১০/০৯/৯৫ইং এর কপি আছে। এই দলিলের গ্রহীতা সৈয়দ আব্দুল কাইয়ুম গং সৈয়দ আব্দুল কাইয়ুম গং নামজারী করিবার জন্য আবেদন করে ২৩/০৯/১৯৯৫ইং তারিখে।

যুগ্ম সচিব গণপূর্ত বিভাগ ০৭/১০/৯৫ইং তারিখে যৌথভাবে নামজারী করা যাইতে পারে মর্মে মত দেন।”

16. P.W.4 Abu Siddique in his deposition testified at a stage that he does not know the suit land.

17. P.W.5 Md. Fazal Hossain in his testimony testified at a stage that, perhaps the suit property has been allotted in favour of Fakir Chand and at that time he was a minor boy of 05 years.

18. P.W.6 Md. Hasan Ali, who is a man of different area; testified at a stage that lie does not know as to whether Fakir Chand was the owner of the suit property and it is also not known to him that, as to whether Fakir Chand entered into a deed of agreement with Altaf Hossain or appointed Salma Akter as of his attorney through a power of attorney.

19. The last witness of the plaintiffs, Momata Rani Chakroborty is an official witness, who is the Assistant Record Keeper, Sadar Record Room, Tejgaon, Dhaka. This witness proved the lease deed No.4643 from the original volume and this deed has been marked as Exhibit-6. She has also proved the general power of attorney No.371 dated 12.01.1970 from the concerned volume which was executed by Fakir Chand in favour of attorney Umme Salma. This document has been marked as Exhibit-7. This witness also proved the sub-kabala deed No.5278 dated 10.09.1995, executed by Salina Akter Khatun on behalf of Fakir Chand in favour of the defendants and this document is marked as Exhibit-8.

20. Vis-a-vis; the defendant's witness D.W.1 is the defendant No.1(Ka) Mst. Rokeya Khatun. This witness corroborated the case of their written statement in her deposition. She has also testified about their title documents which are on records and possession in favour of them.

21. D.w.2 Md. Rafique Ulla testified about the possession of Altai Hossain in the suit property through him who was a tenant under Altaf Hossain. He has corroborated the defendant's case in his testimony.

22. The last witness of' the defendant's, D.W.3 Md. Abul Kashem Akon testified about the case of the defendants as to their right, title, interest and possession in the disputed property. All the D.W.s have been thoroughly cross-examined from the side of the plaintiffs but except some minor discrepancies no such material contradiction or omission is noticed in their testimony by which they can be disbelieved.

23. On the contrary the witnesses produced from the side of the plaintiffs as I have already spelt out has proved the case of the defendants in their depositions and also proved the documentary evidences produced from the side of the defendant-opposite parties to substantiate their case.

24. Going through the evidence on records and connected all other papers it is obvious to note that, the learned courts below in their observation and findings evaluated the evidence on records in its true perspective and after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law rightly and legally decided the merit of the suit and its subsequent appeal against the plaintiffs and in favour of the defendants. I find no such misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. It further appears from the impugned judgment and decree that the learned appellate court under the ambit of Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure on preponderance of evidence arrived at a conclusive decision as to the right, title, interest and possession of' the parties to the suit and in the observation and findings as it appears, there is no ambiguity or illegality by which it can be held that the judgment and decree is perverse.

25. Before parting, however I must observe that, in the foregoing narrative; with regard to the facts and circumstances of this case; due to distinguishable character the case laws referred to from the side of the petitioners does not help them and I have every reason to inclined such a view that the Rule have got no merit to succeed.

26. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 25.11.2014 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No.19 of 2013 disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 13.01.2013 and 20.01.2013 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dhamrai, Dhaka in Title Suit No.34 of 2011 is hereby affirmed.

27. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

28. However; there will be no order as to costs.

29. Send back the lower Court's record and communicate the judgment and order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Moin Uddin, Advocate ----- For the petitioner.
