Although (concur in the main conclusion arrived at by my Lord, my approach to the questions raised in this reference has been some what different and as such I have felt impelled to express it in a separate Judgment.

75. This reference to the Full Bench arises out of a First Appeal, being F.A. No.191/73, in which the defendant is the appellant. The plaintiff-respondent instituted the suit for a decree for the sum of Tk. 11,100/- being the rent and/or compensation and also for ejecting the defendant from the scheduled property which consists of the first floor of Dacca Municipal Holding No. 2 Moulvi Abul Khirat Road under P.S. Kotwali, District Dacca.

76. Shortly stated, the plaintiff's case is that it is a registered Company under the Companies Act, 1913 and the owner of the holding-in-suit; that the defendant was a Director-in-charge of the plaintiff and as such he was allotted the First Floor of the said premises for his accommodation; that he having resigned from the said position on 28-8-1967, he was required to leave the house but he approached the plaintiff for letting out the premises to him to which the latter agreed and the defendant continued to live in the house at a monthly rent of Tk. 300/- and as such he was a tenant under the plaintiff and even if he was not a regular tenant he was only in permissive use and occupation of the premises as an ejectable licensee and therefore liable to be ejected and to pay fair compensation at least @ Tk. 300/- per month for use and occupation of the aforesaid premises.

77. Further case of the plaintiff is that the defendant failed to pay any rent from the very beginning of the tenancy and thus became a defaulter and liable for arrear rents from September, 1967 to June, 30, 1970 for a sum of Tk. 10,200/- and compensation for the months of July 1970- to November, 1970 and for such period as he does not vacate the premises at least at the rate of Tk. 300/- per month. The plaintiff served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendant through its Advocate on 28-5-70 and the defendant having failed to pay rent and vacate the premises, the suit was instituted against him.

78. For the purpose of jurisdiction and court-fee, the suit was valued at Tk. 11,100/- according to the plaintiff's claim and advalorem court-fee was paid thereon and the plaintiff offered to pay further court-fee, if necessary.

79. The defendant filed a lengthy written statement. For our present purpose, it will he sufficient to notice that the material allegations of the plaintiff were denied and the case of the defendant is that his wife Begum Farida Salahuddin has been in peaceful, undisturbed and continuous possession of the suit holding since her acquiring absolute right, title and interest therein by virtue of the gift from her father dated the 19th February 1962. The defendant denied any tenancy under the plaintiff at any time and contended that as such the question of the ejectment from the premises never arose.

80. It will be seen that the defendant never challenged the valuation of the suit as given by the plaintiff both for court-fee and jurisdiction and indeed no issue was raised at the trial in that behalf.

81. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in full but made a finding that the plaintiff was unable to prove that the defendant was a tenant under it as the defendant did not pay rent to the plaintiff and that it was conclusively proved that the defendant had entered into possession of the suit premises as an employee or as servant of the Company. 82. Defendant preferred the aforesaid First Appeal against the decree and, inter-alia, took a ground in the Memorandum of Appeal which reads as follows :

28. "For that the learned subordinate Judge should have held that the suit was not properly valued and adequately stamped inasmuch as the suit was valued at Tk. 11,100/- being only the rent and/or compensation for 37 months at the rate of Taka 300/- per month from November, 1967 to November 1970, vide paragraphs 6 and 7 the plaint, without making any separate valuation for eviction and without payment of any court-fee thereon and as such the suit should have been dismissed on this ground too."

83. As would, however, appear from the order of the referring Bench, the defendant, appellant, in course of the hearing of the appeal raised mainly three points which did not include the above-mentioned ground. But the learned Judges of the Division Bench themselves took up the question of valuation and court-fee on the basis of the said ground. It appears that the plaintiff-respondent conceded that the plaintiff would have to pay another set of court-fee on the valuation put for, a decree for ejectment, the valuation being on the basis of the 12 month's rental at the rate of Tk. 300/- per month. It appears further from the Order that the learned Advocate for the rescinding relied upon the Special Bench decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Rahman Ali v. M/S. Benaras Silk Industiries and another (1) for the proposition that the subject matter in a suit for ejecting a license e is the plaintiff's right to possess the property in suit and not the property itself. Again it appears from the earlier part of the order that the learned Advocate for the respondent claimed that the suit would be governed by Section 7 (xii) of the Court-fees Act, 1870.

84. The learned Judges of the Division Bench felt that the question of valuation and court-fee in a suit for ejectment of a licensee from a house by the full-owner is not a simple one, because, there is sufficient scope for doubt as to whether such a suit is covered by section 7(v) or section 7(xii) of the Court-fees Act.

85. Their lordships seemed to be in doubt about the application of the decision of the Special Bench referred to above in the facts of the present case and embarked upon an examination of the decisions on the point. Having done that, their lordships examined the decision of the Special Bench closely and concluded thus; "In the facts and circumstances of that case, the view taken by the learned Judges appears to be correct and we respectfully agree with the decision".

86. According to their Lordships "In the instant case position is slightly different" and "In that view of the matter and it the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the Special Bench decision does not provide the necessary guidance in the consideration of the question raised before us." The learned Judges ultimately came to the conclusion that "we find that the facts of this case clearly attract section 7(v)(e). For the purpose of Jurisdiction and court-fee, valuation of the suit shall be the market value of the property-in-suit."

87. Now, as to the reason for making a reference to the Full Bench, I may again quote from their Lordships' order thus : "In our opinion the question under consideration is of great public importance, and the same call for consideration by a larger Bench. Accordingly the case is referred to a Full Bench. We frame the following question for consideration :

(1) Whether in a suit instituted by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the house for ejectment of the defendant alleged to be his licensee, after determination and/or revocation of the license, for the purpose of jurisdiction and court-fee, valuation of the suit shall be the market value of the property in suit ?

(2) Whether a suit for ejectment of a licensee after revocation or termination by the plaintiff claiming co be the full owner of the suit house, falls within clause (v) or clause (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1970 ?"

88. At the hearing of the matter before us, the question almost naturally arose about the propriety and competence of the present reference in view of the rules of this court and, more particularly, the facts of the case under consideration as set out above. Mr. T.H. Khan, learned Advocate for the appellant (in the First Appeal) has been somewhat equivocal in his submission on this point but ultimately contended that the referring Bench having in effect differed from the aforesaid Special Bench decision of the Dacca High Court with regard to the application of section 7 (v) of the Court-fees Act, in suits for ejectment of a licensee by a full owner, the reference has been properly made and as such is competent.

89. Mr. F A. Mannan, the learned Advocate for the respondent (in the First Appeal) has submitted that in view of the facts of the present case, the points referred to the Full Bench for determination do not arise at all. Moreover, he has pointed out that their Lordships having agreed with the decision of the Special Bench and having themselves pointed out the difference in the facts of the present case with that of the Special Bench, there is hardly any occasion for a reference of the points of law to the Full Bench.

90. The learned Deputy Attorney General, who appeared in pursuance of our notice to the learned Attorney General who, we were told, was ill, has submitted that the decision of the Special Bench is binding on a Division Bench and if the learned Judges of the Division Bench wanted to take a different view, they could express it in their Judgment and yet follow the decision of the Special Bench and the matter could have been resolved in the ultimate court. In support of his submission, he has referred to the observations of Cornelius, Chief Justice, in the case of Province of East Pakistan v. Sirajul Huq Patwari, (1).

91. Having carefully perused the order of the learned Referring Judges I say with respect, I have felt great hesitation within myself about the propriety of the reference itself. The reason for making this reference to the Full Bench has been stated to be that "the question under consideration is of great public importance". Upon a reference to the Rules of this Court, however, it is found that the only provision regarding reference to a Full Bench is provided in Chapter VII thereof which, inter alia, reads as follows:

Reference to a Full Bench.

(1) Whenever a Division court shall differ from any other Division Court upon a point of law or usage having the force of law, the case shall be referred for decision by a Full Bench.

(2) If the question arises in an Appeal from an Appellant Decree or Order, the Court referring, the case shall state the point or points upon which they differ from the decision of a former Division Court and shall refer the Appeal for final decision by a Full Bench.

(3) If the question arise in an Appeal from an Original Decree or order, the questions of law shall alone be referred, and the Full Bench shall return the case with an expression of its opinion upon the points of law for final adjudication by the Division Court which referred it, and in case of necessity in consequence of the absence of any or either of the eferring Judges, for the ultimate decision of another Division Court.

92. In this connection, it will be pertinent to notice the provisions in Chapter II of the said Rules which, inter alia, read as follows :-

1. A Division Court for the hearing of appeals from the decrees or orders of subordinate Courts shall consist of two or more Judges as the Chief Justice may think fit.

(i) Provided that it shall be competent for one Judge to hear appeals and applications and Lawazimas relating thereto in all matters specified in the subjoined, except where such appeals, applications or matters involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, of the Government of India Act, 1935, or any order in Council made thereunder. He may, however, send any particular case, he thinks fit to be disposed of by two Judges, with his reasons for the same to the Chief Justice for his orders for being placed before a Division Bench.

(ii) Provided further that where at any stage of the hearing of an appeal, application or other matters it appears to the Judge that it involves a substantial question of law relating to the interpretation of the Government of India Act, 1935, or any order in Council made thereunder or the Indian Independence Act, the Award of the Boundary Commission, the Award of the Arbitration Tribunal, the orders made under the Indian Independence Act, or under the constitution of Pakistan or where any question of ultra vires of any provision in any Legislative Act arises he shall send the appeal, application or other matter to the Chief Justice for being disposed of by a Division Bench of at least two Judges.

(iii) Provided also that, on the requisition of any Division Court or whenever he thinks fit, the Chief Justice may appoint a Special Division Court, to consist of three Judges, for the hearing of any particular appeal, Rule, Revision or an application, or any particular question of law arising in any appeal or in any other matter.

<u>93. Now in the instant case, we have not found nor been pointed out any difference of opinion upon a point of law between the referring Bench and any other Division Court. Rather it is found that the learned Judges of the referring Bench not only agreed with the decision of the Special Division Court but made a distinction on facts of the present case with that of the Special Bench case. Their Lordships also pointed out that the decision of the Special Bench case "does not provide the necessary guidance in, the consideration of the question raised before us". Then their Lordships went on to hold that the facts of the case clearly attract section 7(v) (e) of the Court-fees Act. Thus, I do not see why in the absence of any difference on a point of law and inspire of the view taken that the Special Bench case does not provide the necessary guidance, it was considered appropriate to refer the point to the Full Bench for determination which, I say with respect, is not in harmony with the Rules.</u>

94. The learned Judges, it seems, could not agree with the interpretation of the word "subject-matter in the expression "according to the value of the subject-matter" occurring in section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act as given by A. S. Chowdhury, J. in that Special Bench decision. But the interpretation of the word "subject matter" was not the decision of the case, but was only the view of the learned Judge amongst three Judges. What was decided in that case is that the suit of a limited owner seeking to eject a licensee would be governed by section 7(xii) of the Court-fees Act for the purpose of court-fee. There A. S. Chowdhury, J held the view that the word "subject matter" occurring in section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act means the right sought to be established, the wrong to be remedied and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong and in that view of the matter his Lordship found it difficult to apply clause (v) in the case of ejecting a licensee by a limited owner and, therefore, held the residuary clause (xii) to be applicable in that case. The learned Referring Judges are of the view that this interpretation may be justified in .the facts of that case but section 7(v) is applicable in the facts of the instant case where the plaintiff being a full owner is seeking relief in the form of possession of immovable property of which he is out of possession and in such a case the "subject fatter" cannot be the right sought to be established and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong. So the facts of the two cases being different, as found by themselves, the learned Judges were perfectly entitled to their own views as to the application of section 7(v) in spite of the expression of opinion with regard to the phrase "subject-matter" by a learned Judge of the said Special Bench.

95. It is true in this reference we cannot go into the facts of the case but are to decide the points only as referred to us. While examining the propriety of the reference, we have incidentally looked into the facts relevant for the purpose of understanding the points at issue. From the reading of the plaint it appears that the plaintiff was seeking to eject its tenant, the defendant and alternatively it pleaded that even if he was not a regular tenant, he was a licensee liable to be ejected. The suit was valued at Tk. 11,100/- on the basis of the rent/compensation claimed and court, fee was paid thereon. But no separate Court-fee was paid for the relief of eviction and that gave rise to the present question at the time of the hearing of the appeal. The plaintiff-respondent offered to pay court-fee on the basis of twelve months rent next before the institution of the suit. The learned Judges of the Division Bench. I say again with respect, without examining the plaint case or the finding of the Trial Court in. respect of the status of the defendant or even making their own finding whether the defendant was a tenant, licensee or trespasser which is absolutely essential at this stage, for the determination of the fees that are to be paid in the suit and for the valuation thereof, at once proceeded to examine the points under consideration on the assumption that the defendant was a licensee. It may be mentioned that although the Trial Court held that the plaintiff was unable to prove that the defendant was a tenant because he did not pay rent to the plaintiff, it was nowhere found that he was a licensee.

96. In the context of the aforesaid facts, the conclusion which initially found favour with us was that this reference was not perhaps appropriate and, if at all we would be merely answering an academic question. But ultimately, there was some sort of a consensus that we should answer the points raised before us. We have persuaded ourselves to examine the points referred to us for three reasons. Firstly because the answer may have some relevance for the disposal of the First Appeal itself. Secondly, the learned Judges of the Division Bench have expressed some opinion in their order with regard to the questions at issue which, for all practical purposes, is contrary to the view taken by the Special Division Bench (19 D.L.R. Dacca 287) although the learned Judges took pains to mention clearly that' they agreed with the decision of the Special Bench in the facts and circumstances of that case. Lastly, the question being one of general public importance, it is desirable that there should be an authoritative pronouncement to avoid any further controversy on the subject.

97. I have already reproduced the two questions that have been framed by the learned Judges of the Division Bench for consideration. It seems to me that the second question should have preceded the first as the answer to that question would determine whether any answer to the first one is called for. I may also add that the second question is the main question in this reference and that is, whether a suit for ejectment of a licensee after revocation or termination of the license by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (v) or clause (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870. If our answer is that such a suit falls under clause (xii), it is obvious that the first question does not arise. If, however, we hold that clause (v) will govern such a case, then, of course, the first question will be relevant because of the view taken by the learned Judges of the Division Bench with regard to the word "subject-matter" occurring therein in contradistinction to the views expressed by A.S. Chowdhury, J in the Special Bench case reported in 19 D.L.R. Dacca 287.

98. I would, however, like to dispose of the first point first with short observation on the assumption that clause (v) governs the suit in question. Section 7 of the Court-fees Act 1970, as it obtains now, is reproduced herein below in its entirety for facility of discussion:

"7. Computation of fees payable in certain suits: The amount of fee payable under this Act in the suits next hereinafter mentioned shall be computed as follows:

i. for money : In suits for money (including suits for damages or compensation, or arrears of maintenance, of annuities, or of other sums payable periodically)—according to the amount claimed ;

ii. for maintenance and annuities: In suits for maintenance and annuities or other sums payable periodically—according to the value of the subject-matter of the suit, and such value shall be deemed to be ten times the amount claimed to be payable for one year:

Provided that, in suits by widows for maintenance such value shall be deemed to be the amount claimed to be payable for one year.

iii. for movable property having a market value: In suits for movable property other than money, where the subject-matter has a market-value—according to such value at the date of presenting the plaint :

iv. for movable property of no market value : In suits—

(a) for movable property where the subject-matter has no market-value, as, for instance, in the case of documents relating to title;

(b) (Omitted by s.7(l) of the Court-fees (Bengal) Amendment) Act, 1935 (Ben. Act VII of 1935)

(c) for declaratory decree and consequential relief to obtain a declaratory decree or order, whore consequential relief is prayed,

(d) for an injunction to obtain an injunction,

(e) for easement for a right to some benefit (not herein otherwise provided for) to arise out of land, and

(f) for accounts for accounts—according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint or memorandum of appeal (subject to the provisions of section 8 C). In all such suits the plaintiff shall state the amount at which he values the relief sought:

v. for possession of land, buildings, or gardens :

In suits for the possession of land, buildings, or gardens—

(a) according to the value of the subject, matter, and such value shall be deemed to be fifteen  times the net profits which have arisen from the land, building or garden during the year next before the date of presenting the plaint, or if the court sees reason to think that such profits have been wrongly estimated, fifteen times such amount as the Court may assess as such profits or according to the market-value of the land, building or garden, (whichever is greater),

(b) if in the opinion of the Court, such profits are not readily ascertainable or assessable or where there are no such profits, according to the market-value of the land, building or garden;

Explanation in this paragraph "building" includes a house, out-house, stable, privy, urinal, shed, hut, wall and other such structure, whether of masonry, bricks, wood, mud, metal Or any other material whatsoever :

vi. to enforce a right of pre-emption : In suit to enforce a right of pre-emption-according to the market-value of the land building or garden in respect of which the right is claimed:

Explanation—In this paragraph "building" has the same meaning as in paragraph v:

vi. A for partition and separate possession of a share of joint family property etc. In suits for partition and separate possession of a share of joint family property, or of a joint property, or to enforce a right to a share in any property on the ground that it is joint family property or joint property—

if the plaintiff has been excluded from possession of the property of which as clarifies to be a coparcener or co-owner, according to the market-value of the share in respect of which the suit instituted:

vii. for interest of assignee of land-revenue : In suits for the interest of as assignee of land revenue—fifteen times his net profits as such for the year next before date of presenting the plaint.

viii. to set aside an attachment : In suits to set aside an attachment of land or of an interest in land or revenue—according to the amount for which the land or interest was attached

viii. to set aside decrees: In suits to set aside decrees passed for ascertained amounts-according to the amounts of the decrees sought to be set aside, or where such decrees are not for any ascertained amounts, the fee payable shall be the same as paid on the plaints of the suits in which the questioned decrees were passed: Provided that, where such amount exceeds the value of land or interest, the amount of fee shall be computed as if the suit were for the possession of such land or interest:

ix. to redeem: In suits against a mortgage for the recovery of the property mortgaged, to foreclose : and in suits by a mortgagee to foreclose the mortgage or, where the mortgage is made by conditional sale, to have the sale declared absolute according to the principal money expressed to be secured by instrument of mortgage:

x. for specific performance : In suits for specific performance—

(a) of a contract of sale—according to the amount of the consideration :

(b) of a contract of mortgage—according to the amount agreed to be secured :

(c) of a contract of lease—according to the aggregate amount of the fine or premium (if any) and of the rent agreed to be paid during the first year of the terms :

(d) of an award—according to the amount or value of the property in dispute :

xi. between landlord and tenant : In the following suits between landlord and tenant—

(a) for the delivery by a tenant of the counter-part of a lease,

(b) to enhance the rent of a tenant having a right of occupancy,

(c) for the delivery by a landlord of a lease.

(cc) for the recovery of immovable property from attendant including a tenant holding over after the determination of a tenancy,

(d) to contest a notice of ejectment,

(e) to recover the occupancy of (immovable property) from which a tenant has been illegally ejected by the landlord, and

(f) for abatement of rent—according to the amount of the rent of the (immovable property) to which the suit refers, payable for the year next before the dates of presenting the plaint.

xii. in suits not expressly provided for in this section :

In suits not expressly provided for in this section, according the value cl aimed, but such value shall not be less than a value which would attract a court-fee of less than fifteen rupees ;

<u>99. Reading clause (v.) of section 7 as a whole, there remains little doubt that the word "subject-matter" occurring therein is referable only to land, buildings or gardens as the case may be and, if that be so, it is evident that the suit shall have to be valued according to the market value of the property in suit for the purpose of Court-fee where there is no net profit arising out of the land, building or garden dining the year next be-fore the date of presenting the plaint.</u>

100. In the Special Bench case referred to above his Lordship A. S. Chowdhury, J interpreted the expression "subject-matter" to mean a right sought to be established, wrong to be remedied and defence asserted in justification of the wrong and accordingly found it difficult to include a suit for ejectment of a licensee in that clause as the latter part of the clause cannot be made applicable in that can view of the "subject-matter". According to his Lordship, subject-matter is the right en joyed by the plaintiff. It is neither land nor building nor garden but a right that the plaintiff possesses over the same. It must be said, with due respect.to his Lordship, that there is an obvious error in this interpretation of the word "subject-mateer", as occurring in. clause (v), which is bereft of its context. Indeed it has been said by high authorities that statutory language is not read in isolation, but in its context.

101. The following passage occurs in Maxwell's "The Interpretation of Statutes" 12th Edition at page 76:

"The words of a statute, when there is doubt about their meaning, are to be understood in the sense in which they best harmonies with the subject of the enactment Their meaning is found not so much in a strictly grammatical or etymological propriety of language, nor even in its popular use, as in the subject, or in the occasion on which they are used, and the object to be attained."

102. Crawford in his statutory construction (1940) at page 351 stated as follows:

204. The context. The words, phrases, sections, sub-sections, provisos, saving clauses, in fact, every part of the statute, must be interpreted with reference to the context. This means that the court in construing a statute cannot isolate words or give them their abstract meaning or consider the different parts of the statute separately and independently. Every part of the statute must be considered togather, and considered as an integral part of the whole, and kept subservient to the general intent of the whole enactment. Each part or section of the statute subject to construction should be construed in connection with every other part or section, even sections which are invalid, or in conflict. Indeed all of the parts must be given effect according to the intent expressed or clearly revealed."

103. His Lordship's interpretation of the word may be perfectly valid in a different context, but when we read clause (v) as a whole and that being the only permissible manner in which a statute should be read and interpreted, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the subject matter' there is the land, building or garden as the case may be.

104. That the word "subject-matter" in clause (v) is capable of bearing only one meaning as referred to above, but may as well mean a relief claimed in the suit in a different context and for a different purpose has been pointed out by Dasgupta J in two decisions of the Calcutta High Court.

105. In case of Chandi Charan Das v. Sushilabala Dasi (1) in a suit for recovery of possession from a licensee whose license had been revoked, question arose as to what would be the basis of valuation of the suit for the purpose of jurisdiction. It may be noted that both parties agreed that the court-fee payable on the plaint would be in accordance with the provisions of section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act. Das Gupta 3 held that for the purposes of jurisdiction, the subject matter of the suit was not the property in respect of which the plaintiffs claimed relief but the relief itself which was that the licensee should leave the land and the structures thereon. His Lordship found no reason to differ from the view of Macklin J (AIR 1947 Bombay 482) that for purposes of court-tee under clause (v) the subject-matter is the property itself but disagreed with the interpretation in so far as the valuation of such a suit for jurisdiction was concerned. His Lordship highlighted the meaning of "subject-matter" by giving some examples as follows: "In a lecture on the question whether Shakespeare and Bacon were identical person, the subject matter was neither Shakespeare nor Bacon but their identity; a club considering the question whether members should come in Dhoti, the subject matter was the desirability of the members attending the club in Dhoti; also in a suit to enforce a right of irrigation from a tank, the subject matter was neither tank nor the land to be irrigated but the right of irrigation. So also in a suit on a claim of ancient rights enjoyed by a house, the house was not the subject matter but the relief which the plaintiff claimed.

106.- The same learned Judge in the sub-sequent case of Manik Chard Mondal and another v. Sudhir Kumar Mandal and another (1) while considering whether the subject matter of the litigation was not the property but the right of the plaintiff to eject the licensee for purposes of court-fee observed as follows:-

“If the legislature has contented itself by merely saying that in suits for possession of lands; buildings or gardens the amount of fee payable shall be computed according to the value of the subject matter, there would have been much scope for the argument that the word. "subject-matter" should not be taken to be the same as the land, buildings or gardens. The Legislature itself, however, proceeded to add that such value should be deemed to be 15 times the net profits which have arisen from the land, building or garden during the year next before the date of presenting the plaint, or if the court sees reasons to think that such profits have been wrongly estimated, fifteen times such amount as the court may assess as such profits or according to the market value of the land, building or garden, whichever is lower and then if, in the opinion of the, court, such profits are not readily ascertainable, or assessable, or where there are no such profits according to the market value of the land, building or garden, It is true that in some cases of which mention has to be made of a decision of Patna High Court in Mussammat Barkatunnisa Begum v. Musammat Kaniz Fatema (2) and a decision in Ram Raj Tewari v. Giranandan Bhagat and Others (3) the view was taken that it is not the property over which the suit was brought that can be called the subject matter of the suit but the relief itself that is sought which is the subject matter of the suit. In the Patna case the decision was that the subject matter of the suit is the right to eject the defendants and the value of the right is that value at which the defendants right to remain in the house under the license of the plaintiff may be valued. This Court in Satish Kumar v. Sailabasini: Devi (4) took a different view. There also a person claimed possession from a licensee, as in the present case and Sen 3 held that the valuation should be made in one of the ways provided in clause (v) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, and that the market-value of the land is the proper measure. The matter was considered at the Bombay High Court in Ratilal Mandal v. Chandulal Chhotalal (5) Macklin, 3, with whom Bavdekar, J. agreed, held that the market-value of the land itself was the basis on which the court-fees have to be computed -----

Though the view taken above which, as I have stated earlier, was also the view taken by Sen, J. in this court, might result in hardship in many cases, I am unable to see how, on an interpretation of the Statute according to recognised rules, it is possible to escape the co inclusion that this view is right. It is certainly possible to say that the subject-matter of suit is really the relief for which the suit is brought. It was in that view that this Court held in Chandi Charan Das v. Sushila bala Dasi (1) that the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction should be made in such cases where a plaintiff asks for possession of the land from a licensee not on the basis of the market-value of the land but on the valuation of the relief he wants to obtain by getting rid of the licensee. As was, however, pointed out in that very case, the interpretation of the word "subject-matter" may well be different when the question of court-fee has to be considered under section 7(v) of the Court-Fees Act."

107. It appears that different High Courts of India have veered round the view that the "subject-matter" in clause (v) cannot be anything else but the property itself. Without burdening this Judgment by referring to huge cases of the Indian High Courts, I propose to refer to only one case and that is the case of Sisir Kumar Dutta and others v. Susil Kumar Dutta. (2) This was a Special Bench decision in which there was an exhaustive review of all the available decisions on the point. I shall refer again to this case when I take up the second question. But for the present purpose, one passage from that decision may be reproduced here:

"I have already observed that the subject-matter of a suit for eviction against a licensee whose license stands revoked and who thereupon becomes a trespasser is the property which is sought to be recovered. That being so, the value of the relief must be the value of the subject matter, namely, the property and that must be valued in accordance with section 7(v) of the Court-Fees Act."

108. In this connection, only one other case may be noticed. In the case of Jogdish Chandra v. Basant Kumar (1) their Lordships differed from the view taken in an earlier case of the same court. It was held in that earlier case (I.L.R 5 Patna 631AIR 1927 Patna 140) that the subject-matter of the suit is 'the right to eject the defendants and the value of that right is the value of which the defendant right to remain in the house under the license of the plaintiff may be valued. It may be noted that the same view was taken by A.S. Choudhury J. in the Special Bench Case of the Dacca High Court referred to above. But the Patna Full Bench held thus:

"With great respect, I find too difficult to accept the view. The defendant's right as licensees had already come to an end. The subject-matter of the suit was not, therefore, any right of the defendants as licensees: but the subject-matter was the entire property which was sought to be recovered."

109. I have already mentioned that in the context of the entire clause (v), the "subject-matter", of necessity, refers to the property itself i.e. land, buildings or gardens, This view, as seen above, is shared by most of the High Courts of India. Thus I am one with the observation of the learned Judges of the referring Bench that "In such a case the "subject-matter" cannot be the right sought to be established and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong. Hence my answer to the First question is that assuming clause (v) covers the suit of a plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the house for ejectment of the defendant alleged to be his licensee after determination and/or revocation of the license, for the purposes of jurisdiction and court-fee, the valuation of the suit shall be the market value of the property in suit.

110. Now with that answer, we are squarely faced with the second question of the reference which, as stated earlier, is the main question and I better quote it again:-

"Whether a suit for ejectment of a licensee after revocation or termination by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (v) or clause (xii) i) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870?

111. Mr. T.H. Khan has submitted that such a suit falls within clause (v) of section 7 because it provides for suits for possession and once a license is revoked or terminated, the licensee becomes a trespasser and any suit to recover possession from him will clearly attract clause (v). If this view is correct, as Mr. T.H. Khan claims it is, clause (xii) will have no Manner of application. For this proposition, Mr. Khan has placed strong reliance on the Special Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court 65 C.W.N. 1, already referred to above. He has submitted that the Special Bench decision of the Dacca .High Court, 19 D.L.R. Dacca 287, not having considered the ratio of the Calcutta Special Bench Case that a licensee upon revocation or termination of his license becomes a trespasser, cannot be held to be authoritative for the view that clause (xii) will be attracted in such a suit.

112. Yet another branch of Mr. Khan's argument is that it is difficult to apply clause (xii) in such a suit because the expression "Value claimed" as it occurs therein is very vague and can mean anything including value of the property. He has submitted that it is not for the court of supply the omission; but if it does in one way as was done in the Special Bench Case of the Dacca High Court to mean "the 'value of the right sought to be enforced" no exception can legitimately be taken if another court reads "property" instead of 'fright".

113. Mr. F.A. Mannan has, one the other hand, submitted that a suit against a licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated not having been specifically provided for in any of the preceding clauses of section 7, clause (xii) is the only clause which will automatically govern such a case. He has relied on the aforesaid Special Bench case of the Dacca High Court in support of his submission and also contended that the status of the plaintiff, whether a limited owner or full owner, will not make any difference in the matter of application of clause (xii) Mr. Mannan has further submitted that clause (v) will be applicable in those suits where the relief for possession is primary and directly involved; but a suit for ejectment of a licensee not being a suit directly for recovery of possession, clause ( v) is not attracted in such a suit. He has also submitted that the Court-fees Act being a fiscal statute, the court should construe its provisions beneficially in favour of the litigant public and should incline to apply clause (xii) if there is the slightest doubt with regard to the application of clause (v) in such a suit.

114. The learned Deputy Attorney General started by submitting that it is possible to apply both clause (v) and clause (xii) to the clause of suits under consideration. When pointed out by us that the clauses are mutually exclusive, he finally opted for the view that clause (xii) would govern such a case.

115. Section 7 of the Court-fees Act has already been reproduced hereinbefore. It is clear that the section is meant to provide for computation of fees payable in certain suits clause (v) thereof provides for suits for the possession of land, buildings or gardens. After having provided for suits for possession of land, buildings or gardens generally irrespective of the mural relationship of the contestants with regard to the property-in-suit, the legislature, in subsequent clauses has manifestly referred to certain of such relationships and provided for different basis for computation of fees for recovery of possession in those suits other than as in clause (v). A wholesome principle is easily discernible in the matter of realizing fees in suits for possession. Under clause (v) in a suit for possession generally fees are to be computed according to the value of the subject-matter and such value shall be deemed to be fifteen times the net profits which have arisen from the land etc. during the year next before the institution of the suit or according to the market valise thereof. But in the subsequent clauses/ keeping in view certain from of juridical relationship between the contestants and the property in suit, the legislature has provided for different basis resulting in comparatively lesser amount of fees when a plaintiff claims possession of property of which the initial possession of the defendant is lawful but becomes unlawful on the date of the institution of the suit. For instance, it has been provided under clause (ix) that when a mortgagor sues for the recovery of the property mortgaged, he has to pay the court-fee according to the principal money expressed to e secured by the instrument of mortgage. Similarly, under clause (x) in suits for specific performance of a contract of sale, fee is to be paid according to the amount of the commiseration. Recovery of possession is often an usual prayer in such a suit which is always granted in case of success. Then again under clause (xi) in a suit between the landlord and tenant fable recovery of immovable property from a tenant, it is to be computed according to the amount of the rent of the immovable property payable for the year next before the date of presenting the plaint.

<u>116. It is evident that, in like manner, the suit of a licensor to recover possession from his licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated has not been expressly provided for in any of the clauses of section 7. It may be reasonably argued that such a suit being a suit for possession should come under the general provisions for suits for possession under clause (v). But then it has to be conceded that a suit of this nature is not expressly provided for either in clause (v) or in any, other clause. If that be so and indeed it is so, then in terms of clause (xii), a suit of this kind, of necessity, and by the sheer logic of permutation, comes to be governed by that clause.</u>

117. Let us examine to what extent the principle enunciated in the Special Bench Case of the Calcutta High Court, 65 .C.W.N. 1, can be accepted as an authority on which so much reliance has been placed by Mr. T.H. Khan.

The question before that Special Bench was:-

"What is the proper valuation of a suit for ejectment of a licensee upon revocation or termination of his license for purpose of (i) Court-fees and (ii) jurisdiction is there any difference in the matter between a case of revocation of license and a case of termination as distinguished from revocation of licence?"

Their Lordships after reviewing the catena of case-law on the point answered the questions in the following terms:

"I. Valuation of a suit for ejectment of a licensee, upon revocation or termination of his license, either for the purpose of court-fees or for the purpose of jurisdiction shall be made under the provision of section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act." 2. There is no difference in the manner of such valuation between a case of 'revocation of license and a case of termination of license as distinguished from revocation of license.

118. The retio in that decision, to quote from the judgment itself was "The answer to the question before me ought to be sought, in the first place, in what the position of a licensee is, After his license is revoked. In my opinion a licensee, whose license has been revoked, becomes a trespasser, just as a tenant, whose tenancy has been determined becomes a trespasser, unless law Makes him a statutory tenant.... If a licensee whose license stands revoked becomes a trespasser, then a suit for eviction of such a person undoubtedly would be a suit for possession of land house or garden and must be valued according to the value of the subject matter under section 7(v) of the Court fees Act.

119. In the first place, it may be pointed out that their Lordships were considering the case without there being clause (xii) in the Court-fees Act as in our case which was added in the then Pakistan by Ordinance LII of 1962. So, the premises are different. We do not know, said Abdullah J. rightly in the Special Bench Case, what view the Calcutta High Court would have taken if such a provisions was available to them. In that view of the matter, that decision is not quit; relevant for our present purpose. But Mr. T.H. Khan has submitted that even so the proposition of law as enunciated therein with regard to the status of a licensee after termination or revocation of license should be accepted as sound. If the proposition that a licensee becomes a trespasser upon revocation or termination of his license is correct then there is no question that a suit against him for possession would be governed by Clause (v) and not by clause (xii).

120. Upon an examination of the subject of license, I have found myself unable to accept the view that a licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated, becomes a trespasser for the purpose of a suit to evict such a licensee.

121. A license has been defined in section 52 of the Easements Act 1881 in the following terms:

"Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the granter, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license.

It will be seen that a license is a purely personal privilege which enables a licensee to do something in or upon the land of the licensor with his express or implied consent. It is merely a leave to do a thing enabling a licensee to do lawfully what he could not otherwise do except unlawfully. This right does not confer on the licensee an interest in immovable property or an easement appurtenant to some dominant tenement.

122. In Halsburys Laws of England Second Edition (Vol 20 page 8) (Landlord and tenant) it has been stated as uncle?:-

"A grant under which the grantee takes only the right to use the premises without exclusive possession operates as a license, and not as a lease. In deciding whether a grant amounts to a lease, or is only a licence, regard must be had to the substance of the agreement. If the effect of the instrument is to give the holder the exclusive right of occupation of the land, though subject to certain reservation, or to a restriction of the purposes for which it may be used, it is a lease; if the contract is merely for the use of the property in a certain way and on certain terms, while it remains in possession and control of the owner, it is a licence."

123. In the case of Abdullah Bhai and others v., Ahmed Din (1) (at page 172) their Lordships held thus:

"The right of ownership as well as the right of which it is composed are rights in rem and not in persona and by the lease a right in turn is transferred to the lessee. On the other hand a "licence," as will appear from its definition in section 52 of the Easement Act is merely a competence to do something which except for this permission would be unlawful. It does not confer any rights in physical property. There is in the case of a licence only a personal agreement between the licensor and the licensee whereby the licensor agrees not to interfere with the doing a particular acts on property which is in his possession. No right in rem passes to the licensee."

The underlining’s as made above are mine.

124. It may be pointed out that under section 116 of the Evidence Act "no person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time when such license was given."

<u>125. Thus it appears that no interest in immovable property passes to neither a licensee nor the possession of the licensor cease at any point of time. When a license is revoked or terminated and the licensee yet continues to enjoy the personal privilege granted to him. I do not think that in order to stop him from further enjoyment of his privilege, it is necessary to bring an action for recovery of possession in the same way as it is required against a trespasser. Upon revocation of the license, the continuance of the licensee becomes unlawful no doubt; but for the purpose of a suit against him, having regard to the incidents of his right as a licensee, I think a decree for his ejectment is the proper and complete remedy and no further relief in the form of recovery of possession is called for nor required. There is and ought to be a distinction between, a trespasser who causes severance of physical possession of the owner and a licensee who continues unlawfully after termination of the license for the purpose of claiming relief in suits against each of them. In the case of the former, possession needs be recovered but in the case of the latter, there is no question of recovery of possession, for, by revoking the license, the licensor cannot be said to have lost his possession which was and has always been with him; what he needs is to remove an ungrateful creature from the immovable property in respect of which the latter continues to enjoy personal privileges in spite of the revocation/termination of his license. In that view of the matter also, a suit to evict an erstwhile licensee does not come under clause (v) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act.</u>

126. It may be observed that in West Bengal clause (V-A) has been incorporated by the Court-fees West Bengal (Amendment) Act 1963 (West Bengal Act 18 of 1963) in the following manner:

(V-A) In a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property from—

(a) A trespasser, where no declaration of title to the property is either prayed for or necessary for disposal of the suit—according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the provisions of section 8C;

(b) A licensee upon revocation or termination of his license—

(i) Where a license fee is payable by the licensee in respect of the immovable property to which the suit refers, according to the amount of the license fee of the immovable property payable for the year next before the date, of presenting the plaint, or

(ii) where no such license fee is payable 5 by the licensee, according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the provisions of section 8C.

127. It will be seen that the legislature in that Province must have considered the burden which a plaintiff seeking to eject his licensee would have to encounter in paying. court-fees pursuant to the decision of the Calcutta High Court (65 C.W.N. 1) already referred to before and accordingly brought about a change in the law to give relief to the litigants in such suits and, also, I venture to think, to make it more consistent in principle with the other provisions of section 7 of the Court-fees Act. I am of the view that the same purpose has been achieved in our country, in so far as a suit for ejecting a licensee is concerned, by adding clause (xii) to section 7.

128. At this stage, we may dispose of another contention of Mr. T. H. Khan as to on what basis the amount of fee shall be computed under clause (xii). The clause says "according to the value claimed." The value referred to therein is neither the value of the property nor that of the right to be asserted. It is the value of the relief which a plaintiff claims in a suit subject to the limitation contained in the clause itself, namely, such value shall not be less than a value which would attract a court-fee of less than fifteen rupees. This view about the basis of computation approximates with the aforesaid section (V-A) (b) (ii) of the amendment in West Bengal. I would like to recommend more explicit provisions in our own law to cater for suits against licensees with and without fees differently and against a trespasser where no declaration of title is either prayed for or necessary on the line of the amendment in West Bengal referred to above. But until such an amendment is brought about, in a suit to eject a licensee court-fee is to be paid according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the limitation mentioned in clause (xii) itself.

<u>129. I have found in course of the fore-going discussion that a suit of the kind under consideration does not fit in clause v or in any other clause of section 7 and as such the residuary clause (xii) has, of necessity, to be taken recourse to. Even if there is a reasonable doubt as to whether clause (v) would be attracted in such a case then also on the well-established principle of beneficial construction of fiscal statutes, there will be no escape from the conclusion that clause (xii) would be attracted. For this proposition it will be sufficient to refer to a passage occurring in Maxwell's "The interpretation of Statutes" (12th Edition) at pag. 256:</u>

<u>"Statutes which impose pecuniary burdens are subject to the same rule of strict construction. It is well-settled rule of law that all charges upon the subject must be imposed by clear and unambiguous language, because in some degree they operate as penalties; the subject is not to be taxed unless the language of the statute clearly imposes the obligation, and language must not be strained in order to tax a transaction which, had the legislature thought of it would have been covered by appropriate words."</u>

130. For the reasons assigned, my conclusion is that a suit for ejectment of a licensee, after revocation or termination by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870.

End.

full_judgment:
Shahidul Islam J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 4-9-2003 and 7-9-2003 passed by the Assistant Settlement Officer and Appeal Officer (the Respondent No. 4) and signed by the Settlement Officer on 16-9-2003 after rehearing/hearing of settlement Appeal Case Nos. 77717 & 77725 of 2003 & 10121 of 2000 (Annexure-C & C-1) of Tejgaon Settlement Office, Dhaka should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may fit and proper. 

2. Facts in short for disposal of the Rule are that during the last survey operation, land as described in the Writ Petition was recorded in the name of the petitioner and thereafter objection was filed. Ultimately that was rejected, appeal was filed under Rule 31 and that was also rejected. Thereafter when the matter was awaiting for final publication of the record, at that time the Bangladesh Railway came forward by filing an appeal under Rule 31 of SA and T Rule 1995. Thereafter the respondent No. 4 issued notice upon the petitioners for rehearing of the appeal brought under Rule 31 and thereafter the impugned orders were passed. The petitioners being aggrieved by the said order came forward before this Court by filing the Writ petition and has obtained the instant Rule. 

3. The petitioners case in short is that C S Plot Nos. 613, 614 and 616 and other plots were owned and possessed by Mahmud Ali and Amjad Ali having 8 annas share each. The names of tenants were recorded in CS khatian. The Plot Nos. 616, 613 and some portion of 614 were fallen in the Saham of Mahmud Ali who sold 30 decimals of land of Plot Nos. 613/614 to Aftabuddin Ostagar and Jamrat Bibi on 25-5-1939 but the scribe wrongly wrote Plot No. 616, though delivered possession in Plot Nos. 613 and 614. While Aftabuddin and Jamrat Bibi were in possession in Plot Nos 613 and 614 they sold out the same to Jamila Bibi on 24-12-1943 and thereafter Jamila Bibi sold 30 decimals of land to Sk Yousuf Ali on 29-4-1946 who sold the same to Kadam Ali on 13-9-1955. The SA Khatian was prepared in his name and thereafter Kadam Ali sold 9 decimals to the father of the petitioners on 12-7-1962 who mutated his name and paid rents and taxes to the Government. The father of the petitioners filed Title Suit No. 251 of 1976 for correction of Plot No. 616 and got decree on 21-4-1978. During 1979 one Abdul Malek disturbed peaceful possession of the father of the petitioners for which he filed Title Suit No. 476 of 1979 and got decree against that person. During RS record the case land was rightly recorded in the name of the father of the petitioners. Said Abdul Malek filed Title Suit No. 49 of 1983 & TS No. 86/90 against the father of the petitioners and those were dismissed. That father of the petitioners sold 4 decimals of land to the petitioner No. 1 on 11-5-1996 who his name and paid rent & taxes to the Government and got plan from RAJUK for construction of a 5-storied building and petitioner No. 1 as a officer of Agrani Bank got Loan to build 5 storied building and accordingly the petitioner No. 1 constructed a 5 storied building in the suit land. During Moha Nagori Survey and Settlement an area of 4 decimal of land was recorded in the name of the petitioner No. 1, 5 decimals of land in the name of the father of the petitioners against which one Quiyum objection case and that was dismissed. The aggrieved party preferred appeal and that was dismissed by order dated 8-4-2001. The DP Khatian Nos 514 & 515 became final after completing all the stages of survey namely Khana Pun, Bujarat and attestation and after disposal of objection cases and appeals those were sent to the press for publication. 

4. It is the further case of the petitioner that the further of the petitioners gifted his 5 decimals of land to the petitioner Nos. 2-4 vide registered Hiba-bill-ewaz deed on 7-7-1999. Soon after the RS Khatian was finally published, the petitioner No. 1 and the petitioners No. 2-4 separately mutated their names and paid rents and taxes to the Government. The petitioners have been possessing the suit land since 1962 by constructing pucca building and the Government is receiving rents and taxes regularly without any objection. The photo state true copies of the CS, SA, RS, SA Mutation Khatian, RS Mutation Khatian and DP Khatians and last Rent Receipts have been annexed and marked as Annexures- "A- 12 and A-13" respectively. The DP Khatians became final in the year 1999 and against that the objection case and Appeal under section 30 and 31 was also dismissed in the year 2001. The Respondent No. 5 Railway did not file any objection case against D P Khatian. The land as described in the Writ Petition is not the acquired land of the Railway authority did not take any steps against any actions of the petitioners since 1962. Rather the petitioners mutated their names constructed 5 storied building after taking "No objection certificate" from the Railway office did not raise objection against SA or RS settlement Record nor raised objection against recent survey but all on a sudden the petitioner No. 1 and the father of the petitioners got notices for Rehearing of the earlier Appeal No. 10121 of 2000 and hearing of new Appeal Nos. 77717/30 and 777725/30 filed by the Railway Estate Officer, Dhaka The petitioners appeared and submitted all the necessary papers. The Assistant Settlement Officer allowed the appeals of Railway by the impugned orders dated 4-9-2003 and 7-9-2003 which was counter signed by the settlement officer on 16-9-2003. The petitioners obtained the certified copy of the same. The certified copy of the orders of objection case and Appeal filed by Quiyum dated 11-4-2000 & 8-4-2001 and the notices dated 38-7-2003 have been annexed in the Writ Petition and marked as Annexures-"B, B-1, B-2, B-3 & B-4" 

5. It is the further case of the petitioner that the impugned orders is not clear as many appeals were heard analogously but the appeals individually. 

6. It is contended that after exhausting the forum of appeal under Rule 31 of the settlement Rules 1955 there remained no forum open before the Bangladesh Railway to submit the 2nd appeal and, as such, the impugned order was passed unlawfully. 

7. The respondent No. 5, the Bangladesh Railway, Divisional Estate Officer, Dhaka contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in opposition denying the material statements made in the Writ Petition and contended, inter alia, that the land as described in the Writ Petition was acquired by the Railway vide Gazette notification in L A case No. 43/1959-1060 and, as such, the Bangladesh Railway moved the settlement office as per law. It is contended that under Rule 42 and 42(A) of the Settlement Rules 1955, the respondent No. 4 was quite lawfully authorized to accept the appeals filed by the Railway. It is contended that the Respondent No. 4 had scope to accept under Rules 31 till before final publication of the record.

8. Mr Osman Gani, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that the land as described in the Writ Petition has been in possession of the petitioners and their predecessor since 1962 and the S A record, R S record were prepared in their names and they paid rent vide annexure-A series and B series. He further submitted that in against the recent survey held under the revisional settlement, some disputes were made against the DP Khatian and thereafter appeals were also preferred. He submitted that the petitioners being in possession since 1962, the Railway can not dispute the recording of the petitioners name and cannot prefer appeal under Rule 31. He further submitted that Rule submitted that Rule 42 and 42(A) are not applicable in the instant case. He prayed for making the Rule absolute. 

9. Mr Kh Shahriar Shakir for Mr Saifur Rashid, the learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 5 who submitted that the land was acquired by Railway and the gazette notification was made duly and the respondent No. 4 was authorized by law to pass any order as provided under Rules 42 and 42(A) of the SAT Rule 1955. He further submitted that whenever any fraud is detected the remedy becomes available as provided in Rule 42 and 42 A. He prayed for discharged of the Rule. 

10. Mr ARM Hasanuzzaman, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the Government submitted that since the land was acquired for Railway, the respondent No. 4 has exercised his jurisdiction lawfully and the same cannot be called in question before this Court by filing writ. He submitted that the land was acquired in 1960 but the petitioner's predecessor claimed the land thereafter, that is in the year 1962. He submitted that the Writ Petition does not lie. 

11. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates. Upon perusal of the Writ Petition as well as the statements made in the Affidavit-in-opposition, it is admitted that the petitioners are in possession, upon the land as described in the Writ Petition. Front the copy of the gazette notification which has been annexed as Annexure 1, it shows 1 that some property was acquired by Railway. From the copy of the said Gazette notification it is difficult to find out or detect that the land as described in the Writ Petition was acquired by the Railway. The alleged acquired land is unspecified. There is nothing on record to show that the Railway ever exercised its act of physical possession since 1960 upon the land as shown in the Writ Petition. It appears that the petitioner and their predecessors have been exercising their act of physical possession continuously since 1962 as the S A record and the R S records were prepared in their names and they are paying rent to the Government vide Annexure-B series. Annexure-A series are the Khatians. In view of the above facts and circumstances and unless it is shown specifying particular portion of land which was acquired by Railway, it is difficult to accept the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respondents that the scope of enter-taming appeal under 31 of the Settlement Rules, 1955 was not open before the Railway to submit appeals. There is nothing available on record to show that any fraud was committed in getting recorded the names of petitioners in the DP khatian. As such, the application of Rule 42 and 42(A) are not available.

12. Mr Kh Shahriar Shakir, submitted that the Settlement Officer, at the time of passing the impugned order mentioned the question of fraud. The Question of fraud is a question and that got to be decided by a Civil Court after taking down evidence. A Settlement Officer is not empowered to decide any question of fraud. There is no materials before us to accept the question of fraud, if practiced by the petitioners and, as such, the point raised by Mr Shahriar cannot be accept. It further appears that not a single ground was taken towards fraud in the appeal or revision before the settlement appellate authority. Since no question of fraud was agitated, the application of Rule 42(A), in the instant case is not available and, as such, the submissions as made Mr ARM Hasanuzzaman and Shahriar Kabir cannot accepted. Since the respondent (Railway) has raised a question of law that is question of fraud the forum is open before the Railway authority to file a suit before competent Court but they cannot invoke the aid of Rule 31 or 42 or 42 (A) of the settlement Rules 1955. 

13. In view of the above we find merit in the Rule. 

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 4-9-2003 and 7-9-2003 passed by the Assistant Settlement Officer and Appeal Officer (the Respondent No. 4) and signed by the Settlement Officer on 16-9-2003 in the Appeal case Nos. 77717& 77725 of 2003 & 10121 of 2000 (Annexure-C & C-1) of Tejgaon Settlement Office, Dhaka is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The order of stay stands vacated. 

End.
