It was unanimously decided that the Executive Director would receive a monthly remuneration of Taka 12,500 and the other Directors shall receive Taka 5000 each month and the remuneration of the Chairman shall be Taka 5000 per month. He has also taken us through the First Wage Board Award, 1997 dated 29th of May. 1997 showing that an Editor of the newspaper has been placed in special grade-1 together with Deputy/ Joint/Assistant and Executive Editors and their salary has been fixed at Taka 7,000 - 250 - 10,000 under the heading "Bartaman Betan Crom" (বর্তমান বেতনক্রম) showing an increase of 57.14% under the heading (বৃদ্ধির হার)  To counter this argument, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that, Mr Anwar Hossain does not draw his salary. In reply to this Mr Akhtar Imam argued that the restrictions and prohibitions envisaged under Article 147(3) of the Constitution comes into operation the moment a person who had been holding any post of profit becomes a Minister, etc. irrespective of whether or not he draws any salary. The parameter is not whether salary is drawn or not. Rather it is as to whether the post or position carries or does not carry salary. From the resolution and from the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 referred to above it is found that the post of Editor and that of the Executive Director are posts of profit. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq then' argued that the proviso to Article 147(3) of the Constitution has rather removed the disqualification of Minister to hold any post of profit as it applies only to future post or position of profit and not the post and position he has been holding prior to his becoming a minister. Thus, according to him, a Minister can retain his former post and position, but cannot hold any post or position of profit once he becomes a Minister. Mr Akhtar Imam, on the other hand, argues that if this contention be accepted then there will be two categories of Ministers, which he submits is an absurd proposition. Mr Huq then argued that the bar or disqualification imposed under Article 147(3) is only directory in nature and that it is not mandatory because no consequence has been provided for or spelt out in the Article. Mr Akhtar Imam argued that prohibitive or negative word in a statute or Article cannot be directory in nature. It must be mandatory and in support of his contention has placed reliance on the case of Osman Gani Mondol vs Mainuddin Ahmed and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 61 and the case of Akbar Hossain vs Government of Pakistan and another reported in PLD 1976 (SC) 315. In the case of Osman Gani Mondal their Lordships held with reference to Crawford's Statutory Constructions page 516, section 261 that it is the Rule of Statutory Construction that where a Statute is framed in terms of command, and there is no indication from the nature of wording of the Act or the surrounding circumstances itself to receive a permissive interpretation, it would be construed as peremptory and again, in section 263 at page 520 thereof it has been said- "prohibitive or negative words can rarely, if ever, be directory, or, as it has been aptly stated, there is but one way to obey the command "thou shall not" and that is to completely refrain from doing the forbidden act and this is so, even though the statute provides no penalty for its disobedience. Accordingly, negative; prohibitory and exclusive words or terms are indicative of the legislative intent that statute is to be mandatory. In the case of Akbar Hossain where a Justice of the Supreme Court was appointed as the Chief Justice of a Province it was held that none could hold two substantive offices at the same time. When a Supreme Court Judge was appointed as Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan it was held that it must be kept in mind that the rule of interpretation of Constitution and mainly the provisions in it entailing disabilities, should be strictly construed. There is no question of the respondent (meaning the Chief Justice of Sind and Baluchistan) holding the two permanent offices of a Judge of Supreme Court and the Chief Justice of High Court, for such a situation is neither contemplated under the Constitution nor is it factually true as it is evident from the reply of the Ministry of Law, Government of Pakistan. Even as regards others the holding of two offices simultaneously will lead to confusion for the terms and conditions of the two are different as regards age of retirement, remuneration pension, etc. The High Court Judge on appointment as Judge of the Supreme Court ceased to be a Judge of the High Court and the High Court Judge in such case does not resign from the office of Judge of the High Court. But his conduct in accepting office of Judge of the Supreme Court amounts to resignation from the former office and appointment of Supreme Court Judge as Chief Justice of a High Court amounts to resignation from office of Judge of Supreme Court and hence, the appointment does not fall within the mischief of Article 107(1)(a) and that if the Chief Justice of a High Court is ever to revert to Supreme Court such would be a fresh appointment and not in continuation of previous appointment. If the interpretation of Mr Huq that the prohibition applies to future posts of profit and not previous posts and that the prohibition is not mandatory and is only directory be accepted then Article 147(3) would be meaningless. Article 147(3) cannot be a dead letter because no provision of the Constitution is irrelevant or redundant. Mr Abdur Razzaque argued that each and every Article of the Constitution shall have the same force and binding character and effect because it is the Supreme Law of the land as it reflects the will of the people (Article 7).

214. Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh Second Edition page 735 under the heading "Special provisions relating to some Constitutional offices" in paragraph 6. 59B gave his interpretation on Article 147(3) and the proviso thereto stating that the said Article makes some provisions in respect of the office of the President. Prime Minister, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Minister. Minister of State, Deputy Minister. Judge of the Supreme Court, Comptroller and Auditor General, Election Commissioner and Member of Public Service Commission. Thus, it is clear that the proviso did not take away or remove the disability (as has been argued by Mr Huq). The restriction or embargo is still in place. The proviso has been added so that the Minister's, etc. are not handicapped in receiving their salary as Minister. In bringing his point home that a person by becoming a Minister does not lose his previous position of profit and, in support of this proposition, Mr Huq has relied upon the case of Md Abdul Hoque vs Fazlul Quader Chowdhury reported in 15 DLR 355 in which case the question under consideration was as to whether a Member of the National Assembly can retain the said position and claim the privilege and perform the rights and duties allowable there under after being appointed to the President's Council of Ministers. The Rule was made absolute holding, inter alia, that the Minister has already ceased to be the Member of the National Assembly of Pakistan from the date on which he entered upon his respective appointment as Minister.

215. Mr Huq has also cited the case of M Salimullah, Advocate vs Md Abdur Rouf, Chief Election Commissioner and others reported in 1 BLC 229. In the reported case Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause under what authority Mr Rouf was holding the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and also to show cause under what authority he was at the same time holding the office of Chief Election Commissioner of Bangladesh. In the said case, it was held that Mr Justice Abdur Rouf ceased to be the Chief Election Commissioner on 18-4-1995 and returned to his previous post as a Judge of the High Court Division on 19-6-1995 and later on was elevated to the Appellate Division on 19-6-1995 and is now functioning as a Judge of the Appellate Division and, as such, the cause of action regarding the holding of two posts simultaneously for which the Rule was issued does not subsist now as Mr Justice Rouf is not occupying office which was called in question in the Rule on the date when the Writ of quo warranto was issued. It was also held that the post of a Judge of the Supreme Court is not a post of profit. So, this case has no applicability in the present context.

216. Mr Akhtar Imam, with reference to the morality of public office and qualification for ministerial office, has drawn our attention to the Constitutional Law and Administrative Law by Hillary Barnett (Third Edition) and quoted Sir lvor Jennings stating that the most elementary qualification demanded of a Minister is honesty and incorruptibility. It is, however, necessary, not only that he possessed this qualification but also be seen to appear to possess it. Lord Hailsham expressed the same sentiment as follows:

A politician must be trustworthy, and if he is found out telling a lie or if he is discovered in even a small financial dishonesty, he can bow himself out of public life. If a Minister of the Crown or Member of Parliament conducts his personal or official affairs in such a manner that falls below an acceptable standard, the Minister may be required to resign. Prof. SE Finer described such conduct as being a personal misadventure of the Minister which raises such doubt about his personal prudence or integrity as to cause him to resign.

217. As to the conduct of Ministers of the Crown the Nolan Committee introduced the view that the public is entitled to expect very high standard of behaviour from Ministers, as they profound influence over the daily lives of all of us.

218. Amongst others, the committee recommended that the Ministers of the Crown are expected to behave according to the best standard of constitutional and personal conduct. In particular, they must observe certain principles of ministerial conduct such as, Ministers must ensure that no conflict arises, or appears to arise, between their public duties and private interests and they must keep their party and ministerial roles separate. They must not ask a civil servant to carry out party political duties or to act in any other way that would conflict with the civil servant's code.

219. Mr Akhtar Imam. argued that by becoming a Minister Mr Anwar Hossain fell into the category of a person performing the duty and the authority used in Article 102 and it must receive a liberal meaning and has relied on the case of Shri Anadi Mukta Sad guru SMVSJMS Trust vs VR Rudani reported in AIR 1989 (SC) 1607 wherein their Lordships held that the term authority used in Article 226 (Indian Constitution) in the context must receive a liberal meaning in likely term in Article 12. Article 12 is relevant only for the purpose of enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32. Article 226 confers power on the High Court to issue Rules for enforcement of the fundamental rights as well as non-fundamental rights. The words any person or authority used in Article. 226 are therefore, not to be confined only to statutory authorities and instrumentality of the State. They may cover any other person or body performing the duty. The form of the body concerned is not very much relevant. What is relevant is the nature of the duty imposed on the body. The duty must be judged in the light of positive obligation owed by person or authority to the affected parties. No matter by what means the duty is imposed. The scope of Article 226 has been explained by Subbarao J, in Dawarkanath vs Income Tax Officer (1965-3 SCR at pages 540-41) AIR 1966 (SC) 84-85. This Article is couched in comprehensive phraseology and it exfacie confers a wide power on the High Court to reach injustice wherever it is found. The Constitution dizzily used a word/language in describing the nature of the power, the purpose of which and the person or authority against whom it can be exercised. It can issue Rules in the nature of prerogative rights, as understood in England, but the use of the expression "Nature" for the said expression does not equate the Rules that can be issued in India with those in England but only draws an analogy from them. That apart, the High Court can also issue directions, orders or rights other than the prerogative rights. It enables the High Court to mould the reliefs to meet peculiar and complicated requirements of this country. Any attempt to equate the scope of the power of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution with that of the English Courts to issue prerogative rights is to introduce the unnecessary, procedural restriction grown over the years in a comparatively small country like England with unitary form of government into a vast country like India functioning under a federal structure. Such a construction defeats the purpose of the Article itself.

220. Thus, Mr Anwar Hossain, when he was still a Minister, by using his ministerial power as well as the power and influence of his party had a great sway over the conduct of affairs and management of the daily Ittefaq as has been hinted and discussed earlier. Because of the fact that he was still Executive Director-II and from behind the scene had been pulling the strings through the editor-in-charge during his (Mr Anwar Hossain's) absence which term he uses to signify that he has not ceased to hold the office in the Ittefaq and, in so doing, he has been influencing the mode and manner of reporting news and expressing views in the daily Ittefaq to suit his personal and his party interest and convenience which inevitably affects the freedom of the petitioner and the members of the public at large to read objective, impartial and fair news and, as such, there cannot be a bar for the High Court Division in exercising the power of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution. Most importantly, because it affects the fundamental rights of freedom of expression and this is a case in point where the private interest and public duty of a Minister are in conflict.

221. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that the concept of Managing Director is absent and is alien to the Daily Ittefaq. On a reference to Article 50(a) of the Articles of Association it is found under the heading "Managing Director" the directors may from time to time appoint anyone of their body as the Managing Director of the company. While Article 51 provides that the directors may, at any time, appoint a managing agent to manage the entire affairs of the company under the control and direction of the directors, while Article 52 provides that the company in a general meeting may appoint from amongst the directors one or more directors to be Executive Directors. As we have already seen that the petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein and respondent Mr Anwar Hossain were made Executive Director Nos. 1 and 11 respectively and a combination of those two Executive Directors constituted the managing director and as such, the contention of Mr Huq as to the absence of the concept of managing director cannot be accepted. Besides that, section 2(Tha) of the Company's Act has defined what the managing director is. Mr Abdur Razzaque, learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that there is some similarity between Article 147(3) of our Constitution and that of Article 58 of the Indian Constitution.

222. In Article 58(2) it is provided that a person shall not be eligible for election as President if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State or under any legal or other authority subject to the control of any of the said Governments and the explanation added thereto says that for the purpose of this Article a person shall not be deemed to hold any office of profit by reason only that he is the president or vice-president of the Union or the Governor of any state or is a Minister either for the union or for any State. While Article 59(2) provides that the President shall not hold any other office of profit. Article 55 of our Constitution (Bangladesh Constitution) provides that there shall be a Cabinet of Bangladesh having the Prime Minister at its head and comprising also such other ministers as the prime minister may from time to time designate. Sub-Article (2) provides that the executive power of the Republic shall, in accordance with this Constitution, be exercised by or on the authority of the prime minister, while sub-Article (3) provides that the cabinet shall be collectively responsible to Parliament. The oath of office of a minister requires him to say, amongst others, that "I will do right to all manner of people according to law, without fear or favour, affection or ill will", but this becomes different, if not absurd, when a minister holds any office of profit as in the present case. Mr Anwar Hossain while he remained Executive Director-Il and was running and managing the paper through an editor in-charge allegedly during his absence thus claiming that he is the editor for all intent and purposes which as a Minister cannot he done because of his party affiliation and ministerial power and functions.

223. Mr Abdur Razzaque, refers to Halbury's Law as regards the constitutional status of members of parliament, stating that amongst others, those who are members of the House of Commons are subject to the Rules for the registration and declaration of interest in the same way as other members. In addition they are subject to the guidelines and requirements laid down by successive prime ministers in order to ensure that no conflict arises or appears to arise between their private interest and public duties He then referred to the Ministerial Code of Conduct in Australian politics providing that Ministers are required to divest themselves of all shares and similar interest in any company or business involved in the area of their portfolio responsibilities. The transfer of interest to a family member or to a nominee or trust is not an acceptable form of divestment. Ministers should perform their public duties uninfluenced by fear or favour i.e. by any expectation that they will benefit or suffer as a consequence. They should not accept any benefit where acceptance might give appearance that they may be subject to improper influence and they should not exercise the influence obtained from their public office or use official information. Mr Razzaque, then refers to JAG Griffith's Parliament, Functions, Practice and Procedure (Sweet Maxwell 1989) as to the disqualification of the members of the House of Commons. The House of Commons Disqualification Act, 1975 lists office holders of which are disqualified for membership of the House of Commons. He then referred to Article 66 (dd) of our Constitution (Bangladesh Constitution) as to qualification and disqualification for Election to Parliament providing that a person shall be disqualified for election as, or for being, a member of parliament who holds any office of profit in the service of the Republic other than an office which is declared by law not to disqualify its holders. Mr Razzaque, echoing the arguments advanced by Mr Akhtar Imam, submitted that Article 147(3) is referable to salaries of certain constitutional functionaries and that without the proviso, the Ministers would be debarred from drawing salaries as Ministers. This proviso was added with a view to avoiding conflict of interest of a Minister (as in the present case) in his personal ministerial capacities.

224. Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque, the learned Counsels for the petitioner, argued that Annexure-G to Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 i.e. a communication made to petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein as Executive Director-I of the lttefaq Group of Publications Limited by Mr Md Shafiul Alam, Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka was not a refusal to authenticate any declaration as asserted by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. Annexure-G, according to them, was rather a -reply to the letter contained in Annexure-F to Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 raising objection by Executive Director-I to the effect that a letter dated 4-2-97 of the Additional District Magistrate describing/showing Mr Anwar Hossain as the publisher of the daily lttefaq was illegal because Mr Anwar Hossain was, in fact, the Publisher of the said paper for and on behalf of the company and not in his personal capacity that Mr Mainul Hosein was made the printer by resolution dated 19-3-1985 and 29-10-86 of the company, that he found it embarrassing to have his name printed in two capacities as chairman of the board of directors as well as printer and, as such, according to his desire the company entrusted both Mr Mainul Hosein and Mr Anwar Hossain to discharge the duties of Printer and Publisher jointly, that Mr Anwar Hossain, by using his political power and influence as a Minister and by denying the ownership of the other directors and share-holders of the company, has been trying to establish himself as the publisher in place of the company, that he (Mainul Hosein) also brought to the notice of the then Prime Minister certain facts including that of counterfeit currency notes, that the post of Editor is not transferable, that by not printing the name of the editor someone cannot be shown or made to be the editor as there is no sanction of law to do so. Rather, section 6 of the Act of 1973 has made it imperative that the Editor's name must be printed in every copy of the newspaper, that without having his name printed as Editor none can remain or continue to be an Editor, that the name of Mr Anwar Hossain is not being printed as Editor and, as such, he is no longer the Editor of the daily Ittefaq and that the name of Mr Rahat Khan is being printed in the Printers Line and he is the editor and in this behalf he (Mr Mainul Hosein) has given a declaration. This Annexure-F dated 12-3-97 has evoked/prompted the writing of Annexure-G dated 1-4-97 by the Additional District Magistrate Dhaka to Mr Mainul Hosein and it is argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that Annexure-G not being a refusal to authenticate a declaration made under section 12 of the Act of 1973 the contention of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Counsel for respondent Mr Anwar Hossain that instead of a writ petition an appeal against the refusal to authenticate ought to have been preferred is misconceived. I find force and substance in the arguments of Mr Imam and Mr Razzaque and it is accepted.

<u>225. For the sake of convenience, before going into the other arguments of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, I propose to discuss the 4 (four) following arguments advanced by him even at the risk of some repetition. The first argument is, that the Rules in Writ Petition Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are not maintainable under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution. Because the impugned acts by Mr Anwar Hossain were not done in the exercise of his powers and functions in the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority rather, if at all, those were done in relation to the affairs of the daily Ittefaq which is a private limited company. In support of this argument, Mr Huq referred to the case of Sultana Nahar, Advocate vs Bangladesh and others reported in 1998 BLD 363. It was a case involving the eviction of 600 sex workers from a brothel called "Kandu Patti" by an unruly mob led by the local ward commissioner, one Mr Hossain, under the very nose of the law enforcing agencies and the Senior Judge made the Rule absolute declaring that the sex workers were illegally and forcibly evicted and the law enforcing agencies failed to discharge their legal duties by not giving legal protection to them (sex workers) to continue their profession at "Kandu Patti" with a direction to respondent Nos. 1, 2, 8 and 9 to earmark a specified and distinct area for their permanent rehabilitation. There was also a mandatory injunction as a stopgap arrangement to restore possession of the evicted sex workers till their rehabilitation, with a further direction to respondent No.5, officer-in-charge, Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka to lodge an FIR, according to the written complaint of 14 sex workers. This was dissented to by the learned Junior Judge holding, inter alia, that the manner of eviction of the sex workers though is condemnable, this Court, in its writ jurisdiction, is unable to restore their possession because, the place is owned by a private individual and that the Government has now lost its jurisdiction to rehabilitate the sex workers since the action done was not in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority attracting the mischief of Article 102(1 )(9). This decision, I am afraid, cannot be made applicable in the instant case simply because the eviction was carried out by some unruly mob led by the local Ward Commissioner who was neither a person exercising any function in the Affairs of the Republic nor did do anything in discharge of his public duty.</u>

<u>226. Mr Anwar Hossain, the respondent, while holding the post of a Minister, as I have referred to above, has not only taken part in the management of the daily Ittefaq, he has also caused interference in the publication of the paper for long 16(sixteen) days with a view to forcing and compelling the Editor-in-charge and others to print his name as Publisher/Editor. Both Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque argued that a Minister may not be a person in the service of the Republic but, surely and definitely, he has constitutional functions and thus exercises very high public duty. By causing the closure and or stoppage of printing of the paper</u>

<u>from 28-12-1993 to 13-1-1994 he (Mr Anwar Hossain) had violated Article 39 of the Constitution and that brought his action fairly and squarely within the ambit of both Article 102(1) and 102(2) and the writ petition cannot be said to be not maintainable. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that Mr Anwar Hossain did, if at all, do something in connection with the affairs of the Ittefaq and not in connection with the Affairs of the Republic or any local body or authority. True it is that the actions of Mr Anwar Hossain primarily affected the affairs of the company, but at the same time it did affect the readers of the paper who have a right to read fair, neutral objective and impartial news and views which is guaranteed under Article 39(2)(b) of the Constitution. It is inescapable to avoid the mischief of Article 39 which is one of the Articles under Chapter III i.e. fundamental rights and hence, there is an infringement of fundamental right under Article 102 which can be invoked by operation or Article 44 of the Constitution. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq also argued that the post of Executive Editor is not a post of profit and, as such, there can be no bar in holding this post while Mr Anwar Hossain became a Minister. I have already dealt with this point that from a plain reading of the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 it is evident that the said post is a post of profit. Mr Akhtar Imam has taken me through the Articles and Memorandum of Association of the company and with reference to Article 50 argued that the directors may from time to time appoint anyone of their body as the Managing Director provided that the Director shall not take any appointment made or committee constituted under Articles 51 and 52. Article 51 deals with managing agent stating that the directors may at any time appoint agent to manage the entire affairs of the company under the control and direction of the directors upon such terms as they think fit subject to the provisions of this Act provided the director shall not make any appointment under this Article during the subsistence of any appointment made or committee constituted under Article 50 and/or 52. Article 52 deals with Executive Committee and Executive Directors, Providing that company in general meeting may appoint from amongst directors one or more directors to be Executive Director or Directors and may constitute an Executive Committee consisting of such executive director/directors as it thinks fit. Provided that no appointment of an Executive Director shall be made or constitution of an Executive Committee shall be made during the subsistence of any appointment earlier made under Article 50 and/or 51. While clause (d) provides that for the purpose of division of responsibility between Executive Directors, the company's business shall be taken to comprise of the following sections:</u>

<u>(i) Press and Publications.</u>

<u>(ii) Accounts,</u>

<u>(iii) General Section comprising of:</u>

<u>(a) Circulation Department.</u>

<u>(b) Advertisement Department.</u>

<u>(c) Job Department and Purchase Department.</u>

<u>Clause (E) provides that the respective responsibilities of the Executive Director in respect of each. of the sections referred to above shall be defined by the Company in General Meeting and Clause (F) provides that in the event of an Executive Director being unable to discharge his functions due to absence from Dhaka or illness or any other such reason he may nominate, in writing, another Director to exercise his functions during such absence. The expression "due to absence from Dhaka or illness or any other such reason" cannot and must not be allowed to mean during his absence so long he remains a member of the Cabinet.</u>

<u>227. Mr Akhtar Imam argued that a combination of the Executive Directors I and II constituted the post of Managing Director and the argument advanced by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq that there is no post of Managing Director in the Ittefaq Group of Publication is not tenable in law in view of the discussions made above. The second point raised by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq is that since there are three Civil Suits pending between the same parties on the same point as in the writ petitions, all the three Rules are liable to be discharged as those are not maintainable, inasmuch as the petitioner cannot be allowed to invoke both writ jurisdiction and remedies available in the civil Court. Mr Huq has furnished me with a copy showing the details of cases filed by Mr Mainul Hosein. From the said list it appears that serial Nos. 5,6 and 14 are three civil suits i.e. (a) Title Suit No. 59 of 2002, (b) Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 and (c) Title Suit No. 321 of 2002 and the date of filing of the aforesaid three suits are as follows: 11-3-2002, 7-4-2002 and 24-11-2002. So, all the three suits were instituted subsequent to the filing of the three writ petitions. To counter this argument advanced by Mr Huq, Mr Akhtar Imam learned Counsel for the petitioner, has placed reliance on the case of Chairman Civil Aviation Authority vs Kazi Abdur Rouf reported in 46 DLR (AD) 145. The reported case is different and distinguishable from the writ petition before us inasmuch as, in the reported case one Kazi A. Rouf, Headmaster and Secretary of the Staff Welfare High School filed a writ petition challenging a Memo dated 29-7-92 of the School Inspector, Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka to the Chairman, Bangladesh Civil Aviation Authority, Kurmitola requesting the latter to form an Ad hoc Committee in terms of regulation 20 of the Board contending that the Managing Committee could have been constituted in terms of Regulation 4(1) and not in terms of Regulation 20(1). The writ petitioner challenged the impugned memo in a Title Suit and having lost in the injunction matter lost faith in the civil Court and then filed a writ petition and Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, as his Lordship then was, held that there is no bar in filing writ petition after withdrawing a suit. It all depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But it is clear that in the present case writ petitioner filed a suit basically containing highly contentious and disputed question of facts for adjudication by a civil Court and it is not his case before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction that his grievance can be met merely by looking at law on agreed facts, so the pursuit of suit is unnecessary. He came to lay before the writ jurisdiction the same question offact which he earlier laid before the civil Court for adjudication. The writ jurisdiction shall have been denied to him under such circumstances. Mr Imam argued that this decision by implication has held that if there is no disputed question of fact the door of writ jurisdiction is not closed . And in the Civil Suits and the three writ petitions there is no disputed question of facts. The suits and the writ petitions rather involved interpretation of a statute i.e. the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 and the interpretations of Article 39 and Article 147(3) and its proviso. Furthermore, in the instant case, as I have already referred to earlier, the suits having been filed subsequent to the filing of the writ petitions, the arguments advanced by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq that since suits are pending so writ petitions cannot be maintained because under Article 110 of the Constitution all the suits ought to have been brought before this Court for disposal simultaneously. This argument, I am constrained to hold, cuts both ways. It imposes no unilateral or singular obligation on the writ petitioner to file an application under Article 110, inasmuch as, a co-equal and corresponding right has been made available by the aforesaid Article to the respondent as well and the respondent could have, if so advised, brought those suits for adjudication by one and the same Court i.e. the High Court Division. Neither party having done so, this contention of Mr Huq does not appeal to me. In reply to the second point raised by Mr Haq mainly that during the pendency of the civil suits these writ petitions are not maintainable, Mr Akhtar Imam has referred to the case of Dhaka Warehouse Limited and another vs Assistant Collector of Customs and another reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 327 wherein their Lordships held that in principle, where an alternative statutory remedy is available, application under Article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. There are however, exceptions to this rule. Without attempting an exhaustive enumeration of complete extraordinary situation we may note a view of them. In spite of an alternative statutory remedy, an aggrieved person may take recourse to Article 102 of the Constitution where the vires of a statute or a statutory provision is challenged, where alternative remedy is not efficacious or adequate and the wrong complained of is so inextricably mixed up that the High Court Division may for the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice examine that complaint. It is needless to add that the High Court Division is to see that the aggrieved person must have good reason for bypassing an alternative remedy. Mr Imam also placed reliance on the case of MA Hai, Md Wazed Ali Mia and Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh. In that case also it was held that availability of alternative remedy by way of appeal or revision will not stand in the way of invoking writ jurisdiction raising purely a question of law or interpretation of statutes. In the reported case the appellant Abdul Hai, a Senior Executive of the TCB, was provisionally removed from service for inefficiency and corruption. A writ petition was filed under Article 102 against the order of removal taking the ground that under the mandatory provision of Rule 7(11) of the Government Servant (Disciplinary and Appeal) Rules, 1984 he stood discharged from the charge because the specified period is 120 days from the date of communication of the charge-sheet to him within which period the proceeding against him was to be concluded, expired before the impugned order of removal was passed. He claimed that the Disciplinary and Appeal Rules of 1984 are applicable to him since the corporation adopted the rules. The corporation stressed that the proceedings were presented under the Rules of 1976, which did not provide for any time limit, such as 120 days from the date of submission of charge-sheet or 120 days from the date of suspension of the accused. Some other grounds were also taken. The High Court Division upheld the contention of the corporation that the provisions of Rule VII, sub-rule 2 of the Rules of 1984 are applicable and all the writ petitions were dismissed. As against that, the petitioners preferred the instant appeal and their Lordships held that if the writ jurisdiction is sought to be invoked raising purely a question of law or interpretation of stature, as in these cases, availability of an alternative remedy will not stand in the way. In the case before me admittedly the facts are not in dispute and the civil suits as well as the writ petitions call for interpretation of various sections of the statute namely, the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 as well as . the interpretation of some Articles of the Constitution including Articles 39 and 147(3) hence the alternative remedy, as argued by Mr Huq, shall not stand in the way of the writ petitions.</u>

228. The third point argued by Mr Huq is that the Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is liable to be discharged for the petitioner's failure to invoke and to exhaust the alternative statutory remedy by way of appeal before the Press Appellate Board as provided under section 12A of the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973. This point having been elaborately dealt with before, needs no more discussion except saying that Annexure "G" not being a refusal to authenticate the declaration under section 12(3) the same is not an appealable order.

229. The fourth argument of Mr Huq is that Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is hit by the principle of res judicata inasmuch as, the point involved in the present Rule has already been decided against the petitioner by judgment and order dated 6-2-2001 passed in Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 and the petitioner did not prefer any appeal against the said judgment.

230. Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque have refuted this contention of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. Firstly, by saying that the point involved in the two writ petitions are neither the same nor have the Judges of the Division Bench in disposing of Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 decided the question of disability or disqualification of a Minister to hold any post of profit or emolument after his assumption of the office of a minister rather, their Lordships left that Constitutional question unanswered. On a reference to the said judgment dated 6-2-2001 at pages 16 and 17 of the certified copy of the judgment it is found that their Lordships have observed as follows:

"However, in view of provisions of Article 147(3) which runs as under-No person appointed to or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever for the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object. It appears that any person holding or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall not hold any office or take any part in the management or conduct of any company. In the instant case, it appears that during the period respondent No.3 (meaning thereby Mr Anwar Hossain) was holding office of the Minister, also continued to print his name as 'printer' and 'publisher' of the daily Ittefaq which leads (sic) to show, participation in the management and conduct in the business and the affairs of the company having profit and gain. The Respondent No.1 (District Magistrate) having been invited earlier by the petitioner, through his letter dated 21-1-92 evidenced by Annexure-F ought to have taken notice of the fact that respondent No.3 was holding the office of printer and publisher as well as the office of the Minister simultaneously and hence ought to have enquired into the matter and examine (sic) as to whether there was any violation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution at all and thus respondent No.1 (the District Magistrate, Dhaka) failed to see that the daily Ittefaq is not published by the disqualified person."

This being the finding, 1 do not find any reason to hold that the constitutional point raised in the writ petition i.e. the disqualification under Article 147(3) has been decided in Writ Petition No.1481. As such, the question of res judicata does not arise Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has also argued that the petitioner instead of filing writ petition seeking a Writ of quo warranto and questioning as to under what authority Mr Anwar Hossain was holding the post of minister, challenged the retention of his post which he held prior to becoming a minister Mr Huq though admits that Article 147(3) puts a complete and total embargo upon the holding of any post of profit or emolument by the constitutional functionaries enumerated in sub-Article (4) of Article 147 of the Constitution, the bar has been removed and or taken away by the proviso to the said Article i.e. 147(3), and, according to Mr Huq, there is no bar for a Minister or other functionaries mentioned above to retain any post or position which he held prior to becoming a Minister as it happened in case of Mr Anwar Hossain and hence he is not required to give up the post held earlier because the proviso imposed a bar in accepting any post of profit after someone becomes a Minister. Besides that, Mr Huq has argued that there is a marked distinction and difference between Article 104 of the Constitution of Pakistan of 1962 and Article 147(3) of the Bangladesh Constitution. In the Pakistan Constitution there is also an embargo in the retention of post of profit by Constitutional functionaries such as the President, Minister and Governor employing expression as the Minister, Governor, etc. shall cease to hold any office of profit whereas under Article 147(3) of the Constitution of Bangladesh the expression is couched in a different language providing that no person appointed to or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post, position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company association or body having profit or gain as its object.Mr Huq argued that the intention of the lawmakers as it appears from the expression used in Article 147, was not to prohibit a Minister from retaining any post or position he held before becoming Minister rather, the intention was to make it applicable to any post of profit after someone becomes a Minister and, in support of his contention, has referred to the case of Md Abdul Haque vs Fazlul Kader Chowdhury reported in 15 DLR 353 and 16 DLR (SC) 52 which I have discussed at an earlier stage.

231. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq also argued that after Mr Anwar Hossain having ceased to be a minister the determination of the constitutional question under Article 147(3) became purely hypothetical and an academic one and, in support of his argument placed reliance on the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR 319. It is not disputed that in the reported case a hypothetical question was decided by the High Court Division and that was why in paragraphs 58 and 59 of the judgment Mr Justice ATM Afzal, as his Lordship then was, eviscerated the said Judgment in the pronouncement as under:

Naimuddin J: In his judgment found that the Upazila Parishad was not a local Government institution within the meaning of Articles 59 and 9 of the Constitution and, as such, Article 9 cannot be invoked for declaring the repealing Ordinance/Act void under Article 7(2) on the ground of inconsistency with . Article 9. He has not also found that the impugned Ordinance/Act is in conflict with any other provision of Part II of the Constitution containing Fundamental Principles of State Policy. That being so, it was wholly unnecessary to decide whether in view of the provision in sub-article (2) of Article 8 that the principles set out in Part II shall not be judicially enforceable, any legislative act which is in direct conflict with and passed in flagrant violation of the provisions of Part II can be declared void under Article 7(2). Having answered this hypothetical question in the affirmative after taking hypothetical facts into consideration in a lengthy discussion, the learned Judge addressed himself to the real question thus;

"Consequently, if it is found that the impugned repealing Ordinance is violative of Article 9 of the Constitution, it is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution."

232. Then the finding was made that the repealing Ordinance was not violative of Article 9 with which we have agreed. Therefore, the broad decision that a law can be declared void in case of a conflict with any provision of Part II of the Constitution was uncalled for and made on hypothetical facts. This, as a rule, the Courts always abhor. The Court does not answer merely academic questions but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of the matter before it. This should be more so when Constitutional questions are involved and the Court should be ever discreet in such matters. Unlike a civil suit, the practice in Constitutional cases has always been that if the matter can be decided by deciding one issue only no other point need be decided.

Finally, I wish to express my full agreement with the main judgment prepared by the learned Chief Justice."

233. But the issue we are dealing with is neither hypothetical nor academic. I, for one, do not have the slightest hesitation to hold that this is a down-to-earth practical issue and recurrence of such incident may be there again as it did happen twice in the case of Mr Anwar Hossain.

In his Law on Writs, VG Ram Chandran (Fifth Edition) under the caption "Futile writs" at page 984 the author with reference to the case of Munindra Kumar vs Rajiv Govil reported in (1991) 3 SCC 386 (374): AIR 1991 (SC) 1607 said that the selection process adopted by the State Electricity Board having been found to be arbitrary and ultra vires the rule, in view of the fact that even if three more posts (for three petitioners) would have been ordered to be created to afford chance to all the candidates similarly situated, there was a remote chance of the writ petitioners being selected. The Supreme Court therefore, did not issue a Rule observing that "such exercise would be in futility".

The author then said. "This however, does not mean that in no case the Court can consider a question of discretion and not of jurisdiction of the Court (reference may be made to Madhu Limaye's case).

<u>234. In an appropriate case, the Court may also pronounce the constitutionality of a statute even though it may not be necessary in that case. Thus, if a petition is filed by the petitioner against an order passed by the Government withdrawing the benefit granted in favour of the petitioner and that order is revoked, the petition may become infructuous. But if again, that benefit is withdrawn, the petition will not become infructuous. Similarly, although the order has already been passed but if it has a continuing adverse effect on the right of the petitioner, the petition does not become academic in nature. Again, the principle may not apply to an order which is wholly illegal or without jurisdiction.</u>

235. The 2(two) most ticklish points for consideration in these Writ Petitions are the interpretation of Article 147(3), its proviso and the feasibility of the issuance of a Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution against a private person and also interpretation of certain sections including those of sections 2(d), 6, 7 and 12 of the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973. The proviso in question is in the following language : "provided that such person shall not for the purposes of this clause be deemed to hold any such office, post or position by reason only that he holds or is acting in the office above mentioned. According to Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the embargo or prohibition imposed under Article 147(3) has been lifted or removed by the proviso and, as such, for Mr Anwar Hossain, as a Minister, there was no bar to retain the post and position he held before becoming a minister and that the disqualification only applies to his holding any future post or position of profit after assuming of the office of a minister which is seriously contested by the learned Counsels for the petitioner. According to them, this embargo is a total and complete bar and they have referred to the Constitutional Law of Bangladesh Second Edition by Mr Mahmudul lslam at para 659B under the heading special provisions relating to some constitutional offices of the President, Prime Minister, Speaker, etc (discussed beforehand).

236. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq further submits that Mr Mainul Hosein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka against Mr Anwar Hossain and others seeking a declaration that in the absence of a fresh resolution by the Board of Directors Mr Anwar Hossain cannot be said to be holding the post of Executive Director-II of the company and the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq. Defendant Mr Anwar Hossain filed an application for stay of further proceedings under section 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that analogous and co-related matters are involved in Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996, 2746 of 1997 and 3834 of 1999 and those are pending in the High Court Division and the learned Joint District Judge allowed the prayer for stay of the suit. As against that, Mr Mainul Hosein preferred Civil Revision No. 5119 of 2002 and their Lordships held "Although we are not in a position to hold that the matters substantially and directly in issue in the present suit and the matters directly and substantially in issue in the Writ petitions are the same, we are constrained to hold that matters involved in these Writ petitions touching the legality or otherwise of some actions of opposite party No.1 and his position as Executive Director-II of the Company are sub-judice before the High Court Division, the position that boiled down in that analogous and co-related matters in such circumstances (sic) the learned Subordinate Court may feel handicapped and totally fettered (sic) to proceed with the present suit pending decisions in the three writ petitions between the contending parties and accordingly, stayed further proceedings of Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 till disposal of the writ petitions and discharged the Rule. Mention may be made here that Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 was filed long after the filing of the writ petitions and because of the order of stay of all further proceedings of the suit there cannot be any risk of conflicting decisions. Mention may also be made that in the Civil Revision their Lordships also held that moreover the judgment delivered by this Court in Writ Petition NO.1481 of 1994 has practically spelt out the position of opposite party No.1 (Mr Anwar Hossain) as the Executive Director-Il of the Company with reference related to (sic) the provisions of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. We are not, therefore, called upon to elaborate it". It may not be out of place to mention that in Writ Petition NO.1481 of 1994 their Lordships held "the respondent No.1 (District Magistrate. Dhaka) having been notified earlier by the petitioner (Mr Mainul Hosein) through his letter dated 21-1-92 evidenced by Annexure-F ought to have taken notice of the fact that respondent No.3 (Mr Anwar Hossain) was holding the office of Printer and Publisher as well as the office of the Minister simultaneously and hence, ought to have enquired into the matter and examined as to whether there was any violation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution at all and thus respondent No.1 (Additional District Magistrate. Dhaka) failed  to see that the Daily Ittefaq is not published with the disqualified person." It is thus, obvious that the impugned orders and the Rules in the 2 (two) writ petitions are not the same and, as such, the issue remained unresolved.

237. Regard being had to the facts and circumstances, the materials on record, the submissions of the learned Counsels for the parties arid for the foregoing reasons. I agree with my learned brother Mr Abdus Salam Mamun J.

238. In the result, the Rules are made absolute without any order as to cost. All the impugned orders are therefore, declared to have been made or passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

Since the matter in dispute involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, a certificate is hereby issued under' Article 103(2)(a) to enable the respondent to prefer an appeal from the judgment and order passed by me and, in the meantime, the parties are directed to maintain status quo in all respects.

End.

full_judgment:
Amin- Ur- Rahman Khan J.- By an application under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code the petitioners obtained this rule to challenge the order dated 2 5.1985 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Dhaka rejecting an application submitted by the present petitioners as defendant Nos.1and 2 undo, section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No. 314 of 1985. 

2. The Opposite parties numbering 26 filed Title Suit No. 211 of 1983 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka against 36 defendants including Dijendra Narayan Nandi who was defendant Na i for a declaration or their title in 3'71 lands of C S. plot Nets 76 and 94 and for a further declaration that decree dated 23 7 76 passed in Title Suit No. 25 of 19/5 of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka is void The same opposite-p Jules subsequently brought Title Suit No 314 of 1985 against 34 principal defendants and 64 pro-defendants making the present petitioner defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in which they sought declaration of title in schedule 13-1 lands i e the entire land of C.S. p1or No.94 and part of C.S plot No 76 as also for declaration of title in the lands of schedule D-11 namely lands of plot Nos.92, 93. and 149 measuring P44, schedule E i.e., lands I. f C.S. plot No.141 with a further declaration that the decree dated 24 3.78 passed in Title Suit No 50 of 107e of first Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and mutation of the name of the defendant No.31 in S.A. Khatian No.178 on the basis of that decree was void 

3. The present petitioners being defendant Nos.1 and 2 in the subsequent suit, i e., Title Suit Vo.314 of 1985 made an application under section10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying the proceeding of the subsequent Suit i.e, Suit  No. 314 of 1985 pending disposal of the earlier instituted suit namely, Title Suit No. 211/83, In their application the present Deletions submitted that though defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were not parties in the earlier instituted suit but Dijendra Narayan Nandi figured as defendant No, 1 in that suit and the present petitioners having claimed title on the basis of purchase from the Vendee of Dijendra Narayan Nandi who were parties in that suit and also since there was a common matter and commas) issue in respect of title over the lands of C.S, plot Nos. 76 and 94 involved in both the earlier instituted suit and the subsequently instituted suit, it was necessary according to the provision of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to stay the proceedings of the later instituted suit until the disposal of the earlier suit while the parties and their successors were same Upon the said petition the plaintiff Opposite parries filed a written objection against the stay prayer upon the ground that most of the lands over which declaration of title was prayed for in the subsequent suit namely, title suit No 314 and many of the parties who were defendants in that suit were not the subject matter and parties in the earlier suit namely. Title Suit No. 211/83 and thus all the subject matter and all the facts in issue were not common in both the suits and so section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code was quite inapplicable and no stay could he granted as prayed for by the defendant Nos. t and 2 under the provision objection 10 of the Cede of Civil Procedure. 

4. The learned Subordinate Judge after considering the petition of the defendants and 2 and the objection of the plaintiffs and also after considering the provision of section 10 of the C P.C. gave his finding that the cause of action and matter in issue of the two suits are different arid upon such finding be rejected the prayer to; stay of tin suit.

5. Being aggrieved by that order the pre-sent Rule was obtained by the defendant Nos, 1 and 2 by an application under section ll5 of the Code of Civil Procedure 

6. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submitted that the main matter in both the suit was the claim of title in C.S plot Nos. 94 and 76. As in the earlier Suit No 211/8 the declaration of title was sought only in respect of those 2(two) plots title while in the subsequent suit also the declaration of title was sought in respect of those two plots though declaration was also sought for in respect of some other plots in the subsequent suit. 

7 He further submitted that though pre-sent defendant' Nos r and 2 were not party in the former suit but still the defendant Nos. I and 2 claimed title through the persons who were parties in the former suit. In such a situation the provision of section 10 of the C P.0 was well applicable and according to the said provision the learned Subordinate Judge was required by law not to proceed with trial of the subsequent suit and consequently he should have granted the prayer under section 10 of the C P.C. In other words Mr Ishtiaq Mimed submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge committed error of law in failing to exercise the jurisdiction vested in him by failing to stay the proceedings of the subsequent suit. 

8. On the other hand, Mr. Khondker Mahabubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submitted that except the prayer for declaration of tide in respect of C.S plot Nos. 94 and 76 which was the only issue that was common in both the suits all other mistress and issues of the subsequent suit were not at all concerned or involved in the earlier suit so when there were severs different issues involved in the subsequent suit which were not at all involved in the earlier suit the provision of section 10 of the C.P C was quite inapplicable. 

9. Section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code is in the following language t, "No Court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter ID issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigation under the same title where such suit is pending in the same or any other Court In Bangladesh having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed or in any Court beyond the Ironist of Bangladesh established or contained by the Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court". 

10. According the said provision, the matter in issue in the subsequently instituted suit must be directly and substantially in issue in the previously instituted suit. This really means that the entire matter issue in both the suits must be same. Besides that the parties in both the suits should be the same or at least the parties must be such under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title ID this case all the matters in issue in the subsequent suit are not at all matters in issue in the former suit because in the subsequently instituted suit declaration of title has been claimed in respect of C S. plots No. 92, 93, 149, 56, 97 and 141 and none of these plots are subject-matter in the earlier instituted suit Similarly, in the earlier instituted suit there was the prayer for declaration that the decree in Title Suit No. 25/1975 was void and this matter is riot present at all in the subsequent suit. Again in the subsequently instituted suit declaration was sought in respect of a decree in Title Suit No. 50/1978 of the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka as being void and this matter was not till present in the earlier instituted suit. Further, regarding the parties, in the earlier suit only 36 persons were defendants while in the subsequent suit there were 34 defendants as also 6; pro-defendants, Thus it is found that all the matters in issue in the previously instituted suit were not matters in issue in the subsequent suit and also all the parties of the subsequently instituted suit were not parties in the earlier suit and thus most of the matters, issues and parties were different in the two suits. In fact out of several matters and issues only one matter and issue regarding the C.S. plot Nos. 76 and 94 were common in the two suits and every other matter and issue was different in the two suits. 

11. The expression "matter in issue" has referred to the entire subject controversy between the parties and the application for stay of suit under this section is bound to show that all the matters in issue in the suit are directly and substantially in issue in the previously instituted suit. It is not sufficient that there are some issues common to the two suits but all the matters in issue in the two suits should be identical and Court cannot apply this section where there are some issues in common and also other different issues. Even when one of the issues in the two suits are common that is not sufficient to attract the operation of this section unless it could be shown that the entire subject in controversy was the same in both the suits. 

12. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed cited a decision in the case of Muhammad Younas Vs. Nargis Sultana, reported io PLD Lahore 1970, page 41 where also it has been held that every matter in dispute should be directly and substantially in issue in both suits and that one of several issues being common is insufficient for stay of subsequent suit. Another case has been referred to by Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed which is the case of Ch. Muhammad Afzal Vs. Mst. Sardar reported in PLO 1949 Lahore at page 16 wherein it has been held that section 10 of the C P.C. bars the trial of a suit when all the issues in both the suits are common and that the mere fact that one or two issues are common in the two suits is not sufficient for bringing the suit within the scope of section 10. The same being the accepted principle it is found that the present case cannot be held to be a case wherein section 10 of the C.P.C. can be applied. Thus it is found that the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error of law in rejecting the defendant petitioner's prayer for stay and rather that was the only legal and proper order that could be passed. 

13. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that in view of the fact that section 10 was not applicable and also in consideration of the fact that at least one issue was common in both the suits, so, he thought it to be most appropriate to seek an analogous hearing of both the suits and that an application for analogous hearing of the two suits has been already filed on behalf of the opposite parties before the learned Subordinate Judge which remains to be disposed of by him. Since the said petition is already before the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal we think it will not be proper to give our views in respect of the said petition. As he is competent to dispose of the same we refrain from making any comment in respect of the said prayer for analogous hearing and the said petition will be disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge in accordance with law In the result, the Rule is discharged with-out any order as to costs 

A.T.M. Afzal, J.—I agree. 
End.

Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Defendants-Appellants
Vs
