full_judgment:
This case has been remanded to this Court for disposal of the matter afresh on the basis of materials on record by order dated 16-3-2015 passed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3278 of 2014.

2. This Rule was issued calling upon the defendant-opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 21-11-2007 (decree signed on 27-11-2007) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 96 of 2002 affirming the judgment and decree dated 16-4-2002 (decree signed on 22-4-2002) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Boalmari , Faridpur in Title Suit No. 44 of 2000 decreeing the suit in preliminary form allotting 50 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff and 18 decimals of land in favour of the defendant No. 1 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. Facts of the case, briefly, are that the opposite party No. 1, as plaintiff instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 44 of 2000 before the learned Assistant Judge, Boalmari, Faridpur imploding the defendants for partition of the suit land as descried in the schedule of the plaint. The case of the plaintiff in short is that the suit jama was originally belonged to Jaliluddin Mollah, who transferred 1.76 acres of land including 68 decimals of land of the suit plot to his son, Abdus Samad Mollah (defendant No. 3) by a registered deed of gift dated 5-2-1974 and thereafter, the defendant No. 3 sold out 1.05 acres of land including 50 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1157 to the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by the registered Kabala dated 22-8-1991. The suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds. The plaintiff mutated his name and paid rent to the Government, the plaintiff possessed 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side. The defendant No. 1 purchased some land from the defendant No. 3 and there was dispute in respect possession in the suit land and therefore, on 15-5-2000 the plaintiff requested for amicable partition but the defendant No. 1 refused to do so and hence, the suit.

4. The petitioner as defendant No. 1 entered appearance in the suit and filed a written statement denying all the material averments of the plaint stating, inter-alia, that the defendant Nos. 2, 3 are full brother of the plaintiff, the suit jama was originally belonged to Jaliluddin, who transferred 1.76 acres of land including 68 decimals of land of the suit plot in favour of his son (defendant No. 3) by way of a registered deed of gift dated 5-3-74 and thereafter, the defendant No 3 sold out 60 decimals of land of the suit plot and 05 decimals of land of non suit plot No. 1161 to the defendant No. 1 (petitioner) and handed over possession to him. The defendant-petitioner has possessed the suit land by bargadars and the current record of right prepared in his name, the plaintiff has no right, title and possession over the suit land, the plaintiff filed the instance suit for depriving the defendant No. 1 after creating a benami sale deed and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Boalmari, Faridpur on the pleadings of the parties framed the following issues for determination:—

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form and manner?

2. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties?

3. Whether the suit is bad for defect of hotchpotch?

4. Where the plaintiff has right, title and possession over the suit land?

5. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get the reliefs as prayed for or any other reliefs.

6. At the trial the plaintiff himself was examined as PW 2 and 4 other witnesses were examined including the deed writer and the defendant No. 1 himself was examined as DW 1 and 2 other witnesses were examined as DW 2 and DW 3 and both the parties exhibited certain documents to prove their respective cases.

7. The Trial Court after closing of the evidence and hearing argument of the parties decreed the suit on contest in preliminary form allotting 50 decimals of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1 and 18 decimals of land in favour of the defendant-petitioner.

8. on appeal, the learned. Additional District Judge, Faridpur by his judgment and decree dated 21-11-2007 passed in Title Appeal No. 96 of 2002, concurred with findings with learned trial Judge and dismissed the appeal holding that the trial Court has rightly decreed the suit in preliminary form allotting 50 decimals of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 and 18 decimals of land in favour of the defendant No. 1 and the instant Revision application is directed against that judgment and decree.

9. Mr AKM Shamsul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner submits that both the Courts below having failed to consider that the suit was not maintainable for not bringing the entire property left by Daliluddin Mollah into hotchpotch. He further submits that there is ample evidence on record showing possession of the defendant petitioner in the disputed lands and the defendant No. 3 in collusion with the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 created the fraudulent kabala dated 22-8-1991 in order to defraud the defendant-petitioner and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree of affirmance is perverse being contrary to law and facts, the same is liable to be set-aside. Mr AKM Shamsul Haque in support of his submission has relied on a decision reported in 41 DLR 447.

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 submits it is on record that kabala dated 22-8-1991 in favour of plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 is an admitted kabala and it has not been set-aside by any competent Court, the plaintiff proved his possession by adducing sufficient corroborative evidence over 50 decimals of the suit land and both the Courts below taking into consideration of the evidence and materials on record found that the defendant No. 3 sold out 1.05 acres of land including 50 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1157 to the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by the registered Kabala dated 22-8-1991, the suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds, the defendant No. 1 purchased some land from the defendant No. 3, the plaintiff-petitioner mutated his name and paid rent to the Government, the plaintiff possessed 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side and such concurrent findings of fact on possession and title are based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record and, as such, the question of interference does not arise at all.

11. Finally, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan submits that according to the admitted facts of the case it is crystal clear that the record of right was wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants and the same was brought to the notice of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 after filing the suit. He adds that the proposition of law is by now well settled that record of right is not a document of title it does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence, it may support an evidence of title and in this case both the Courts below on the facts of the case and on consideration of the legal position rightly decided this point in favour of the plaintiff. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan to fortify his argument has relied on the decisions reported in 28 DLR (AD) 61, 13 MLR (AD) 6.

12. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgments of both the Courts below, deposition of witnesses and other materials on record. Now, for convenience I will first take up the question whether the suit was bad for defect of parties and hotchpotch.

<u>13. On scrutiny of the record, it appears that the contesting defendant No. 1, petitioner raised a plea of defect of parties and a further plea that the entire properties of the parties were not brought into hotchpotch in his written statement although, the DWs including the defendant No. 1 (petitioner) as DW 1 in their respective deposition did not utter any single word as to prove such plea of defect of parties and hotchpotch. It further appears that the trial Court below on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record decreed the suit on the clear finding that the defendants could not show that for non inclusion of any certain plot or party, any of the parties in the suit will be prejudiced and in that view of the matter the suit is not bad for defect of parties and hotchpotch.</u>

14. On a close perusal of the entire evidence and materials on record, I find nothing on record to suggest that during trial the defendants raised any point for non inclusion of any certain plot or party, any of the parties in the suit will be prejudiced and thus, sitting under revisional jurisdiction, I do not find any reason to hold a different view. Moreover, on query from the Court, Mr AKM Shamsul Haque the learned Advocate for the petitioner finds it’s difficult to show any error or illegality in finding of the trial Court on the point of defect of parties and hotchpotch.

15. Now, let me look at the crux of the matter whether the Court of appeal below committed any illegality in dismissing the appeal on the finding that the trial Court has rightly decreed the suit in preliminary form allotting 50 decimals of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 and 18 decimals of land in favour of the defendant No. 1.

16. In the instant case the opposite party No. 1, as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 44 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Boalmari, Faridpur on the averments that the suit jama was originally belonged to Jaliluddin Mollah, who transferred 1.76 acres of land including 68 decimals of land of the suit plot to his son, Abdus Samad Mollah (defendant No. 3) by a registered deed of gift dated 5-2-1974 and thereafter, the defendant No. 3 sold out 1.05 acres of land including 50 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1157 to the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by registered Kabala dated 22-8-1991, the plaintiff mutated his name and paid rent to the Government, the plaintiff possessed 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side. The defendant No. 1 purchased some land from the defendant No.3 and there was dispute in respect of possession in the suit land, the suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds and thus, on 15-5-2000 the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 1 for amicable partition but in vain.

17. Let me now advert to the evidence on record.

18. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 to prove his case examined 5 witnesses including himself as PW 2 and exhibited some documents. PW 1, Ayub Ali, as inspector of Boalmari Krishi Bank exhibited the original kabala No. 2685 dated 22-8-91 as exhibit No. 1. PW 2, plaintiff, Md Ahad Molla stated in his deposition that: এই জমি দলিল উদ্দিন ৩নং বিবাদী ছামাদ মোল্যাকে দান করে দখল বুঝায়ে দেই ইং ৫-২-৭৮ তারিখে। উক্ত দলিলের সহিমোহর নকল দলিল দিয়েছি। প্রদর্শনী-১(ক)। সামাদ মোল্যা (৩নং বিবাদী) স্বত্ববান দখলীকার থাকাকালে ইং ২২-৮-৯১ তারিখের দলিল মূলে আমার নিকট ৫০ শতক জমি বিক্রয় করে দখল দেয়। উক্ত দলিলের সহিমোহর নকল জমা দিয়ে উহা প্রদর্শনী-১ চিহ্নিত হয়। This witness in his deposition also stated that a shalo machin and water house stood in his 50 decimals of suit land, he mutated his name and paid rent to the Government. PW 3 stated in his deposition that he is a deed writer of Boalmari sub-registry office, on 22-8-1991 the parties of the deed went to him and he written the deed in question and on that date the sub-registrar registered the same. PW 4, Md Fazlul Haque Mollah, stated in his deposition that: আমি মোকদ্দমার পক্ষদের ও নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী দাগের উত্তর পাশে জমি আছে। নালিশী জমির মধ্যে পশ্চিমাংশে ৫০ শতক জমি আহাদ মোল্যা ১০/১১ বৎসর দখল করে।বাকী জমি সামাদ মোল্যা খাইত। এই জমিতে আহাদ মোল্যার শ্যালো ম্যাশিন ও হাউজ আছে ৭/৮ বৎসর ধরে। নালিশী দাগের পূর্বাংশে সবুর মোল্যা ৩ বৎসর যাবৎ সামাদের দখলকারী অংশ দখল করে।PW 5, Md Ali Afzal stated in his deposition that: আমি মোকদ্দমার পক্ষদের চিনি ও নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী জমির নাল পশ্চিমে আমার জমি তবে ঐ ভিন্ন মৌজা মুরাইল পশ্চিম খন্ডের মধ্যে। নালিশী জমির মধ্যে আহাদ মোল্যা ১১/২ পাখির একটু বেশী পশ্চিম নাল দিয়ে দখল করে ৩০ শতক পাখি। সবুর ঐ দাগের পূর্বাংশে সামাদের দখলীয় জমি ৩/৪ বৎসর খায়। এর আগে সবুর কোন জমি খাইত না।

19. Defendant petitioner, Md Abdus Sobur himself was examined as DW. 1, who stated in his cross examination that:  আহাদ (plaintiff) নাম পত্তন করাইয়েছে কিনা তা সে জানে, আমি জানিনা। আহাদের ২২-৮-৯১ তারিখের দলিলের বিরুদ্ধে আমি কোন মোকদ্দমা করিনি। This witness in his cross-examination also stated that ১২-১০-৯১ইং তারিখের আমার দলিল মূলে আমি আমার পক্ষে নাম পত্তন করায়নি বা খাজনা দিইনি।

20. From the above, it transpires that the defendant No. 3 sold out 1.05 acres of land including 50 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1157 to the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by registered Kabala dated 22-8-1991. The plaintiff possessed 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side the plaintiff mutated his name and paid rent to the Government. Moreover, on going through the evidence of DWs. it appears that DW. 1 (defendant No. 1, petitioner), DW.2 and DW 3 in their respective evidence admitted the possession of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 over 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side.

21. As regards the plaintiff's case of title to the suit land it is based on the kabala (Ext. 1) dated 22-8-1991.

22. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record found the claim of the plaintiff is true and decreed the suit and the appellate Court below as last Court of fact on consideration of the evidence on record, facts and circumstances, held that "trial court has rightly decreed the suit in preliminary form allotting 50 and 18 decimals of land of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff-respondent and defendant-appellant respectively and I find nothing to interfere with judgment passed by the learned trial Court." Both the trial Court and lower appellant Court came to a common finding that the plaintiff has been succeeded to prove his right, title, possession as well as share of 50 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 1157 at its western side.

23. The learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner could not refer to any principle which has been allegedly violated by the Courts below nor to any fact which has either been ignored or wrongly relied upon. Therefore, I find no reason to interfere therewith.

24. Now, it remains for me to consider whether the record of right was wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants.

25. From the facts as disclosed in the paint, written statement, deposition of witnesses, it becomes clear that the record of right was wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. The court of appeal below after a detailed discussion of the attending circumstances borne out by records held "mere preparation of record of right as contended by the appellant does not create any right and title on the suit land". Furthermore, it appears from the record that the original kabala dated.22-8- 1991 was mortgaged to Krishi Bank, Boalmari Branch and it was called for comparison, the trial Court has decided that the kabala of the plaintiff is earlier to the kabala of the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff's kabala has been duly acted upon.

26. The proposition of law is well settled that a registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over other records of rights, until and unless such kabala is cancelled on specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit and in this case the defendant petitioner admitted in his evidence that he did not file any such suit for declaration of title and cancellation of registered kabala dated 22-8-1991 (Ext. 1).

27. In the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 32 DLR 252, it has been held as follows:

"The records of rights of the Government which at best are evidence of possession at the time when such records are prepared and not an evidence of title. This is a well established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit."

28. In this case it is also found that (Ext.1) was the original kabala dated 22-8-1991, which mortgaged to Krishi Bank, Boalmari Branch by the plaintiff and it was called for comparison at the trial and that registered document is more than 20 years old document. No dispute was raised in the trial Court as to its registration (kabala dated 22-8-1991). Therefore, sitting under revisional jurisdiction, I am unable to accept the contention of Mr AKM Shamsul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the defendant No. 3 in collusion with the plaintiff-opposite party created the fraudulent kabala dated 22-8-1991 (Ext.1) in order to defraud the defendant-petitioner or the kabala dated 22-8-1991 (Ext. 1) was not acted upon.

29. By now I have covered the points raised by Mr AKM Shamsul Haque. Now, let me advert to some of the submissions as made by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan. One of the main submission made by him relying on the decision reported in 17 BLD (AD) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134 is that a finding of fact whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division in Revision except in certain well-defined circumstances such as non-consideration and misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case and in the present case the judgments of 2 Courts below are well based on correct evaluation of the facts and materials of the case and, as such, the question of interference does not arise at all.

30. Mr AKM Shamsul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner while elaborating his submission this Court asked him to address on the point that whether the judgments of two Courts below are based on misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record. Mr Haque could not satisfy me upon referring evidence from the record that the judgments of two Courts below are based on misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record. The trial Court and the lower appellate Court are the final Court of facts. The suit having been concluded on concurrent findings of fact, it is very difficult to interfere with such findings sitting under the revisional jurisdiction, unless it is found that the concurrent findings of fact are perverse being contrary to law or evidence and materials on record.

31. At the end of the day, Mr AKM Shamsul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner having himself realized the difficulties submits that both the Courts below failed, to consider the defendant-petitioner's case from a correct angle, which resulted in an error in the impugned decisions occasioning failure of justice and thus, on such ground the suit may be sent back on remand to the trial Court for deciding it on all points after holding the trial afresh.

<u>32. To this, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate relying on the decisions reported in 54 DLR (AD) 73, 55 DLR (AD) 20 and 41 DLR (AD) 124 submits that the defendant-petitioner got ample opportunity to adduce evidence before both the Courts below and since the deed of the plaintiff was proved in accordance with law and both the Courts below after due consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit and the evidence on all material points are there on record, it would not be justified sitting under revisional jurisdiction to send the suit back on remand.</u>

33. In the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs Montaj Ali reported in 55 DLR (AD) 20, it has been held as follows:

"Though the learned Judge of the High Court Division quoted the relevant portion of the deposition of DW 1 as noticed by us, but he failed to consider the same properly resulting in error in his finding. Further, the legal position is that where evidence has been duly placed before the trial Court and it has decided the suit on merit the revisional Court has no power to remand by shirking its duty, particularly solely for the purpose of writing the judgment afresh. This appeal, therefore, must succeed."

34. In the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue and Asstt. Custodian Vested Property, Chandpur vs Tafurnessa, wife of Ali Ahmed Mia reported in 41 DIR (AD) 124, it has been held as follows:

"But a remand order is not to be granted as a matter of routine. Section 29 All 184 PC and 17 All 112 PC Mr Moksudur Rahman found it difficult to pinpoint the area of investigation which could be done on remand. The crucial question is as to the physical presence of the vendor. It is presumed under section 60 that the registration was done in accordance with law and the requirement of the law was fulfilled. It is a rebuttable presumption, no doubt, but Mr Moksudur Rahman could not argue, how the evidence as it is, has rebutted the presumption. The defendants got ample opportunity at the trial stage and no such rebuttal evidence was adduced. Hence the prayer for remand does not merit consideration. Since the point has been settled already on which the leave was granted, Mr Ahmed is correct in saying the appeal has become of mere academic interest."

<u>35. In the case of Akitullah vs Zafala Begum reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74, it has been held that remand as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not of matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in any party's pleading.</u>

<u>36. In the case of Golam Rahman vs Hazera Khatoon, reported in 1 MLR (AD) 211 = 47 DLR (AD) 108, it has been held that remand of a suit for fresh trial to provide opportunity for introducing a new case of adverse possession is not sustainable.</u>

<u>37. In view of the long line of judicial decision is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible, I am unable to accept the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner on the point of remand since both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record to decide the case on merit. The Court of appeal below having decided the case on consideration of the materials on record and in accordance with law the same calls for no interference. Therefore, I find no substance in either of the contentions as raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

38. In view of my discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant Rule must fail.

39. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of affirmance dated 21-11-2007 (decree signed on 27-11-2007) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 96 of 2002 is hereby maintained.

Let a copy of the judgment along with lower Courts record be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 14-9-2017 passed by the learned District Judge, Habiganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 01 of 2017 allowing the appeal and thereby setting aside the order dated 9-1-2017 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Lakhai, Habiganj in Title Suit No. 137 of 2015 returning the plaint should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite party No. 1, Most. Abeda Khatun as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 137 of 2015 in the court of Assistant Judge, Lakhai, Habiganj, against the petitioner as defendant for decree of declaration of title in the property and for a declaration that register deed bearing No. 100/2006 is 'void ab initio, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff along with recovery of possession. The suit has been valued at Taka 1,73,000 being the value of the registered deed under challenge for the purpose of jurisdiction of the court and for payment of court fees. The defendants in suit appeared and contesting the suit by filing written statement. In usual course the trial court framed issues for determination of the dispute and proceeded with hearing of the suit. After framing issues the defendant petitioner filed an application on 22-9-2016 under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial court praying for rejection of the plaint raising objection as to valuation of the suit and payment of court fees.

3. The trial court has enquired the matter of valuation through sherestadar of the court who submitted report obtaining information from the concern Sub-Registrar office. There-after, the trial court heard the application filed by the defendant-petitioner under Order 7 Rule 11(d) and the valuation matter. After contested hearing the trial court rejected the application filed by the defendant under Order VII, rule 11(d) and accepted the report of the sherestadar and returned the plaint in suit to the plaintiff for presenting the same before the appropriate court by its order dated 9-1-2017 being the pecuniary jurisdiction of the suit is beyond the trial court.

4. Being aggrieved the plaintiff moved against the order before the District Judge, Habiganj by filing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 01 of 2017. The learned District Judge, Habiganj, heard the appeal and on contested hearing allowed the same by setting aside the order of the trial court by the impugned judgment and order dated 14-9-2017. At this stage, the defendant-respondent-petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.

5. Mr. Foyej Ahmed learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner at the very outset drawing attention of the court to the prayer made in the plaint submits that the suit is for a declaration of title in the property and recovery of possession. As such the suit has to be valued on the market price of the property in question. But the plaintiff valued the suit on the value of a sale deed valued at Taka 1,73,000 and paid court fees on the said valuation. He further submits that the market price of the suit property as per report submitted by the sherestadar is Taka 10,89,040 which is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the trial court. The trial court by accepting the said report returned the plaint as it has no jurisdiction to try the suit. He submits that the trial court rightly returned the plaint to the plaintiff for presenting the same before the court having jurisdiction to try the same and to pay appropriate court fees on the said value.

6. It is also argued that the appellate court while allowing the appeal has misconceived the provisions of law regarding valuation of the suit and payment of court fees and on such an erroneous view wrongly found that the value of the suit would be the value of the sale deed under challenge and not the market price of the property and as such, the judgment and order passed by the appellate court is liable to be set aside.

7. Mr. Saifur Rashid, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 submits  that the cause of action of the suit in fact arises out of a registered kabala under challenge on the basis of which the defendant No. 1 claims title in the property and dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land. The dispute in the instant case is based on a document and both the declarations are closely related to each other and the title of the plaintiff could be declared by the court only if the court finds that the kabala under challenge is not at all binding upon the plaintiff.

8. He further submits that the substantive relief sought for in the instant suit is a declaration in respect of a sale deed in the name of the defendant and as such, the value of the suit would be the value of the deed not the market price of the suit property. He also argued that the plaintiff rightly valued the suit on the basis of the value of the sale deed in question as the substantive relief of the plaintiff against the defendant was in respect of the sale deed. In support of his such contentions he has referred to the case of Ahmed Kabir vs Haji Mazahar Ahmed reported in 43 DLR 500 and Syed Ahmed vs Keshab Chandra reported in 1988 BLD 60.

9. Heard the learned Advocate for the parties, perused the revisional application, impugned judgment and order of the courts below, plaint in suit and written statement filed by the defendant as annexed to the application.

10. Going through the prayers made in the plaintiff in suit, it appears that the suit is for declaration and recovery of possession. To appreciate the facts involved in this case, prayers as made in the plaint may be reproduced below for easy understanding, which run thus:

“১২। অতত্রব বাদীপক্ষ প্রার্থনা করেন যে,

ক) বিরোধীয় নিম্ন তপশীল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে বাদীপক্ষের জোতম্বত্ব সাব্যস্থে তাহা declared হওয়ার;

(খ) বিরোধীয় নিম্ন তপশীল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে ১/২নং বিবাদীকে অন্যায় অনধিকারী জবরদখলকার গণ্যে তাহাদিগকে তথা হইতে অপসারণ করতঃ তথায় ১/২নং বিবাদীর নির্মিত পাকা কি কাঁচা গৃহাদিসহ যাবতীয় প্রতিবন্ধকতাদি অপসারণে বিরোধীয় ভূমির নির্দায় বাদীনির খাস দখল পাওয়ার;

(গ) ১/২নং বিবাদীপক্ষ মাননীয় আদালতের নির্দেশে বিরোধীয় ভূমির যাবতীয় প্রতিবন্ধকতাদি অপসারণে উহার নির্দায় খাস দখল বাদীপক্ষের অনুকূলে পরিত্যাগ না করিলে মাননীয় আদালত মাধ্যমে বিরোধীয় ভূমির খাস দখল পাওয়ার;

(ঘ) বিগত ও হাজতীকালের মহাশীলাতের প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি হওয়ার;

(ঙ) বিরোধীয় ভূমি প্রসঙ্গে ৩নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক ১/২নং বিবাদী বরাবরে সম্পাদিত ও রেজিস্ত্রীকৃত  লাখাই এস.আর, অফিসের ১০০/২০০৬ইং নং যুক্ত রেজিঃ দলিলটি শুরু হইতে বাতিলযোগ্য এবং বেআইনীগণ্যে বিরোধীয় ভূমি প্রসঙ্গে উক্ত দলিলটি বাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে কার্যকরি নহে মর্মে declared  হওয়ার;

(চ) বিরোধীয় ভূমি প্রসঙ্গে সহকারী কমিশনার (ভুমি), লাখাই কার্যালয়ের ৪৯৩/২০১৩-২০১৪ইং সনের নামজারী মামলা মূলে ১/২ নং বিবাদীর হাসিলা, নামজরী সংক্রান্ত আদেশ ও তদানুবলে প্রাপ্ত নামজারী পরচা বেআইনী ও যোগাযোগী-গণ্যে উক্ত নামজারী পরচা বিরোধীয় ভূমি প্রসঙ্গে বাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে কার্যকরি নহে মর্মে declared হওয়ার;”

11. It appears that the 1st prayer is a declaration of title in the property 2nd prayer is recovery of possession, 4th prayer is a declaration in respect of a sale deed by which the defendant No. 1 claims title in the suit property. From the prayers it seems that the title of the plaintiff in suit could only be declared unless a declaration is given to the effect that the sale deed in question is void, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff.

12. In the present case substantive prayer of the plaintiff is declaration of title and a declaration to the effect that the sale deed to be illegal and void and both the prayers have nexus with each other. In this situation this Court in the case of Ahmed Kabir vs Haji Mazahar Ahmed reported in 43 DLR 500 held that;

"the objective standered of valuation is the consideration money of the kabala or market price prevailing at the time of institution of the suit which is less".

And in the case of Syed Ahmed vs Keshab Chandra reported in 1988 BLD 60 it has been held that;

"in a suit where the relief is sought for is that certain kabalas are not binding upon the plaintiff and for recovery of possession, where the market price of the property is either more than or equal to the consideration money then consideration money will be the objective standered for valuing the relief sought for but if the market price less, then market price would be the objective standard for valuing the relief sought."

<u>13. The plaintiffs, no doubt, have challenged the legality of the defendant's title in the property on the basis of the sale deed under challenge. This, in fact, for tracing the title of the real title holder, declaration of the plaintiff's title was sought for, in the suit. If the said declaration is not granted then the other reliefs such as declaration of title in the property or recovery of possession cannot be granted independently in favour of the plaintiff. As such, this court has no hesitation to hold that the relief by way of declaration to the effect that the sale deed is void illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff along with declaration of title are the principal reliefs in the suit and recovery of possession which is incidental and consequential relief. If the relief against sale deed is refused then the other reliefs sought for cannot be granted.</u>

14. In view of such situation the plaintiff is required to value the suit on the value of the sale deed not on the market price of the property in question. Relying on the decisions referred to on behalf of the opposite party this court finds that the trial court wrongly returned the plaint and the appellate court rightly held that the suit has been properly valued for the purpose of jurisdiction and payment of court fees and the Assistant Judge has jurisdiction to try the said suit. The trial court accepted the valuation of the suit at the time of filing of the same and the defendant did not raise any objection at the earliest but admitting jurisdiction filed written statement and the court framed issues for determination of the dispute. Moreover, the defendant did not file any application praying for return of the plaint but prayed for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure which was rejected by the trial court.

<u>15. Valuation of a suit and payment of court fees is primarily a question between the plaintiff and the government because it involved government duties only. The defendant who may believe and even honestly, that proper court fees has not been paid by the plaintiff, still has no right to move the superior court of appeal or in revision against the order adjudging payment of court fees payable on the plaint. The impugned judgment and order passed by the appellate court speaks with clarity and there is no infirmity of reasoning whatsoever or any error of law, which would warrant interference of this court in exercise of jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

16. In the light of the legal position as stated above this court finds that the principal relief claimed by the plaintiff opposite party in title suit is of declaration that a sale deed is void, ab initio, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff along with other relief of declaration of title and recovery of possession are incidental and consequential to the principal relief. In such view of the matter the plaintiff is entitled to value the suit on the basis of the principal relief claimed by him and the other reliefs are merely incidental to the said relief.

17. In the backdrop of the above discussion this court finds that the learned appellate court rightly came to the correct finding that the plaintiff is at liberty to value the suit in accordance with the declaration of relief of his choice. Thus, the impugned judgment and order does not call for any interference.

18. Taking into consideration the above, this court finds no merit in the Rule as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

19. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to costs.

20. Order of stay granted at the time issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate a copy of the judgment to the court concerned.

End.

full_judgment:
Khizir Ahmed Choudhury J: In this revisional application rule has been issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 4-3-2014 passed by learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 274 of 2009 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 26-7-2009 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 208 of 2005 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The petitioners herein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 208 of 2005 before the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet impleading the present opposite parties as defendant praying for declaration that they are entitled to hold and possess the 2nd schedule land which is within first schedule land and the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 12 of 1992 being affirmed In Title Appeal No. 199 of 1996 are void, ineffectual and plaintiffs are not bound by those decrees.

3. The case of the plaintiffs in brief, is that, first schedule land belonged to Sree Sree Gobinda Jew Deity within which Gandha Singha was jote tenant whose behalf his son Krishna Kumar Singha built a seemi pacca structure. Thereafter, Gandha Singha transferred the 2nd schedule land to his sister Sharna Kumari by oral gift and left for India. Sharan Kumari while performing Seba Puja died leaving son Monoronjon Singha and daughter Monika Debi. Monika Debi after marriage went to her husband's residence and, as such, Monoronjon Singha became exclusive possessor over the 2nd schedule land. Thereafter, Monoronjon Singha transferred the said land to Dr Motilal Singha by deed dated 8- 1071966 and Dr Motilal Singha continued to perform Seba Puja and other the rituals over the 2nd schedule land. Dr Motilal by receipt dated 11-9-1989 transferred 2nd schedule land and structure thereon to plaintiff and since then the plaintiff are performing Seba Puja and other religious formalalities by residing with family members therein. He also paid municipal holding tax and other taxes. Defendant No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 97 of 1985 before the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet for declaring his right of shebapuya, maintenance and administer the affairs of the deity. Father of defendant Nos. 2-3 Navo Kumar Singha was defendant No. 2 and defendant Nos. 4-8 was also defendant that suit, the suit was transferred to Artha Rind Adalat, Sylhet renumbered as Title Suit No. 12 of 1992. Utpal Singh, proforma defendant No. 9 as plaintiff also filed a title suit being Title Suit No. 11 of 1992 for declaration of title of deity and for recovery of khas possession. Both the suits were heard analogously and the trial Court dismissed the suits. Defendant No.1preferred Title Appeal No. 199 of 1996 before the District Judge wherein defendant Nos.1-8 filed a solenama with collusion with each other and by that solenama defendant Nos. 1-8 a partitioned the suit properties amongst themselves which is illegal, ineffectual and not binding by the plaintiff. In both suits the plaintiffs were not made parties and, as such, the findings and reasonings of those suits are not binding upon the plaintiff.

4. The opposite parties as defendant Nos. 1-8 filed a written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff contending that suit land belonged to Gandha Singh, the predecessor interest of defendant who after purchase established a family deity over there namely Sree Sree Gobinda Jew Deity. Subsequently, Bhim Singh and his son Radha Charon Singha and thereafter, Pitambar Singha son of Radha Charon Singha, and his heirs were substituted as defendant Nos. 1ka to 1Gha and ultimately they became heirs of the recorded owners and they are administering the affairs of the deity The heirs of Gandha Singha i.e. present defendants have been administering and maintaining the affairs of the deity and they allowed 20 families as licensee for residing in the suit land and the plaintiff secretly and collusively beyond the knowledge of the Sebayet started living in the suit land. When the defendants asked them to quit.the suit land, he took some time but ultimately refused to vacate the suit land. The plaintiffs also did not pay the rents regularity by taking advantage of the litigation and thereafter, a arbitration was held at the intercession of the elderly people of the locality and the plaintiffs undertook to vacate the suit land On 14-5-2005 but ultimately filed the instant suit with a view to the illegal gain.

5. The, trial Court framed as many as 4 issues for disposal of the suit and after hearing dismissed the suit finding the claim of the plaintiffs not sustainable. The appellate Court affirmed the findings and reasonings of the trial Court and after hearing dismissed the appeal against which the instant rule.

6. Mr Md Mahbub Ali, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that admittedly the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land and they have been residing therein with their family members by raising structures. He also submits that original owner of the suit land Garidha Singa has established deity and by successive transfer Monoronjon Singha got the Suit land and he sold the possessory right of the suit land to the present plaintiff on 8-10-1996. He next submits that admittedly the Plaintiffs are occupant in the suit land along with other 20 families and according to the admission of the defendants the present plaintiff used to pay rent to them and the plaintiff are in possession of the suit land. He next submits that in the earlier suits solenama has been filed by the plaintiffs and defendants of that suit collusively beyond the knowledge of the present plaintiffs and since they are not parties in the earlier suits they are not bound by the findings of the suits. He next submits since the plaintiff are in possession in the suit land, he was necessary party therein for resolving the disputes completely and effectually and, as such, the present plaintiffs are not bound by the decrees. He averred that Meanwhile the defendants have filed title Suit No. 51 of 2015 before the Joint District judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet impleading the present petitioner as defendant praying for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession and as such, question of title and possession and dispossession are to be adjudicated in that title suit. He next submits since the defendants have filed title suits and, as such, until and unless they can get a decree in that suits they cannot claim the office of shebiet legally. He finally submits that the present petitioners are not claiming title in the suit land rather their claiming their possessory right over there and if they can prove possession in the suit land for quite long period they can get a decree in respect of their possessory right.

7. The opposite party Nos. 2-4 filed a counter affidavit denying the claim of petitioner. Mr Md Mustaque Ahmed, learned advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that admittedly suit land belonged to the predecessor of the present opposite party namely Gandha Singha who after purchase of the suit land established deity namely Sree Sree Gobinda Jew Deity and he himself remained as Sebayet of the deity and continued administer Seba Puja and other religious rituals by himself. On the death of Gandha Singha, eldest brother Bhim Singha and thereafter Radha Charon Singha and on his death Pitambar Singh became heirs of the original owners and like their predecessor they have been performing Seba Puja in the suit premises as legal heirs of the original owners. He next submits that the plaintiff were not inducted into possession by the present opposite party rather one Motilal Singha inducted the present plaintiff in the suit land who has got no title over there and the said Motilal Singha was neither Sebayet nor any way related with the deity and, as such, he possession of the present plaintiff cannot be termed as lawful one He next submits that record of right has been prepared in the name of the predecessor of the present opposite parties in the SA record as well as the present record of right from which it can be inferred that the defendants have got absolute right as Sebayet of the deity. He further submits that when dispute arose between the defendants they filed the suit and ultimately they resolved the disputes by compromise where the plaintiffs have got no right to be impleaded as they are in no way related with the deity or the property of the deity and, as such, the decree as granted by the Courts below cannot be set aside at the instance of the present plaintiffs. He next submits that the opposite parties are paying rents record of right has been prepared in their names and municipal holding and other papers are in their names and, as such, the present petitioners claim of possessory right is not sustainable. He finally submits that the plaintiffs are living in the suit land as trespasser as they are not paying rents for quite long period and, as such, their suit is not maintainable in its present forum.

8. Having gone through the pleadings, evidence, exhibits and other materials it appears that suit property belonged to Gandha Singha who established the deity over the suit land. The claim of the plaintiff is that Gandha Singha orally gifted the suit property to his sister Sharan Kumari and on his death son Monoronjon was heir who transferred the suit land to Motilal who transferred the same to the present plaintiffs. To substantiate such claim, the plaintiffs are required to proof Sharan Kumari's acquiring title in the suit land but fact is that under Hindu Law property cannot be transferred bural gift and it is not also proved how Motilal got the property and whether Motilal has transferable right over the suit land but these facts have not been proved by the plaintiffs by convincing evidence.

9. On the other hand the defendants by showing record of right and other documents tried to establish that they are the lenient descendants of Gandha Singha and they being the Sebayet got right to hold and possess Debutter property. On going through the supplementary affidavit submitted by the opposite parties it appears that record of right has been prepared in the name of the predecessor of the present opposite parties although in the record of right the name of the deity is absent but from admitted fact from both the parties it appears that the suit property comprises homestead, garden, and mondir. The plaintiff are also not claiming title over the suit land, but their specific contention is that they are in possession of the suit land for quite long period and they have got possessory right over the suit land along with other families as Pujaries of the deity. It is also facts that till date not step has been taken for evicting other occupants who are residing in the suit land for quite long period.

<u>10. So far possessory right is concerned, persons who claim possessory right cannot claim it against lawful owner as possessory right can be claimed against persons who have no title over the suit land. In the case of Alexander vs Nair Service Society Ltd. AIR 1966 Karala 286 it is held that,</u>

<u>"just as a true owner who is dispossessed can, within the period limited by law, being a suit for possession against the person in possession notwithstanding that the latter is not the immediate but only a subsequent intruder, irrespective of the number of nature of the intervening adverse possessory titles, so can a possessory owner against all but the true owner. Does it make any difference then that, in between, there was an interval during which the true owner was in possession? Would that extinguish the title of all earlier possessory owners so as to entrench a subsequent trespasser and give him good title against all but the true owner? We think not. For, the title of a possessory owner springs from the fact of his possession and that is not erased by the true owner regaining possession. The possessory owner's title continues to exist; only it is an imperfect title which is of no avail against the perfect title of the true owner; but against the inferior title of any subsequent possessor, it is a good title. Halsbury (Simonds Edition, Bo. 24 paragraph 492 at page 255) says on the authority of Asher vs Whitlock, (1865) 1 QB 1 and 1907 AC 73."</u>

11. Here the questions of title have not been resolved completely in the earlier suit as well as in the appeal. Earlier suits between the defendants opposite parties ended with compromise decree and by virtue of solenama, opposite parties got right to perform puja and other religious rites. The contention of the opposite parties is that since the present plaintiffs have no title over the suit land, they were validly left out from being added as defendants.

<u>12. It appears that the present opposite parties has filed a suit being Title Suit No. 51 of  2015 before the Joint District Judge 2nd Court, Sylhet seeking declaration of title and recovery of khas possession by evicting the present plaintiffs. Since the defendants have filed a title suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession, this aspect of the matter will be dealt with by the competent Court at the time of peremptory hearing of the suit.</u>

13. Admittedly till date no steps were taken by the opposite parties for eviction of the present petitioners, this aspect will also be considered and adjudicated in Title Suit No. 51 of 2015. The petitioners although claimed that they are in possession of the suit land by a deed dated 8-10-1966 from Dr Motilal Singh, the title of Motiall has not been proved in the Courts below, so only their claim is left.regarding their possession, as such all these points will be decided in Title Suit No. 51 of 2015.

14. In the above facts and circumstances, since a suit has been filed in competent Court seeking title and recovery of khas possession, all the aspects will be decided and resolved in that suit. Accordingly, the instant rule is disposed of in the terms and observation made herein before. Findings made herein will have no bearing in deciding Title Suit No. 51 of 2015, pending in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet.

15. The order of status-quo granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby re-called and vacated.

16. Send down the lower Courts records. Communicate the order.

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 11-6-2014 passed by the learned Special District Judge, Sylhet in Civil Revision No. 69 of 2011 disallowing the revision and affirming the judgment and order dated 11-10-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present Opposite Party No. 01 as Plaintiff filed a Title. Suit being No. 170 of 2009 before the 2nd court of the learned Joint District Judge, Sylhet against the defendant-petitioner and others for a declaration that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 220 of 1973 dated 26-5-1977 is inoperative, not effective and not binding upon the plaintiff contending inter alia that the plaintiff to the above mentioned Title Suit No. 220 of 1973 on a false allegation and on the basis of some forced anti dated papers filed the Title Suit being No. 222 of 1973 in the 2nd court of the learned Joint District Judge, Sylhet and in that suit behind the back of present-plaintiff who was the defendant No. 25 to that suit collusively after practicing fraud upon the present plaintiff obtained a collusive decree and the plaintiff-government of Bangladesh getting knowledge of that suit and decree on 29-3-2009 have preferred the Original Suit being No. 170 of 2009. After service of summons notices upon the defendants of the Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 the defendants No. 1-11 after making their appearance filed an application for rejection of plaint under Oder VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned trial court. The learned trial court i.e. the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd court, Sylhet hearing the parities to the suit by his judgment and order dated 11-10-2011 rejected the application for rejection of the plaint filed by the defendant-petitioner and others.

3. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred a civil revision No. 69 of 2011 in the court of the learned District Judge, Sylhet which was transmitted for hearing and disposal to Janonirapotta Bignokari Oporadh Damon Tribunal and Special Judge, Sylhet and the learned Special Judge, Sylhet by the impugned judgment and order dated 11-6-2014 disallowed the civil revision and affirmed the order of the learned trial court.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the 1st court of revision, the defendant No. 01 as petitioner with leave of this court has preferred 2nd revision under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained a Rule with an interim order of stay.

5. During hearing of the Rule, Mr Md Abdus Samad, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mr Md Abdul Hai, the learned Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr Md Shahidul Islam Khan, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party.

6. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned trial court as well as the 1st court of revision during disposal of the application for rejection of plaint and subsequent revisional application under section 115(2) of the code of Civil Procedure committed illegality. The learned advocate further submits that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 222 of 1973 has been affirmed by this court in Civil Revision 273 of 1982 and, as such, the courts below committed wrong in holding the view that the declaratory suit filed' by the defendant-government challenging the judgment and decree passed in earlier Tile Suit No. 222 of 1973 is maintainable. The learned Advocate also submits that the government claimed that the suit property is a vested and non-resident property, but after the promulgation of 'Arpito Sompotti Prottarpon Ain, 2001', it has been clear that the suit property is not a vested property, since it is not enlisted in the "Ka" schedule list, published in the official Gazette and, as such, there is no reason to file the original suit from the side of the government treating the property as vested property. The learned Advocate lastly after referring some decisions of our Apex court submits that the plaint submitted from the side of the defendant No. 25 in the declaratory suit being Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 is liable to be rejected under the ambit of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Deputy Attorney-General opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced form the side of the learned counsel for the petitioner and submits that, neither the trial court nor the 1st court of revision during passing their judgment and orders committed any illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the present-petitioner and others behind the back of the government without service of summons notice practicing fraud upon the court and the parties managed to obtain a collusive judgment and decree on 26-5-1977, which is not binding upon the defendant-government to that suit and challenging that judgment and decree the government instituted a Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 for getting a declaration that the judgment and decree passed in favour of the present-petitioner and others is ineffective, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also submits that, the area of the suit land is 12.36 acres in which the Government of Bangladesh has right, title, interest and possession, and stating the facts as to how and why the suit property is the government property, and the present-petitioner and others how has practiced fraud in getting their decree in their suit, filed the plaint in the Title Suit being No. 170 of 2009 which is pending for disposal on merit. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also submits that there is no scope to entertain the application for rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is no ingredient in the instant application for rejection of the plaint by which such application can be allowed. The learned Deputy Attorney-General lastly submits that against the judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 273 of 1982 of this court an appeal being No. Civil Appeal No. 360 of 2002 is pending before the Honorable Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh vide "Annexure-D-1". Therefore, it cannot be said that the Government is not empowered or have no locus standi or legal character to challenge the judgment and decree in their Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 before a competent court of law. The learned Deputy Attorney-General in the conclusion of his submission submits that, the decisions referred to from the side of the present-petitioner are not applicable in this case, since the facts and circumstances of this case is quite different with that of the facts and circumstances from where the decisions were given.

8. Considering the submission of the learned Advocates having gone through the  judgment and order passed by the trial court as well as the 1st court of revision and all other connected papers including the plaint of Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 (Annexure-A), the judgment and order passed by this court in Civil Revision No. 3780 of 2000 (Annexure-D), the schedule of the plaint of Title Suit No. 170 of 2009 and the certified copy of the order passed by their Lordships in Civil Appeal No. 360 of 2002 (Annexure-D-1), the application for rejection of pliant under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Annexure-B-1) it transpires that, the learned trial court during disposal of the application for rejection of plaint held that there is an allegation of fraud, raised from the side of the government; which is required to be looked into, and the application for rejection of plaint having no merit is liable to be rejected.

9. Subsequently, the 1st court of revision holding the view that there is a contention from the side of the government in their declaratory suit that the plaintiff to the former suit have practiced fraud and there is a collusion in the service of summons-notice upon the court. Besides this, the question of abatement of the suit which is raised from the side of the defendant-petitioner is required to be adjudicated at the time of trial of the original suit. The learned 1st revisional court finding no material for rejection of plaint affirmed the order of the trial court by the impugned judgment and order.

10. In this context, going through the contents of the application for rejection of plaint I find that the defendants No. 1-11 in their application under Order VII Rule 11 of the-Code of Civil Procedure contended that they have obtained the decree against the government and others without practicing any fraud or suppression of summons and the government who is the defendant No. 25 was well aware about the suit, but inasmuch as the Government has no title and interest in the suit property, they did not contest the Title Suit No. 222 of 1973. It was further contended in the application for rejection of plaint that there is no fraud or collusion in getting the decree in Title Suit No. 222 of 1973 and the decree has been affirmed by the Honorable High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Civil Revision No. 273 of 1982 and the Government only to stay the further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 04 of 2000 have instituted the subsequent Title Suit No. 170 of 2009.

11. It is to be mentioned here that, Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has empowered the court to reject the plaint in appropriate case, and the provisions lay down in the relevant Rule runs as follows:

The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:—

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

12. In the instant case as I have come across from the connected papers that here in this case, there is no such reason or ground as cited above, by which it can be held that the learned trial court as well as the 1st court of revision committed any illegality or infirmity in passing their judgment and orders. Furthermore, the contention which is given in the application for rejection of plaint is a mixed question of facts and law, which is required to be adjudicated by evidence and prior to that, at this stage there is no scope to draw such inference that the plaint is vexatious or the suit preferred by the government is barred by any law or there is no cause of action to prefer the suit as instituted from the side of the present-opposite party No. 01.

<u>13. In the case of rejection of plaint, the plaint alone and not the application of defendant shall be the basis of rejection of plaint. In the instant case I find that the present-opposite party No. 01 in their plaint has raised a specific cause of action which is their date of knowledge. The allegation raised by the defendant-petitioner is not proved or the plaint cannot be said mala fide at this stage. Apart from this, the plaint cannot be rejected outright before judging the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties to substantiate their pleadings. I find support in the decision of our Apex Court passed in the case of Nurul vs Moin 39 DLR (AD) 1.</u>

<u>14. Besides this, the application for rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has a very limited scope. Only where the ingredients spelt out earlier is apparent from the face of the record, the court is empowered to reject the plaint under the ambit of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

15. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and discussions referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that the decisions referred to from the side of the learned council for the petitioner have got no nexus in the instant case due to distinguishable facts and circumstances of the case.

16. Accordingly, the Rule has got no merit to succeed.

17. In the result; the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 11-6-2014 passed by the learned Special District Judge, Sylhet in Civil Revision No. 69 of 2011 is hereby affirmed.

18. The order of stay granted earlier by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment and order at once.

End.
