parties:
ABUL KHAIR TOBACCO AND OTHERS
Vs.
REGISTRAR OF TAXES AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin, J: This Rule has been issued calling upon opposite parties to show cause as to why order no.20 dated 23.02.2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 45 of 2010, should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that opposite party no.2 herein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.45 of 2010 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka, praying for perpetual injunction against infringement of Trade Marks and passing off goods under the Trade Marks Act, 2009, impleading the petitioner as defendant no.1 contending inter alia that the plaintiff company incorporate in Bangladesh having engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing tobacco and registered proprietor of the brand and trademark BRISTOL with its design and get up; The Trade Mark has been registered in the office of the Registrar of Trade Marks as TM 25519 dated 21.06.1987 under Class 34; The name BRISTOL was first registered by the plaintiff in 1942 and thereafter with changing demand of the consumers, new packs of. BRISTOL cigarettes were introduced; on 06.08.2009, plaintiff applied for Trade Mark registration of a new pack design of BRISTOL and obtained value. added tax (hereinafter called 'VAT') approval in this regard; On 10.08.2010, plaintiff again applied for Trade Mark registration of a new pack design as BRISTOL; By virtue of long usage and registration of the mark BRISTOL in respect of cigarettes, plaintiff has acquired exclusive right over the trade mark BRISTOL along with its design, style and get up; Recently plaintiff came to know that the defendant no.1 distributing leaflets in various trade outlets across the country introducing a new product namely BRISDOL with almost same get up as plaintiffs product BRISTOL; Plaintiff requested defendant no.2 in writing with copies to the defendant no.3 and other concerned authorities not to grant approval of the Mushak-1 form of BRISDOL submitted by defendant no.1; Defendant nos. 2 and 3 have not replied; In the meantime, defendant no.1 started manufacturing and marketing similar goods by adopting- BRISDOL as a trade mark with similar colour, design and get up; Defendant no.1 by using a deceptively and phonetically similar trade mark infringing trade mark of the plaintiff and also passing of their product as the product, of plaintiff and thus infringing plaintiffs intellectual property right and causing irreparable loss and damage to the plaintiff; Hence, the suit.

3. Defendant no. l filed written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint and contending inter alia that the defendant is a limited company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act and engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing various tobacco products in Bangladesh since 1998; In course of business, defendant adopted its trademark BRISDOL and started using the same on its product; On 27.09.2010, defendant applied to the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT, Comilla Division for fixation of price of the goods contains 10 sticks in a pack and VAT authority determined and fixed the value vide Memo dated 05.10.2010; Defendant applied to the Registrar of Trade Marks for a report whether any application pending for trademark similar to or identical with the defendant's trademark BRISDOL; No report was available indicating that there is any registered trademark BRISDOL; Following the search, defendant applied to the Registrar of Trademarks for registration of its trademark BRISDOL on 27.09.2010 and the same has been registered as Trademark Application No.136200 under class 34; Defendant's further applied for amendment of the application in prescribed form TM-16 on 13.10.2010; Following fixation of retail price by the VAT authority and by virtue of pending application before the Registrar of Trade Marks, defendant manufactured and marketed  its products bearing the trade mark BRISDOL in the month of September, October 2010 and paid huge amount of revenue to the Government exchequer; Upon enquiry, defendant came to know that plaintiff applied for the first time on 19.08.2009 for fixation of price of cigarettes bearing the trademark BRISTOL containing 20 sticks in each pack; VAT authority in the course of price fixation process afforded a hearing wherein plaintiff confirmed that the trademark BRISTOL has not been used for the last 22 years which is apparent from averments of the plaint filed by the plaintiff; As such, plaintiff's trademark is liable to be struck off from the register; Though plaintiff obtained price declaration for BRISTOL in the month of September, 2009, it never marketed its product under the said brand name until the defendant produced and marketed its product with trade mark BRISDOL on 27.09.2010 and obtained price approval from the VAT authority on 05.10.2010; Defendant no.1 manufacturing and marketing its product under trade name of BRISDOL identifying the same as a product of Abul Khair Tobaco Company Limited as such, there had not been any infringement of any trademark of the plaintiff inasmuch as the plaintiff had lost its trademark due to non use of the same for a long time; Furthermore, design and get up of the defendant's product is distinctive and dissimilar from that of the plaintiff's as such, there had not been any violation on the part of the defendant of any provision of the Trademarks Act, 2009; Defendant is the prior user of the trademark BRISDOL; Suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. On 23.03.2012, defendant no.1 filed an application in the suit under Section 102 of the Trademarks Act, 2009 read with section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for stay proceeding of the suit contending inter alia that defendant no.1 being petitioner filed Trademarks Application No.5 of 2010 impleading the plaintiff as opposite party in the High Court Division of Bangladesh Supreme Court under Section 98(1) read with section 42(1)(Kha) of the Trade Marks Act, 2009, for rectification of the Register of Trade Marks by way of striking off the Trade Marks No.10335 in Class-34 and being application no.135119 dated 10.08.2010. Upon hearing the applicant, this Division issued rule and stayed operation of the Registration of Trademark no.10335 dated 11.11.1942, Trade Mark No.25519 dated 21.06.1987 and Trade Mark No.28744 dated 10.05.1989 in respect of BRISTOL under Class-34, for a period of 3(three) months vide order dated 31.10.2010. Being aggrieved, Opposite party no.2 of the application i.e. plaintiff of the Title Suit filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2527 of 2010. After hearing the petitioner, Appellate Division stayed operation of the order passed by the High Court Division till 31.3.2011. As such, proceeding of Title Suit No.45 of 2010 for infringement of trademark is required to be stayed till disposal of the rectification proceeding pending in the apex court.

5. After hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/documents, learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, rejected the application holding that Title Suit and Trademarks application are two different types of cases with separate relief.

6. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order, defendant no.1 as petitioner preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present rule with an order of stay.

7. Mr. Tanjib-Ul- Alam appearing with Mr. Md. Hassan Habib, learned advocate for the petitioner by filing supplementary affidavit annexing Trade Marks Application no.5 of 2010 with annexures appended thereof and the order passed by 'the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2527 of 2010 submits that the court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order. Without considering that the Title Suit for infringement of trademark is required to be stayed till disposal of the rectification proceeding regarding the trademark now pending in the High Court Division. He also submits that the court below committed an illegality in not considering that the matter in issue in Title Suit No.45 of 201.0 is directly and substantially an issue in the Trade Marks Application no. 5 of 2010 and as such, proceeding of Title Suit should be stayed till disposal of the Trade Marks Application by the High Court Division. He again submits that a suit for infringement of the trademark with regard to validity of registration between the parties should be stayed under Section 102 of the Trademarks Act, 2009, read with Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure when rectification proceeding regarding the same Trade Mark is pending in the higher court. He next submits that the fact that trademark application filed after institution of the suit is immaterial for the purpose of stay. He further submits that court can stay proceeding of a suit even if it does not come within the purview of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for ends of justice to avoid unnecessary harassment to any party. In support of his submissions, learned Advocate referred to the case of Chandra Bhan Demblia Trading, Delhi, vs. Bharat Sewing Machine Co., Bikaner, reported in AIR 1982 Delhi, 230 and the case of Mst. Arifa Begum vs. Khulque Mohammad Naqvi, reported in 21 DLR (WP) 209.

8. On the other hand Mr. A. M. Aminuddin with Mr. M. Mushfiqur Rahman, learned advocates appearing for the opposite party no.2 submits that Appellate Division vide order dated 15.05.2013 passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2527 of 2010 send the Trade Marks Application no.05 of 2010 to this Division for early disposal on merit but the petitioner did not take any step for hearing of the application. He also submits that if the Title Suit is stayed till disposal of the Trade Marks Application then the opposite party no.2 shall suffer irreparable loss and injury inasmuch as Title Suit is filed for permanent injunction against infringement of trademark and passing of goods by the defendant no.1.

9. Heard the learned advocates. Perused revisional application, supplementary affidavit and annexures appended thereof.

<u>10. It appears that upon hearing the Trade Marks Application no. 5 of 2010 filed by the petitioner, this Division issued rule and also stayed operation of the registration of the opposite party no.2 relating to its product under trade name BRISTOL for a period of 3(three) months. Against the order, opposite party no.2 as petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2527 of 2010 before the Appellate Division of this court and prayed for stay of the order passed by this Division. Upon hearing the petitioner, Hon'ble Judge-in-Chamber stayed order of this Division till 31.03.2011. After hearing the parties, Appellate Division disposed of the leave petition with following observation.</u>

<u>"Upon hearing the learned Advocate, we are of the view that the ends of justice would be best served, if the Rule itself is disposed of on merit by the High Court Division.</u>

<u>Let this rule be heard and disposed of by the High Court Division as early as possible. The parties, if so advised may take steps for early disposal of the said Rule without any adjournment. However, the order of stay granted earlier by the learned Judge in Chamber be continued till disposal of the said Rule".</u>

11. It is apparent that in spite of said order by the Appellate Division, neither the petitioner nor the opposite party no.2 took step for disposal of the Trademarks Application no.5 of 2010.

12. Opposite party no.2 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit no.45 of 2010 for permanent injunction against infringement of the trademark and passing off goods under the Trade Marks Act, 2009, claiming defendant no.1 of the suit infringing plaintiffs intellectual property right and thereby causing irreparable loss to the plaintiff.

13. On the other hand, defendant no.1 of the suit i.e. present petitioner filed written statement denying the allegation contended that defendant is the prior user of the trademark BRISDOL, design and get up of the same is distinctive and different. Further contending that plaintiff did not use the trademark BRISTOL for a long period of 22 years as such, defendant's trademark is liable to be struck off from the register.

14. The petitioner filed Trade Marks Application no.5 of 2010 under Section 98(1) read with Section 42(1) l(Kha) of the Trade Marks Act, 2009 for rectification of the Register of Trade Marks. After filing written statement, defendant no.1 of the Title Suit filed an application under Section 102 of the Trade Marks Act, 2009 read with Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to stay proceeding of the suit till disposal of the Trademark Application.

15. Section 102 of the Trade Marks Act runs as follows:

"102. Stay of proceeding where the validity or registration of the trademark is questioned-(1) Where in any suit for the infringement of a trademark, the defendant pleads that the registration of the plaintiff trademark is invalid; or the plaintiff' pleads the invalidity of the registration of the defendant's trademark the Court trying the suit hereinafter referred to as the Court, shall:

(a) if any proceedings for rectification of the Register in relation to the plaintiffs or defendant's trademark are pending before the Registrar or the High Court Division, stay the suit pending the final disposal of such proceedings.

(b) if no such proceedings are pending and the Registrar is satisfied that the plea regarding the invalidity of the registration of the plaintiffs or defendant's trademark is prima facie tenable, raise an issue regarding the same and adjourn the case for a period of 3(three) months from the date of framing of the issue in order to enable the party concerned to apply to the High Court Division for rectification of the Register.

<u>16. Since plaintiff instituted Title Suit no.45 of 2010 praying permanent injunction against the defendant no.1 i.e. petitioner of the Trademark Application for infringement of Trade Mark and passing off goods under the Trade Marks Act and the defendant of said suit as applicant filed Trademark Application no.5 of 2010 before this Division under Section 98(1) read with Sections 48(1)(kha) of the Trade Marks Act, for rectification of the register of Trade Marks, I cannot agree with the finding of court below that Title Suit filed by the plaintiff and the Trademarks application filed by the defendant no.1 of the suit as applicant are two different type of cases and reliefs are also different.</u>

17. It appears that Title Suit no.45 of 2010 and Trademarks Application no.05 of 2010 are between the same parties challenging Trademark of one another. Defendant no.1 stated in his written statement that plaintiff did not use the trademark for the last 22 years as such plaintiff's trademark is liable to be struck off from the register. Defendant no.1 of the suit as applicant filed Trade Marks Application no.05 of 2010 under Section 98(1) read with Section 42(1)(kha) of the Trade Marks Act, 2009, for rectification. Title Suit and Trade Marks Application arising out of same dispute between the same parties. Suit is for infringement of Trade Mark and Application is for rectification challenging validity of registration of Trade Marks of each other. When rectification proceeding is pending before this court, Suit for infringement of Trademark pending in the Court below should be stayed in view of Section 102 of the Trade Marks Act, 2009. I find support of this view in the case of Chandra Bhan Dembla Trading, Delhi, -Vs-Bharat Sewing Machine Co. Bikaner, reported in AIR 1982 DELHI 230, wherein it is held:

"A suit for infringement of trademark, in which the contest between the parties is with regard to validity of registration of each other, can be stayed when rectification proceedings regarding the trademarks are pending."

18. Under the facts and circumstances of the case and for the reasons stated above, I am of the view that Court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order.

19. Accordingly, rule is made absolute.

20. Order dated 23.02.2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge; 2nd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit no.45 of 2010 is set aside.

21. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule and extended from time to time is hereby vacated.

22. In view of the order passed by the Appellate Division, the parties are directed to take necessary step for early hearing of Trade Marks Application no.5 of 2010.

23. Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concern at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 10.03.2013 and 14.03.2013 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 214 Court, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No.10 of 2002 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 29.11.2001 and 05.01.2002 respectively passed by the learned. Assistant Judge, Chitalmari, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.51 of 1998 decreeing the suit in part should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the predecessor of the present respondent-opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted the original Title Suit being No.51 of 1998 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Chitalmari for partition, contending inter alia, that one Narayan Chandra Bala was the recorded tenant in S.A. khatian No.125, under Mouza. Khoromkhali of Chitalmari Upazila under Bagerhat District along with his other co-sharers in the suit holding in 50% share comprising an area of 2.01 acres of land. He was also a recorded tenant in 3/4 share comprising an area of 1.78 acres of land in S.A. khatian No.I99 of the same Mouza. The father of Narayan Chandra namely Bhaggya Dhar Bala during his life time obtained 0.52 acres of land in plot No.202 appertaining to C.S. khatian No.73 corresponding to S.A. khatian No.201 and 299 from a recorded tenant of the suit holding one Malek Mia and others. Thereafter, the father of the plaintiffs erected his dwelling but on 0.52 acres of land and subsequently died leaving behind his son Narayan Chandra Bala. During peaceful possession of the plaintiffs while one Darikanath Bala tried to dispossess the plaintiffs, the plaintiffs filed a civil suit which was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs up to the appellate court. In the subsequent record of right the land of plot No.202 of C.S. khatian No.73 while not recorded in the name of Narayan, he filed a suit being Title Suit No.285 of 1985 and during pendency of that suit he died leaving behind two sons Bankim Chandra Bala and Suklal Bala. Bankim Chandra in the aforesaid suit alleged that he is the sole successor of his father Narayan Chandra Bala. At the death of Suklal, Bankim Chandra did not substitute the heirs of Suklal. Subsequently, Bankim Chandra by a registered sub-kabala dated 20.06.1990 transferred 0.16 acres of land from plot No.201 and .06 acres of land from plot No. 197 of S.A. khatian No.199 and 0.10 acres of land from plot No.202 of S.A. khatian No.201/299 measuring the total land 0.12 acres in favour of the plaintiffs and delivered possession therein. It is also the case of the plaintiffs that Suklal transferred 0.25 acres of land of the suit holding in favour of one Moazzem Hossain and Moniruzzaman by a registered kabala dated .24.11.1985, who subsequently transferred the same in favour of the plaintiffs by a registered transfer deed dated 15.06.1988. In this way; the plaintiffs after acquiring right, title, interest and possession in the land measuring 0.50 acres by a mutation proceedings mutated their names and opened a separate khatian being No.199/1. The further case of the plaintiffs is such that Suklal by a kabala dated 12.04.1997 transferred 0.26 acres of land from suit plot No.202 in favour of the plaintiffs and thereafter the plaintiffs acquired in all 0.86 acres of land in the suit holding and Civil Suit being No.59 of 1997 which was filed against the decree of Title Suit No.285 of 1985 was dismissed for default and that the defendant No.1 created a false nadabi-paira from Suklal on 16.10.1997 and that due to the difficulty of ejmali possession with the defendants the plaintiffs requested the defendants for amicable partition but they refused, which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit for partition in respect of 0.86 acres of land in the suit holding.

3.The contrary case of the defendant No.1, who contested the suit and who is the petitioner of this revisional application in short is thus that he is the sole successor in interest of the recorded tenant Narayan Chandra Bala and Suklal never executed any kabala on 12.04.1997 and also not filed Title Suit No.59 of 1997. The further case of the defendant-petitioner is such that by way of false personification the aforesaid kabala deed was obtained and the defendant by a transfer deed dated 20.06.1990 transferred 0.16 acres of land from plot No.251 and 0.06 acres of land from plot No.196 measuring 0.22 acres in all, and the plaintiffs fraudulently inserted the land which is the homestead property in the kabala and that the defendant never delivered possession to that land from suit plot No.222 and the defendant-petitioner did not take any consideration money for the aforesaid land from the plaintiffs. Against that kabala dated 20.06.1990 the defendant has filed a Title Suit No.82 of 1998. It is the case of the defendant-petitioner that the plaintiffs are possessing only 0.22 acres of land in the suit holding.

4. During trial of the original suit the learned trial court after framing 05(five) different issues decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs to the extent of 0.73 acres of land in the suit holding by the judgment and decree dated 29.11.2001.

5. Being aggrieved the defendant-petitioner preferred a Title Appeal being No.10 of 2002 in the Court of learned District Judge, Bagerhat, which was transmitted to the 2nd Court of learned Joint District Judge, Bagerhat for hearing and disposal and the learned appellate court hearing the appeal by the impugned judgment and decree dated 10.03.2013 disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the defendant-appellant-petitioner have preferred this revisional .application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay.

7. During hearing of this Rule Mr. Sadananda Rana the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while none appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned trial court as well as the appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed illegality in holding the view that the suit is liable to be decreed. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit was bad for defect of party, but neither the trial court; nor the appellate court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit suffers from defect of party. The learned Advocate argued that, with regard to the defect of party the witness No.1 of the plaintiffs in his deposition admitted that there are some necessary parties, who are left out from the plaint. The learned Advocate also submits that the defendant-appellant-petitioner categorically alleged in his pleading that in the kabala deed dated 20.06.1990 the plaintiffs fraudulently included 0.10 acres of land which is a homestead in plot No.202 and against that fraudulent kabala deed the defendant has filed a Title Suit being No.82 of 1998 and for that, the defendant-petitioner prays for calling the volume book of the concern kabala deed for comparison. The learned Advocate during hearing of the Rule has submitted for additional evidence and lastly submits that for the reason mentioned earlier both the courts below erred-in-law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be interfered with.

9. In order to appreciate the submission of the learned Advocate having gone through the judgment and decree passed by the trial court as well as the Appellate Court and the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties and all other relevant papers including the case records I find that, admittedly the suit land along with other property originally belonged to Narayan Chandra Bala and it transpires that Narayan Chandra died leaving behind two sons Bankim Chandra Bala and Suklal Bala who inherited the property left behind their father.

10. Consulting the relevant papers it also transpires that the petitioner's case is such that his full brother Suklal Bala executed a nadabipatra in his favour and Bankim Chandra by dint of this paper claimed his exclusive title and interest in the suit land and claimed him the sole successor-in-interest of Narayan Chandra Bala. The learned Appellate Court with regard to this rightly appraised the legal aspect that a nadabipatra as alleged does not create or extinguish any title and interest in favour of anybody in respect of property. It is found that from a kabala deed dated 24.12.1985 which has been marked as Exhibit-3 and the kabala deed dated 15.06.1988 (Exhibit-8) the plaintiffs have become co-sharers in the suit holding to the extent of .0.21 acres of land in plot No.201 and 199 and 0.04 acres of land in plot No.196.

11. Both the parties to the suit, to substantiate their respective claim have adduced witnesses and the plaintiffs have examined 05(five) witnesses and submitted their basic documents marked as exhibits. On the other hand, the defendant-petitioner has examined 03 witnesses in support of his case and submitted some documentary evidence, which are also have been marked as exhibits by the learned trial court. It is the concurrent findings and decisions of both the courts below that in the lands of S.A. khatians No. 201, 299, 199 and 125 the predecessors of the parties have got their interest and title: In the land measuring 1.78 acres the predecessor of the parties namely Narayan Chandra had 1.1866 acres of land corresponding to S.A. khatian No.199 and two sons at the demise of their father acquired .59333 acres of land. It further appears from the observation and findings of the courts below that the learned trial court under the ambit of section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872 compared the signature of Suklal Bala and scrutinized the signature with the registered sub-kabala deed dated 24.12.1985 with the signature as it appears in kabala deed dated 12.04.1996' which has been marked as Exhibit-5 and after comparison of the signatures, conclusively held that the signatures as it appears with the deed under challenge in Title Suit No.82 of 1998 is the product of same individual and it is decided concurrently by the trial court as well as the Appellate Court that the allegation of forgery as raised from the side of the defendant-petitioner is not proved by any tangible evidence and as a result the plaintiffs to the suit obtained 0.26 acres of land in the suit plot No.202 by virtue of the kabala deed dated 12.04.1997 and the plaintiffs have succeeded to establish their plaint case by cogent evidence and that they have title and possession to the extent of 0.22 acres of land in suit plot No.197 and 201 by the purchase deed dated 20.06.1990.

12. Having gone through the evidence on records I find that P.W.1 Md. Amir Ali, who is the predecessor-in-interest of the present opposite parties No.1-4, testified in support of their pleading. During his deposition he testifies at a stage that the Bankim Chandra Bala without including his brother instituted Title Suit No.56 of 1997 alone, which was subsequently decreed. It was further testified that for the reason stated above, the decree was not enforceable against Suklal Bala, the brother of Bankim Chandra Bala. This witness purchased 83 decimals of land from the heirs of Suklal and Bankim. He also purchased 32 decimals of land from Bankim Chandra on 20.06.1990. P.W.1 in his deposition testifies at a stage that he requested the defendant on 15.07.1998 for amicable partition, but the defendant denied. P.W.1 in his cross-examination testified at a stage that they did not include one Kalidas, Debdas, Horish Mokter Shekh and Ashok Roy in their suit. This witness also testified that one Choitanyo and Sumanta Tarafder are not parties.

13. P.W.2 Sk. Fayekuzzaman is the possession witness of the plaintiffs and this witness testified that he knows the parties and the suit land which is being possessed by the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs have garden in the suit property.

14. P.W.3 Yosuf Ali Sikdar is a deed-writer of Chitalmari Registry Office. He deposed in support of the deed No.1006 dated 12.04.1997 executed by Suklal. This witness as scribe of the deed identified his signature in the said deed.

15. P.W.4 Montanzir Hossain is a Bank Emplyee who as per direction of the Court has brought a deed dated 15.06.1988 which was submitted in their bank for obtaining loan as mortgage and the plaintiff Amir All mortgaged that deed and obtained loan from the bank. This witness compared the photocopy of the deed with the original, which has been marked as Exhibit-8.

16. P.W.5 Abdur Rob Sheikh testified in support of 32 decimals of land transferred by a kabala executed by the defendant-petitioner in favour of the plaintiff Amir Ali. This witness deposed that the consideration money was paid in his presence, which was Tk.25,000/- and the plaintiff possess that land.

17. Vis-à-vis; the D:W.1 of the defendant, who is the defendant No.1 himself Bankim Chandra Bala in his testimony testified that he is the defendant to the suit and the total land of plot No.232 of the C.S. khatian No.73 consists of 52 decimals originally belonged to one Abdul Goni and Bhaggya Dhar was a tenant under him. This witness testified in support of his written statement.

18. During cross-examination the defendant Bankim Chandra conceded that Narayan Chandra died leaving behind 02 sons, he (D.W.1) and Suklal at the time of death of Narayan Chandra were in India. This witness further admitted that at the death of their father, in Title Suit No.285 of 1985, he (D.W.1) claiming himself the only heir of Narayan Chandra substituted. This witness in a reply to a question from the side of the plaintiffs testified that, he cannot say as to what date Suklal went to India and he (D.W.1) will not be able to produce any lawful paper to substantiate that Suklal migrated to India.

19. D.W.2 is one Santosh Kumar Howlader. This witness deposed about the possession of the defendant-petitioner in 52 decimals of land of the suit holding.

20. D.W.3 Gojen Chandra Roy also stated in support of the possession of the defendant-petitioner in 52 decimals of land.

21. During cross-examination this witness frankly testified that in the khatian No.299 total quantum of land is 3.22 acres and beside plot No.202 he cannot recollect anything about the land of remaining plots.

22. On meticulous assessment of the evidence on records along with other materials to the original suit I find that the courts below with regard to possession of the property rightly held that, in a suit for partition constructive possession is enough and possession of one co-sharer amounts of possession of all the co-sharers of the suit holding.

<u>23. Apart from this; from the testimony of the witnesses it transpires that the plaintiffs to the suit in order to succeed in their case examined their witnesses as stated above, who were thoroughly cross-examined from the side of the defendant and from the trend of their cross-examination as well as from their testimonies, no such material contradiction, omission or ambiguity is noticed by which it can be held that the plaintiff's witnesses are not competent, trustworthy or credible. The courts below concurrently in their findings arrived at a decision that the plaintiffs to the suit by sufficient tangible evidence have been successfully discharged' their onus in proving their title and interest to the extent of 0.73 acres of land in the disputed holding pursuant to their three title documents marked as Exhibits-4, 5 & 8. With regard to left out parties to the suit it was observed by the learned courts below that the plaintiffs has no claim against the recorded tenants who has been left out from the plaint of the plaintiffs and there is no chance from the side of the contesting defendant No.1 of prejudice, in absence of the persons who were not included as party to the suit. The persons in whose presence an effective and proper adjudication into the matter-in-dispute is possible, they are already on record inasmuch as they have been made party to arrive at an efficacious relief to the parties.</u>

<u>24. It is to be noted in the context of defect of parties that Order I Rule 9 and 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides that, a party may be considered a necessary party if the following two conditions are satisfied. Firstly; there must be right to some relief against him in respect of the matter involved in the suit and secondly; his presence should be necessary in order to enable the court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit. In the case of Johan —vs.- Shamsu, 27 DLR (SC) 129, our Apex Court has clearly held that in the above mentioned two cases only the presence of the party is required to be looked into strictly.</u>

25. Apart from this; a suit cannot be defeated by reason of mis-joinder or non-joinder of parties if it is found that in absence of those persons proper efficacious relief can be awarded. [Ref: Safaruddin —vs.- Fazlul 49 DLR (AD) 51, Sufia —vs.- Amin 10 BLC(AD) 41, Motilal —vs.- Benodini 28 DLR (SC) 5, Akhtanur —vs.- Habib, 31 DLR(AD) 88, Abu —vs.- Government 31 DLR (AD)218 and Abdus —vs.- Sohrab 1 BLD (AD) 77].

26. In our revisional jurisdiction, where glaring in consistency with the evidence on records is noticed and where it appears that there has been misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, in that case only this Court invoking its revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is entitled to exercise this jurisdiction to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the learned courts below. Otherwise, the Appellate Court being the final court of facts, the judgment and decree passed by this court is immune from interference.

27. In the instant case, I find no such glaring inconsistency or misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with.

28. Having, regard to the facts, circumstances and discussions referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that the Rule has got no merit to succeed.

29. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The judgment and decree dated 10.03.2013 and 14.03.2013 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No.10 of 2002 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 29.11.2001 and 05.01.2002 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Chitalmari, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.51 of 1998 is hereby 'affirmed.

30. Let the order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

31. However; there will be no order as to costs.

32. Communicate the judgment and order at once and send down the Lower Court's Records immediately.

End.

MILON CHANDRA BANIK @ DHAR AND ANOTHER
Vs.

full_judgment:
Khizir Ahmed Choudhury, J: The instant rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-7 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order No.11 dated 13.03.2016 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 450 of 2014 rejecting the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedures should not be set aside.

2. Opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted other suit No. 450 of 2014 in the 1st Court of Joint district Judge, Chittagong praying for declaration of title; right to use the pond in the suit land jointly; judgment and decree passed by learned Additional Assistant Judge, Chittagong in Other Title Suit No. 41 of 1992 will not create any obstruction in the peaceful possession of the plaintiff and the defendants are not entitled to take any step by virtue of execution case No.01 of 2014 pending in the Court of Assistant Judge, 1st Additional Court, Chittagong and other reliefs.

3. The case of the plaintiff in brief is that suit property originally belonged to 2 brothers namely Ananta Mohan and Kashi Mohan whose name record of right is prepared. Ananta Mohan had no issue and Kashi Mohan died leaving behind his son Porikkhit Banik and as such the Schedule property devolved to Porikkhit Banik and he had been enjoying the property as rightful owner and possessor for a considerable period of time and his name also appeared in the P.S. Khatian No.341/1, 5878/2 and Khatian No. 341/2 as well as B.S. Khatian No. 2978. Suit land consists of house, pond and Viti type. Due to financial stringency Porikkhit Banik relinquished his right title and interest over the suit property to opposite party No.1 vide registered deed No.1655 dated 24.08.1997 who has been enjoying and possessing the suit property without any let or hindrance. On 27.06.2014 the defendant along with some others tried to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land on the pretext of a decree in respect of the suit land in a suit for specific performance of contract. To avoid untoward incidence the plaintiff filed a case under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and subsequently in order to remove the cloud constrained to file the instant suit.

4. The defendants entered appearance and by filing an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure prayed for rejection of the plaint contending that the suit property originally belonged to Mohendra Lal Dey and on his death it devolved upon his three sons Kali Shankar Dey, Hari Shankar Dey and Narayan Chandra Dey. Petitioner's father instituted Other Class Suit No. 45 of 1990 before the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, having renumbered as Other Class Suit No.41 of 1992 having transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, first Additional Court, Chittagong, seeking specific performance of contract contending that the owners proposed to sell the suit property to the father of the petitioners and accordingly entered into a agreement on 07.12.1989 fixing Tk.60,000/- as consideration money out of which Tk.35,000/- was paid as baina money and it was stipulated that after obtaining requisite permission from Income Tax authority and observing other formalities the owners will execute and register deed of sale on receiving Tk.35,000/-. Father of the petitioner after complying terms and condition and observing formalities demanded execution and registration of deed of sale on the basis of oral contract but the owner of the property declined to execute and register deed of sale. Petitioners' father demanded on several occasions for execution and registration of the Kabala and lastly on 18.03.1990 he approached the predecessor of the defendant to execute and register deed of sale and ultimately constrained to file the suit which was decreed in favour of the predecessor of the petitioners on 31.08.1992 against which the defendants of that suit preferred Other Appeal No.521 of 1992 which was allowed whereby Judgment and Decree passed by the trial Court was set aside, against which the petitioners father filed Civil Revision No. 4756 of 1995 before the High Court Division and after hearing rule was made absolute which was challenged before the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave To appeal No.81 of 2011 by the predecessor of the defendants and the Appellate Division also upheld the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division which was again challenged by the predecessor of the defendants by filing Civil review petition before the Appellate division which was also dismissed. The predecessor of defendant No.10 and 11 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.98 of 1992 before the senior assistant Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong impleading the predecessor of present petitioner as defendant, praying for declaration of title and permanent injunction which was decreed in his favour on 27.04.1996.

5. The father of the defendant No.1 and 2 preferred Other Appeal No.153 of 1996 and after hearing the Appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereafter Parikkhit Banik preferred Civil Revision No.4903 of 1999 before the High Court Division but subsequently he withdrew the said Civil Revision. The further contention of the petitioners is that, present plaintiff deposed as DW.2 in Other Suit No.41 of 1992 and knowing well about the decree obtained by the predecessor of the petitioners purchased the suit land by registered deed of sale dated 24.08.1997 being deed No. I655 and as such the suit is barred by resjudicata and also barred under clause (b) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. Defendant-opposite parties by filing written objection against the prayer for rejection of plaint stated that the contents of the application does not come within the purview of order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and since the statement made in the application requires to prove by evidence it cannot be resolved through application filed under order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They further averred that the valuation as given in the plaint is reasonable and sustainable and as such the application of Order 7 Rule 11 for rejection of plaint is liable to be rejected.

7. Learned Joint District Judge by order dated 13.03.2016 rejected the application for rejection of plaint on the ground that resjudicata is a mixed question of law and facts and it can only be decided after adducing evidence at the time of peremptory hearing, and hence the instant rule.

8. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury along with Ms. Sonia Parvin and Ms. Bithi Roy appeared for the petitioners. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury learned advocate for the petitioners submits that, in a suit for specific performance of contract, the predecessor of the petitioners got decree in his favour which was upheld up to appellate division and thereby the predecessor of the present petitioners became absolute owner and possessor of the suit property, apart from this Porikkhit Banik, who is transferee of the present plaintiff filed Title Suit No.98 of 1992 seeking declaration of title and other reliefs regarding the suit land where he got decree which was reversed by the appellate court which he challenged in the high court division and ultimately he had withdrawn the civil revision and thereafter he transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff and as such the suit is clearly barred by the principle of resjudicata. He also submits that since the original owners lost in the earlier proceedings, the present suit filed by the transferee of the previous owners is malafide which is filed to cause harassment to the present petitioners and as such the suit is not maintainable. Ile next submits that the present plaintiff-opposite party as DW. 2 deposed in earlier suit having filed for specific performance of contract and he had full knowledge about the decree obtained by the predecessor of the petitioners and as he purchased the property knowing fully well about the decree, the plaint is liable to be rejected as vexatious one. He next submits that in the instant matter all the facts and circumstances amply justifies that the present suit has been initiated by a person whose predecessor lost up to appellate division and he cannot get any title from persons who lost in earlier proceedings and so the present proceeding is bound to fail and as such learned Joint District committed error in not rejecting the plaint. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury further submits that Porikkhit Banik has withdrawn Civil revision No.4903 of 1999 from the High Court division without taking permission to sue afresh and as such his subsequent transferee is precluded to initiate fresh suit on the self same cause of action and as such the suit filed by the opposite party claiming purchase of the same from Porikkhit Banik cannot be proceeded with and the plaint was required to be rejected but the Joint District Judge without adverting that vital aspect of the case rejected the application simply contending the question of resjudicata is to be decided during trial.

9. Learned advocate in support of his contention referred the case of Abdul Matin Vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh 13 BLC 30, Rezaul Karim and others Vs Moulana Md. Harun-ur-Rashid and others 12 BLC 705, Syed Md. Shah Jalal Nure Alam and others Vs Salimullah Chowdhury and others 10 MLR AD 91 and also a decision reported 22 DLR in the case of Zohural haque Moral and ors Vs Abdul Karim Molla and ors 545, A.Z.M. Khalilur Rahman Vs Md. Syed Hossain and ors 25 DLR 485.

10. Per contra Mr. Probir Neogi, learned advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that in the application filed by the predecessor of the present petitioners for rejection of plaint was on the ground of being barred by resjudicata and admittedly the question of resjudicata is to be resolved by taking evidence and as such the application filed under Order 7 Rule 11 being not entertainable the court of first instance rightly rejected the application. He further submits that in considering application under order 7 Rule 11 of the C.P. Code, the statement made in the plaint is only to be relied upon, any other applications and materials are to be kept out of consideration and the trial Court rightly rejected the application relaying upon the established principles. He submits that in the plaint a clear cause of action has been delineated by the plaintiffs and as such the statement made by the defendant-petitioner in the application filed under Order 7 Rule 11 is not to be considered by the Trial Court. He further submits that the present opposite party No.1 has purchased the suit land from Porikkhit Banik who was admitted owner of the suit property and he has got every right to retain and enjoy the suit property as absolute owner and as such without establishing right title and interest by producing papers and by adducing reliable evidence, the present petitioner are not entitled to interfere in the rightful title and possession of the plaintiff. He next submits that the valuation as made in the plaint is correct and proper valuation and the defendant-petitioner failed to show any paper to the effect that the valuation is not correct and even for undervaluation, plaint should not be rejected as the valuation can be raised an updated at any point of time since the suit was pending in the Court of Joint District Judge who possess unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction for entertaining any suit. He next submits that the present opposite party No.1 is a bonafide purchaser from the owner of the suit land and he having possessed the suit land after purchase as rightful owner, his title cannot be denied by any devices. Mr. Probir Neogi in support of his contention referred the case of Chandu Lal Agarwalla and another Vs Khalilur Rahman and others 3DLR 403, Rezaul Karim and others Vs Moulana Md. Harun-ur-Rashid and others, 12 BLC 705, Sree Chandan Ranjan Sarker Vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others 18 MLR 49, Mahbubul Haque (Md) Vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR AD 49, Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another Vs A.K.M. Habibur. Rahman and others 13 BLD AD 217 and Razia Sultana and another Vs Mir Shahinul Islam 22 BLC 288 in support of his contention.

11. Having gone through the pleadings, relevant papers, application and supplementary affidavit it appears that the present opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No.450 of 2014 impleading the petitioner as defendants praying for declaration of title, challenging decree passed in Other Suit No.41 of 1992 and along with a prayer for permanent injunction restraining the defendants not to dispossess him from the suit land. Admittedly the plaintiffs claimed to have purchased the suit land from Porikkhit Banik, the predecessor of defendant No. 9 and 10 of the suit by a sale deed dated 24.08.1997 being sale deed No.1655. It also appears that Porikkhit Banik prior to sale of the suit land to the present opposite party No.1 instituted title Suit No.98 of 1992 before the Senior Assistant Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong praying for declaration of title confirmation of possession and permanent injunction where he got decree in his favour on 27.04.1996 and the said decree was challenged before the District Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.153 of 1996 which is transferred to Joint District Judge, Commercial Court, Chittagong and after hearing the appeal was allowed by judgment and decree dated 24.10.1999 setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. Thereafter Porikkhit Banik preferred Civil Revision No.4903 of 1999 before the High Court division and ultimately he withdrew the said Civil Revision on 11.05.2010. While allowing the withdrawal, the High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court as well as the Trial Court. Now it is vitally important to look into the contents of the application for withdrawing the Civil Revision. The contents of the application for withdrawal was to the effect that on perusal of the record the plaintiff-petitioner have understood that they should not have filed the suit and now on proper understanding of overall situation have decided not to proceed with the suit. The transferor of the present plaintiff did not sought any permission to refile the suit due to any formal defect or any other reasons, rather it has been mentioned in clearest terms that they should not have filed the suit and decided not to proceed with the same. Now it is to be considered in absence of any leave from the court whether a fresh suit can be instituted by the same person or his transferee claiming title in the suit since no permission was taken for instituting a fresh suit. It appears that Porikkhit Banik who filed the earlier suit has transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff who after purchase again filed the suit seeking declaration of title, permanent injunction and other identical reliefs being made in the earlier suit. It is clear that the vendor of the petitioner filed title Suit No.41 of 1992. Since vendor of the present petitioners withdrew Revisional application as well as his suit, the present petitioner being successor-in-interest is not entitled to file the instant suit. For better understanding order 23 rule 1 is reproduced bellow:

"R.1 Withdrawal of suit or abandonment of part of claim (1) At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim.

(2) Where the Court is satisfied-(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or

(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim, it may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim.

(3) Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim.

(4) Nothing in this rule shall be deemed to authorise the Court to permit one of several plaintiffs to withdraw without the consent of the others."

12. Since no permission is accorded for instituting fresh suit, the present suit filed by the transferee of the previous plaintiff is not maintainable.

13. In the case of Moon Garments Industries vs Janata Bank 50 DLR it is held that

"We have considered the language of Order 23, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which clearly gives an unqualified right to a plaintiff to withdraw from suit at any time. When the plaintiff withdraws from his suit without seeking permission to sue afresh as contemplated under rule 1(2), the plaintiff is precluded from instituting any fresh suit? In respect of the subject-matter or the claim made in the suit so withdrawn"

14. Now the question arises whether in an application under Order 7 Rule 11 this fact can be examined and scrutinized in absence of any evidence to be adduced by parties at the time of peremptory hearing. So far the factual aspect is concerned nobody is denying the suits and proceeding being carried on by the parties but only legal point to be considered whether the application under Order 7 Rule 11 can be entertained and disposed of on the point of the suit being barred by resjudicata as mentioned in the application before taking the suit to the peremptory hearing. Since the parties are not disputing the papers and documents filed by them, the documents are taken to be admitted. Now the questions come whether the suit should be carried on to the peremptory hearing or can be disposed of upon the papers and documents as kept in the record. It is fairly established here that the parties indulged in various litigation in as many as courts in respect of the suit property and in all the proceedings, the present petitioners got verdict in his favour. The present plaintiff is not claiming title otherwise from Porikkhit Banik whose predecessor lost up to appellate division and after losing in the appeal, Porikkhit Bank himself has withdrawn the revisional application. In a landmark decision reported in 53 DLR AD 12 our appellate division clearly held that if ultimate result of the suit is as clear as daylight, it should not be proceeded further rather it should be buried at its inception. The facts and circumstances of that suit are quite identical with the facts and circumstances of the present suit. In that suit the predecessor of the plaintiffs by filing title suit went up to appellate division and got decree in their favour but the defendants subsequently by filing another suit tried to challenge the decree of the earlier suit and in the circumstances our appellate division clearly held that the defendant should not be allowed to proceed with the suit as their predecessor has fought up to appellate division unsuccessfully. Similar and identical scenarios have been emerged in the present suit, so apart from order 7 rule 11 of the code of Civil Produce the court can invoke inherent jurisdiction to do justice.

15. It is fairly evident that evidence is not necessary for resolution of disputes in this matter. Although by filing application under Order 7 Rule 11 code of Civil Procedure, the petitioners raised the question of resjudicata but in fact this particular matter clearly comes within the ambit of inherent power of the Court which can take a decision in an appropriate case since the case in hand is quite identical with the facts and circumstances of the reported decisions of 53 DLR AD 12. The facts and circumstance and factual matrix as mentioned in the application clearly made out a case for exercising inherent power.

16. Mere mentioning wrong provision in the application does not invalidate any application or order where actually source of power exists, so it is a fit case for exercising inherent power of the Court and this court the suit as filed by the opposite party No.1 should not be proceeded with. Apart from this in the case of Md. Shahjahan Siraj Vs Md. Rafique Quoraishi and others 2 ALR AD 202 our appellate division held that plaint can be rejected on the ground of resjudicata and the Court is quite to consider resjudicata in an application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Relevant paragraph of the said decision is here under,

"Having gone through the plaints of both the suits, we are of the view that the plaints of both the suits were rightly rejected by the learned Additional District Judge but that should have been done by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil procedure. Therefore, the plaints of both the suits shall be deemed to have been rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the materials on record justify to do so."

<u>17. The principles enunciated in the decision of 22 BLC 288, 18 MLR 49 are that the Court cannot travel beyond the averments made in the plaint and cannot take into consideration regarding maintainability of the suit but by this time it is fairly settled that in an appropriate case Court can reject plaint by invoking inherent power under section 151 of the code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case inherent power of the Court has been invoked given the facts and circumstances of the case and as such the referred decision is distinguishable here. The decision referred in 13 BLD AD 217, 12 BLC 705, 3 DLR 403, 52 DLR AD 49 are regarding the principals of resjudicata wherein it has been held that resjudicata is mixed question of law and fact and such plea is to be considered upon taking evidence but meanwhile it is propounded in the decision referred in 2 ALR AD 203 as referred above, that in an appropriate case the Court can reject the plaint on the question of resjudicata by invoking inherent power of the Court and the instant case being appropriate one for invoking such power given the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the decision as referred above is not applicable here as the case clearly came within the perimeter of the principals as enunciated in the decision of 2 ALR AD 203 and 53 BLR AD 12.</u>

18. Another striking feature is that the present plaintiff deposed as DW.2 in earlier proceeding whereby the predecessor of the present opposite party got decree in their favour in a suit for specific performance of contract, so he cannot be termed a person who is unaware about the litigation and outcome of the suits. Apart from this Porikkhit Banik transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff although Porikkhit Banik by filing title suit seeking declaration of title lost in that suit, so it is clearly established that a clever design and many waver has been Exercised by Porikkhit Banik and present plaintiff regarding suit land for depriving the lawful owner of the suit land. The plaintiff also can't be termed as bonafide purchaser.

19. Above factual scenarios clearly establish case in favour of the petitioners. The application filed by the plaintiff for rejection of plaint merits consideration and accordingly the rule is made absolute.

20. The plaint of title Suit No.450 of 2014 pending in the court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong is rejected. The parties will bear their respective cost.

21. Communicate the order.

End.
