full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgement and decree dated 07.07.2015 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No.03 of 2013 dismissing the appeal.

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of the instant civil petition for leave to appeal, are that Gopal Chandra Majumder, the predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos.1-7 and respondent Nos.8,9 and 12-16 herein as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.484 of 2012 impleading the present petitioners and respondent Nos.17-28 as defendants praying for declaration of title in the 'ka' schedule property and further declaration that registered deeds of sale No.4132, No.4134, No.4130, No.4139 all dated 07.09.1996 and No.3510 dated 31.08.1998, as described in the "kha" schedule to the plaint are inoperative, valueless, ineffectual and the plaintiffs are not bound by those deeds and also to pass a decree for evicting defendant Nos.1-11 from schedule Ga(1)-Ga(5)land.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in brief, is that the suit properties belonged to Satish Mohon Roy, who has two sons namely Sushil Mohon Roy and Narayan Chandra Roy, 4 daughters namely Purno Shashi, Charu Bala, Swadeshi Bala and Bina Bala. Purno Shashi was married with Shubol Chandra Das, son of Subodh Chandra Das. Except Purno Shashi Das, the sons and other daughters left for India, where they started residing as their permanent abode and in spite of earnest request by Satish Mohon Roy, they did not return to Bangladesh. Purno Shashi Das and her husband Subol Chandra Das came to the homestead of Satish Mohon Roy and started to reside there taking care of Satish Mohon Roy. Subsequently, Satish Mohon Roy executed a Will in favour of Purno Shashi Das on 03.01.1962 appointing Subol Chandra Das as executor of the Will. Purna Shashi Das and her husband Subol Chandra Das continued to reside with Satish Monon Roy by looking after him. Thereafter, Satish Mohon Roy died and, subsequently, Subol Chandra Das, executor of the Will initiated Probate Case No.19 of 1963 and the learned District Judge granted probate on 01.07.1963 in favour of Purno Shashi Das. Subsequently, Subol Chandra Das, transferred the suit land to Gopal Chandra Majumder, Dilip Majumder and Joydeb Majumder-plaintiff Nos.1-3, Jitendra Chandra Majumder, father of plaintiff Nos.4-6 and grandfather and father-in-law respectively of plaintiff Nos.7 and 8 vide five sale deeds and delivered possession thereof. The plaintiffs mutated their names in the record of rights, paid rent and continued to hold and possess the same by themselves and through tenants. The defendants were monthly ejectable tenants, but they were habitual defaulter in payment of rent and in spite of repeated demand they didn't pay rents. Subsequently, on being approached, the Martial Law authority issued notice to the defendants to quit the suit properties.

4. Challenging the notices, the defendants instituted Title Suit No. 98 of 1984 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka, which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 237/90 and lastly as Title Suit No. 93 of 1991, wherein they filed an application for amendment of plaint claiming to have purchased the suit land from Narayan Chandra Roy through registered deed of sale, but their application for amendment of plaint was rejected. They preferred Civil Revision No. 1810 of 2000 before the High Court Division. In the plaint they admitted to be tenants, but subsequently they claimed ownership to the suit land by filing amendment application and as such their claim was rightly rejected. The plain-tiffs have been holding and possessing the suit land, but due to creation of collusive deeds, title of the plaintiffs was clouded, hence, they issued notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act. But in spite of getting notice, the defendants did not pay heed thereto which constrained the plaintiffs to file the instant suit.

5. Defendant Nos.1 and 2, 10-12 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that Satish Mohon Roy being owner of the suit properties died leaving behind two sons namely Sushil Mohon Roy and Narayan Chandra Roy, wife Naresh Bala Roy and four daughters, namely Tanu Bala Roy, Shadeshi Bala Roy, Bina Bala Roy and Purno Sashi Das. The defendants were tenants under the original owner and, subsequently, under Narayan Chandra Roy son of Sushil Chandra Roy. Thereafter, they used to pay rent to Narayan Chandra Roy through plaintiff No. 1. Narayan Chandra Roy transferred .017 acre of land on 07.09.1996 in favour of Romesh Chandra Das vide deed of sale No. 4131, .0175 acre of land in favour of Nur Mohammad Gazi vide deed of sale No.4132, .0175 acre of land in favour of Shanti Ranjan Sarker vide deed of sale No.4133 and .0175 acre of land in favour of Khorshed Alom vide deed sale No. 4134 and, thereafter, transferred .1697 acre of 1 land in favour of Shanti Ranjon Sarker and aforementioned other purchasers vide deed of sale No.3510 dated 31.08.1998. Defendant Nos.1-2 in the meantime filed Civil Suit No.94 of 1984 before the Subordinate Judge, First Court Dhaka, praying for declaration of title and challenging notice dated 06.03.1984 issued from the office of Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka for evicting defendant Nos.1-2. Satish Mohon Roy without executing any Will died leaving behind his aforesaid heirs and hence, the Will as mentioned in the plaint is fraudulent and the plaintiff probated the Will through deceitful means without serving any notice to the next of kin of Satish Mohon Roy. With a view to grab the suit property, the plaintiffs created the deed of sale showing Subol Chandra Das as vendor, who had no saleable interest in the suit land and as such the suit is liable to dismissed.

6. The trial Court, upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record by its judgement and decree dated 04.11.2012 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved, the defendants filed First Appeal No.03 of 2013 before the High Court Division, which upon hearing the parties was dismissed. Hence, the defendants are now before us having filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal.

7. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submitted that the High Court Division failed to consider that the plaintiffs failed to prove the existence of the probate case and while the trial Court during trial called for the records of the pro-bate case, the concerned office could not produce the records and it transpires that the Will as well as probate case is totally false and forged. He further submitted that the plaintiffs claimed that Satish Chandra Roy executed a Will in favour of his daughter Purna Shashi Dasya on 03.01.1962 by appointing Subol Chandra Das as executor and they got probate on 01.07.63, but at that time the legal heirs of Satish Chandra Roy were not made party in the probate proceeding, and as such the probate was illegal and no right accrued in favour of Purna Shashi against the right of inheritance of Narayan Chandra Roy, and as such the impugned judgement and decree is illegal and cannot be sustained in law. He also submitted that the High Court Division failed to notice that the daughter of the executor of the Will had no right to transfer any land to any body and daughter of Satish Mohan did not execute any deed in favour of the plaintiffs and even did not give any power for which the plaintiffs never acquired any right, title and interest in the suit land and as such the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession is not maintainable, but the High Court Division erred in decreeing the suit and thus the same is liable to be set aside.

8. Mr. A.M. Amin Uddin, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1, 8, 10 and 14 made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and decree of the High Court Division.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

10. We note from the judgement of the trial Court that upon elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances and the evidence on record it was found that the predecessor of the plaintiffs obtained title to the suit land through probate of the Will executed by the original owner of the land, namely Satish Mohon Roy. It was observed by the trial Court that the suit property was recorded in the name of Purna Shashi Dasya, daughter of Satish Mohon Roy, in the S.A. Khatian and neither the defendants nor the predecessor of the defendants namely Narayan Chandra Roy raised any question regarding the S.A. Khatian. It was further observed that neither Satish Mohon Roy nor any of his heirs challenged the Will executed by Satish Mohon Roy. It was also observed that the name of Puma Shashi Dasya was recorded in R.S. Khatian No. 2529 and on her behalf her husband Subol Chandra Das transferred the suit land by way of 5 separate deeds in the year 1981 in favour of the plaintiffs, who thereafter mutated their names in respect of the suit land. The trial Court concluded that Narayan Chandra Roy therefore had no title to transfer by way of the disputed deeds dated 1996 and 1998. Accordingly, the trial Court decided that the plaintiffs were able to prove their title in the suit property and decreed the 5 disputed deeds detailed in schedule that to the plaint as void.

11. In the course of its elaborate discussion the trial Court noted that upon receiving notice from the Martial Law Authority to vacate the suit properties, the present defendants as petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 93 of 1991 wherein they admitted that they were tenant under the plaintiffs and their predecessor. However, they subsequently sought to amend their plaint claiming that they have purchased the suit property from Narayan Chandra Roy. However, that application for amendment was rejected up to the revisional Court.

<u>12. The High Court Division observed that in challenging the eviction notices by way of Title Suit No. 93 of 1991 the defendant intended to assert that they tendered rent to the plaintiffs on behalf of Narayan Chandra Roy, son of Satish Chandra Roy, but that contention is not sustainable as they failed to submit any paper showing payment of rents to Narayan Chandra Roy. Subsequently, they sought to amend the plaint claiming purchase of the suit property from Narayan Chandra Roy by a registered instrument. The High Court Division concluded that the above conduct of the defendant shows that they shifted from their earlier position raising a claim of ownership and thereby forfeited rights as tenant in the suit property.</u>

13. It is clear from the facts and circumstances discussed above that the defendants by their own admission made in Title Suit No. 91 of 1993 (originally Title Suit No. 98 of 1984) were tenants in the suit property. It is also apparent from the evidence and materials on record, as observed and decided by the trial Court, that Purna Shoshi Dasya's name was recorded in the record of rights in respect of the suit property and that she had title in the suit property by way of Probate Case No.19 of 1963. The trial Court found that Narayan Chandra Roy did not have any title to pass to the defendants and hence, the disputed deeds were void.

14. We also note that the beneficiaries of the Will did not come forward to challenge the order of the probate case. Although the defendants alleged that the probate case was false, they did not adduce any evidence or produce any witness to substantiate their claim. Moreover, the claim of the defendants that they purchased the property is contradicted by the plaint of the suit which they filed earlier wherein they claimed to be tenants in the property. Their subsequent attempt to amend the plaint to establish their claim of proprietary right over the property failed. Hence, the trial Court and appellate Court rightly decreed the suit.

15. In view of the discussion above, we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division.

16. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 26.02.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.557 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J. This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 26.02.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 557 of 1997 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are:

<u>3. The predecessors of appellant No.1 herein as the plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 30 of 1991 in the Fifth Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong for a decree of declaration of the plaintiffs title over the suit schedule-1 land measuring .38 acre and also for declaration that the plaintiffs were entitled to receive the compensation money for the requisition of schedule-1(Ka) land under schedule-1, measuring .26 acre and the principal-defendants have no right in that.</u>

4. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that the suit land belonged to one Gani Mia, who sold the same land by a registered deed of sale dated 05.05.1925 to Lal Mia. After that, Lal Mia sold the same by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925 to Najir Ahmed, the father of the plaintiffs. Subsequently, Najir Ahmed settled the said land with Abdur Rahman by a registered patta. Abdur Rahman used to stay in Burma. During the R.S operation, the R.S. Khatian for the suit land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs father, Najir Ahmed and his four brothers, though they had no title to the suit land and they also did not possess the land on the basis of the wrong recording. Abdur Rahman sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975 and the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. The recent B.S. Khatian was recorded in their names. Proforma defendant Nos.11 and 12 acquired 0.26 acre of land described in schedule 1(Ka) in L.A. Case No.13 of 1986-87. A Compensation Assessment Roll was duly prepared in the names of the plaintiffs. The principal defendants taking the advantage of the wrong recording of the land in R.S. and P.S. Khatians raised objection against the plaintiffs' right to get compensation for the acquired land and as such, the suit was filed to remove the cloud in the suit land.

5. Defendant Nos.2-8 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit. Their case, in short, is that the suit land belonged to C.S. recorded tenant Oli Mia, who by an amicable partition with Gani Mia was in possession of the suit land and subsequently, Oli Mia died leaving behind 5 sons namely, Najir Ahmed and his four brothers and the R.S. record was rightly made in their names. Abdur Rahman, son of Oli Mia, sold 0.08 acre of suit land to this defendant by a registered deed of sale dated 28.05.1986 and out of said land 0.05 acre was acquired by the Government and that mutation khatian in respect of 0.08 acre of suit land was prepared in the name of the defendant. The plaintiffs father, Najir Ahmed was entitled to get share in the suit land and that the alleged deeds of transfer and the deed of settlement are forged and ineffective and Najir Ahmed had never possessed the suit land.

6. The trial Court, upon hearing the par-ties, by the judgment and decree dated 11.11.1991 dismissed the suit.

7. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial court, the plaintiffs preferred Other Appeal No.706 of 1991 before the learned District Judge, Chittagong. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court and Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong, who upon hearing the appeal, by the judgment and decree dated 05.08.1996 allowed the appeal setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, the defendants moved the High Court Division by filing a revisional application and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.557 of 1997. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing both the sides by the judgment and order dated 26.02.2007 made the Rule absolute.

9. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiffs as the leave-petitioners have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1864 of 2007 before this Division and obtained leave on 24.07.2008 resulting in Civil Appeal No. 67 of 2009.

10. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division committed error in dismissing the suit without adverting to the findings arrived at by the Court of appeal which decreed the suit on consideration of possession of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the High Court Division erred in law in applying the amended provision of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and in the instant case lease had been granted by the landlord by executing and registering a patta in the year 1925 and that execution of a lease deed, by the lessor as well as by the lessee was not mandatory before 1929. He then submits that the Court of appeal below decreed the suit by taking into consideration that Abdur Rahman was in possession of the suit land on the strength of the patta executed by the Nazir Ahmed and that as soon as the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force, he became a rayiat under the Government and thus while making the Rule absolute, the High Court Division failed to consider the aforesaid finding of the appellate Court. He lastly submits that the High Court Division committed error in rejecting exhibit-3, the registered patta dated 18.07.1925 by the landlord treating the same as a lease deed under section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and committed error in not considering that when the Bengal Tenancy Act was in operation, the landlord had authority to grant patta in respect of the suit land and a patta is always a document executed only by the landlord under the then circumstances.

11. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, submits that the trial Court as well as the High Court Division on meticulous consideration of the materials on record, came to the finding that the plaintiffs could not prove their title to and possession in the suit land and as such, no interference is called for.

12. We have considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

<u>13. The trial Court came to the finding that on consideration of evidence on record, it appeared that the plaintiff could not prove that at the time of R.S. operation, Abdur Rahman was in Burma (now Myanmar). The trial Court also came to the finding that the plaintiff could not prove that Abdur Rahman possessed the suit land himself or through 'bargader' and as such, the contention of the plaintiff-appellants that taking advantage of Abdur Rahman's staying in Burma, the R.S. khatian was wrongly prepared in the names of Nazir Ahmed and his four brothers. The trial court also found that exhibits-2, 2ka and 3 were never acted upon. The trial Court, therefore, concluded that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their title to and possession in the suit land.</u>

14. The appellate Court, on the other hand, came to the finding that as per C.S. khatian Gani Mia (Guno Mia) was in exclusive possession of plot No.3182. The Appellate Court also found that in the C.S. khatian the four boundaries of the plot were clearly given which exclusively proved that Gani Mia, the C.S. recorded tenant was in exclusive possession of the suit plot No.3182. The appellate Court held that the suit land did not belong to Oli Mia but that it actually belonged to Gani Mia, who sold it to Lal Mia, who again sold it to Najir Ahmed. The Appellate Court also held that as Najir Ahmed had succeeded in proving his title by way of purchase on the basis of registered deed (exhibit-2ka) the initial presumption attached to R.S. khatian, exhibit-1(ka) was rebutted. The appellate Court also held that Najir Ahmed as tenure-holder in R.S. plot No.4429 (suit plot) was entitled to transfer the same by way of settlement which he did accordingly by executing patta exhibit-3 dated 18.07.1925, by which 18 gondas of land were transferred to Abdur Rahman. The appellate Court also held that the allegations of fraud by Najir Ahmed was not proved by cogent evidence and that the appellate Court also held that one who alleged fraud must bear the burden of proving it and the burden is comparatively heavier when it is against old registered documents. The appellate Court also held that by three documents (exhibits-2, 2ka and 3) no land of Oli Mia was attracted and that the chance of fraud in view of the given circumstances seemed to be too remote. Therefore, the appellate Court concluded that the plaintiffs had been able to prove their title to and possession in the suit land and accordingly, the appellate Court decreed the suit.

15. The High Court Division concurred with the findings arrived at by the trial Court and held that the appellate Court was not justified in reversing the findings of the fact arrived at by the trial Court. The High Court Division held that as the suit land was settled permanently, it was required to be registered under section 107 of the Transfer of the Property Act and that the patta was not executed by the ten-ant Abdur Rahman and as such, it was not valid in the eye of law.

16. The High Court Division also found that the plaintiffs could not prove their title on the basis of exhibits-2, 2ka and 3 and also possession in the suit land. Therefore, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree delivered by the appellate Court concurring with the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

17. The plaintiffs claimed that land of C.S. khatian No.3182 belonged to Gani Mia who sold it to Lal Mia by a registered deed of sale dated 05.05.1925. Lal Mia also sold the land of the said plot to Najir Ahmed by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925. Najir Ahmed settled the suit land to Abdur Rahman by a registered patta dated 18.07.1925. Abdur Rahman owned and possessed the suit land by paying rent to Najir Ahmed, the predecessor of the plaintiffs. But during S.A. operation, the land of said patta was wrongly recorded in the names of Najir Ahmed and his four brothers as Abdur Rahman at the relevant time was in Burma. Subsequently, Abdur Rahman sold the suit land as shown in schedule-Ka to the plaint to the plaintiffs by a registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975.

18. On the other hand, the defendants claimed that their predecessor Oli Mia was the recorded tenant of C. S. khatian and that Oli Mia by amicable settlement with Gani Mia got the suit land as shown in the 1st schedule to the plaint and that he died leaving behind Najir Ahmed, Sadik Ahmed, Abdur Rahman, Abdul Khaleque and Md. Nasir. Subsequently, the suit land was correctly recorded in the names of Najir Ahmed and his four brothers. Najir Ahmed was the owner of 1/5th share of the suit land. In order to deprive his brothers, Najir Ahmed collusively created the deeds dated 05.05.1925 and 16.06.1925 and that those documents were not acted upon. The registered patta dated 18.07.1925 standing in the name of Abdur Rahman is also collusive. Therefore, the claim of the plaintiffs on the basis of registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975 is void, collusive, inoperative and without any consideration.

19. Abdur Rahman, son of Oli Mia, sold .08 acre of land to the defendants by a registered deed of sale dated 28.05.1986. The 1st schedule land to the plaint has been recorded in C.S. plot No.3182 corresponding to R.S. plot No.4429. The C.S. record, exhibit-1 shows that the recorded tenants were Gani Mia, Oli Mia and Karimjan. The C. S. record (exhibit-1) reveals that the recorded tenants were in specific possession of the different plots of the khatian. Oli Mia was in possession of C.S. Plot Nos.3114 and 3380. Gani Mia was in specific in C.S. plot Nos.3182 and 3184 and the remaining plots were possessed by Karimjan. In the C.S. Khatian four boundaries of plots were clearly given so as to denote actual possession of each of the tenants. C.S. plot No.3182 exclusively stands in the names of the Gani Mia which is bounded on north by a road and on the south and east by Oli Miah and on the western side by Abul Hossain. Therefore, the aforesaid entry in C.S. khatian proved possession of Gani Mia, the C. S. recorded tenant exclusively in C. S. plot No.3182 and his title to the said plot would follow from the established possession. Gani Mia as an exclusive owner sold 18 gondas of land of C.S. plot No.3182 to Lal Mia by giving a defined boundary on 05.05.1925. Out of 96 decimals of the C.S. plot, 36 decimals of land were transferred which is proved by exhibit-2. While in possession of the said land, Lal Mia sold it to Najir Ahmed by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925 (exhibit-2ka) and handed over possession thereof.

<u>20. The aforesaid findings proved that the suit land did not belong to Oli Mia but it actually belonged to Gani Mia, who sold it to Lal Mia, who again sold it to Najir Ahmed. As Najir Ahmed has succeeded in proving his title by way of purchase on the basis of registered deed (exhibit-2ka) the initial presumption attached to the R.S. khatian exhibit-1(ka) was rebutted. Therefore, Najir Ahmed was legally entitle to settled the suit land to Abdur Rahman by exhibit-3, the registered patta dated 18.07.1925. The appellate Court on consideration of evidence on record found that the allegation of fraud was not proved in obtaining the suit land by the plaintiffs. The appellate Court also discussed the evidence adduced by P.Ws.1, 2 and 3 and found that they could prove that the Abdur Rahman was in actual possession of the suit land. The appellate Court also noted that P.Ws.2 and 3 were not cross-examined by the defendants in respect of their evidence as regards possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The appellate Court also noted that the defendants did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence during the trial. The appellate Court also considered exhibits-4 and 4ka, the rent receipts in respect of the suit land and found that the plaintiffs paid rent before filing of the suit and that rent receipt not only proved possession of the plaintiffs but also proved as collateral evidence of title to the suit land. The appellate Court noted that respondent No.3 filed three rent receipts relating to P.S. plot No.3080 for an area of .08, .22, .10 and .05 acre of land and that from those rent receipts, the plaintiffs' claim of possession was not affected so far as regards the quantum of land in P.S. khatian No.3082. The appellate Court also held that the defendants had not come out with positive proof regarding exclusive possession of P.S. plot No.4429 and as such, their onus was not discharged.</u>

<u>21. The High Court Division came to the finding that the patta dated 18.07.1925 should have been a bilateral document and that it should have been executed by both the landlord Najir Ahmed and tenant Abdur Rahman and as such, it was not valid according to section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. This finding of the High Court Division is erroneous as the patta, exhibit-3 dated 18.07.1925 was executed and registered before 1929. A lease deed is required to be executed and registered by both the tenant and landlord under section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act on and from 1929.</u>

22. In the light of the findings made before, we find substance in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgment delivered by the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court is restored.

23. There is not order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 9th day of November, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 4793 of 1998 and 4787 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. These two appeals, by leave, are from the judgment and order dated the 9th day of November, 2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.4793 and 4787 of 1998 making the Rules issued in the respective civil revision absolute.

2. Facts essential to dispose the appeals are that Md. Nurul Miah, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos.1(a)-(g) and Bazlu Miah, predecessor-in-interest of respondent No.2(a), as pre-emptors filed Miscellaneous Case Nos.3 and 4 of 1991 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act, 1950) for per-emption of the respective case land transferred to the pre-emptee appellant herein (in both appeals) by kabalas dated 20.01.1990, 21.01.1990 respectively.

3. The case of the preemptors was that the land of C.S. Khatian No. 17 comprising an area of 28.94 acres land originally belonged to Abu Miah, Yakub Ali, Hasana Banu, Saburrennessa and Salima Khatun to the extent of six annas, four annas, two annas, two annas and two annas share respectively. Yakub Ali, out of his 7.23½ acres land, sold 2.20 acres land to Ibrahim Khalil Majumder and others. Our of the remaining 4.53½ acres land, the heirs of Yakub Ali, Abdul Bari Miah, Abdul Ali Miah and Karamat Ali Miah, sold 4.53 acres land by two registered sale deeds dated 17.04.1926 in favour of Karimuddin Bepari, father of the pre-emptee and others and Karimuddin Bepari got only 0.5766 acre land. Karimuddin Bepari died leaving behind four sons including the pre-emptee two daughters and the pre-emptee got only 0.113 acre land in his share from his father, Karimuddin Bapari. The pre-emptee also purchased .0188 acre land from his two brothers and one sister. The pre-emptors transferred .10 acre land to one Abdul Ghani Master by registered sale deed dated 13.12.1953 and also sold .07 acre land to one Nurul Islam by registered deed of transfer dated 06.02.1987 and the pre-emptee sold more that his share in C.S. Khatian No. 17. The pre-emptee was a stranger to the case holding, so the pre-emptors were entitled to pre-empt the case land.

4. Subsequently, the preemption application was amended incorporating the fact the heirs of Yukyb Ali Munshi had shown transfer in respect of an area of 3 kanis, 2, gonads, 2 karas and 2 krantees equivalent to 3.76 acres land out of the disputed C.S. Khatian Nos. 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21 along with Khas Khatian No.1 and the schedule to the sale deed had shown that 2.63 acres land was sold from C.S. Kharian No.17. The pre-emptee had no interest in the case holding, whereas the per-emptors were co-sharers by inheritance as will as by purchase and as such, they were entitled to preempt the case lands.

5. The miscellaneous cases were contested by pre-emptee by filing separate written objection contending, inter alia, that he was a co-sharer in the case holding by inheritance, so preemption applications against him were not maintainable. Karimuddin Bepari, predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptee and his three brothers purchased 3.76 acres land from the heirs of C.S. recorded tenant, Yukub Ali by registered deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 and Karimuddin got 0.94 acre land in the case holding in his share and he died leaving behind four sons named Abdul Ghani Master, the pre-emptee, Abdul Kader and Nurul Haque, two daughters-Zinnatunnessa and Arabunnessa and a widow, Faridunnessa died leaving behind four sons and two daughters named above. The pre-emptee inherited .18¾ acres land from his father, Karimuddin Bepari. The pre-emptee purchased .02¾ acre land from his sister-Zinnatunnessa. In the above manner, the pre-emptee became the owner and the possessor in respect of .21 2/15 acre land. The pre-emptee sold .17 acre land by two sale deeds and he remained the owner and possessor in respect of .21 2/15 acre land as co-sharer in the case holding. The pre-emptors and others got their holding separated on mutation in Mutation Case Nos.303 of 1987-88 and 296 of 1987-88 and opened new khatians being Khatian No.195 in respect of 4.30 acres land and Khatian No.188 in respect of 4.13 acres land and paid rents separately. Because of the separation of jamas, the per-emptors on longer remained a co-sharer in the case holding in S.A. Khatian No.10 covered by sale deed dated 20.01.1990 and 21.01.1990 (the deeds under preemption). Shamsuddin and his brothers-Fazlur Rahman and Khorshed Alom also got their 2.18 acres land separated from S.A Khatian No.10 in Mutation Case. No.301 of 1987-88 and paid rents separately. After purchase of the respective case land by separate deed under preemption, the pre-emptee made much improvement thereon, i.e. excavated pond, raised the land and constructed house and thereby incurred an expenditure of take 1,22,500.00.

6. Both the miscellaneous cases were tried analogously and both the cases were dismissed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur by the order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, dated 16.09.1992. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order, the pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal Nos.64 of 1992 and 65 of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Chandpur. The pre-emptee also filed a cross-objection in Miscellaneous Appeal No.65 of 1992 against the finding of the trial Court as to the co-sharership of the pre-emptors in the case holding. The learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chandpur by his judgment and order dated 13.02.1996 allowed both the appeals, but rejected the cross-objection and sent both cases to the trial Court for retrial giving chance to the parties to produce evidence.

7. After remand, the cases were heard afresh and the learned Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur by the order dated 11.01.1997 dismissed both the cases. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order of the learned Assistant Judge, the pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal Nos.2 and 3 of 1997 before the District Judge, Chandpur and the learned District Judge, Chandpur by the judgment and order dated 02.08.1998 dismissed both the miscellaneous appeals and affirmed those of the learned Assistant Judge.

8. Against the judgment and order of the Appellate Court, the pre-emptors preferred Civil Revision Nos.4793 of 1998 before the High Court Division and a Single Bench by the order dated 09.11.2006 made both the Rules absolute and miscellaneous cases, i.e. allowed the prayer for preemption. That the pre-emptee appellant preferred civil petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.602 and 604 of 2007 before this Division and this Division by the judgment dated 29.07.2008 dismissed both petitions. Thereafter, the pre-emptee filed Civil Review Petition Nos.4 and 5 of 2009 for reviewing the judgment passed by this Court in the said leave petitions and leave was granted to consider the following submissions made on behalf of the appellants by their learned Counsel:

"Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in both the petitions submits that though land of cadastral Survey Khatian Nos.18-21 had been shown as tenanted land in the sale deed dated 17.04.1926 under Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 but the said under tenancies subsequently got no existence as under tenancies and the said land went to khan holding of Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 and those land of under tenancies stood recorded in State Acquisition Khatian No.10 in the names of tenants or heirs of transferors Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 and not in the names of heirs of any under tenants of Cadastral Survey Khatian Nos.18-21 and the deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 is a positive proof that Karim Uddin and his three (3) brothers purchased 3.76 acres of land from sons of Yakub Ali and Karim Uddin got. 94 acres of land in the case holding and pre-emptor-petitioner inherited .18-2 acres of land from his holding and father Karimuddin and pre-emptor petitioner still remains owner and co-sharer by way of inheritance in respect of li acres of land after transfer of .17 acres of land and pre-emptor petitioner having been a co sharer by way of inheritance, pre-emption cases by pre-emptor respondent is not at all maintain-able and both the trial Court and the Lower Appellate Court concurrently found that the pre-emptor petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance and those findings rested upon correct construction and reading of the sale deed dated 17.04.1926, share of Yukub Ali in the case holding and materials on record but the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division totally misdirected himself in his approach in resolving the legal battle involved in pre-emption cases and committed a substantial error in holding that pre-emptor-petitioner inherited .13 acres of land and transferred .17 acres of land and thereby exhausted all his interest in case holding and became a stranger and this Division did not at all explore the legal controversy and in a summary way dismissed the leave petitions and judgment under challenge in Civil Review Petition may kindly be reviewed in the interest of justice.

Mr. Huq submits that the pre-emptor-respondent-side in Mutation and sub Division of Joint Tenancy and holding case Nos.303 of 1987-1988 and 296 of 1987-1988 got Joint Tenancy and Holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10 separated and sub division and got their names mutated in separate Khatians in respect of 4.13 acres respectively and predecessor vendors of per-emptee-petitioner Shasuddin and others in Mutation and Sub Division of Holding Case No.301 of 1987-1988 got their Holding Sub-division and separated on opening of new Khatian in respect of 2.18 acres of land and the original Joint Tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10 gat no existence and pre-emptor respondent side and predecessor vendors of pre-emptor-petitioner who stepped in to shoes of predecessor vendor-respondents, no longer remained co-sharer of the transferred holding and the pre-emptor respondent side ceased to be co-sharer of the tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10, and thus, had legal character and locus standi to exercise right of Pre-emption against Pre-emptee petitioner and though the learned Trial Court Judge and the Appellate Court Judge took into stock this fundamental aspect of the matter neither the High Court Division nor the Appellate Division took into consideration the same and ruminated the vital and core legal aspect of the matter and that in the event of consideration and meditation of this important aspect of the matter, the fate of Civil Revisions and Civil Petitions For Leave to Appeal would have been otherwise and Per-petitioner would have been graced with favorable verdict and, as such impugned judgment may kindly be reviewed to secure ends of justice."

9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel for the appellants, has made his submissions in line with the leave granting order and in support of his submissions, he has referred time and again to the kabala dated 19.02.1962, i.e. exhibit-'6'. He has also referred to the mutation khatians by which the per-emptors got their land of the case khatian separated to emboldened his submission that by separating the jamas of the pre-emptors from the case khatian, they ceased to be co-sharers therein and therefore, they were not entitled to preempt the case land as co-sharers, but the High Court Division failed to consider this vital factual and legal aspect of the case in allowing the miscellaneous cases and this Court also failed to notice the said legal and factual aspect of the case and thus fell into an error in dismissing the leave petitions and the appeals merit consideration and the same be allowed.

10. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned Advocate fir respondent Nos.1(a) and 1(b) in both the appeals, has supported the judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the judgment of this Division dismissing the leave petitions. He has submitted that against the finding of the trial Court that the per-emptors were co-sharers in the case holding, the pre-emptee filed a cross-objection before the District Judge and that was rejected. Therefore, the same question cannot be re-opened before this Court in these appeals, because the finding of the Appellate Court as to the co-sharership of the pre-emptor shall be a resjudicata in view of the provisions of section 11 of Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention, he has referred the case of G.H. Hook-Vs-Administrator General of Bengal and others, AIR 1921, Privy Council, H. Mr. Khair has further submitted that it is true that the pre-emptors got their jamas separated from the case khatian, but on their application, the lands of the khatians were again amalgamated during the pendency of the miscellaneous case, thereby, before the date of hearing of the cases, the co-sharership of the pre-emptors in the khatian was restored. Therefore, the High Court Division rightly allowed the miscellaneous cases and there being no merit in the appeals, the same be dismissed.

11. From the leave granting order quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that leave was granted to decide two points; one: whether the pre-emptee remained as a co-sharer in the case holding after transfer of the land by him as claimed by the pre-emptoes and two: whether the per-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in case holding after separation of the khatian in their names and whether the subsequent amalgamation of the khatian the pendency of the miscellaneous cases could have any legal consequence in restoring the co-sharership of the pre-emptors in the case khatian and thus give them locus standi to file the application for preemption as co-sharers.

12. We would like to deal with the second point first, because if it is found that the pre-emptors ceased to co-sharers in the case holding due to splitting of the jamas long before filing the miscellaneous cases and that the subsequent amalgamation of the khatians could not have any legal consequence on the pre-emptors claim of cosharership in the case khatian, that the other point need not be answered.

13. Admittedly, the jama of the pre-emptors was separated from the case khatian being S.A. Khatian No.10 and this is very much apparent from exhibit-'5', i.e. the order sheets of Miscellaneous Case No.2 of 1991-1992 in which the jamas were allegedly amalgamated. The two orders passed in the miscellaneous case read as follows:

স্থানীয় তহশীলদারকে উপরোক্ত আদেশ মোতাবেক তহশীল প্রেরিত অনুমোদিত প্রস্তাব বাতিল করিয়া সাবেক ১০নং খতিয়ানে উল্লেখিত মােকদ্দমার ভূমি একত্রীকরণ এবং সরকারের প্রাপ্য আদায় করার জন্য নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেলে I

14. Besides the orders passed in the above miscellaneous case, the fact of separation of khatian is further clear from the mutation being Nos.188, 195, 193 of the office of Assistant Commissioner (Land), Shahrasti, Chandpur.

15. Mr. Mahbubey Alam has pointed out that after the miscellaneous cases for pre-emption were filed on 16.05.1991, the pre-emptors with the other co-sharers filed an application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Shahrasti, Chandpur for reconsideration of the cases by which their janas were separated with the further prayer for cancellation of the mutation cases and also for amalgamation of S.A. Khatian No.10 and accordingly, a proceeding under the said section of the Act, 1950 was started. From the first order as quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that the jamas of the pre-emptors from the case khatian were separated and were approved, but they prayed for amalgamation on the plea that the jamas were separated on mistaken calculation of share of the co-sharers. The second order dated 30.03.1992 shows that the jamas were amalgamated by cancelling the earlier approved khatians after one year, two months of filing the miscellaneous cases and without assigning any cogent reason too for such amalgamation far from any finding that the jamas separated earlier was done on wrong calculation of share of the co-sharers. The only funny reason assigned by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) was that amalgamation was made to facilitate realization of government revenue and for maintaining the records properly ignoring the fact that after separation of the khatians, the pre-meptors paid rents for three years and during this period neither the Government nor the applicants before him faced any difficulty in paying rents as well as in realizing the same by the Government from the applicants.

16. It further appears that the jamas in question were separated on 20.01.1988 and 21.01.1988 respectively, whereas the prayer for preemption vide the miscellaneous cases were filed on 16.02.1991, i.e. the date on which the miscellaneous cases were filed, the pre-emptors were not co-sharers in the case khatian. Therefore, they were not entitled to preempt the case lands as co-sharers in the case khatian. It also appears to be very significant that the written objection in the respective miscellaneous case by the pre-emptee was filed on 05.08.1991 stating categorically that the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the case khatian as because they separated their khatians from the case khatian, whereas the application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 was filed on 18.03.1992. Thus, it is clear that the pre-emptors made a very smart move to review the order of separation of the khatians passed earlier in the above mentioned mutation cases just to obviate the legal stigma that since they ceased to be co-sharers in the khatian would have no locus standi to pray for preemption of the case lands transferred by the kabalas in question.

17. In the context, we find substance in the submission of Mr. Mahbubey Alam that if this kind of smart move by a pre-emptor(s) is allowed, the very act of separation of the khatians shall become an absolute mockery and in the process, the factual stand taken by the per-emptee in a preemption proceeding through the written objection as to the locus standi of the pre-emptor(s) shall be rendered ineffective and nugatory by the post facto move of the pre-emptor(s) and a Court of law cannot be a party to such a move of the pre-emptor(s).

18. Besides the above, the order of amalgamation passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) prima facie was not done in accordance with law inasmuch as from the order dated 18.03.1992, it is clear that the application was filed by the pre-emptors along with others under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 for reviewing the earlier order of separation of the khatians, but the order was passed for amalgamation of the khatians. This move was possibly taken by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) as proviso (c) to section 150(1) has clearly provided that an order shall not be modified or reversed on a review until reasonable notice has been given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter, but the orders as quoted hereinbefore do not show that any notice was at all given to the parties concerned and a date was fixed for such hearing after service of notice.

19. In the context, we would like to point out that section 150 of Act, 1950 is in Chapter XVIII under the head Jurisdiction, Appeal, Revision and Review, whereas amalgamation, subdivision and consolidation of holdings is in Chapter XV and for the amalgamation of a holding, completely separated procedure has been laid down in this chapter, whereas the procedure of review as provided in section 150 is quite different. More significant thing is that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 150 has clearly provided that an application for review of an order shall not be entertained unless it is made within thirty days from the date of such order or, when such application is presented after the expiry of the said period of thirty days, unless the applicant satisfies the Revenue Officer that he had sufficient cause for not making the application within the said period. But unfortunately the orders of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) do not show any reflection whatsoever of the said provisions of clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 150. In the instant case, the application for review was filed long after 3(three) years of the separation of the jamas, but the orders show that no application was filed for condoning the delay after such an inordinate delay. Therefore, the order of amalgamation made by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) having not been done in accordance with law, the same was illegal and an inconsequential order and the same could not in any way save the pre-emptors to be strangers in the case holding in view of the separation of the khatian made earlier.

20. It is also an admitted fact that after separation of the khatians for long three years, the pre-emptors enjoyed its benefit and paid rents, but they shifted from their said stand only to avail their right of pre-emption as co-sharers in the case holding by filing application under section 150(1) for reviewing the case of separation of the jamas. Such a move was absolutely malafide just to negate the provisions of law and cannot be approved by a Court of law. We conclude that the very date on which the cause of action to file the pre-emption applications arose the pre-emptors not being co-sharers in the case khatian, were not entitled to pray for preemption of the case lands as co-sharers in the case kharian.

21. Now, the next point to be considered is whether the point as to the cessation of co-sharership of the pre-emptors due to the splitting of jamas as raised in the leave granting order and argued by Mr. Mahbuber Alam can be said to be barred under the principle of resjudicata. In this regard, it is very pertinent to look at the relevant finding of the co-sharership of the pre-emptors by the trial Court in the first order. The relevant finding reads as under:

“অন্য দিকে প্রার্থী পি, ডব্লিউ-১ এর জেরা হইতে দেখা যায় তাহার নাম খরিদ (sic) করিয়া ১৮৮ ও ১৯৫ নং খতিয়ান প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ছিল 1 প্রদর্শনী-৫ দৃষ্টে দেখা যায় নালিশা ১০ নং এস, এ , খতিয়ানের (sic) যে ১8.৮৩ একর ভূমি ১৯৮৭-৮৮ সালের ২৬৭, ২৯৬, ৩০১ , ৩০২ এবং ৩০৩ নং মোকাদ্দমা বলে পৃথক বা খারিজ করা হয় উহা আবার মূল ১০ নং খতিয়ানে একত্রী করণ করা হয় ৷

উপরোক্ত আলোচনার পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে প্রার্থীগণ যে নালিশা জমায় শরীক নয় উহা বরিতৈ (sic) পারি না তবে ১ নং প্রতিপক্ষ যে নালিশা জমায় আগন্তক নয় উহা বলিতে পারি । ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ ও প্রার্থী পক্ষের ন্যায় নালিশা জমায় ওয়ারীশ সূত্রে শরীক ৷

22. This finding of the trial Court clearly shows that it did not at all consider the fact that the pre-emptors though filed the application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 for reviewing the cases of earlier separation of khatian, but the order was passed for amalgamation just in a casual manner on the reasons reasons already discussed above. The trial Court also failed to consider that the application for reviewing the separation of the khatian was filed after one year, four months of filing the application for preemption and also after filing the written objection by the pre-emptee where he specifically pleaded that pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the case holding due to the separation of the jamas from the case khatian. It is true that a cross-objection was filed by the pre-emptee against this finding before the District Judge when pre-emptors filed the miscellaneous appeals against the order of the trial Court rejecting the prayer for preemption and the same was rejected, but as it appears that the Appellate Court like the trial Court did not at all consider the provisions of section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 as discussed above and the glaring attending fact that the application under the said section was filed long after filing the miscellaneous cases and filing the written objection taking objection that the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the kharian as they separated their jamas from the case khatian and without giving any explanation for filing the same after such a long delay. This will be clear from the finding of the first Appellate Court. The finding so far as it relates to the rejection of cross-objection by the first Appellate Court is as under:

“প্রতিবাদী পক্ষে ক্রস আপীলদায়ের করিয়া উল্লেখ করিয়াছে যে প্রার্থী আপীলকারী নালিশী সি/এস ১৭এবং এস, এ, ১০ নং খতিয়ানের শরীক প্রজা নহে ৷ তাহার অংশের জমা বিভাগ হইয়া তাহার নামে  আলাদা খতিয়ান সৃষ্টি হইয়াছে । তৎপর তিন বৎসরের খাজনা দিয়াছে ৷ ১৯৯০ ইং সন পর্যন্ত খাজনা আদায়ের পর ১৯৯১ ইং সনে ঝি(Sic) মােকদ্দামা ২টি আনায়ন করা হয় ৷ তৎপর ১৮/৬/১৯৯২ ইং সনে সম্পূর্ন অবৈধভাবে জমা খারিজ বাতিল (sic) করা হয় ৷ তাহা যােকাদ্দমার চলিতবস্থায় কার্যক্রম বিধায় লিসপেনডেনসী নীতিতে বরাত (sic) ৷ বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত এতদ সংক্রান্তে সঠিক সিদ্ধান্তে উপনীত না হইয়ইি প্রার্থককে নালিশা (sic) জমার শরীক নহে উহা বলিতে পারি না উল্লেখে এক সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করেন যাহা আইনত সম্মত হয় নাই ৷

প্রার্থী পক্ষের ১নং সাক্ষীর সাক্ষেরে জেরায় অংশে সঈকৃত(Sic) হইয়াছে যে, তাহার নামে খারিজা খতিয়ান সৃষ্টি হইয়াছিল এবং সে নিত (sic) বৎসর খজনা আদায় করিয়াছে ৷ পরবর্তীতে খারিজা (sic) খতিয়ান বাতিল ক্রমে তাহা ১০ নং মূল খতিয়ানের একত্রি করন করা হয় । একত্রি করন মিছ মোকদ্দমা চলিতবস্থায় সংঘটিত হয় ৷

পিয়েমশান (sic) মোকদ্দমার ক্ষেত্রে লিসপেনডেন্সী নীতি প্রযোজ্য নহে বিধায় সিদ্ধান্তে উপনীত হওয়া যায় সে মোকাদ্দমা চলিতাবস্থায় খারিজী খতিয়ান বাতিলক্রমে মূল খতিয়ান একত্রি করণের আদেশ বেআইনী নহে এবং অনুরূপ আদেশদানের এখতিয়ার রেভেনিউ কর্তপরে (sic) রহিয়াছে I ফলে ১নং প্রতিবাদী পক্ষের ক্রস আপীল ব্যর্থ হইল ৷

<u>23. The finding of the Appellate Court clearly shows that it did not also at all consider the facts and circumstances of the case under which the order of amalgamation of the khatians was passed. Since the Appellate Court failed to consider provisions of section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 in rejecting the cross-objection filed by the pre-emptee against the finding of the trial Court as the co-sharership of the pre-emptors its finding in that respect was perincuriam. Further the Appellate Court totally misconceived the doctrine of lis pendens and also totally failed to consider that the act of amalgamation of the khatains of the  pre-emptors on the basis of an application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 during the pendency of the miscellaneous cases was not a case of lis pendens within the meaning of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, but a malafide and smart move made by the pre-emptors to acquire the locus standi to file the application for preemption by resorting to amalgamating the khatains which stood separated long three years before and had already been acted upon. Therefore, we find no sub-stance in the submission of Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood that the question of re-opening the separation of khatians touching the cessation of co-sharership of the pre-emptors would be a resjudicata within the meaning of section 11 of the Code. The facts and circumstances of the case under which the Privy Council propounded the principle of resjudicata in the case of G.H. Hook (supra) are absolutely distinguishable from the instant case and hence the principle of law enunciated therein has no manner of application in the instant case.</u>

24. In view of our decision on the second point as formulated hereinbefore, the first point does not require any decision.

25. For the discussions made above, we find merit in the appeals and accordingly, both the appeals are allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and those of the Courts below are restored and the miscellaneous cases are dismissed. The judgment passed by this Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.603 and 604 of 2007 stands reviewed accordingly.

26. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27th of May, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 665 of 1996.
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgement and order dated 27.05.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.665 of 1996 making the Rule Nisi absolute.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the respondent herein as petitioner filed Writ Petition No.665 of 1996 before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the property in question was allotted to her father late Md. Nazir on June 26, 1962. The writ petitioner's father gifted the property to her and in support thereof he affirmed an affidavit on April 9, 1964 before the Magistrate, First Class, Dhaka. The writ petitioner's father died in 1971. Before his death, all the installments of the lease amount were cleared and to that effect a letter was written on March 4, 1982 by the Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur Housing Estate. The writ petitioner filed Succession Case No.111 of 1984 and obtained a certificate that she is the sole heir of late Md. Nazir. While residing in the property in question, she came to know that the property was listed as abandoned property, and thereupon in 1982 she made representation for release of the property from the list of abandoned property. The authority, by letter dated January 4, 1984 asked the writ petitioner to file the papers including a certificate from the local Ward Commissioner to the effect that the writ petitioner is a legal claimant of the property in question.

3. Since the property was listed as abandoned building, the writ petitioner filed a case before the Court of Settlement seeking release of the building and the same was dismissed on the finding that the writ petitioner is not "aware to (sic) the relevant facts about the particulars of the original allottee and as such her statement to the effect that she is the daughter of Nazir cannot be reliable", that "it is evident from her own application that she was not in possession of the case house and as such applied for release of the property from the abandoned property list. Therefore, the claim of the petitioner about physical possession in the case property appears to be false", that "at present one Harunur Rashid is in possession of the house", that "neither the petitioner has been able to prove that she is the daughter and heir of the original owner Md. Nazir, nor she has possession in the case property. Rather, it appears from the Government files and records that the property of Md. Nazir was found abandoned after commencement of P.O.16/72 and the Government took control and management of the property from the very beginning. There is no evidence before us to show that Md. Nazir died in this country and that he was available after the war of liberation". Then the writ-petitioner filed the aforementioned writ petition upon which Rule Nisi was issued.

4. After hearing the parties and upon consideration of the evidence and materials, by the impugned judgement and order, the High Court Division made the Rule Nisi absolute.

5. Hence, the writ respondents as petitioners filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1995 of 2001 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Attorney General for the petitioners:

"I. That the findings of the Court of Settlement having been based on the materials on record, the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the findings of the Court of Settlement on artificial reasoning.

II. That the claimant of the property having failed to discharge the onus of rebutting the presumption that the property rightly vested to the Government as abandoned property, the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute.

III. That the High Court Division not being the Court of appeal sitting in writ jurisdiction erred in law in setting aside the findings of the Court of Settlement and making the Rule Nisi absolute without any cogent reason."

6. Mr. Goutom Kumar Roy, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further submitted that the claimant claimed that she had been in possession of the case building all along, whereas in her petition to the Ministry of Works in about 1986, she had claimed that she was living with her husband in Sowari Ghat, Dhaka. Hence, her claim of possession is false and the building was rightly included in the 'Ka' list of abandoned building. He submitted that the Court of Settlement found the building to be abandoned based on records produced before it. The High Court Division acted illegally in setting aside such findings.

7. Mr. A.M. Aminuddin, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division. He submitted that at the time of hearing, the respondent was examined as P.W.1 on 27.2.1994, while she was very sick and extremely nervous on that date, she made some statements by way of her deposition which were apparently inconsistent with her stand in the case and that accordingly an application was made on her behalf soon thereafter on 3.5.1994 with a prayer for her re-examination in the case by cancelling her earlier deposition on 27.2.1994, and as such the Court of Settlement being satisfied vide order dated 3.5.1994 allowed the prayer for re-examination. Although a consider-able time had elapsed, her deposition was not taken on re-examination, rather the hearing of the case was concluded ultimately dismissing the case on the basis of her initial deposition, although the Government acting through the Ministry of Works failed to produce any material on the basis of which, the building in question could be regarded as an abandoned property. He submitted that the Court of Settlement dismissed the case of the respondent on the finding that she was not the rightful claimant of the building in question and she was not the legal heir of the original allottee, late Md. Nazir and also held that the respondent could not prove that she was in possession of the building in question, and relying on the Government assertion to the effect that one Harunur Rashid was in possession of the building for the Government, as such the Government treated the same as abandoned property since 1972, as a matter of course. These findings of the Court of Settlement were arrived at obviously on the strength of certain observations, annotation, addendum and commentary in the concerned files of the Government and not on the basis of any valid evidence, documentary or otherwise rather these findings are contrary to the available documentary evidence on record. He submitted that the respondent conversely has been able to prove her title to the building in question, on the strength of Lease Agreement dated 19.4.1962, letter of possession dated 20.6.1962 (Annexures-A and A-1) demonstrating grant of lease of the said building in favour of her father, Md. Nazir. The respondent in the memo of the instant writ petition has also annexed letter dated 4.3.1982 vide Annexure-C, issued by the Mohammadpur Housing Estate, which makes it obvious that all the Government dues up to 1982 so far as it relates to the building in question were already paid by said Md. Nazir. The respondent also annexed a Succession Certificate and a certificate from the Chairman of Ward No.12 concerned, in which the building is situated vide Annexure-E and E-1, which revealed that the respondent was the lone legal heir of said Md. Nazir as his only daughter. All these Annexures are in original and were very much available before the Court of Settlement. He submitted that Annexure-E and F are the Government letters in original addressed to the respondent showing the said building as her address and that possession of all these original papers/documents provided a valid rebuttable presumption that the respondent is the genuine claimant of the building in question as the heir of said Md. Nazir vis-a-vis the respondent's consistent claim to be in possession of the building, although the Government claims that the same was in possession initially through Chand Mia and presently through one Harunur Rashid, but the Government could not produce any of them before the Court of Settlement, in spite of Court's order passed on 31.12.1994 in this regard. He submitted that the Court of Settlement arrived at the aforesaid finding that the petitioner/respondent is not the heir of Md. Nazir, merely on suspicion, caused by some of her oral testimony which she made, because of her illness and fright, in utter disregard to the documentary evidence, viz. Annexure-B and D, i.e. Affidavit dated 09.04.1964 sworn before the Magistrate, First Class as well as Succession Certificate obtained from Third Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. He submitted that the Court of Settlement having passed the order on 03.05.1995 to re-examine the respondent, deprived her of a hearing by the order dated 23.11.1995 and thus the same is violative of practice and is clearly violative of the law and the principles of natural justice as well. He submitted that the Court of Settlement was satisfied that the deposition of the petitioner/respondent was not correctly recorded and as such passed the order dated 03.05.1994 allowing re-examination of the petitioner, but ultimately passed the impugned decision on the basis of the said incorrect initial deposition. He submitted that the Court in order to ascertain the factum of possession passed an order on 03.12.1994 to issue notice upon the persons claimed by the Government to be in possession of the building in question and also passed an order for personal attendance of the respondent, but ultimately passed the impugned decision without recording any satisfaction in respect of service of notice upon them, or without hearing any of them, which is neither proper nor legal. He submitted that the Court of Settlement arrived at the iniquitous and wrong decision only on consulting the Government records, without giving the respondent any opportunity and access to that. Conversely the Court of Settlement felt the necessity of ascertaining the factum of possession by examining persons alleged to be in possession of the building in question, but without examining any such per-son came to finding in respect of possession of the building on the basis of Government records concerned.

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the appellants and the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

9. On perusal of the decision of the Court of Settlement, we note that the Government challenged the identity of the petitioner before the Court of Settlement, Musammat Amikun (respondent herein). It was claimed by the Government that the petitioner before the Court of Settlement was a fictitious person. Upon considering the oral testimony of the petitioner, the Court of Settlement noted that she was not aware to the relevant facts about the particulars of the original allottee, and as such, her statement to the effect that she was the daughter of Md. Nazir was not reliable. In this regard, we also note that before the Court of Settlement, the petitioner deposed that she was born in Mymensingh, whereas in her petition filed before the Chairman of the Court of Settlement, she had stated that she was born in Dhaka.

10. With regard to the possession of the building in question, the Court of Settlement found that the petitioner before it was unable to prove her possession therein and relied upon the Government's claim that the building was under its possession through one Chan Miah as caretaker of the building and later through one Harunur Rashid. The Court of Settlement noted that it was evident from the petition before it that the petitioner was not in physical possession of the building.

11. The High Court Division reversed the decision of the Court of Settlement taking into consideration that the petitioner before the Court of Settlement (respondent herein) was in possession of all the original papers which in its estimation "raises valid equitable presumption that the petitioner is the genuine claimant of the house as the heir of Md. Nazir." The High Court Division observed that the Court of Settlement arrived at the finding that the petitioner is not the heir of Md. Nazir only on suspicion caused by some of her oral testimony which she made because of her illness, nervousness and panic, in utter disregard of the documentary evidence. At this stage, we have to say that we do not find any evidence to suggest that the petitioner before the Court of Settlement was suffering from any illness, nervousness or panic at the time when she deposed before the. Court of Settlement.

12. Mr. A.M. Aminuddin has drawn our attention to the fact that the petitioner had filed an application for taking her evidence again. Although the case was adjourned for re-examining the petitioner, she was not re-examined. In this regard, we must make it clear that re-examination of any witness may, at the discretion of the Court, be allowed for the purpose of clarifying any evidence or for producing fresh evidence which was not produced/provided earlier. In other words, a witness may be recalled to supplement his or her evidence, but not to correct what he or she stated earlier. The fact that the petitioner, while deposing before the Court of Settlement contradicted her own statement made in her petition, could not be corrected on her re-examination. On the other hand, the contradiction speaks a volume about the veracity of her statement.

13. With regard to the original documents, which the High Court Division relied upon in finding that the respondent herein was in possession of the case building, we are constrained to hold that in the facts of the present case, simply being in possession of the original documents relating to a building which has been declared abandoned, does not ipso facto prove the entitlement of the possessor of the original document to be entitled to a declaration that the building was not lawfully declared as abandoned. Merely proving the title of Md. Nazir does not help the petitioner before the Court of Settlement in establishing that the building was not lawfully declared abandoned when she made fundamental errors about her predecessor and her own place of birth. We also note that the respondent herein firstly claimed that she had acquired the building in question by way of gift from her father. But subsequently, she attempted to prove her ownership by way of inheritance by producing a succession certificate. We also note that the respondent filed Succession Case No.111 of 1984 when Md. Nazir is claimed to have died in 1971. All these facts tend to support the view taken by the Court of Settlement that the respondent, Most. Amikun was not a genuine heir of Md. Nazir.

<u>14. By the impugned judgment, the High Court Division reversed the decision of the Court of Settlement as if it was sitting in appeal. In the case of Mostafa Kamal (Md.)-Vs-First Court of Settlement and others, 48 DLR(AD)61, this Division endorsed the legal principle that the High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction cannot sit as a court of appeal over the judgement of the Court of Settlement for re-settling the questions of fact. In that case also the Court of Settlement on consideration of the materials on record arrived at a finding that the petitioner in that case was not the daughter and heir of the original lessee and that she had not been in possession of the house in question at the relevant time. The respondent herein had to prove not only her title in the building but also that she was the genuine and legal heir of the original allottee of the building.</u>

<u>15. It has been held time and again that when a building is declared abandoned, the onus is on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not abandoned. In the instant case, the respondent failed to prove her claim to be the heir of the original allottee and also that the building was unlawfully declared abandoned. She could not prove that she was in possession of the building. We note from annexure-F that the letter dated 7 September, 1982 from the Section Officer of the Ministry of Home Affairs addressed to the applicant's mother that she was living at 6/3 Champatali Lane, Sowari Ghat, Dhaka, which is the address given by the claimant as her husband's address. That would mean that the applicant's mother was at that time with her son-in-law and not in the case building. The Court of Settlement, having called the relevant records for the building in question, came to a finding that the building was in the possession of the Government and declared it as having been lawfully declared as abandoned property.</u>

16. In the facts and circumstances discussed above, we find merit in the appeal, which is accordingly allowed, without however, any order as to costs.

17. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside.

End.
