case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J. This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are:

3. Krishnapada Biswas and others, the predecessors of the respondents herein as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.1208 of 1983 against Saburannessa Bibi and others, the predecessors of the appellants, seeking declaration of title in the suit land, which consisted of 30 decimals of land situated in plot No.307 and also 03 decimals of land situated in other plot, both under khatian No.133 of Mouza and P.S. Jhenaidah and also for recovery of khas possession thereof on the averments that above plot No.307 measuring 63 decimals of land belonged to Fazar Ali and others. Subsequently, Sattendra Nath became the owner of the same, and then on 15th Chaitra B.S, 1354, Sattendra Nath leased 30 decimals of land situated on the northern side of plot No.307 to Haripada, his servant, who then constructing a house started living therein. But the survey record was wrongly prepared in the name of Sattendra Nath. On 15th Kartick,1375 B.S, Jagadish disclosed to Haripada that the record of right in respect of the suit land stands in the name of Sattendra and he had purchased the suit land from Sattendra Nath along with other lands. After coming to know about the same, Haripada filed Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 under section 143(a) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for correction of the record of right and then the above miscellaneous case was stayed with a direction to the other side to file a regular title suit by 20.05.1970 and such suit not being filed, decision was given in favour of Haripada on 15.06.1970. During the liberation war, Haripada was shot dead in his own house. From suit plot No.307, which contained 60 decimals of land(but wrongly written 63 decimals in khatian), Jagadish purchased only 33 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath but he in his kabala from Sattendra Nath, fraudulently included the entire land of the plot, which was owned by Haripada and Amanat Mollah. Haripada died leaving his wife Bimala Bala, who sold 03 decimals of land to Manju Rani, respondent No.6 of Civil Revision No.286 of 2001. Then Bimala Bala on 24.7.73 sold 10 decimals and on 01.09.1975 sold 17 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 and Basanti Bala. They dug a pond in 15 decimals of purchased land. Basanti Bala on 14.7.1976 sold 02 decimals of land to Monto Kumar. The defendant earlier filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981, which ended on filing a solenama which was forcefully obtained by the defendants from the plaintiff. Thereafter, defendants forcibly took possession of the suit land on 15.11.1981. Then on 10.10.1982 defendant constructed a straw-hut on the bank of the pond which is situated within the suit land.

4. Defendant (Saburannessa) contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit. Her case, in short, is that Sattendra Nath, the owner of the suit land along with other lands, sold 91 decimals of land to Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 6.9.1963 and also sold 30 decimals of land from the suit land to Amanat Mollah by a registered deed of sale dated 17.4.1964. Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 28.11.1969 sold 91 decimals of land to Saburannessa and she, during the period of liberation war, went to India and then on coming back to Bangladesh, having found her house destroyed, lived in the hospital where she was an employee. In the meantime taking advantage of the death of her husband, Bimala Bala constructed a house on the northern side of the suit land by dispossessing her there-from. The defendant came to know that Haripada fraudulently created dakhila in relation to 33 decimals of land which included 30 decimals of land in the suit plot and also got exparte decree for correction of record in his favour. Then, she filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 for declaration of her title in the suit land and also for recovery of khas possession. The above suit was compromised and a solenama was filed by the parties, on the basis of which, the plaintiff gave possession of only 15 decimals of land to her and took one month time for removal of the house from the suit land in order to handover possession of the balance land but, on 10.05.1982. The plaintiff refused to do so disclosing that in terms of the condition of the solenama, she would get only 15 decimals of land and the rest would go to the plaintiff. Then she, on obtaining the certified copy of the solenama on 25.8.1982, found that the solenama was not correctly written in terms of the agreement made between her and the plaintiff and accordingly, she filed Title Suit No.772 of 1982. The trial Court, upon hearing Title Suit Nos.772 of 1982 dismissed it by the judgment and decree dated 28.04.1991. Against the aforesaid judgment, the defendant filed Title Appeal No.84 of 1992 which was dismissed on 11.06.1994 for want of tadbir, against which the defendant filed Miscellaneous Case No.35 of 1994 which was also dismissed on 02.02.1995.

5. The trial Court, upon consideration of materials on record, decreed Title Suit No.1208 of 1983. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.85 of 1992 and the learned lower appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, respondent Nos.1-6, the successors of Haripada, moved the High Court Division by filing a revisional application and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing both the sides by the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 made the Rule absolute.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the successor of the plaintiffs as the leave-petitioners have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1767 of 2008 before this Division and obtained leave on 16.08.2009 resulting in Civil Appeal No.288 of 2010.

8. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the appellate Court came to the finding that after lease of 30 decimals of land from suit plot No.307 in favour of Haripada, Satendra Nath had title over 33 decimals of land in the said plot and Krishnapada, the plaintiff in Title Suit No.1208 of 1983 failed to produce any supporting document in respect of the lease made by Sattendra Nath in favour of Haripada and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the appellate Court further held that P.W.2, Lutfor Rahman, the only solitary witness of the plaintiff, son of Amanat Molla, is an interested witness and that the lower appellate Court on proper calculation of the age of P.W.2 came to the finding that the P.W.2 at the time of the alleged settlement was a boy of 9/10 years old and that the High Court Division on the basis of erroneous calculation held that at that time the age of P.W.2 was only 14/15 years and that on that wrong calculation believed his evidence and that Krishnapada totally failed to prove the lease in favour of Haripada by submitting any document and that exhibit-D, on which, Krishnapada relied on is merely the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 which did not create any title in his favour even then the High Court Division made the Rule absolute only on the basis of exhibit-D.

9. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, submits that exhibit-D, the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969, proved that in fact, dakhila was granted to Haripada and that the said dakhila was lost during war of liberation and that the High Court Division erroneously concurred with the finding of the trial Court which held that exhibit-D proved the settlement of Haripada and as such, no interference is called for.

10. We considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment an the materials on record.

11. The trial Court relying on exhibit-D, the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 and also on the evidence of P.W.2 came to the finding that settlement of Haripada was proved. Haripada filed some dakhilas in the miscellaneous case and that those dakhilas were lost and that the said contention of the plaintiffs could not be disbelieved.

12. The trial Court also came to the finding that Haripada took settlement of 30 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath and that after the death of Krishnapada, his wife Bimala became owner of the said land and that the plaintiff, subsequently, purchased the suit land from Bimala Bala.

13. The appellate Court, on the other hand, came to the finding that the plaintiff claimed that Haripada took settlement of 30+3=33 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath and that on perusal of the record it appeared that no document could be produced to substantiate the claim of settle-ment. The appellate Court also came to the finding that admittedly Haripada was a servant of Sattendra Nath and that it was not believable that Sattendra Nath after settling the suit land to his servant would get the R.S. khatian recorded in his own name in respect of the said land. The appellate Court held that it was believable that subsequently by two deeds of sale, Jagadish and Amanat Molla purchased the entire land of suit plot No.307 measuring 63 decimals of land.

14. The High Court Division, on the other hand, concurred with the finding of the trial Court holding that P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman at the relevant time of settlement was aged about 13/14 years and that P.W.2 stated in his evidence that his father Amanat Molla was serving in serestha of Sattendra Nath as 'Gomasta' when Haripada purchased the suit land from Sattendra Nath and that his father Amanat Molla, wrote dakhila on 15th Chaitra,1354 B.S. and that during cross-examination by the defendant, this witness Lutfor Rahman could not be shaken. Therefore, the High Court Division concurred with the judgment of the trial Court and made the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court.

15. Admittedly, C.S. plot No.307 measuring 1.33 acres of land belonged to Sattendra Nath. The plaintiff claimed that Sattendra Nath settled .30 acre of land from the suit plot to Haripada on 15th Chaitra, 1354 B.S. and subsequently, Haripada constructed his dwelling house on that land and after his death his wife Bimala Bala became the owner of the suit land. The plaintiff also claimed that on 24.07.1973 and 01.09.1975 Bimala Bala transferred .10 acre and .07 acre of land to plaintiff No.1 and Basanti Bala respectively. Bimala Bala also transferred .03 acre of land to Monjo Rani and Basanti Bala transferred .02 acre of land to Monto Kumar Das. The plaintiff also claimed that the defendant filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 and that on the basis of forged sole-nama filed in that suit, the plaintiff on 15.11.1981 entered into the suit land and on 15.10.1982 erected a straw-house on the bank of the tank appertaining to the suit land.

16. On the other hand, the defendant claimed that on 06.09.1963 Sattendra Nath sold the suit land along with .91 acre of land of other plots to Jagadish and also sold .30 acre of land to Amanth Molla. Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 28.11.1969 sold the suit land to defendant No.1. Defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 which was decreed on compromise. On the basis of the sole-nama, the plaintiff relinquished possession of .15 acre of land and that the plaintiff refused to relinquish the remaining portion of the suit land on 10.05.1982. Subsequently, the defendant obtained certified copy of the solenama and came to know about the forgery. Subsequently, this defendant filed Title Suit No.772 of 1982.

<u>17. The plaintiff claimed that Sattendra Nath settled .33 acre of land to Haripada on 15th Chaitra, 1354 B.S. The plaintiff, however, could not produce any registered deed or dakhila and not even oral evidence to substantiate his claim. P.W.1 in his evidence stated that he did not have any personal knowledge about the alleged settlement. P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman in his evidence stated that when Sattendra Nath settled the suit land to Haripada, his father wrote the dakhila and that his father was the 'Gomasta' of Sattendra Nath and that on the date of his deposition, he was aged at 56/57 years. The appellate Court computed the age of P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman and found that at the time of alleged settlement his age was about 9/10 years. Therefore, the appellate Court discarded his evidence as being a child witness. The plaintiff claimed that Haripada took settlement of .30 acre of land from the suit plot and .03 acre of land from other plot but it appears that the khatian was prepared in the name of Sattendra Nath. It is also admitted that Haripada was admittedly the servant of Sattendra Nath. Therefore, it creates doubt that Sattendra Nath after giving the settlement of the suit land to his servant Haripada would get the suit land recorded in his own name. On the contrary, it appears to be believable that subsequently Sattendra on the basis of two registered kabalas sold the entire land of the disputed plot to Jagadish and Amanath Molla.</u>

18. The learned Assistant Judge relied upon exhibit-D, the certified copy of the Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969. But before institution of the aforesaid miscellaneous case, Sattendra Nath sold the entire land of the suit plot to Jagadish and Amanth Molla. Therefore, after relinquishment of the right of Sattendra Nath in respect of the suit land, Haripada filed the miscellaneous case for correction of khatian against Sattendra Nath. The appellate Court, therefore, held that this miscellaneous case was collusive and fraudulent and as such, the decision of the miscellaneous case for correction of khatian was ineffective. It was revealed that the defendants were not parties to the said miscellaneous case and that the defendant disputed the very existence and effectiveness of the said miscellaneous case for correction of khatian. The appellate Court also came to the finding that possession of this defendant is admitted in .15 acre of land out of the suit land measuring .30 acre of land. On the other hand, the plaintiff claimed that he was dispossessed from 05/06 acre of land. Record reveals that the plaintiff purchased the suit land in 1973 and 1975 and prior to that the defendant acquired title thereto. The appellate Court also noted that D.W.2, a child witness, tried to prove the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land but that his evidence was dis-carded by the appellate Court on the ground that at the relevant time he was child witness aged about 9/10 years.

19. In the light of the findings made before, we find substance in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and order delivered by the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court is restored.

20. There is no order as to costs.

End.

BADRUDDIN MIMED BEING DEAD HIS HEIRS-MOST. SAJEDA BEGUM AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 20th November, 2007 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 86 of 1995 affirming those dated 30.11.1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 136 of 1994 dismissing the suit.

2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that the Railway filed the aforesaid suit for declaration of its title in respect of the land as described in the schedule to the plaint and for further declaration that the ex-parte decree dated 24.09.1984 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 279 of 1970 was collusive, fraudulent, inoperative and the same is not binding upon the plaintiff stating, inter alia, that the suit land, along with other lands, was acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1870 and possession of the same was delivered to the Railway, the requiring body. The Railway took over possession of the said land by a declaration dated 02.09.1882 and, thereafter, it constructed Dhaka-Joydebpur Rail line which crossed the suit land and other lands. For the purpose of construction of double track rail line, the Railway authority requested the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to acquire more lands and, accordingly, L.A. Case Nos. 62 of 1964-65 was started for acquisition of more lands. Since the land of Plot No. 121 was acquired in 1882 and the Railway took over possession of the same and Rail line was constructed on the said land and other lands, it was not necessary to acquire the said land again. The defendant Nos. 1 to 3, getting fraudulent ex-parte decree in Title Suit No.279 of 1970, demanded compensation claiming that the Government has acquired the suit land in L.A. Case No.62 of 1964-65 so, according to them, they are entitled to get compensation due to such acquisition. Meanwhile, the Railway constructed double track rail line which crossed the suit land and other lands. In Title Suit No.279 of 1970, the defendant Nos. 1-3 claimed that they got settlement of the suit land from Bhawal Raj Estate. In C.S. operation, the land of Plot No.121 was duly recorded in the name of Railway. In S.A. operation, the same was again recorded in the name of Pakistan Railway. Neither the Railway nor the Government surrendered their right in the disputed property in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate. The story of settlement by Bhawal Raj Estate in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-3 is absolutely false and concocted. Hence, was the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and the same was barred by the provision of res-judicata and also barred by limitation. They further contended that the suit land originally belonged to Bhawal Raj Estate. It permitted the then East Bengal Railway Company to use the said land for alignment of Dhaka- Mymensingh Railway line. In S.A. operation, the same was recorded in the name of the Railway. Thereafter, the Railway surrendered 5.14 acres of land in favour of Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury in 1914. Thereafter, Bhawal Raj Estate settled 3.54 acres of land in favour of Feroja Begum, Anwar Hossain and Badruddin on 09.03.1938 receiving salami of Tk. 460/-. S.A. record of right was prepared in their names in S.A. khatian No.199. At the time of constructing Dhaka- Tongi one track Railway into two track, the Railway took over possession of 5.14 acres of land from Firoza Begum, Anowar Hossain and Badruddin in L.A. Cases No.62/64-65 and 14/65-66. The defendants were under impression that the said land of Plot No. 121 was duly acquired in L.A. Case No.62 of 1964-65 as such they were entitled to get compensation. These defendants and Firoja Khatun, claiming title in the suit land, filed Title Suit No. 279 of 1970 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for getting compensation. The defendant of that suit, that is, the plaintiff of this suit, appeared in the said suit and contested the same. In written statement of the said suit, they admitted that the Railway surrendered 5.14 acres of land and, thereafter, the Government acquired 4.94 acres of land for construction of double track rail line. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. These defendants, who were the plaintiffs in that suit, preferred First Appeal No.68 of 1972 in the High Court Division which was remanded to the Subordinate Judge. In the said suit, the present plaintiff appeared but finally did not contest the same. Accordingly, the suit was decreed ex-parte on 24.09.1984. Since the present plaintiff in earlier Title Suit No.279 of 1970 admitted the story of surrender of the suit land in favour of Bhawal Raj and the defendants took settlement of the said land from Bhawal Raj and that the plaintiff of this suit, knowing fully well about the said Title Suit No. 279 of 1970, appeared in the same and finally did not contest when the same was taken up for hearing and consequently, the said suit was decreed ex-parte, this suit should be dismissed.

The trial Court dismissed the suit. The Railway preferred First Appeal in the High Court Division which was also dismissed. Then, the Railway preferred this appeal getting leave.

4. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel appearing with Mr. Shahed Alam learned Counsel for the appellant, submits that the suit land along with other lands were acquired by the Government in 1882 and the Government handed over possession of the said land to the Railway and the Railway, taking over possession of the same, constructed Rail line which crossed the suit land. In C.S. operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of Railway Department. Neither the Government nor the Railway surrendered the suit land in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate. The claim of the defendants, so far the story of relinquishment of title and possession in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate, is absolutely false and that the defendants' claim of taking settlement of the suit land from Bhawal Raj Estate is also false and fabricated. He further submits that in Title Suit No.297 of 1970 the Railway appeared and filed written statement. Both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective cases and the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the suit. In the First Appeal, the present defendants, who were the plaintiff-appellants in the said appeal, filed application for admitting additional evidence and the High Court Division remanded the suit for consideration of the application for additional evidence. In view of such circumstances, the trial Court was not authorized to decree the suit ex-parte. Mr. Mahbubey Alam lastly submits that the defendants, in collusion with some officials of the Railway, made an attempt to grab the Railway property and created some papers inasmuch as there was no provision in law to surrender of the acquired property, the learned courts below committed error of law in not holding that suit land is the property of the Railway.

5. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents, submits that it is true that the Government acquired the suit land for Railway but the Railway did not use the said land and the same remained fallen. At one stage, the Railway surrendered the suit land in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate. 'Thereafter, in 1938 Bhawal Raj Estate settled the suit land to the defendants. The Government, admitting the story of surrender and subsequent settlement, prepared a proposal for acquiring the same for the purpose of construction of double track rail line in 1964-65 and accordingly, these defendants and Firoja Khatun, claiming title in the suit land, instituted Title Suit No.297 of 1970 for realization of compensation and got decree. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali submits that in view of the admission of the Railway in the written statement submitted in Title Suit No.297 of 1970 and in different documents, the Railway is not legally permitted to say that the Railway did not surrender the suit land in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate who settled the same to these defendants, the learned courts below rightly dismissed the suit.

6. Admittedly, the suit land along with other lands were acquired by the Government for the purpose construction of Rail line, that is, the same was acquired for public purpose and public interest. Exhibit-1 is attested photostate copy of Calcutta Gazette dated 06.09.1882 regarding acquisition of the suit land. P.W.1 proved the Ext. 1 and the defendants did not raise any question regarding genuineness of Ext. 1. It is also admitted that the Railway Department, taking over possession of the suit land, constructed rail line thereon which crossed the same and a portion of the disputed plot remained as unused. It is the case of the defendants that the Railway surrendered the suit land in favour of Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury in 1914. In support of the claim of surrender the defendants failed to produce any instrument of surrender or any other evidence. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali submits that the Railway admitted that it surrendered the title and possession of the suit land in favour of Bhawal Raj Estate. Mr. Mahbubey Alam submits that the defendants, in collusion with some dishonest officials of the Railway, created those papers admitting the story of surrender inasmuch as there was no law to effect such surrender.

7. We have gone through the related laws. Those are the Land Acquisition Act, 1870 and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1870 provides that when the Collector has made an award under section 14 or a reference to the Court under Section 15 of the said Act he may take possession of the land, which shall thereupon vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. It is the case of the defendants that the Railway surrendered the suit property and officials of the Railway admitted so in different letters. But we do not find, within four corners of the Land Acquisition Act, 1870, any such provision of relinquishment/surrender of title and possession of the acquired land rather it is provided that after completion of acquisition the right, title and possession of acquired land shall be vested in the Government free from all encumbrances. In such circumstances, the only way was to transfer the acquired land to the incumbent by the Government by executing an instrument of transfer. Similar provision was provided in Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 which stated that when the collector made an award under Section 11 of that Act he may take possession of the land, which shall thereupon vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. In the case of Fruit and Vegetable Merchants Union Vs. the Delhi Improvement Trust reported in AIR 1957 SC 344 it was observed that in the cases contemplated under sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 the property acquired becomes the property of the Government without any condition or limitations either as to title or possession. The legislature has made it clear that the vesting of the property is not for any limited purpose or limited duration. Section 16 clearly lays down that after making an award, the Collector may take possession of the land which shall thereupon vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. We do not find any such provision in those laws, exercising which, the Railway Authority or the Government was permitted to surrender the title and possession of the acquired land in favour of original owners or to any one. Where Government took over possession of the land soon after the award they are not at a liberty to withdraw from the acquisition of the land. There is no provision by which land statutorily vested in the Government reverts to the original owner. (ref: AIR 1970 SC 1576, Lt. Governor of Himachal Pradesh and another Vs. Sri Avinash Sharma). In absence of any such provision in the aforesaid laws, it is difficult to accept that the Railway Authority legally surrendered title and possession of the suit land in favour of the Bhawal Raj Estate. The only course open to the Government or Railway after possession has passed on to it is to retransfer it to the original owner or someone else, with his consent, in the regular mode in which transfers are effected. If any attempt was at all made to surrender the suit property, the same was a nullity. The land having once vested in the Government, the Government cannot divest itself of it withdrawing from the acquisition which is already complete. Once possession of the land is taken by the Government, the fact, that owner of the land entered upon land and resumed possession, does not have effect of obliterating consequences of vesting.

Moreover, in C.S. operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of Railway. C.S. khatian shows that in the column of  অত্র স্বত্বের বিবরণ ও দখলকার the words ভারত সম্রাট পক্ষে ইস্ট বেঙ্গল ইস্ট রেলওয়ে in the column of ”অত্র স্বত্বের শ্রেণি বিশেষ নম্বর অনুষঙ্গ” the words  ”নারায়ণগঞ্জ ময়মনসিংহ রেলওয়ে মালিক” and against plot No. 121 “জমির রকম”  was mentioned as  রেল লাইন and the land was measuring an area of 5.54 acres. As per provision of Section 103 8(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. The entry in the C.S. khatian has a' probative value. The presumption under Section 1038(5) of the B.T. Act being a statutory one cannot be taken away merely by an allegation. The defendants failed to adduce any evidence to rebut such presumption.

8. Thus, the position stands that the suit land was acquired by the Government and possession of the same was handed over to the Railway and, in such view of the matter the title and possession of the same was vested in the Government free from all encumbrances. There is no instrument in the record to prove that the Government/ Railway surrendered the suit land and even there was no such law of surrendering acquired land. Accordingly, C.S. khatian was rightly prepared.

9. It is the is further case of the defendants that Bhawal Raj Estate settled the suit land to the defendants or their predecessor in 1338 B.S. but the said story of settlement as pleaded by the defendants has not been proved.

10. These defendants earlier filed Title Suit No.297 of 1970 for getting compensation stating that the suit land was acquired in 1964-65 in the L.A. Case No.62 of 1964-65 and 14 of 1965-66. It appears from the materials on record that the said suit was dismissed and the trial Court specifically found that these defendants committed gigantic fraud for grabbing the suit land and that the suit land was acquired land for the Railway. These defendants preferred appeal which was remanded by the High Court Division for consideration of the prayer for admitting additional evidence filed by these defendants, that is, the plaintiffs of that suit.

11. The High Court Division in its order of remand made following observation and direction:

"Since we have decided to allow the application for additional evidence on the Ground that the evidence was not available to the party at the time of trial and the fresh evidence that is sought to be adduced are materials for determination of the case. We feel that for the ends of justice the plaintiff appellant should be allowed to adduce documentary evidences which have been annexed with the petition while allowing additional evidence. We are aware that fresh evidence should not be allowed unless two conditions are satisfied.

First one is that the new evidence was not available to the parties seeking to adduce it at the trial or that reasonable diligence could not have made it so available. The second condition is that fresh evidence, if true, would have had, or would have been likely to have had a determining effect to the court below. We feel that in the interest of justice the application to adduce further evidence should be allowed and hence we allow the application and permit the plaintiff appellant to produce the evidence as had been annexed in the application and to prove the same before the court below in accordance with law. Since we have allowed the application permitting the plaintiff appellants to adduce further evidence we need not enter into the merits of the case. We therefore, set aside the judgment and decree of the court below and remand the suit to the trial court for hearing after taking further evidence. The learned Subordinate Judge shall take additional evidence as may be adduced by the parties beside the evidence already on record.

Let the application for additional evidence along with the annexures be sent down to the court below for receiving them in evidence in accordance with law.

In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is remanded to the court below for hearing in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above.

There will be no order as to costs."

12. After the order of remand, the trial Court, amongst others, passed the following orders and ex-parte decree:

"Plaintiff files hajira. Defendant (Govt.) prays for time.

Heard the learned Advocate for the plaintiff and perused the record. None appears on behalf of the defendants to move the petition for time on calls. It appears that the defendants-Govt. filed written statement long ago and thereafter the suit was dismissed on contest vide judgment dated 24.08.1971. Subsequently the plaintiffs as appellants moved the Hon'ble High Court in F.A. No. 68/72 whereby the Hon'ble Court remanded the suit for trial afresh with a direction to accept some documents as additional evidence on behalf of the plaintiff. But the plaintiffs have not filed the said documents in the Court. Again the suit has been fixed for ex-parte hearing as because the defendants did not come forward for hearing after it is received on remand. Considering the circumstances, the defendant’s prayer for time to file written statement is rejected. Fix 23.09.1984 for ex-parte hearing.

72....23.9.84 plaintiff filed hajira. Defendant takes no step. No time today. Put up tomorrow for ex-parte hearing.

73 24.9.84 plaintiff files hajira. The suit is taken up for ex-parte hearing. The plaintiffs have filed suit for declaration of their title to the suit property and for further declaration that they are entitled to receive proper compensation for acquisition of the suit property in L.A. Case No.62/64-65 and 14/65-66. Previously, the suit was dismissed on contest against the defendant No.1 and ex-parte against the rest vide judgment dated 24.08.1971, but on appeal the Hon'ble High Court in F.A. No. 62/72 was pleased to set aside the said judgment and decree and thereby remanded the suit to this court for fresh trial with a direction to accept some documents as additional evidence on behalf of the plaintiffs. But lastly the defendants did not come to contest the suit.

The plaintiffs claim title to the suit land by way of rayati settlement from the ex-land lord Bhawal C/W estate. Previously the plaintiff No.1 Badaruddin Ahmed was examined as P.W/ 1 and some documents were marked as exts.1, 1(a), 1(b),2-2(b),3,4,5,6-6(a) and for identification as X,X(1), Yand Y(1). Today, another P1W, i.e. P/W.2 Moslehuddin Ahmed is examined and some other documents marked as exts. 7, 8, 9-9(a) and 10-10(a). Now, from the evidences on record it appears that the plaintiffs have proved their alleged rayati settlement in the suit land. Thus they acquired title to the same by operation of law with the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The case is, therefore proved. Court fee paid is correct. Hence, Ordered.

That the suit be decreed ex-parte without any cost. It is declared that the plaintiffs having sixteen annas right, title and interest in the suit property are legally entitled to receive proper compensation in L.A. Case No. 62/64-65 and 14/65-66 of the L.A. Collector, Dhaka."

<u>13. Since both the parties adduced evidence and the defendant (the present plaintiff) contested the suit by filing written statement and cross-examined the plaintiffs witnesses, the Court was not authorized to decree the suit ex-parte. It appears that the High Court Division remanded the suit with a direction to accept some documents as additional evidence on behalf of the plaintiffs. From order No. 71 dated 07.08.1984 it appears the plaintiffs had not filed those documents in the Court. Since, the defendant failed to appear, the Court should have proceeded with the case on merit without proceeding with the matter under Order IX Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiffs were bound to prove their case to the satisfaction of the Court and their burden was not lightened because the defendant was absent. In the case in hand, learned Subordinate Judge, without disposing the suit on merit considering the evidence adduced by the parties, most illegally decreed the same ex-parte. Once it is found that a judgment and decree has been obtained by practicing fraud on the court, it is trite that the principles of res-judicata shall not apply.</u>

14. Furthermore, the present defendants in that suit sought for declaration of their title and compensation for acquisition of suit land in L.A. Case No.62 of 1964-65 and 14/65-66 but actually the same was not acquired in those L.A. Cases so the question of entitlement of getting compensation does not arise. Thus the said suit itself was misconceived and the same was filed by misrepresentation of facts and by suppression of material facts. The defendant-respondents got decree for realization of compensation stating that the suit land was acquired by the Government in the aforesaid L.A. cases but they failed to produce any papers regarding acquisition of disputed plot in those L.A. cases. Moreso, we have already held that the Land Acquisition Acts do not authorize the Government to surrender the acquired land and that if any such event ever occurred, the same was inoperative and a nullity, we are of the view that the defendants have had no title in the suit land.

15. In the case of S.P. Chengalvalvaraya Naidu V. Jagannath (1994)1 SCC I it was observed that the principle of "finality of litigation' cannot he pressed to the extent of such absurdity that it becomes an engine of fraud in the hands of dishonest litigants. The Courts of law are meant for imparting justice between the parties.----we have no hesitation to say that a person, whose case is based on falsehood, has no right to approach the court. He can be summarily thrown out at any stage of litigation." The High Court Division, in our opinion, committed error of law in shutting the doors of justice in view of the discussions made above. 16. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the title and possession of the Railway in the suit land remained intact in view of the acquisition of 1882, the courts below committed error of law in not decreeing suit holding that the Railway had has lawful title and possession in the suit land.

17. Accordingly, we find substance in the appeal.

18. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the courts below is hereby set aside.

End.
